## Chapter 6.

### Concerning the Immensity of the Heavens in Relation to the Size of the Earth.¹²)

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram positioned to the right of the text. It depicts a circle (representing the horizon) with two intersecting diameter lines. The endpoints on the circumference are labeled: "b" at the top left, "a" at the top right, "c" at the bottom left, and "d" at the bottom right. The central point of intersection is labeled "e" (representing the Earth or the observer).</image-desc>

That the vast mass of the Earth is of no account in relation to the size of the heavens can be recognized from the fact that the boundary circles—for that is what the <term>horizontes</term> <note>original Greek: "ὁρίζοντες" (horizontes) meaning "bounding circles" or horizons.</note> of the Greeks mean—bisect the entire celestial sphere; which could not happen if the size of the Earth, or its distance from the center of the world, were significant in comparison with the heavens. For a circle that bisects a sphere passes through the center of the sphere and is the largest of the circumscribed circles. Let *a b c d* be a bounding circle, and let the Earth, from which we view it, be *e*: then this *e* is the center of the horizon, through which everything that appears is separated from that which does not appear. If one now looks through a <term>diopter</term> <note>An ancient sighting tube or instrument used for measuring angles and alignment.</note> set up at *e*, or a <term>horoskop</term> <note>In this context, an instrument for observing the time or the position of the stars (a horoscopium), not a modern astrological chart.</note>, or through...

...[using] a water-level <note>A leveling instrument used to ensure the observer's horizontal plane is accurate.</note>, the rising of the beginning of Cancer <note>One of the twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note> at point *c*: then at that same moment, one sees the beginning of Capricorn setting at point *a*. If, during another rotation, the beginning of Capricorn rises at *b*, the setting of Cancer will be observed at *d*, and *bed* will be a straight line, namely the diameter of the ecliptic. However, it has already been shown that *aec* is the diameter of the same circle; consequently, it is clear that the center of the circle lies at the common point of intersection. Thus, the horizon always bisects the ecliptic, which is a great circle of the sphere. Now, since a circle on a sphere is itself a great circle if it passes through the center of another great circle, the horizon belongs among the great circles, and its center is simultaneously that of the ecliptic.

But because the line passing through the surface of the Earth is necessarily different from the line passing through its center, yet both are—due to the Earth's insignificance relative to the immensity of the heavens—effectively like parallel lines which seem to be a single line because the distance between them is too small to perceive at the boundary (as the gap they enclose is imperceptible relative to their length, in the manner shown in optics): this seems to prove beyond doubt that the heavens are immeasurably large compared to the Earth, gaining the appearance of an infinite magnitude, and that the Earth relates to the heavens, according to the judgment of the senses, as a point to a body, and as a finite quantity to an infinite one.<sup>13)</sup>

However, nothing more than this has been proven, and it specifically does not follow that the Earth must remain at rest in the center of the world. On the contrary, it should rather amaze us if such an immeasurably vast world moved through space in twenty-four hours instead of its very small part, which is the Earth. For the claim that the center is motionless and that what is near the center moves more slowly does not prove that the Earth rests at the center of the world; it is no different than saying the heavens move but the poles remain still, and what is near the poles moves very slowly; just as the Pole Star appears to move much more slowly than the Eagle <note>original: "der Adler," referring to the constellation Aquila or its brightest star, Altair.</note> or Sirius, because the former, being near the pole, describes a smaller circle. All of these belong to a sphere whose movement, decreasing toward its axis, does not allow for an equal movement of all its parts, while the movement of the whole carries them all around in equal times, but through unequal spaces. Upon this rests the basis of the proof that the Earth—insofar as it constitutes a part of the celestial sphere and shares in its nature and movement—moves very little as a neighbor to the center. ## Chapter 7.

### Why the Ancients believed the Earth rests in the center of the world, as if it were the center? 15)

For this reason, the ancient philosophers <note>Referring primarily to Aristotle and Ptolemy, whose geocentric views dominated science for over 1,500 years.</note> have tried to prove by several other reasons that the Earth stands in the middle of the world. As the main cause, however, they cite <term>heaviness and lightness|In Aristotelian physics, "gravity" (heaviness) was the natural tendency of earth and water to move toward the center of the universe, while "levity" (lightness) was the tendency of air and fire to move upward</term>. The element of Earth is indeed the heaviest, and all weighable things move, according to their impulse, toward its innermost center. Since the Earth is spherical—and heavy objects from all sides move toward it perpendicularly to its surface by their own nature—they would meet at its center if they were not held back at the surface; because, in fact, a straight line that is directed perpendicularly to the <term>tangent plane|A flat surface that touches a sphere at exactly one point without crossing it</term> at the point of contact leads to the center. For the—

--- Page 47 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether the Earth is at the center of the universe. Having previously discussed the immense size of the heavens compared to the Earth, the text now examines the physical arguments used by ancient philosophers to claim that the Earth must remain stationary at the center.</meta>

For those bodies that move toward the center, it seems to follow that they would rest at the center. All the more so, then, the entire Earth will rest at the center, and, whatever falling bodies it receives into itself, it will remain immovable by its own weight. Similarly, they <note>Referring to the ancient geocentric philosophers.</note> base their proofs on the principle of motion and its nature. Aristotle <sup>16)</sup> says that the movement of a simple body is simple; of simple movements, one is rectilinear <note>original: "gradlinig"; moving in a straight line.</note> and the other is circular. Of rectilinear motion, one is upward and the other is downward. Therefore, every simple motion is either toward the center (downward), away from the center (upward), or around the center (circular). It belongs only to earth and water, which are considered heavy, to move downward—that is, to seek the center. Air and fire, however, which are endowed with lightness, move upward and away from the center. It seems clear that rectilinear motion must be granted to these four <term>elements|The classical building blocks of matter: earth, water, air, and fire</term>; regarding the celestial bodies, however, they rotate in a circle around the center. This is Aristotle's view. 

If therefore, says the Alexandrian Ptolemy <sup>15)</sup>, the Earth were rotating, at least in a daily revolution, then the opposite of what was said above would have to occur: specifically, the motion that would traverse the entire circumference of the Earth in twenty-four hours would have to be incredibly violent and its speed unsurpassed. But things set into such a sudden, rapid rotation seem entirely unsuited for staying together; rather, they would be scattered, unless the connected parts were held together with great firmness. And long ago, he says, the loose earth would have been flung beyond the heavens themselves—which is quite ridiculous—and even less would living creatures and other detached masses have remained unshaken in any way. Furthermore, bodies falling in a straight line would not reach their intended place perpendicularly, because the ground would have been pulled away from beneath them with such great speed in the meantime. We would also see the clouds and anything else floating in the air always moving toward the west.

What is in accordance with nature produces effects that are the opposite of what happens through violence. Things upon which violence or an external impulse is exerted must be destroyed,

<meta>This page continues the argument against the geocentric view (that the Earth is the center of the universe). and cannot long endure; but what occurs by nature does so rightly and remains in its best state of connection. Therefore, Ptolemy $^{15}$ fears without reason that the Earth and all terrestrial objects set in rotation would be scattered by the activity of nature, since nature's activity is entirely different from that of art <note>In this context, "art" refers to human engineering or artificial, forced motion, as opposed to the inherent laws of the natural world.</note>; or from what could be produced by the human mind. 

Why, then, does he not fear the same thing—and to an even higher degree—for the universe, whose motion would have to be so much swifter as the heavens are larger than the Earth? Or have the heavens become immeasurable precisely because they were driven away from the center by the unspeakable force of motion; whereas otherwise, if they stood still, they would collapse? Certainly, if this were the case, the size of the heavens would increase into infinity. For the more they were driven upward by the outward impulse of motion, the swifter the motion would become, because of the ever-increasing circle they would have to traverse in the span of twenty-four hours; and conversely, if the motion grew, so too would the immensity of the heavens grow. Thus, speed would increase size, and size would increase speed, into infinity. 

According to that physical principle: that the infinite can neither be traversed $^{17}$ nor move for any reason,$^{18}$ the heavens would necessarily have to stand still. But it is said $^{19}$ that outside the heavens no body, no place, no empty space, and indeed nothing at all exists, and therefore there is nothing for the heavens to expand into; yet it is truly wonderful that something can be enclosed by nothing. If, however, the heavens were infinite and limited only at their inner cavity <note>This refers to the boundary between the celestial spheres and the lower elements of the Earth.</note>, it would perhaps be all the more confirmed that nothing exists outside the heavens, since every thing, whatever size it may be, is within them; but in that case, the heavens will remain motionless. 

For the primary thing upon which one relies for proof of the finiteness of the universe is motion. Whether the universe is finite or infinite, we shall leave to the dispute of the natural philosophers <term>Physiologists|From the Greek 'physiologia'; in the 16th century, this referred to natural philosophers who studied the physical laws of the universe</term>; for us, this much remains certain: that the Earth, enclosed between poles, is bounded by a spherical surface. Why then do we still hesitate to grant it a mobility that belongs to it by nature and corresponds to its form, rather than assuming that the whole universe, whose boundary is not known and cannot be known, is in motion? And why do we not confess that the appearance of a daily rotation belongs to the heavens, but the reality of it belongs to the Earth? It is just as when Virgil’s Aeneas $^{20}$ says: 

> “We sail out of the port, and lands and cities recede.” 

Because, when a ship sails calmly along, everything outside of it is seen by the sailors as if it were moving in imitation of the ship's motion, and the sailors, conversely, [think they are at rest]...

This expanding motion is directed from the center toward the periphery; therefore, if something consisting of earthy parts is set on fire, it moves from the center upward.

<meta>This page continues the argument for the Earth's rotation. Following the previous discussion on the atmosphere and how it might move in tandem with the Earth, the author now addresses the classical Aristotelian laws of motion to prove that the Earth moving is more "natural" than the heavens moving.</meta>

...motion, however, seizes those bodies which have moved away or been pushed from their natural place, or have somehow fallen outside of it. Nothing resists the order and the form of the whole world so much as being outside of one’s own place. **Rectilinear motion** <note>Movement in a straight line, which Aristotle believed was the only movement possible for the four "corruptible" elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> therefore only occurs when things are not behaving correctly and are not fully in accordance with their nature, by separating themselves from their whole and leaving its unity. Furthermore, those bodies which are driven upward or downward, apart from circular motion, do not perform a simple, uniform, and steady movement; for they cannot govern themselves according to their lightness or the pressure of their weight; and if they have a slower motion at the start of a fall, they increase their speed as they fall; while, conversely, we see the earthly fire driven into the heights—and we know no other—immediately become sluggish, as if the cause of the power of the earthy matter were showing itself therein. **Circular motion**, on the other hand, always proceeds uniformly because it has an unceasing cause. Those other movements, however, decrease as they progress, and they cease once they have reached their place and are no longer "heavy" or "light"; therefore, their motion stops. If, then, circular motion belonged to the universe, but rectilinear motion also belonged to its parts, we could say that circular motion exists alongside the rectilinear, just as an **animal exists with a disease**. The fact that Aristotle <gloss>16) Likely a reference to Aristotle's 'On the Heavens'.</gloss> divided simple motion into three types—away from the center, toward the center, and around the center—seems to be merely an intellectual abstraction, just as we distinguish a line, a point, and a surface, while yet the one cannot exist without the other, and none of them can exist without the body. It must also be added that the state of **immobility** is considered nobler and more divine than that of change and instability; the latter, therefore, belongs more to the Earth than to the universe. I would add further that it seems absurd to attribute motion to that which contains and sets things in place, and not rather to that which is contained and placed, which is the Earth. Finally, since the planets clearly come closer to the Earth at times and move further away at others, then the motion of one and the same body, which takes place around the center (which is supposed to be the center of the Earth), will also be directed away from and toward that center. One must therefore conceive of motion around the center more generally, and it is enough if each individual motion has its own center. One sees, then, that from all this, the **motion of the Earth** is more probable than its rest, especially regarding the daily rotation, which is most characteristic of the Earth.

<meta>This page transitions from discussing the physical nature of the Earth's movement to the cosmological implications of such movement. ## Chapter 9.

### Whether several motions can be attributed to the Earth; and on the center of the universe.

Since, therefore, nothing stands in the way of the Earth’s mobility, I believe we must now investigate whether it possesses several motions, so that it might be considered one of the planets. That it is not the center of all circular motions is proven by the seemingly irregular movements of the planets and their changing distances from the Earth, which cannot be explained by <term>concentric circles</term> <note>Perfectly nested circles sharing a single center, as proposed by earlier astronomers like Eudoxus or Aristotle.</note> with the Earth at the center. Since multiple centers exist, no one will be without reason to doubt whether the center of the universe is that of terrestrial <term>gravity</term> <note>In this context, gravity refers to the "heaviness" or natural tendency of objects to fall toward a center, rather than the universal force later described by Newton.</note> or another point. At the very least, I am of the opinion that gravity is nothing other than a natural longing, implanted in the parts of the world by the divine providence of the Master of the Universe, by which they seek their unity and wholeness by coming together in the form of a globe. And it is to be assumed that this inclination also resides within the sun, the moon, and the other planets, and that through its effect they remain in the spherical shape in which they appear, while they nonetheless complete their orbits in various ways. 

If, then, the Earth also possesses other motions besides the one around its center, these must be motions that appear in many ways externally, and among these we recognize the annual revolution. For if one grants the immobility of the sun and transfers the annual revolution from the sun to the Earth, the rising and setting of the zodiac signs and fixed stars—through which they become morning and evening stars—will result in the same way. It will then appear that the stations, <term>retrogressions</term> <note>The appearance of a planet moving backward in the sky, which Copernicus explains as an optical illusion caused by the Earth overtaking other planets in their orbits.</note>, and progressions of the planets are not their own movements, but rather those of the Earth, which lends its motion to their appearances. Finally, one will be convinced that the sun itself occupies the center of the universe. All of this is taught to us by the law of the sequence in which the planets follow one another, and the harmony of the universe, if we only look at the matter, as they say, with both eyes open.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of planetary order from Chapter 10. Copernicus is examining the traditional geocentric arguments regarding the placement of the planets—particularly the "inner" planets Mercury and Venus—relative to the Sun, before he eventually presents his own heliocentric alternative.</meta>

...are distant, as is proven by Euclid in his *Optics* <note>Euclid’s *Optics* (c. 300 BCE) used geometry to explain how the distance of an object affects its perceived size and position.</note>. Therefore, they <note>Referring to traditional geocentric astronomers like Ptolemy.</note> believe that the Moon, because it stands closest to the Earth and moves in the smallest circle, completes its circuit in the shortest time; whereas Saturn, as the highest planet, traverses the largest path in the longest time. Below Saturn lies Jupiter, followed by Mars.

Regarding Venus and Mercury, however, there are differing opinions, because they do not, like the others, move away from the Sun through all degrees of the zodiac <note>Unlike Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, which can appear opposite the Sun in the sky, Mercury and Venus are always seen in close proximity to the Sun.</note>. For this reason, some place them above the Sun, as Timaeus does in Plato <note>Refers to the cosmological model described in Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*.</note>, while others place them below it, such as Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), whose geocentric model dominated astronomy for over a millennium.</note> and a large portion of the moderns <note>In this context, "moderns" refers to medieval and Renaissance scholars who followed the Ptolemaic tradition.</note>. Alpetragius <note>Al-Bitruji, a 12th-century astronomer from Al-Andalus who proposed an alternative to Ptolemy's system.</note> places Venus above the Sun and Mercury below it.

Now, since those who follow Plato believe that all planets are otherwise dark bodies that shine by light received from the Sun, they argue that if these planets were located below the Sun, they would—due to their relatively small distance from it—be seen as half-circles or at least not perfectly round. This is because they would usually reflect the received light sideways, that is, toward the Sun, just as we see in the waxing and waning Moon. They also say that the Sun would occasionally have to be eclipsed by their passing in front of it, and its light would suffer a loss in proportion to the size of the planet. Since such a thing is never observed, they are of the opinion that these planets never come between us and the Sun.

On the other hand, those who place Venus and Mercury below the Sun defend their view by pointing to the vast amount of space they find between the Sun and the Moon. They have determined that the greatest distance of the Moon from the Earth—sixty-four and one-sixth parts (where one part is the distance from the center of the Earth to its surface) <note>These "parts" are Earth radii, the standard unit of measurement in ancient and medieval astronomy.</note>—is contained nearly eighteen times within the shortest distance of the Sun. This shortest distance to the Sun amounts to 1,160 such parts, meaning the space between the Sun and the Moon is 1,096 parts. 

To ensure that such a vast space does not remain empty, they calculate the size of the planetary orbits based on the differences in their distances. They find that these dimensions are nearly sufficient for the furthest distance of the Moon to be followed by the nearest distance of Mercury, and for Mercury's furthest distance to be followed by the nearest distance of Venus, which then finally, at its furthest distance, almost touches the Sun at its nearest point. They believe the orbit of Mercury encompasses 177 of the aforementioned units, and that the remaining space is almost entirely filled by the diameter of the orbit of Venus, measuring 910 units.

Therefore, they do not concede that the planets possess any inherent darkness like that of the Moon. Instead, they maintain that the planets either shine with their own light or are saturated with sunlight throughout their entire bodies. Furthermore, they argue that the planets do not eclipse the Sun because it is extremely rare for them to be positioned directly in front of the Sun's disk, as they usually deviate in latitude <note>In astronomy, latitude refers to how far a celestial body is north or south of the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path.</note>. Additionally, they are small bodies compared to the Sun; Venus, which is larger than Mercury, could hardly cover a hundredth part of the Sun, according to Albategnius <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD), a famous Arab astronomer whose measurements were highly regarded by Copernicus.</note>, the follower of Aratus...

<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s critique of the geocentric (Earth-centered) model. Specifically, he is questioning how traditional astronomers like Ptolemy and Averroës accounted for the positions of Mercury and Venus, noting the massive gaps in their spatial calculations.</meta>

...[Alpetragius] claims <note>Al-Bitruji (Alpetragius) was a 12th-century astronomer who challenged Ptolemy's complex systems of epicycles.</note>, who holds the diameter of the Sun to be ten times larger than previously thought. Therefore, it is not easy for such a small spot <note>Referring to the transit of a planet across the Sun.</note> to be seen within the prevailing light—although Averroës <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a Spanish-Arabic philosopher and polymath.</note>, in his paraphrase of Ptolemy, recalls having seen something darkish when he had calculated the conjunction of the Sun and Mercury <note>Averroës likely mistook a sunspot for the planet Mercury passing in front of the Sun.</note>. 

Thus, it is traditionally decided that these two planets move below the solar circle <note>In the geocentric model, the "solar circle" is the path the Sun takes around the Earth.</note>. But how uncertain and unsure this conclusion is becomes clear from the fact that, while according to Ptolemy the Moon's minimum distance is 38 Earth radii, by a more correct estimate it is more than 49 <note>Copernicus is correcting Ptolemy’s measurements of the Moon’s distance from Earth using more precise observations.</note>—as will become clear below. Yet, we still do not know if anything else is contained in such a large space other than air and, if one wishes, that which is called the <term>fiery element</term> <note>In ancient and medieval science, the "fiery element" was the fourth and lightest of the terrestrial elements, thought to exist in a sphere just below the Moon.</note>. 

Furthermore, the diameter of Venus's orbit—based on the size of its deviation from the Sun on either side by about 45 degrees—must be six times larger than the line that can be drawn from the center of the Earth to the lowest point of Venus's orbit, as will be proven in its proper place. What then should be contained in this entire space, which is all the larger because it includes Earth, air, ether, Moon, and Mercury, plus the immense <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient astronomy to explain the retrograde motion of planets.</note> of Venus circling the stationary Earth? 

How little convincing Ptolemy's reasoning is—according to which the Sun should occupy the middle position between those planets that deviate in every direction and those that do not—is shown by the Moon, which, though it deviates in every direction, reveals the untruth of that claim. 

What cause can those provide who place Venus and then Mercury below the Sun (or arrange them in another order), to explain why these planets do not follow independent orbits, free from the Sun, like the other planets? This is especially problematic if the ratio of their speed and slowness does not accurately represent their order. In such a case, either the Earth would not be allowed to stand in the center (to which the order of the stars and orbits is referred), or there would be no reason for their order at all; nor would it be apparent why Saturn deserved the highest place more than Jupiter or any other planet. 

Therefore, it seems to me by no means negligible what Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century Latin author whose encyclopedia, *The Marriage of Philology and Mercury*, was a foundational text for the medieval liberal arts.</note>, who wrote an encyclopedia, and several other Latins knew very well. For he believes that Venus and Mercury circle the Sun as their center, and for that reason cannot move further away from it than the circles of their orbits allow; they do not circle the Earth like the others, but have alternating, returning distances. What else can this mean but that they revolve around the Sun as the center of their orbits? Thus, Mercury's orbit would indeed be enclosed by that of Venus, which is more than twice as large, and would find a sufficient place within that expansion.

<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s argument for a heliocentric (Sun-centered) model. Having discussed the inner planets (Mercury and Venus) on the previous page, he now turns to the outer planets and the revolutionary idea of placing the Earth in motion among them.</meta>

By taking this opportunity to relate Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars to the same center—while keeping in mind the vast extent of their orbits, which also contain and encompass the Earth—one will not fail to find the explanation for the regular order of their movements. For it is well-established that these planets are closest to Earth when they rise in the evening—that is, when they enter into <term>opposition</term> <note>Opposition occurs when a planet is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun; the planet is at its brightest and closest to us during this time.</note> with the Sun and the Earth stands between them and the Sun. Conversely, they are furthest from Earth when they set in the evening—that is, when they are hidden by the Sun, because the Sun is positioned between them and the Earth. This proves sufficiently that their center belongs rather to the Sun, and is the same center to which Venus and Mercury relate their orbits.

Since all these planets relate to a single center, the spherical space remaining between the outer boundary of Venus and the inner boundary of Mars must necessarily be filled. This space, which is <term>concentric</term> <note>Meaning spheres that share the same center point, like the layers of an onion.</note> with the others on both its surfaces, receives the Earth along with its companion, the Moon, and everything found below the Moon. We cannot separate the Moon from the Earth, as it is indisputably closest to it, especially since we find more than enough room for it in that space.

Therefore, we do not hesitate to assert that everything the Moon encompasses, along with the center of the Earth, moves in a great yearly orbit around the Sun among the other planets. It moves around the center of the universe, in which the Sun rests motionless. Thus, everything that appears to be a movement of the Sun is actually found to be a movement of the Earth. Furthermore, the scale of the universe is so vast that the distance between the Earth and the Sun—though significant relative to the size of the other planetary orbits—completely vanishes when compared to the <term>sphere of the fixed stars</term> <note>In the Copernican system, the stars are so far away that the Earth's movement around the Sun doesn't cause a visible shift in their positions (parallax), which was a major objection to his theory at the time.</note>. I believe this is easier to comprehend than if the mind were splintered into an almost endless multitude of circles, which those who held the Earth fixed at the center of the world were forced to do. One must instead follow the wisdom of Nature; she is very careful to produce nothing superfluous or useless, but often endows a single object with many effects.

If all this should seem difficult, almost incomprehensible, and contrary to the opinions of many, we shall, God willing, make it clearer than the sun—at least to those who are not ignorant of mathematics. The first law remains unchallenged, and no one will bring forth a more fitting one: namely, that the size of the orbits is measured by the duration of the orbital period. The sequence of the spheres, beginning from the highest, is arranged in the following way.

The first and highest of all spheres is that of the fixed stars, containing itself and everything, and therefore motionless, as the place of the

...circling family of stars. Nor is the Earth deprived of the service of the Moon; rather, as Aristotle says in *On the History of Animals* <note>original: *de animalibus*</note>, the Moon has the closest kinship with the Earth. Meanwhile, the Earth receives [light and heat] from the Sun and becomes "pregnant" with an annual birth. We find, therefore, in this arrangement an admirable harmony of the world, and a reliable, harmonious connection between the motion and size of the orbits, such as cannot be found elsewhere. 

For here the careful observer can notice why the advancing and retreating <note>This refers to "retrograde motion," the optical illusion where planets appear to move backward in the sky because the Earth is overtaking them in its orbit.</note> appears greater in Jupiter than in Saturn, and smaller than in Mars; and again in Venus greater than in Mercury; and why such a reversal appears more frequent in Saturn than in Jupiter, but rarer in Mars and Venus than in Mercury. Furthermore, it explains why Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are closer to the Earth when they rise in the evening <note>This occurs when they are in "opposition" to the Sun, meaning the Earth is directly between the planet and the Sun.</note> than when they disappear and reappear. All of this results from the same cause, which lies in the movement of the Earth. However, the fact that none of this movement is visible in the fixed stars proves their immense distance, which makes even the path of the Earth’s annual motion—or its reflection—vanish from our eyes. This is because everything visible has a certain distance as a limit beyond which it cannot be perceived, as is proven in <term>optics</term>. The fact that much still lies between the highest planet, Saturn, and the sphere of the fixed stars is proven by the twinkling brilliance of the latter, a quality by which they differ most from the planets; for there must be the greatest difference between that which moves and that which is unmoving. Truly, so great is this divine, best, and greatest workshop.

## Chapter 11.

### Proof of the triple motion of the Earth.

<margin>1)</margin> Since so many and such weighty testimonies taken from the planets speak for the mobility of the Earth, we now wish to present this movement in general, insofar as the phenomena can be demonstrated through it, as if by a hypothesis. One must generally assume it to be a triple motion: 

The first, which we have said is called <term>nychthemeron</term> <note>A Greek term (Nychthemerinon) for a full 24-hour cycle of day and night.</note> by the Greeks, is the actual rotation of day and night. This occurs around the Earth's axis from west to east, just as it was previously believed that the universe moved in the opposite direction. This rotation describes the <term>equator</term> <note>referred to here as the *Nachtgleichenkreis* (circle of equal nights) or *Taggleichenkreis* (day-equalizing circle).</note>, which some call the day-equalizing circle, because...

The second motion is the annual movement of the Earth's center along with everything related to it. As previously stated, this motion follows the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, serving as the path the Sun appears to follow.</note> around the Sun, also moving from west to east—that is, in a "forward" direction—traveling between the orbits of Venus and Mars. Because of this, as we have said, the Sun itself appears to move through the Zodiac in a similar fashion. <margin>3)</margin>
There follows, therefore, the third motion, that of **Declination**, which also occurs in an annual cycle but is "retrograde"—that is, it moves in the opposite direction to the movement of the Earth's center. Through these two nearly equal but opposing motions, it happens that the axis of the Earth (and thus also the Equator, as the largest parallel circle) remains pointed toward almost the same region of the heavens, as if it were unmoving. Meanwhile, the Sun appears to move through the slant of the Zodiac because of the motion with which the Earth’s center advances; it is just as if the Earth's center were the center of the universe, provided one remembers that the distance from the Sun to the Earth has already surpassed our ability to perceive it relative to the <term>Sphere of Fixed Stars</term>. If one imagines this correctly, the inhabitants of Earth will see the Sun (located at the center ***e***) reaching its winter solstice in Capricorn; this is caused by the greatest northern declination, ***h***, being turned toward the Sun. For this reason, some have believed that the sphere of fixed stars also moves, leading them to assume a ninth, higher sphere; and because even this is not enough, modern thinkers are now adding a tenth sphere. Yet they still have not reached the goal that we hope to achieve through the motion of the Earth, by using it as our principle and assumption in the following development. <margin>38)</margin>

# Chapter 12.

## **On the Straight Lines which are Chords in a Circle.<sup>39)</sup>**

Because the proofs we employ throughout nearly this entire work deal with straight lines and arcs, as well as plane and spherical triangles, and although much on this subject is already available in Euclid's *Elements*, it does not contain the specific method we need most: namely, how to find the sides from the angles, and the angles from the sides. This is necessary because an angle does not measure the chord, nor does the chord measure the angle; rather, it is the arc that measures the angle. Consequently, a method has been devised to determine the chord of any given arc. From the chord, and with the help of the angle, one can find the corresponding arc; and conversely, from the arc, one can find the chord belonging to a specific angle. Therefore, it should not be surprising that we deal with these lines here. Furthermore, regarding the sides and angles of both plane and spherical triangles, we will examine here once and for all—and as far as is necessary for the clarity of our future discussions—what Ptolemy has provided in scattered examples.

Following the common custom of mathematicians, we divide the circle into 360 parts. The ancients assumed the diameter consisted of 120 parts. However, to avoid the complexity of very small fractions when multiplying and dividing these lines—which are usually <term>incommensurable</term> <note>meaning they cannot be expressed as a simple ratio of whole numbers, like the square root of two</note> in length as well as in power—later scholars, from the time when <term>Hindu-Arabic numerals</term> <note>original: "indische Zahlzeichen"; the base-10 system we use today, which replaced the more cumbersome Roman or Greek numerals</note> came into use, introduced a diameter of either 1,200,000 or 2,000,000 parts, or some other rational number. Such a numerical system surpasses all others, both Greek and Latin, in its particular usefulness and fits every kind of calculation best. For this reason, we have considered 200,000 parts of the diameter to be sufficient to exclude any noticeable error. Since values that do not relate to one another like one whole number to another can only be approximated, it is enough to obtain a close value. We will now explain the following six theorems and one problem, mostly following the methods of Ptolemy.

## **First Theorem.**

If the diameter of a circle is given, then the sides of the <term>triangle, square, hexagon, pentagon, and decagon</term> which that same circle circumscribes <note>meaning the shapes are drawn inside the circle so their corners touch the edge</note> are also given. For the radius, being half of the diameter, is equal to the side of the hexagon. The square of the side of the triangle is three times the square of the side of the hexagon, and the square of the side of the square is twice the square of the side of the hexagon, as is proven in Euclid's *Elements*.<sup>40)</sup> The side of the hexagon is thus 100,000 parts in length; that of the square is 141,422 parts; and that of the triangle is 173,205 parts.

<summary>Copernicus introduces the mathematical necessity of trigonometry (chords and arcs) for his astronomical models and establishes a standard diameter of 200,000 units to allow for precise calculation using Hindu-Arabic numerals. He begins by defining the lengths of the sides of basic geometric shapes inscribed within a circle.</summary>

<keywords>chords, trigonometry, Euclid, Ptolemy, Hindu-Arabic numerals, diameter, radius, inscribed polygons, geometry, mathematical precision</keywords>

--- Page 61 ---

It also noted the convention of dividing the circle into 360 degrees and the diameter into 200,000 parts to ensure precision in calculation.</meta>

parts. Let the side of the hexagon be *ab*. According to the first proposition of the second book, or the tenth proposition of the sixth book of Euclid,⁴¹) let this line be divided in <term>extreme and mean ratio</term> <note>Today known as the "golden ratio," where a line is divided so that the ratio of the whole line to the larger segment is the same as the ratio of the larger segment to the smaller one.</note> 

<image-desc>A horizontal line segment diagram illustrating geometric proportions. Five points are labeled with italicized lowercase letters above vertical tick marks. at point *c*,⁴²) and let the larger segment be *bc*. To this, we add the segment *bd* = *bc*. Then the entire line *abd* will also be divided in extreme and mean ratio, and the smaller, added segment will be the side of the decagon <note>A ten-sided polygon</note> inscribed in the circle to which the hexagon side *ab* belongs,⁴³) as is clear from the fifth and ninth theorems of the 13th book of Euclid. The line *bd* itself is obtained in the following way: if one halves *ab* at *e*, it is known from the third theorem of the same book of Euclid that the square of *ebd* is five times the square of *eb*.⁴⁴) Since *eb* has a length of 50,000 parts, the fivefold square results in the line *ebd* having a length of 111,803 parts. If the 50,000 parts of line *eb* are subtracted from this, *bd* remains with 61,803 parts, which is the sought-after side of the decagon. The side of the pentagon—the square of which is equal to the sum of the squares of the sides of the hexagon and the decagon⁴⁵)—contains 117,557 parts. Thus, if the diameter of a circle is given, the sides of the triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, and decagon that can be inscribed in that same circle are also given, which was to be proven.

### Corollary.

From this it is evident that if the chord of any arc is known, the chord belonging to the arc that completes the semicircle is also given. This is because the angle in a semicircle is a right angle. In right-angled triangles, the square of the side opposite the right angle (that is, the diameter) is equal to the squares constructed over the sides enclosing the right angle. Since the side of the decagon, which is the chord of an arc of 36 degrees, has been proven to contain 61,803 parts (of which 200,000 make up the diameter), then the chord of the arc of 144 degrees (which completes the semicircle) is given as 190,211 such parts. And from the side of the pentagon, which spans 72 degrees with 117,557 parts of the diameter, the chord of the arc of 108 degrees (completing the semicircle) is found to be 161,803 parts.

## Second Theorem.

If a quadrilateral is inscribed in a circle, the rectangle formed by the diagonals is equal to the sum of the two rectangles formed by the pairs of opposite sides. Let *abcd* be the quadrilateral inscribed in the circle; I maintain that the rectangle formed by the diagonals *ac* and *bd* is equal to the sum of those formed by *ab* and *cd*, and by *ad* and *bc*. For if we make the angle *abe* equal to *cbd*, then the entire angle

angle **abd** is equal to the whole angle **ebc**, since angle **ebd** is added to each of them. Also, the angles **acb** and **bda** are equal to one another, as angles within the same segment of a circle; for this reason, the two similar triangles **bce** and **bda** will have proportional sides, thus **bc** : **bd** = **ec** : **ad** and **bc** · **ad** = **bd** · **ec**. But the triangles **abe** and **cbd** are also similar, because the angles **abe** and **cbd** were made equal, and **bac** and **bdc** are equal as angles subtended by the same arc. Therefore, again, **ab** : **bd** = **ae** : **cd** and **ab** · **cd** = **ae** · **bd**. It has already been demonstrated, however, that **bc** · **ad** = **bd** · **ec**. Taken together, therefore, **bd** · **ac** = **ad** · **bc** + **ab** · **cd** <note>This is the famous Ptolemy’s Theorem, which states that for a cyclic quadrilateral, the product of the diagonals is equal to the sum of the products of the opposite sides.</note>, which is useful to have proven.

### Third Proposition

For from this it follows: if the <term>chords</term> <note>A straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc.</note> of unequal arcs in a semicircle are given, the chord of the arc by which the larger exceeds the smaller is also given. In the semi-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a semicircle with diameter ad. Inside, an inscribed quadrilateral abcd is formed by chords ab, bc, and cd, along with the diameter.</image-desc>

circle **abcd** with the diameter **ad**, let the chords of the unequal arcs **ab** and **ac** be given. If we now wish to find the chord **bc**, then from what was said above, we obtain the chords of the arcs **bd** and **cd** which complement the others to form a semicircle, with which the quadrilateral in the semicircle **abcd** meets. Its diagonals **ac** and **bd** are obtained along with the three sides **ab**, **ad**, and **cd**; and within this, as already proven, **ac** · **bd** = **ab** · **cd** + **ad** · **bc**. Now, if **ab** · **cd** is subtracted from **ac** · **bd**, there remains **ad** · **bc**. If we then divide by **ad**, as far as this is possible, we obtain the sought-after chord **bc** in numbers. Since, according to the earlier sections, for example, the sides of the pentagon and hexagon are given, it follows in this way that the chord of 12 degrees—by which the two differ—amounts to 20,905 parts of the diameter.⁴⁶)

## Fifth Proposition.

If, again, the chords of two arcs are given, then the chord of the whole arc composed of them is also given. Let the chords given in the circle be **ab** and **bc**; I assert that the chord of the entire arc **abc** is also given.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram with center point f. Two diameters, afd and bfe, are drawn. Points a, b, c, d, and e are marked on the circumference. Chords connect a to b, b to c, c to d, and d to e. Internal diagonal chords bd and ce are drawn, as well as a chord connecting b and e, forming the quadrilateral bcde.</image-desc>

For after we have constructed the diameters **afd** and **bfe**, we draw the straight lines **bd** and **ce**, which follow from the previous steps because **ab** and **bc** are given, and **de** is equal to **ab**. The line **cd** closes the quadrilateral **bcde**, whose diagonals **bd** and **ce**, along with the three sides **bc**, **de**, and **be**, are given. The remaining side **cd** is found by the second proposition, and from it, **ca** is found as the chord of the complement to the semicircle, or of the entire arc **abc**, which was sought. Since the chords of three, one and a half, and three-quarters of a degree have been found so far, one could further produce a table <note>original: "Verzeichniss"</note> for the intervals through very precise calculation. Therefore, one might rightly doubt regarding the chords of these parts whether one should proceed by whole degrees and add one to the other, or by half-degrees, or by some other rule, because the subtle calculations by which they might be derived fail us. However, nothing prevents us from achieving this in another way, free from any perceptible error or any contradiction of the calculated numbers. Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose "Almagest" defined Western astronomy for centuries.</note> also sought this concerning the chords of one degree and half a degree, which is what first inspired us.

## Sixth Proposition.

The ratio of a larger arc to a smaller arc is greater than the ratio of their corresponding chords. Let **ab** and **bc** be two unequal, connected arcs in a circle, with **bc** being the larger; I assert that...

<meta>This page continues the mathematical demonstration regarding the ratios of arcs and chords, building upon the calculations of specific chord lengths (12, 6, 3, and 1.5 degrees) established on the previous page to prove a fundamental trigonometric inequality.</meta>

...that the ratio of the arcs **bc : ab** is greater than the ratio of the chords **bc : ab**, which form the angle **b**, which is bisected by the line **bd**. We draw the line **ac**, which intersects **bd** at point **e**. Likewise, we draw lines **ad** and **cd**, which are equal to each other because they are the chords of equal arcs. Since in the triangle **abc**, the line **bd**—which bisects the angle—intersects **ac** at **e**, the segments of the base **ec : ae** relate to one another as the sides **bc : ab**. Because **bc** is greater than **ab**, **ec** is also greater than **ae**. Now, let **df** be drawn perpendicular to **ac**; this line bisects **ac** at point **f**, which must lie within the larger segment **ec**. And since in every triangle the larger side lies opposite the larger angle, in triangle **def**, the side **de** is greater than **df**, and **ad** is greater than **de**. For this reason, an arc described around the center **d** with the radius **de** will intersect **ad** and extend beyond **df**. Let it intersect **ad** at point **h**, and let it be extended to the straight line **dfi**. 

Now, since the sector **edi** is larger than the triangle **edf**, but the triangle **dea** is larger than the sector **deh**, the triangle **def** has a smaller ratio to triangle **dea** than sector **dei** has to sector **deh**. And since sectors are proportional to their arcs or their central angles, while triangles with the same vertex are proportional to their bases, the ratio of the angle **edf** to **ade** is greater than that of the bases **ef** to **ae**. Consequently, the ratio of the combined angle **fda** to **ade** is also greater than that of **af** to **ae**. In the same manner, the ratio of angle **cda** to **ade** is greater than **ac** to **ae**, or by subtraction, the ratio of angle **cde** to **eda** is greater than **ce** to **ea**. However, the angles **cde** to **eda** relate to each other as the arcs **cb** to **ab**, whereas the bases **ce** to **ae** relate as the chords **cb** to **ab**. Consequently, the ratio of the arcs **cb** to **ab** is greater than that of the chords **bc** to **ab**, which was to be proven.

### Task.

Because the arc is always larger than its chord—given that the straight line is the shortest path between two points—this inequality converges toward equality as one moves from larger to smaller sections of the circle. Thus, finally, at the point of contact with the circle <note>This refers to the geometric limit where a tangent line and an infinitesimal arc meet.</note>, the straight line and the curved line vanish simultaneously. 

It is necessary that they first differ from one another by a noticeable margin. For instance, if **ab** is an arc of three degrees and **ac** is an arc of one and a half degrees, it is proven that the chord **ab** contains 5,235 parts when the diameter <term>diameter</term> <note>The author uses a standard scale where the diameter of the circle is divided into 200,000 units to allow for high-precision integer calculations before the common use of decimal points.</note> counts 200,000, and **ac** is equal to 2,618 such parts. If we assume the arc *ab* to be one and a half degrees and *ac* to be three-quarters of a degree, we then have the chord *ab* equal to 2618 and *ac* equal to 1309 parts. Since we seem to have reached the point where the difference between the straight line and the curved line eludes our perception—as if both were one and the same line—we do not doubt that the chords (taken as 1309 for three-quarters of a degree) follow the same ratio for one degree and the remaining parts. This is all the more practical since half-chords are used much more frequently than whole chords in geometric proofs and calculations.

# Chapter 13.

## On the Sides and Angles of Plane Rectilinear Triangles.

->1.<-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle with a triangle inscribed. The vertices of the triangle are labeled a (left), b (top), and c (right).</image-desc>

If the angles of a triangle are given, the sides are also determined. For instance, let there be a triangle **abc**, around which a circle is circumscribed according to the fifth proposition of the 4th book of Euclid. <note>Euclid's Elements, Book IV, Proposition 5, describes the method for drawing a circle that passes through all three vertices of a given triangle.</note> Therefore, the arcs **ab**, **bc**, and **ca** will also be given, such that 360 parts are equal to two right angles. <note>In this system, 360 degrees represents the sum of the angles in a circle relative to the diameter, which corresponds to 180 degrees in modern notation.</note> When the arcs are known, the sides of the inscribed triangle are also determined as the chords, using the provided table in parts, of which 200,000 make up the diameter. <note>The "table" refers to the chord tables previously calculated by the author; early trigonometry used the length of chords in a circle rather than modern sine or cosine functions.</note>

->2.<-

If, however, any one angle is given along with two sides of the triangle, the third side and the remaining angles are found. For the given sides are either equal to one another or they are unequal. Furthermore, the given angle is either a right angle, an acute angle, or an obtuse angle; and the given sides either include the given angle or they do not.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of an isosceles triangle with vertex a at the top, vertex b at the bottom left, and vertex c at the bottom right. The letter z is located near the middle of the left side ab.</image-desc>

First, let the two given sides **ab** and **ac** in triangle **abc** be equal, and let them include the given angle **a**. Then the remaining angles at the base **bc** are also given—since they are equal—as half of the difference between two right angles and angle **a**. And if one angle at the base is originally given, the one equal to it is immediately known, and from these, the remainder of the two right angles is found. But the sides of a triangle with given angles are known; therefore, the base **bc** is known, specifically according to the table in parts, where **ab** or **ac** (as radii) comprise 100,000 parts, or the diameter 200,000 parts.

->3.<-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a right-angled triangle. Vertex a is at the top right, vertex b is at the bottom left, and vertex c is at the bottom right. A horizontal dashed line connects b and c. The letter z is placed near side ab.</image-desc>

The same result follows if the angle **bac** is given as a right angle along with its including sides. Because it is known that the <term>squares<gloss>The area of a square with a side of the same length.</gloss></term> of **ab** and **ac** are equal to the square of the base **bc**, then **bc** is determined according to its length, and conversely, the sides themselves according to their ratio. <note>This is a reference to the Pythagorean theorem.</note> The segment of the circle that contains the right-angled triangle is a semicircle, the diameter of which is the base **bc**. If, therefore, **bc** is [divided] into 200,000 parts... <note>The sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the geometric rules for solving the sides and angles of plane triangles using inscribed circles and chord tables. It demonstrates how to determine unknown properties of a triangle when certain angles or sides are already known, referencing Euclidean geometry and the Pythagorean theorem.</summary>
<keywords>trigonometry, plane triangles, Euclid, inscribed circle, chords, diameter, isosceles triangle, right-angled triangle, Pythagorean theorem</keywords>

--- Page 72 ---
<meta>This page continues the geometric proofs of Chapter 13, specifically demonstrating how to solve for unknown sides and angles in various types of plane triangles using the table of chords and the properties of right-angled triangles.</meta>

...divided: thus **ab** and **ac** result as the **chords** <note>In early trigonometry, the "chord" of an angle was used where we would use the "sine" function today. It represents the length of a straight line between two points on a circle's circumference.</note> of the two other angles **b** and **c**, which the arrangement of the table <note>Referring to the "Table of Chords" provided in the preceding chapters.</note> shows in parts, of which 180 are equal to two right angles. The same result will be obtained if **bc** is given along with one of the sides enclosing the right angle, which seems sufficiently clear to me.

### 4.

If the acute angle **abc** is given alongside the sides **ab** and **bc** that enclose it: drop a perpendicular from **a** to **bc**, or, if necessary, onto its extension,

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of triangle abc with vertex a at the top. A perpendicular line ad is dropped from vertex a to the base line. Point d is the foot of the perpendicular on the base line. Points b, e, d, and c are labeled along the base. The diagram illustrates the decomposition of a triangle into two right-angled triangles abd and adc.</image-desc>

depending on whether it falls inside or outside the triangle; let this be **ad**. By this means, two right-angled triangles **abd** and **adc** are distinguished; and because the angles in **abd** are given—namely **d** as a right angle and **b** according to the premise—it follows that **ad** and **bd** emerge as chords of angles **a** and **b** in parts, of which **ab** (as the diameter of the circle) contains 200,000, according to the tables. And in the same way that **ab**, **ad**, and **bd** are given according to their length, **cd** is also found as the difference between **bc** and **bd**. Consequently, from the known sides **ad** and **cd** of the right-angled triangle **adc**, the sought-after side **ac** and the angle **acd** are also found according to the previous development.

### 5.

The process will be no different if the angle **b** is obtuse, in that the perpendicular **ad** from **a** to the extension of **bc** forms a triangle

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing triangle abc where angle b is obtuse. A perpendicular line ad is dropped from vertex a to the extension of the base line bc to the left. Point d is the foot of the perpendicular, creating a large right-angled triangle adc and a smaller right-angled triangle abd external to the original triangle.</image-desc>

**abd** with known angles. For the exterior angle **abd** is known through **abc**, and **d** is known as a right angle; thus **bd** and **ad** result in parts, of which **ab** contains 200,000. And because **ba** and **bc** have a given ratio to one another, **bc** is also found in the same parts as **bd**, and consequently the entire line **cbd** is known. Since two sides **ad** and **cd** are now given in the right-angled triangle **adc**, the sought-after **ac** and the angle **bac** emerge, along with the other angle **acb**, which was required.

### 6.

If one of the given sides **ac** and **ab** lies opposite the given angle **b**: it follows from the table that **ac** is found in parts, of which the diameter of the circle circumscribing the triangle **abc** contains 200,000; and since the ratio of **ab** to **ac** is given, **ab** is found in the same parts. Consequently, from the table, the angle **acb** and the other angle **bac** are found, from which in turn **bc** results as a chord; and by this means they are given according to any chosen scale.

### 7.

If all the sides of a triangle are given, the angles can be determined. Regarding the equilateral triangle, it is too well known to require much emphasis that its individual angles each measure one-third of two right angles <note>In modern terms, 60 degrees, as two right angles equal 180 degrees.</note>. In the isosceles triangle, it is also clear; for the ratio of the equal sides to the third side is the same as the ratio of the radius to the **chord** <note>The "chord" in ancient trigonometry is a straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc; it is related to the modern sine function.</note> of the angle. From this, the angle enclosed by the equal sides is found in the table in parts, of which 360 around a center point are equal to four right angles. Subsequently, the remaining angles at the base are found as halves of the remainder of two right angles. It now remains to prove the same for scalene triangles <note>A triangle where all three sides have different lengths.</note>, which we again divide into right-angled triangles. Let **abc** be a scalene triangle with given sides, and upon the longest side—for example, **bc**—let a perpendicular **ad** be dropped. The 13th proposition of the second

<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing a triangle with vertices labeled a (top), b (right), and c (left). A perpendicular line, representing the altitude, drops from vertex a to point d on the base line segment bc.</image-desc>

book of Euclid <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book II, Prop. 13: This theorem is essentially a geometric version of the Law of Cosines for acute triangles, relating the sides of a triangle to the segments created by an altitude.</note> tells us, however, that the square of side **ab**, which lies opposite an acute angle, is smaller than the sum of the squares of the other two sides by twice the rectangle <note>In classical geometry, the "rectangle" of two lines refers to the area formed by multiplying their lengths.</note> of **bc** and **cd**. Angle **c** must be acute; otherwise, **ab** would be the longest side, contrary to our assumption, as can be seen from the 17th proposition of the first book of Euclid and the two following propositions. Thus, **bd** and **dc** are found, and for the right-angled triangles **abd** and **adc**, the sides and angles are known (as has been frequently repeated), whereby the sought-after angles of triangle **abc** are determined.

Alternatively, the same can be derived from the second-to-last proposition of the third book of Euclid <note>Referring to Euclid III, 36, which deals with the power of a point relative to a circle.</note>, perhaps more conveniently for us. If we describe a circle with the shorter side **bc** as the radius, centered at point **c**, it will intersect either the other two sides or just one of them. First, let the circle intersect both: **ab** at **e** and **ac** at **d**. We extend the line **adc** to **f** to complete the diameter **dcf**. From this construction and that proposition of Euclid, it is clear that the rectangle formed by **fa** and **ad** is equal to the rectangle formed by **ba** and **ae**, since each is equal to the square of the tangent drawn from **a** to the circle. The entire line **af** is given because all its segments are given: for **cf** and **cd** are equal to **bc** (as radii of the circle), and **ad** is the difference between **ca** and **cd**. Therefore, the rectangle of **ba** and **ae** is also given, and consequently **ae** is given by its length, and the rest

<image-desc>Two geometric diagrams illustrating the geometric proof. Both diagrams feature a circle centered at point c. In each, a line segment passes through c, defining points d and f on the circle. A triangle abc is drawn where b is on the circle's circumference and a is outside. The side ab intersects the circle at point e. The two figures show different orientations and side lengths for the triangle.</image-desc>

*be*, the **chord** <note>original: "Sehne"; a straight line connecting two points on a curve.</note> of the arc *be*. If we draw *ec*: we then have an **isosceles triangle** *bce* with given sides. From this, the angle *ebc* is determined, and through this, the remaining angles *c* and *a* in the triangle *abc* are also found according to the previous methods. If, however, the circle does not intersect *ab*, as in the other figure where *ab* meets the convex arc: then *be* is nonetheless given, and in the isosceles triangle *bce*, the angle *cbe*—as well as the exterior angle *abc*—is known. In the same manner as before, the remaining angles are immediately found. And let this suffice for **plane triangles** <note>original: "gradlinigen Dreiecke"; literally "straight-lined triangles."</note>, upon which a great part of **geodesy** <note>original: "Geodäsie"; the science of measuring and monitoring the Earth's size and shape.</note> rests. We now turn to spherical triangles.

## Chapter 14.
### On Spherical Triangles.

We take here that convex triangle which is enclosed on the surface of a sphere by three arcs of **great circles** <note>A circle on the surface of a sphere whose plane passes through the center of the sphere, such as the equator or meridians.</note>; the difference and magnitude of the angles, however, are measured on the arc of the great circle which is described from the point of intersection as if from a pole, and which arc is enclosed by the **quadrants** <note>One-quarter of a circle, or 90 degrees.</note> of the circles forming the angle. For as the arc so enclosed relates to the whole circumference, so the angle at the point of intersection relates to four right angles, which, as we have said, contain 360 equal parts.

-> 1. <-

From three arcs of the great circles of a sphere, of which any two taken together are greater than the third, it is evident that a spherical triangle can be composed. For what is asserted here regarding the arcs is proven by the 23rd proposition of the eleventh book of **Euclid** regarding angles <gloss>54)</gloss> <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book XI, Prop. 23: Concerning the construction of a solid angle from three plane angles.</note>; since the ratio of the angles and the arcs is the same, and great circles are those which pass through the center of the sphere: it is clear that those three circular sectors, to which those arcs belong, form a vertex at the center of the sphere. Thus, what has been asserted is certain.

-> 2. <-

Every arc of a triangle must be smaller than a **semicircle** <note>An arc of 180 degrees.</note>. For a semicircle does not form an angle at the center, but projects itself as a straight line. Furthermore, the two remaining angles to which the arcs belong cannot enclose a vertex at the center, and therefore cannot form a spherical triangle. And this, I believe, was the reason why **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose work "Almagest" defined trigonometry for over a millennium.</note>, in investigating this type of triangle, proves particularly through the figure of the spherical sector that arcs assumed to be larger than semicircles do not exist.

<summary>This page marks the transition from plane geometry to spherical trigonometry, defining how triangles are formed by great circles on a sphere. It establishes that the sum of two sides must exceed the third and that no side can exceed a semicircle.</summary>
<keywords>chord, geodesy, spherical triangles, Euclid, quadrants, circular sectors, Ptolemy, spherical sector, great circles</keywords>

--- Page 75 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to spherical trigonometry from Chapter 14. While the previous page defined the basic components of a spherical triangle, this page provides a formal geometric proof for the proportional relationships between sides and angles in a right-angled spherical triangle, relying on Euclidean solid geometry.</meta>

### 3.

In spherical triangles that contain a right angle, the **chord of double the side** <note>Historical mathematicians like Copernicus used the "chord of double the arc" (chord 2α) where modern trigonometry uses the Sine (sin α). Mathematically, sin α = 1/2 chord 2α.</note> which lies opposite the right angle relates to the chord of double one of the two sides enclosing the right angle, as the **diameter** of the sphere relates to the chord of double the angle enclosed by the remaining side and the first side on the **great circle** <term>Great circle|A circle on the surface of a sphere that has the same circumference as the sphere and shares its center, such as the equator.</term> of the sphere. For let *abc* be a spherical triangle whose angle *c* is a right angle; <image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating a spherical triangle abc and its projection from the center of a sphere f. The diagram includes several arcs and straight lines connecting points labeled with lowercase letters: a, b, c, d, e, f, g, i, and k. Lines fa, fb, fc, fd, fe radiate from the center f. Arcs represent segments of great circles. Point g lies on fa, i on fc, and k on fe.</image-desc> and I assert that the chord of double *ab* is to the chord of double *bc*, as the diameter of the sphere is to the chord which, in a great circle, belongs to double the angle *bac*. One should take *a* as a **pole** <note>The point on the sphere's surface exactly 90 degrees from every point on its corresponding great circle.</note>, describe the arc of the great circle *de*, and complete the **quadrants** <note>Quarter-circles of 90 degrees.</note> of the circles *abd* and *ace*. From the center of the sphere *f*, draw the common intersection *fa* of the circles *abd* and *ace*; let the intersection of circles *ace* and *de* be *fe*, and let *fd* be the intersection of *abd* and *de*. Furthermore, draw *fc* from the circles *ac* and *bc*. Thereupon, *bg* is drawn perpendicular to *fa*, *bi* perpendicular to *fc*, and *dk* perpendicular to *fe*, and *gi* is connected. Now, because two circles intersect at right angles when they pass through each other's poles: the angle *aed* will be a right angle; but *acb* is also a right angle by assumption, and consequently each of the two planes *edf* and *bcf* stands perpendicular to the plane *acf*. Therefore, if a **plumb line** <note>original: "Loth"; a line perpendicular to a given plane or line.</note> is erected on the common intersection line *fke* in the base plane (*afe*), it encloses a right angle with *kd*, according to the definition of perpendicular planes. Therefore, *kd* also stands perpendicular to the plane *aef* according to the fourth proposition of the eleventh book of **Euclid** <note>Euclid’s "Elements" was the standard textbook for geometry for over 2,000 years. Book 11 deals with three-dimensional (solid) geometry.</note>. For the same reason, *bi* also stands perpendicular to the same plane, and therefore *dk* and *bi* are parallel to one another according to the sixth proposition of the same book. But *gb* is also parallel to *fd*, because *fgb* and *gfd* are right angles; and consequently, according to the tenth proposition of the eleventh book of Euclid, the angle *fdk* is equal to *gbi*. But since angle *fkd* is a right angle, *gib* is also a right angle by the definition of a **perpendicular** <note>original: "Perpendikels".</note>. Now, the sides of **similar triangles** <note>Triangles with identical shapes but different sizes, whose sides are in constant proportion to one another.</note> are proportional, and thus *df* is to *bg* as *dk* is to *bi*. But *bi* is half of the chord of the double arc *bc*, because *bi* stands perpendicular to the line drawn from the center *f*, and for the same reason *bg* is half of the chord of the double side *ba*, and *dk* is half of the chord of the double arc *de* (or of the double angle *a*), and *df* is half of the diameter of the sphere. Thus it is evident that the chord of the double side *ab* relates to the chord of the double *bc*, as the diameter relates to the chord of the double angle *a* or the double arc *de*; to have proven this will be advantageous.

#### 4.

When in a right-angled triangle another angle and any side are given: the third angle and the other two sides also result.

<image-desc>
A geometric diagram showing arcs on a sphere. A spherical triangle *abc* is depicted, with arcs extending from it. One arc passes through *c*, *a*, and *d*. Another arc passes through *c*, *b*, and *e*. The arcs *ab* and *de* are extended until they intersect at a point labeled *f*.
</image-desc>

For let *a* be the right angle in triangle *abc*, and furthermore let one of the two other angles—for example, *b*—be given. Because of the given side, we make a threefold distinction. For either the side lies adjacent to both given angles, such as *ab*; or only to the right angle, such as *ac*; or it lies opposite the right angle, such as *bc*. 

First, let *ab* be the given side, and from the **pole** <note>The point on the sphere's surface exactly 90 degrees from every point on its corresponding great circle.</note> *c*, the arc of a **great circle** <term>Great circle|A circle on the surface of a sphere that has the same circumference as the sphere and shares its center.</term> *de* is described. After the **quadrants** <note>Quarter-circles of 90 degrees.</note> *cad* and *cbe* are completed, *ab* and *de* are extended until they intersect at *f*. The pole of the circle *cad* will therefore again be at *f*, because the angles at *a* and *d* are right angles. 

Since, when great circles on a sphere intersect each other at right angles, they bisect each other and pass through each other’s poles: both *abf* and *def* are quadrants of circles. Since *ab* is given, the remainder of the quadrant *bf* is also given, and the angle *ebf* is equal to the given angle *abc* as a **vertical angle** <note>Also called vertically opposite angles; they are the angles opposite each other when two lines cross.</note>. 

According to the preceding proof, however, the **chord of double** <note>Historical trigonometry used the "chord of double the arc" where we now use the Sine. Mathematically, sin(α) = 1/2 chord(2α).</note> *bf* relates to the chord of double *ef*, as the diameter of the sphere relates to the chord of double the angle *ebf*. Three of these quantities are given: the diameter of the sphere, the chord of the double arc *bf*, and the chord of the double angle *ebf* (or their halves). 

Therefore, according to the 15th proposition of the sixth book of **Euclid** <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book VI, Prop. 15 deals with the ratios of sides in triangles with equal angles.</note>, the half of the chord of the double arc *ef* also results, and from the "tables" the arc *ef* itself is found. From this, the remainder of the quadrant *de*—which is the sought-after angle *c*—is determined. 

In the same way, the chords of double *de* relate to *ab* as *ebc* relates to *cb*. The chords of *de*, *ab*, and the circle quadrant *ebc* are already given; thus, the fourth chord of double *cb* results, and the sought side *cb* itself is found. 

Now, since the chords of double *cb* relate to *ca* as *bf* relates to *ef*—because each of these two ratios is equal to that of the diameter of the sphere to the chord of double the angle *cba*, and ratios that are equal to the same thing are also equal to each other—and since the three values *bf*, *ef*, and *cb* are already given: the fourth *ca* results, and from it the third side *ca* of the triangle *abc*. 

Now let the side *ac* be assumed as given, and let the sides *ab* and *bc* and the angle *c* be sought: again, the chord of the double arc *ca* will have the same ratio to the chord of the double arc *cb* as the chord of the double angle *abc* to the diameter, by which the side *cb* results, and from the quadrants of the circles the remainders *ad* and *be*. Likewise, the chord of double *abf* (that is, the diameter) relates to the chord of double *bf*,

### 5.

In a triangle where the angles are given, and one of them is a right angle, the sides are also found. Let us retain the previous figure, in which, because of the given angle **c**, the arc **de** is found, and **ef** remains as the rest of the quadrant of the circle. Thus, **bf** is found, and **ab** remains as the rest of the quadrant; and through the preceding steps, it is proven that in the triangle **abc**, the remaining sides **ac** and **bc** are likewise found.

### 10.

Any two triangles on the same sphere have individually equal angles if their sides are respectively equal to one another. For because three sections of great circles on both sides form <term>pyramids<note>The author visualizes the triangle on the sphere's surface as the base of a solid pyramid whose point (apex) is at the very center of the sphere.</note></term> which have their summits at the center of the sphere, but whose bases are planar triangles enclosed by the <term>chords<note>Straight lines connecting the corners of the triangle by cutting through the interior of the sphere.</note></term> of the arcs of the spherical triangles, these pyramids are also similar and equal to each other, according to the definition of equal and similar solid figures. The reason for this similarity lies in the fact that they contain angles which, however they may be taken, are respectively equal to one another; consequently, the triangles themselves also contain respectively equal angles. Especially since those who define the similarity of figures more generally wish to find it in the fact that they contain planes inclined in some consistent way and equal angles within them. From this it seems clear to me that spherical triangles which have respectively equal sides are <term>similar<note>In this historical context, "similarity" for triangles on the same sphere implies they are identical in both shape and size (congruent).</note></term>, just like planar triangles.
