## 13.

Finally, in a triangle where all sides are given, the angles are also determined. In triangle **abc**, let all sides be given; I claim that all angles can also be found. For either the triangle has equal sides, or it does not.

Let sides **ab** and **ac** be equal first: thus it is clear that the halves of the <term>chords<note>A straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc. In historical trigonometry, the sine of an angle was often represented as half the chord of double the arc.</note></term> of the double sides are also equal. Let these be **be** and **ce**, which intersect at point **e**, because their distance from the center of the sphere on the common intersection **de** of the circles is equal, which follows from the 4th Definition of the third book of Euclid and its converse. But according to the third <term>proposition<note>A formal statement or theorem to be proven; here referring to the established rules of geometry in Euclid's Elements.</note></term> of the same book, the angle **deb** in the plane **abd** is a right angle,

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a spherical segment with vertical line segment ad. Points b and c are on the surface, with chords connecting them to points e and d on the central axis. This illustrates a case with equal sides ab and ac.</image-desc>

and **dec** is likewise a right angle in plane **acd**. Therefore, according to the 4th definition of the eleventh book of Euclid, the angle **bec** is the <term>angle of inclination<note>The angle between two intersecting planes, measured in a plane perpendicular to the line of intersection.</note></term> of these planes, which we find in this way: For since the chord **bc** is a straight line, we have a rectilinear (straight-lined) triangle **bec** with given sides—because their arcs are given—and consequently with given angles. Thus we obtain the sought angle **bec**, which is the spherical angle **bac**, and the remaining angles are found according to what was shown previously.

But if the triangle is <term>scalene<note>A triangle where all three sides have different lengths.</note></term>, as in the second figure, it is clear that the half-chords of the double arcs do not meet at the same point. Because if arc **ac** is larger than **ab**, the half-chord of double **ac** (which is **cf**) falls lower; if smaller, it falls higher, depending on whether these straight lines meet closer to or farther from the center, according to the 15th theorem of the third book of Euclid. Then, however, a parallel line **fg** is drawn to **be**, which intersects the common intersection of the circular segments at **g**, and **c** is connected to **g**. Now it is obvious that angle **efg** is a right angle, namely equal to **aeb**; and since **cf** is the half-chord of double **ac**, angle **efc** is also a right angle.

<image-desc>A second geometric diagram showing a spherical segment with unequal sides. Vertical line segment ad contains points e, f, and g. Lines connect b to e, and c to f and g. Line segment fg is parallel to eb.</image-desc>

Consequently, **cfg** is the angle of inclination of the circles **ab** and **ac**, which we thus also find. For the ratio of **df** to **fg** is the same as the ratio of **de** to **eb**, because of the <term>similarity<note>Geometric similarity: when two shapes have the same angles and proportional sides, meaning one is a scaled version of the other.</note></term> of triangles **dfg** and **deb**. Thus **fg** is obtained in the same units of measurement in which **fc** is given. But...

...the ratio of **dg** to **db** is also the same. Therefore, **dg** is also expressed in the same units in which **dc** is given, namely 100,000 <note>In historical trigonometry, 100,000 was often used as the standard value for the radius (Sinus Totus) to allow for integer-based calculations without decimals.</note>. Consequently, according to the last proposition of plane triangles, we find the angle **gfc**, which is the sought-after spherical angle **bac**, and then we obtain the remaining angles according to the 11th proposition of spherical triangles.

### 14.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a circle with center **d**. A vertical diameter connects points **b** (top) and **h** (bottom). Points **a** (right) and **c** (left) are on the circular arc. A chord connects **a** and **c** and intersects the diameter at point **e**. From points **a** and **c**, perpendicular lines (**af** and **cg**) are dropped to the diameter. A line **dk** is perpendicular to the chord **ac** at point **k**. Other connection lines exist between **d** and **a**, and **d** and **c**. A point **i** is marked on the left edge of the circle.</image-desc>

When a given circular arc is cut anywhere, such that each of the two segments is smaller than a semicircle, and the ratio of the <term>half-chord of the double<note>This phrase refers to the classical definition of the sine. Historically, the sine of an angle was defined as half the length of the chord that subtends twice that angle.</note></term> of one segment to the half-chord of the double of the other is given: then the arcs of the segments themselves are also determined. 

For let the arc **abc**, whose center is **d**, be given, and let it be cut at any point **b** such that the segments are smaller than a semicircle. Let the length ratio of the half-chord of the double of **ab** to the half-chord of the double of **bc** be given in some manner: I then claim that the arcs **ab** and **bc** are also determined. 

For one should draw the straight line **ac**, which intersects the diameter at point **e**; from the endpoints **a** and **c**, let <term>perpendiculars<note>Lines meeting at a 90-degree angle.</note></term> be dropped to the diameter, namely **af** and **cg**: these must be the halves of the chords of the doubles of **ab** and **bc**. The angles of the <term>right-angled triangles<note>Triangles containing one 90-degree angle.</note></term> **aef** and **ceg** at the <term>vertex<note>original: "Scheitel"; the point where the two lines intersect opposite each other.</note></term> **e** are equal, and therefore the triangles themselves are equiangular and similar. Their sides opposite equal angles are proportional—for example, **af** is to **cg** as **ae** is to **ec**. In whatever numbers **af** or **cg** are given, we also have **ae** and **ec** in those same numbers, and from these, the whole line **aec** is also found. 

But the chord of the arc **abc** is found in the units in which the radius **deb**, the half **ak** of **ac**, and the remainder **ek** are found. One should draw **da** and **dk**, which are likewise found in the same units as **db**—acting as the half-chord of the segment remaining from the semicircle when **abc** is subtracted from it—which is encompassed by the angle **dak**. Consequently, the angle **adk** is found, which encompasses half of the arc **abc**. Furthermore, in the triangle **edk**, which contains two given sides and the right angle **ekd**, the angle **edk** is found, and from this, the entire angle **eda** which encompasses the arc **ab**. This also reveals the remainder **cb**, which is what we aimed to demonstrate.

### 15.

In a triangle where all the angles are given, even if none of them is a right angle, all the sides can also be determined. Let *abc* be a triangle whose angles are all known, none of which is a right angle. I maintain that all its sides are also determined. For, through any of the angles—for example, through *a*—and through the poles of the arc *bc*, let one construct an arc *ad*, which therefore intersects the arc *bc* at right angles. This arc *ad* falls within the triangle, unless one of the angles at the base (*b* or *c*) is obtuse and the other is acute; but if this is the case, the circle must be drawn through that same obtuse angle toward the base. 

<image-desc>A spherical geometry diagram illustrating a triangle abc on a curved surface. A perpendicular arc ad is dropped from vertex a to the base bc. The arc is extended upwards to a point e. From e, additional arcs ef and eg are drawn to points f and g located on the extensions of sides ab and ac, creating a complex figure of intersecting spherical arcs with right angles indicated at f, g, and d.</image-desc>

After the <term>quadrants<note>A quadrant is an arc of 90 degrees, representing a quarter of a circle.</note></term> *baf*, *cag*, and *dae* are completed and *b* and *c* are taken as poles, one constructs the arcs *ef* and *eg*. The angles *f* and *g* are therefore right angles. In the right-angled triangles, the <term>half-chord of the double arc<note>This is the historical definition of the sine. To find the sine of an angle, early mathematicians looked at the chord of twice the arc's value and took half of it.</note></term> *ae* will be to the half-chord of the double arc *ef* as the half-diameter <note>The radius</note> of the sphere is to the half-chord of the double angle *eaf*. Likewise, in the triangle *aeg* containing the right angle *g*, the half-chord of the double arc *ae* is to the half-chord of the double arc *eg* as the half-diameter of the sphere is to the half-chord of the double angle *eag*. 

And for the same reason, the half-chord of the double arc *ef* is to the half-chord of the double arc *eg* as the half-chord of the double angle *eaf* is to the half-chord of the double angle *eag*. And because the arcs *fe* and *eg* are given—namely, they are the remainders by which the angles *c* and *b* differ from right angles—we thereby have the ratio of the angles *eaf* and *eag* (that is, *bad* and *cad*, which are <term>vertical angles<note>Opposite angles formed by the intersection of two lines.</note></term> to them) as given. The whole angle *bac* is indeed given, and thus, according to the previous proposition, the angles *bad* and *cad* are determined. Furthermore, by means of the 5th proposition, we obtain the sides *ab*, *bd*, *ac*, *cd*, and the entire side *bc*.

This may suffice for the time being regarding triangles, insofar as it is necessary for our purpose. If this were to have been treated more extensively, it would have required a separate volume.

# Nicolaus Copernicus’ On the Revolutions.

## Book Two.

Since we have demonstrated in the previous book that the Earth has a total of three movements, through which we promised to explain all the appearances of the stars, we now wish to fulfill this to the best of our ability by examining and investigating these movements in order, individually and piece by piece. We begin, however, with the most well-known <term>circular motion<note>Copernicus uses the term "revolutions" to describe the circular paths or rotations of celestial bodies.</note></term>—that of day and night. We have already mentioned that the Greeks called this cycle the <term>Nychthemeron<note>original: "Nychthemeron." From the Greek words for "night" and "day," referring to the full 24-hour cycle of one rotation.</note></term>. We have assumed this motion to be most intimately and directly belonging to the globe of the Earth, because from it months, years, and other various divisions of time arise, just as numbers arise from the concept of "unity." 

Therefore, regarding the inequality of days and nights, the rising and setting of the sun, the parts of the <term>Zodiac<note>original: "Thierkreis." The band of constellations through which the Sun, Moon, and planets appear to move from our perspective on Earth.</note></term>, the constellations, and similar things resulting from this circular motion, we will say only a little; especially since many others have written quite abundantly on these subjects, and their conclusions amount to the same as ours. Indeed, it matters not if we reach the same goal by looking from the opposite point of view at those things which others explain by means of a stationary Earth and a rotating universe. This is because in reciprocal systems, it so happens that opposite perspectives can still agree on the observed result. Nevertheless, we will not omit anything that is necessary. No one should be surprised if we still simply use terms like "the rising and setting" of the sun and stars and similar phrases; rather, they should know that we are merely speaking in the customary manner. This language can be maintained by everyone, as long as they keep in mind that:

> To us, who with the Earth do wheel,
> The Sun and Moon seem passing by,
> The stars in changing turns return,
> Or sinking, leave the vaulted sky.
<note>This verse captures Copernicus's central argument: what looks like the movement of the heavens is actually a reflection of the Earth's own rotation.</note>

<summary>Copernicus introduces Book Two, shifting from mathematical proofs to the practical application of Earth's three movements. He focuses first on the 24-hour rotation (Nychthemeron), explaining that while he uses traditional language like "sunset," it is actually the Earth that moves.</summary>

## Chapter 1.

### **On the Circles and Their Names.**

The Equinoctial circle (Equator) is the name given to the largest of all the parallel circles of the terrestrial sphere described around the poles of the daily rotation. The Zodiac (Ecliptic), however, is the circle described through the middle of the signs, in which the center of the Earth itself advances in its annual orbital motion. Because the Zodiac stands at an angle to the Equinoctial circle, according to the measure of the tilt of the Earth’s axis against it, it describes two circles that touch it on either side by virtue of the daily rotation of the Earth. These serve, as it were, as the outermost boundaries of its slant, which are called the <term>Tropics<note>From the Greek 'tropos,' meaning 'turn.' These are the latitudes where the sun appears to stop and reverse its north-south direction.</note></term> (turning circles). For the sun appears to make turnings <note>original: "τροπάς" (tropás)</note> in these circles—namely, a winter turning and a summer turning. Therefore, it was customary to call the one lying to the north the <term>solstitial<note>original: "solstitialis," relating to the summer solstice when the sun reaches its highest point.</note></term> tropic, and the other southern one the <term>brumal<note>original: "brumalis," from the Latin 'bruma,' meaning the shortest day or winter solstice.</note></term> tropic, as was explained further above in the overview of the Earth's circular motions.

Following this is the so-called Horizon, which the Latins call <term>finientem<note>original: "finientem," meaning "the limiting" or "the bounding" circle.</note></term>; because it has its center on the surface of the Earth and its pole at our <term>zenith<note>original: "Scheitel." The point in the sky directly above an observer.</note></term>, it bounds the part of the world visible to us against that which is hidden, and upon which everything that sets appears to rise. However, because the Earth is not to be compared with the immensity of the heavens—since, according to our assumption, not even the space lying between the Sun and the Moon can be compared with the size of the heavens—the horizon appears to bisect the heavens as if it passed through the center of the world, just as we demonstrated at the beginning.

Insofar as the horizon stands at an angle to the Equinoctial circle, it also touches two parallel circles: one northern and always visible, and one southern and always invisible. Proclus and the Greeks call the former the Arctic and the latter the Antarctic; and these circles grow larger or smaller according to the slant of the horizon or the height of the pole of the Equinoctial circle. There remains the Meridian, which passes through both the poles of the horizon and the poles of the Equinoctial circle, and is therefore perpendicular to both circles. When the sun reaches this circle, it determines noon and midnight. Since both of these circles—namely, the horizon and the meridian—have their center at the surface of the Earth, they always follow the movement of the Earth and our eye. For the eye considers itself everywhere to be the center of the sphere of everything visible around it. Furthermore, all circles assumed on the Earth project their corresponding circular images onto the heavens, as is demonstrated more clearly in <term>cosmography<note>The science that maps the general features of the universe, including both geography and astronomy.</note></term> regarding the dimensions of the Earth. Indeed, these circles also have their own names, as...

## Chapter 2.

### On the Obliquity of the Ecliptic, the Distance of the Tropics, and How They Are Measured.

Since the <term>Ecliptic<note>The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere as seen from Earth.</note></term> now appears as a slanted circle between the <term>tropics<note>The two latitudes where the sun reaches its northernmost and southernmost points; the 'turning points' of the sun's path.</note></term> and the <term>Equator</term>, I now deem it necessary for us to investigate the distance between the tropics and then the magnitude of the angle of inclination between the Equator and the Ecliptic. This, however, must necessarily be accomplished through the senses and through the application of instruments. Regarding the latter, the most important requirement is that a square be prepared from wood, or preferably from another, more solid material such as stone or metal, so that wood—which is unstable during changes in the air—cannot deceive the observer. One surface of it is to be leveled as precisely as possible, with a width of perhaps three to four cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18–22 inches; a larger instrument allowed for more precise markings.</note>, so that it is sufficient for the divisions to be applied. Once the center point has been established in one of the corners, a <term>quadrant<note>An instrument shaped like a quarter-circle used for measuring the altitudes of celestial bodies.</note></term> is described as large as possible; this is divided into 90 equal degrees, and each of these again into 60 minutes, as accurately as possible. Following this, a very well-turned cylindrical pin is erected at the center point, perpendicular to that surface, so that it protrudes about a finger’s width or less. After this instrument has been so arranged, one determines the midday line (meridian) on a pavement laid in a horizontal plane, which has been leveled as accurately as possible by means of a water level or spirit level, so that it does not slope in any direction. Specifically, after a circle has been described on this pavement, a pin is erected at its center, and observations are occasionally made during the morning to note where the outermost tip of the shadow hits the circumference of the circle. We do the same in the afternoon and bisect the arc of the circle lying between the two marks. In this way, the straight line drawn from the center through the bisection point will unfailingly indicate the south point and north point. On this basis, the plane of the instrument is erected and fixed vertically, in such a way that, after the center is turned toward the south, the straight line descending from this center meets the midday line exactly at right angles. In this way, one ensures that the surface of the instrument contains the <term>meridian circle<note>The great circle passing through the celestial poles and the observer's zenith; it is the line the sun crosses at true solar noon.</note></term>.

Now, on the day of the <term>solstice<note>From the Latin 'solstitium,' meaning 'sun-standing'; the two times a year when the sun reaches its highest or lowest point at noon.</note></term> and on the shortest day, the shadows cast at noon by that pin or cylinder from the center point in the sunlight must be observed. After some object has been attached to the lower circumference of the quadrant to more accurately mark the position of the shadow, note

...we find the center of the shadow as precisely as possible in degrees and minutes. Once we have done this, the arc that is marked between the <term>solstitial<note>Referring to the summer solstice, the longest day of the year.</note></term> and <term>brumal<note>Referring to the winter solstice, the shortest day of the year.</note></term> shadows shows us the distance between the <term>tropics<note>The boundaries of the Sun's northern and southern path.</note></term> and the entire <term>obliquity of the ecliptic<note>The angle between the Earth's rotational axis and its orbital plane; essentially, the "tilt" of the world.</note></term>. If we take half of this value, we have the distance of the tropic from the Equator; thus, the magnitude of the angle of inclination of the Equator against that circle which passes through the middle of the signs <note>The "circle through the middle of the signs" is the Ecliptic.</note> becomes known. Ptolemy took this interval, which lies between the aforementioned northern and southern limits, to be 47° 42' 40", just as he found it previously observed by Hipparchus and Eratosthenes—namely, as 11/83 of the whole circle; and half of this difference, which is 23° 51' 20", gave the distance of the tropics from the Equator and the angle of inclination against the Ecliptic. Therefore, Ptolemy believed that this remained unchangeable and would always stay so. But it is evident that these distances have continually decreased from that time until our own. For the distance of the tropics has been found by us and some others of our contemporaries to be no greater than 46° 58', and the angle of inclination to be 23° 28 2/5'; so it is sufficiently clear that the obliquity of the Ecliptic is variable. We shall discuss this further below, where we will also show that, according to sufficiently probable conjecture, it was never greater than 23° 52' and will never be smaller than 23° 28'.

## Chapter 3.

### **On the Arcs and Angles of the Intersecting Circles of the Equator, the Ecliptic, and the Meridian; in which Declination and Right Ascension consist, and on their Calculation.**

Just as we have said of the horizon—that the parts of the world rise and set upon it—so we now say that the <term>Meridian<note>An imaginary great circle on the celestial sphere that passes through the north and south celestial poles and the observer's zenith.</note></term> bisects the heavens. In a period of 24 hours, it traverses both the Ecliptic and the Equator, intersecting their arcs starting from the <term>equinoctial points<note>The points where the Ecliptic and Equator cross, marking the start of Spring (vernal) and Autumn.</note></term>, and in turn, the arc enclosed by them is intersected. Since all these circles are <term>great circles<note>The largest possible circles that can be drawn on a sphere, such as the equator on Earth.</note></term>, they form a right-angled spherical triangle; for the right angle arises because the Meridian, by its definition, passes through the poles of the Equator. One calls the enclosed arc of the Meridian (or any circle passing through the poles) the **Declination** <note>The celestial equivalent of latitude: how far north or south an object is from the celestial equator.</note> of that part of the Ecliptic. However, that arc on the Equator which corresponds to the arc of the Ecliptic that begins and moves with it from the same point is called **Right Ascension** <note>The celestial equivalent of longitude: the position of a star measured eastward along the celestial equator.</note>. All of this can be easily demonstrated with a spherical triangle. Let **abcd** be a circle passing simultaneously through the poles of the Equator and the Ecliptic, which most call the <term>Colure of the Solstices<note>A great circle on the celestial sphere that passes through the celestial poles and the two solstices.</note></term>; let **aec** be the...

...half of the <term>Ecliptic<note>The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere over the course of a year.</note></term>; *bed* the half of the <term>Equator</term>; the vernal equinox is at point *e*; the summer solstice at *a*; the winter solstice at *c*; *f* is the pole of the daily circular motion; and on the ecliptic, let the arc *eg* be taken as, for example, 30° degrees, and through it the circle quadrant *fgh* be placed. 

Then it is obvious that in the triangle *egh*, the side *eg* is equal to 30° and the angle *geh* is given—since the latter, due to the <term>declination<note>The angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator; similar to latitude on Earth.</note></term> *ab*, is at least 23° 28' (where 360° makes four right angles)—and the angle *ghe* is a right angle. Consequently, according to the fourth proposition of spherical triangles, the triangle *ehg* consists of given angles and sides. 

It is, namely, proven that the <note>original: "Sehne des doppelten"</note> <term>chord of double<note>In ancient and medieval trigonometry, calculations were made using chords of arcs rather than modern sines. The "half-chord of the double arc" is mathematically equivalent to the sine of the angle.</note></term> *eg* relates to the chord of double *gh* as the chord of double *age*—or the diameter of the sphere—relates to the chord of double *ab*, and their halves likewise. Because half the chord of double *age* equals 100,000, and half the chord of double *ab* equals 39,822, and half the chord of double *eg* equals 50,000, and because, when four numbers are proportional, the product of the inner terms equals the product of the outer: we have the half of the chord of the double arc *gh* equal to 19,911. From this, according to the tables, the arc *gh* itself is 11° 29', which is the declination corresponding to the segment *eg*. 

Following this, the sides in triangle *afg* are also given: *fg* equals 78° 31' and *ag* = 60° as the remainder of the quadrant, and the angle *fag* is a right angle; thus, the chords of the doubles *fg*, *ag*, *fgh*, and *bh* (or their halves) are likewise proportional. Since three of these are given, the fourth results as *bh* = 62° 6' as the <term>Right Ascension<note>The distance of a point delivered eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox; similar to longitude on Earth.</note></term> from the solstitial point, or *he* equals 27° 54' from the vernal equinox. 

Likewise, we obtain from the given sides and the circle quadrants: *fg* equals 78° 31', *af* equals 66° 32', angle *agf* is very nearly equal to 69° 23.5', and the <term>vertical angle<note>Also known as opposite angles, formed by two intersecting lines.</note></term> *hge* is equal to this. In the future, we shall proceed according to this same scheme. 

This, however, must not be forgotten: that the <term>meridian</term> intersects the ecliptic at right angles at those points where the latter touches the <term>tropics<note>original: "Wendekreise"</note></term>. For at those points, as previously stated, it passes through their poles. At the <term>equinoctial points<note>The two points (Spring and Autumn) where the Ecliptic and Equator intersect.</note></term>, however, it makes an angle that is smaller than a right angle in proportion to how much the ecliptic is inclined against the equator—as the angle at the smallest <term>obliquity<note>original: "Schiefe"</note></term> amounts to 66° 32'. 

It is also to be noted that for equal arcs of the ecliptic, whether they are measured from the point of intersection with the equator or from the point of contact with the tropics, the angles and sides of the triangles turn out to be equal. If we, for example, describe the arc of the equator *abc* and the ecliptic *dbe* so that they intersect at the equinoctial point *b*, and take equal arcs *fb* and *bg*, and through the poles of daily motion two circle quadrants *kfl* and *hgm*...

...placed: thus two triangles *flb* and *bmg* are formed, in which sides *bf* and *bg*, the angles at vertex *b*, and the right angles at *l* and *m* are equal. Consequently, according to the 6th theorem of spherical triangles, the triangles have equal sides and angles. Therefore, *fl* and *mg* are equal <term>declinations<note>The angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator.</note></term>, *lb* and *bm* are equal <term>right ascensions<note>The distance of a point measured eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox.</note></term>, and the third angle *f* is equal to the third angle *g*. — If the arcs from the points of contact of the <term>tropics<note>The solstitial points where the sun reaches its highest or lowest point relative to the equator.</note></term> are taken as equal, then everything follows in the same way as if *ab* and *bc* on either side of the <term>equinox<note>The point where the ecliptic (the sun's path) crosses the equator.</note></term> *b* were taken as equal; for if we draw the <term>quadrants<note>Arcs of 90 degrees, or one-quarter of a circle.</note></term> *da* and *db* from the pole *d*

[A diagram showing a spherical triangle or wedge shape with vertices labeled d, a, c and an interior point b on the base arc ac.]

of the equator, two triangles *abd* and *dbc* are formed, in which the bases *ab* and *bc* are equal, the side *bd* is common to both, and the angles at *b* are right angles. According to the 8th theorem of spherical triangles, the triangles themselves are found to have equal sides and angles, from which it is clear that the angles formed by one and the same quadrant at the <term>ecliptic<note>The path the sun appears to follow across the sky over a year.</note></term> correspond to each other, and the designated arcs correspond to the remainders of the quadrants of the whole circle. 

Now we wish to present a draft in table form. In the first column, the degrees of the ecliptic are placed; in the following, the declinations corresponding to those degrees; in the third, the minutes by which they exceed those specific declinations that arise at the greatest <term>obliquity of the ecliptic<note>The angle between the Earth's equator and its orbital path, which changes slightly over long periods of time.</note></term>, and which can amount to at most 24 minutes. We shall do the same in the table of right ascensions and angles. For it is necessary that, in proportion to the change in the obliquity of the ecliptic, everything depending on it must also be changed—including the right ascension, for which this very difference is found to be small, as it does not exceed a 10th part of a degree, and this amounts to only a 150th part of an hour's duration. 

The ancients called the parts of the equator that correspond to the parts of the ecliptic—of which there are 360 to every circle, as we have often said—"times" <note>original: "Zeiten"; ancient astronomers often measured the equator in "time" because 15 degrees equals one hour of the Earth's rotation.</note>; to distinguish them, however, most have called the parts of the ecliptic "degrees" and those of the equator "times," a convention we also wish to maintain. Although this difference is so small that it might rightly be neglected, we have not begrudged the effort to include it. From these differences, the right ascensions for any other obliquity of the ecliptic are then derived, if corresponding parts are added to the individual values in proportion to the progression from the smallest to the largest obliquity of the ecliptic. For example, if I wish to know, at an obliquity of 23º 34', which declination corresponds to the 30th degree of the ecliptic, reckoned from the equinox...

## Chapter 4.

### **How to find the Right Ascension and Declination of any star outside the Ecliptic, provided its longitude and latitude are known, and with which degree of the Ecliptic it stands in the same Meridian.**

---

This has now been developed concerning the <term>Ecliptic<note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note></term>, the <term>Equator<note>The projection of Earth's equator into space.</note></term>, and the <term>Meridian<note>An imaginary great circle on the celestial sphere passing through the north and south celestial poles.</note></term>, and their mutual intersections. However, regarding the daily circular motion, one must not only know what appears within the Ecliptic itself—by which not only the cause of solar phenomena is explained—but one must also derive the <term>Declination<note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note></term> and <term>Right Ascension<note>The distance of a celestial body measured eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox.</note></term> of those fixed stars and <term>planets<note>original: "Wandelsterne", literally 'wandering stars'.</note></term> which lie outside the Ecliptic, for which, however, longitude and latitude are given. Therefore, let one describe through the poles of the Equator and the Ecliptic a circle **abcd**; let the half-equator be **aec**, and its pole **f**; the half-ecliptic **bed**, and its pole **g**; let their intersection with the Equator be **e**.

<image-desc>
A geometric diagram of a celestial sphere represented as a circle. The circle contains points a, b, c, d along its circumference. A horizontal arc labeled aec represents the equator with its pole f at the top of the circle. A tilted arc bed represents the ecliptic with its pole g to the left of f. The two arcs intersect at the center point e. An arc ghkl descends from pole g, passing through a point h and intersecting the ecliptic at k and the equator at l. Another arc fmn descends from pole f, also passing through point h, intersecting the ecliptic at m and the equator at n.
</image-desc>

From pole **g**, let an arc **ghkl** be placed through the star, and let the position of the star be at point **h**; through this, construct a quadrant of a circle **f h m n** from the pole of the daily circular motion. Then it is evident that the star positioned at **h** enters the meridian simultaneously with points **m** and **n**; the arc **hmn** itself is the Declination of the star, and **en** is its Right Ascension, which we are seeking. Since in the triangle **kel**, side **ke** and angle **kel** are given, and angle **ekl** is a right angle: then, from the 4th theorem of spherical triangles, the sides **kl** and **le** result, along with the third angle **kle**; thus the entire arc **hkl** is given. And because in triangle **hln**, two angles—**hln** and the right angle **lnh**—along with side **kl** are given: then also from the 4th theorem of spherical triangles, the other side **hn** results as the Declination of the star, and **ln**, and the remainder **ne** as the Right Ascension calculated from the <term>Equinox<note>original: "Aequinoctium"; the point where the ecliptic and equator intersect.</note></term>. 

Or in another way: If one takes the arc of the Ecliptic **ke** from the preceding as the Right Ascension of the arc **le**, then arc **le** is conversely found from the table of Right Ascensions, and **lk** as the Declination corresponding to **le**, and angle **kle** from the table of Meridian Angles; from these, the rest can be recognized as already proven. Following this, from the Right Ascension **en**, the degrees of the Ecliptic **em** are obtained, with which the star stands in the same meridian as with point **m**.

## Chapter 5.
### **On the Sections of the Horizon.**

The horizon of the <term>right sphere<note>A celestial sphere as viewed from the equator, where the celestial poles lie on the horizon and the equator passes directly overhead.</note></term> is different from that of the <term>oblique sphere<note>A celestial sphere as viewed from any latitude between the equator and the poles, where the equator is tilted relative to the horizon.</note></term>. Specifically, the horizon of the right sphere is that to which the <term>Equator<note>The celestial equator.</note></term> stands perpendicular, or which passes through the poles of the Equator. We call the horizon of the oblique sphere that to which the Equator is tilted. At the right horizon, therefore, everything rises and sets, and days and nights are equal; for this horizon bisects all circles described parallel to the daily motion, as it passes through their poles; and everything we have already established regarding the <term>Meridian<note>The imaginary great circle passing through the celestial poles and the observer's zenith.</note></term> applies here as well. However, we calculate the day here from the rising of the sun to its setting, not as in common life from light to darkness—that is, from dawn until the lighting of lamps; we will, however, say more about this when discussing the rising and setting of the constellations.

Where, on the other hand, the <term>Earth's axis<note>The imaginary line around which the Earth rotates, pointing toward the celestial poles.</note></term> stands perpendicular to the horizon <note>This describes the vantage point from the North or South Pole.</note>, nothing rises or sets; instead, everything remains constantly visible or invisible as it moves in circles, except for what is brought about by another motion—such as the annual motion around the sun. It follows that there, the day lasts uninterrupted for half a year, and the remaining time is night; and this serves no further purpose than to distinguish between winter and summer, because there the Equator coincides with the horizon. 

But in the case of the oblique sphere, some things rise and set, while others remain always visible or invisible, and days and nights become unequal. Where an oblique horizon exists, it touches two <term>parallel circles<note>Circles of constant declination or latitude on the celestial sphere.</note></term> according to its inclination; the one lying toward the visible pole defines the limit of what is always visible, and the other, toward the invisible pole, defines what is always invisible. The horizon, falling across the entire width between these boundaries, divides all the parallel circles lying between them into unequal arcs—except for the Equator, because it is the largest parallel circle, and great circles bisect each other. In the upper hemisphere, the oblique horizon cuts larger arcs from the parallel circles lying toward the visible pole than from those lying toward the southern and invisible pole, and vice-versa in the invisible hemisphere; and since the sun appears in these arcs during its daily motion, this causes the inequality of days and nights.

## Chapter 6.
### **Which differences exist between the midday shadows.**

There are also differences between the midday shadows, according to which some people are called <term>Periscians<note>From the Greek 'peri' (around) and 'skia' (shadow); refers to those in polar regions where the shadow moves in a circle.</note></term>, others <term>Amphiscians<note>From the Greek 'amphi' (both sides) and 'skia' (shadow); refers to those in the tropics whose shadows can fall both north and south.</note></term>, and still others <term>Heteroscians<note>From the Greek 'heteros' (other) and 'skia' (shadow); refers to those in temperate zones whose shadows always point in one direction at noon.</note></term>. We can call the Periscians "those with shadows all around," as they

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the horizon's orientation, moving from the definitions of the right and oblique spheres to the practical effects of geography on sunlight and shadows. It explains how the tilt of the Earth's axis creates different "shadow-zones" for the inhabitants of the world.</meta>

...cast sun-shadows all around themselves; these are those whose <term>Zenith<note>The point in the sky directly above an observer.</note></term> or pole of the horizon is no further from the Earth’s pole than a <term>Tropic<note>One of the two latitudes (Cancer or Capricorn) marking the farthest points north or south where the sun can be directly overhead.</note></term> is from the <term>Equator</term>. For there, the <term>parallel circles<note>Lines of latitude on the celestial sphere.</note></term> which the horizon touches, and which form the boundaries of the stars that are always visible or always invisible, are larger than or equal to the Tropics. Since, therefore, in summer the sun appears in those parallel circles that are always visible, it casts the shadows of <term>gnomons<note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow, usually a vertical rod.</note></term> in all directions during that time.

But where the horizon touches the Tropics, these very circles become the boundaries of what is always visible and always invisible. Therefore, at the <term>Solstice<note>The moment when the sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky at noon, marked by the longest and shortest days.</note></term>, the sun seems to graze the Earth at midnight, at which moment the entire <term>Ecliptic<note>The apparent path of the sun across the sky over the course of a year.</note></term> coincides with the horizon; immediately thereafter, six <term>signs of the zodiac<note>original: "Himmelszeichen"</note></term> rise at once, and just as many set simultaneously on the opposite side, and the pole of the Ecliptic coincides with the pole of the horizon.

The **Amphiskier** <note>From the Greek *amphi* (both) and *skia* (shadow)—people living in the tropics whose midday shadows can fall either north or south depending on the season.</note>, who cast their midday shadows toward both sides, live between the two Tropics, a region the ancients called the "middle zone." And because the Ecliptic stands perpendicular to the horizon twice a year throughout that entire region—as proven in the second theorem of **Euclid’s *Phaenomena*** <note>An ancient Greek treatise on spherical astronomy.</note>—the shadows of gnomons disappear there twice; as the sun passes from one side to the other, the gnomons cast shadows sometimes toward the south and sometimes toward the north.

We others, who live between these [the tropics] and those [the polar regions], are **Heteroskier** <note>From the Greek *heteros* (one of two) and *skia* (shadow)—people whose midday shadows always point in the same direction.</note>, because we cast midday shadows toward only one side, namely the north. The ancient mathematicians, however, used to divide the world into seven <term>Climates<note>In ancient geography, "climates" were zones defined by the length of the longest day, rather than by temperature.</note></term>, specifically by the individual parallel circles passing through **Meroë** <note>An ancient city in modern-day Sudan.</note>, through **Syene** <note>Modern-day Aswan, Egypt.</note>, through **Alexandria**, through **Rhodes**, through the **Hellespont**, through the middle of the **Pontus** <note>The Black Sea.</note>, through the mouth of the **Borysthenes** <note>The Dnieper River.</note>, through **Byzantium**, and so on.<sup>58)</sup> These divisions were based on the differences in the longest days, the length of shadows observed on gnomons during the <term>Equinoxes<note>The two times a year when day and night are of equal length.</note></term> and the two solstices, and according to the <term>height of the pole<note>A measurement of latitude; how high the North Star appears above the horizon.</note></term> or the latitude of each section.

Since these measurements have changed somewhat over time, they are no longer the same as they once were, due to the already mentioned variable <term>obliquity of the ecliptic<note>The tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit, which Copernicus correctly noted is not perfectly constant over centuries.</note></term>, which the ancients did not know; or, to speak more correctly, because of the changing inclination of the Equator toward the Ecliptic, upon which the former depends. But the heights of the pole—or the latitudes of places—and the equinoctial shadows agree with those recorded in ancient times, which had to be the case because the Equator follows the pole of the Earth. For this reason, those sections are not sufficiently accurately defined and bounded by any measurements of shadows and days, but more correctly by their distances from the Equator, which always remain the same. That change in the Tropics, though very slight, causes a small difference in the days and shadows in southern regions, but it becomes noticeable to those traveling northward. It is

<meta>This page transitions from describing the physical movement of shadows to the mathematical principles of spherical astronomy. It connects the geometry of shadows (gnomonics) to the determination of geographical latitude and the variations in the length of days throughout the year.</meta>

From this it is also evident, regarding the appearance of the shadows of <term>gnomons<note>A vertical rod or pillar used in ancient times to measure the sun's altitude by the length of its shadow.</note></term>, that for any given height of the sun, a specific shadow length is perceived, and vice versa. If, for example, **ab** were a gnomon casting the shadow **bc**: then, since the rod itself stands perpendicular to the horizontal plane, **abc** would always be a right angle, according to the definition of lines perpendicular to planes. If one therefore connects **a** with **c**: one has a right-angled triangle **abc**, and if the height of the sun is given: one also has the angle **acb**. And according to the first theorem of plane triangles, the ratio of the gnomon **ab** to its shadow **bc**, and thus the length of **bc** itself, is given. And conversely, if **ab** and **bc** are given: then according to the third theorem of plane triangles, the angle **acb** and the height of the sun which casts that shadow at that time are also determined. In this manner, the ancients <note>original: "die Alten"; referring to classical astronomers like Ptolemy or Hipparchus</note>, when describing those sections of the terrestrial globe, noted for each of them the lengths of the midday shadows, both for the <term>Equinoxes<note>The two times of year (spring and autumn) when day and night are of equal length.</note></term> and for both <term>Solstices<note>The times of year when the sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky at noon, resulting in the longest and shortest days.</note></term>.

# Chapter 8.
## Concerning the Hours and Parts of the Day and Night.

From this it is clear that if one takes the difference read for the sun's declination <note>The sun's angular distance north or south of the celestial equator.</note> in the table under the prescribed **polar altitude** <term>Polhöhe: the latitude of the observer</term>, and adds it to the **circular quadrant** <note>90 degrees</note> for northern declination, or subtracts it for southern, and multiplies the result by two: one obtains the length of the day in question; the remainder is the size of the nocturnal arc. Each of these two figures, divided by 15, shows how many equal hours each consists of. If one takes the twelfth part, however, one obtains the duration of a **temporal hour** <note>Also known as "unequal hours," these varied in length depending on the season so that there were always 12 hours of daylight and 12 hours of darkness.</note>, which always retain the name of the day of which they are the twelfth parts. Therefore, one finds **Solstitial**, **Equinoctial**, and **Brumal** <note>Winter</note> hours mentioned by the ancients. Originally, no others were in use except the twelve between sunrise and sunset, while the night was divided into four **vigils** or watches; and the use of such hours was maintained by the silent agreement of all nations for a long time. For this reason, **water clocks** <note>clepsydrae</note> were invented, by which one determined the hours of the day through the subtraction and addition of the varying drips of water, so that the division of time remained perceptible even in fog. Later, common and equal hours were generally adopted for both day and night; and because these are easy to observe, those temporal hours fell so far into oblivion that if one were to ask a common person today which was the first, third, sixth, ninth, or eleventh hour of the day, he would either be unable to answer or would say something entirely irrelevant. Some count the number of these equal hours from noon, others from evening, others from midnight, and some from sunrise, according to the laws of each state.

# Chapter 9.
## Concerning the Oblique Ascension of the Degrees of the Ecliptic, as it results for any rising degree or degree passing the Meridian.

Having thus explained the length of days and nights and their differences, the explanation of **oblique ascensions** <term>The arc of the celestial equator that rises with a specific degree of the ecliptic in a non-equatorial horizon</term> follows in proper order. For during those times, the **dodecatemoria**—that is, the twelve parts of the **ecliptic** <note>The sun's apparent path across the sky</note>—or any other arcs of the same, rise; there is no other difference between right and oblique ascension than that between the equinoctial and the varying day, as we have shown. Now, the dodecatemoria have been designated with borrowed animal names <note>The signs of the Zodiac</note> belonging to the **fixed stars**...

<summary>This page explains how to calculate the length of days and nights using solar declination and discusses the historical shift from "temporal hours" (which changed length with the seasons) to the modern system of equal hours. It also introduces the concept of oblique ascension in relation to the zodiac signs.</summary>

<keywords>temporal hours, water clocks, polar altitude, ecliptic, dodecatemoria, oblique ascension, vigils, equinoctial hours</keywords>

<page-num>80</page-num>
named, starting specifically from the vernal equinox: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and so on, as they follow in order. Let us again, for the sake of greater clarity, take the meridian *abcd*, with the half-equator *aec*, and the horizon *bed*, which intersect at point *e*; but let us place the equinoctial point at *h* and lay through it the ecliptic <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note> *fhi*, which intersects the horizon at *l*. Through this intersection, let the quadrant *klm* of a great circle pass from the pole *k* of the equator. Now it is evident that with the arc *hl* of the ecliptic, the equator rises by *he*; but in the case of the right sphere <note>The celestial sphere as seen from the equator</note> it would rise by *hem*; the difference between these is *em*, which we have previously proven to be half the difference between the equinoctial and the variable day. But what was added there for northern declination is subtracted here, and conversely added to the right ascension <term>Right Ascension: the distance of a point east of the First Point of Aries, measured along the celestial equator</term> for southern declination, in order to obtain the oblique ascension; and how long a whole sign or another arc of the ecliptic takes to rise becomes evident from the ascensions counted from the beginning to the end. From this it follows that, if any degree of the ecliptic which is rising is given, calculated from the equinoctial point, that degree which passes through the meridian is also produced. For if the rising point *l* of the ecliptic is given, its declination is also produced by means of *hl*, its distance from the equinoctial point, and the right ascension *hem*, and consequently, since *ahem* is the entire half-day arc, the remainder *ah* is also produced, which is the right ascension of *fh*, and which is likewise produced from the table; or the angle of inclination *ahf* is produced along with the side *ah*, and the angle *fah* is a right angle. Consequently, the entire arc *fhl* of the ecliptic, which lies between the rising point and the point passing through the meridian, is given. Conversely, if the degree passing the meridian, and thus the arc *fh*, were given, we would also know the rising degree; for the declination *af* would be known, and because of the angle of inclination of the sphere *a/b*, the remainder *fb* would also be known. In the triangle *bfl*, however, according to the above, the angle *bfl* is given, *fbl* is a right angle, and the side *fb* is known; thus the sought side *fhl* is produced. Another way shall be specified further below.

# Chapter 10.

# On the angle of inclination of the ecliptic toward the horizon.

Since the ecliptic is, moreover, a circle directed obliquely toward the axis of the sphere: it forms various angles with the horizon. That it stands twice perpendicular to the latter for those who live between the tropics, we have already mentioned on the occasion of the...

...discussed the diversity of shadows. However, it seems sufficient for our purposes if only those angles are demonstrated which serve the "one-sided-shadow" inhabitants <note>original: "ein-seitig-schattenden Bewohnern"; a reference to the Heteroscii, people living in temperate zones where shadows always fall in one direction at noon</note>—that is, ourselves—to easily understand their overall relationship. Now, in the case of the oblique sphere <note>the celestial sphere as seen from a location not on the equator</note>, when the equinox or the beginning of Aries rises, the ecliptic is more inclined and approaches the horizon more closely the greater its maximum southern declination is (which belongs to the beginning of Capricorn, passing through the meridian at that time). Conversely, it stands higher and forms a larger angle in the east when the beginning of Libra rises and the beginning of Cancer passes through the meridian; this, I believe, is sufficiently clear. Now, because the three circles—the equator, the ecliptic, and the horizon—intersect at the poles of the meridian, the arcs of the meridian bounded by them determine how large that eastern angle must be calculated to be.

But so that the method for measuring the remaining parts of the ecliptic may also become clear: let *abcd* again be the meridian, the half of the horizon be *bed*, and the half of the ecliptic be *aec*, of which any given degree rises at *e*; we are to find how large the angle *aeb* is, assuming four right angles equal 360 degrees. Since the rising point *e* is given, the point passing through the meridian also follows from the preceding demonstrations, as do the arc *ae* and the altitude *ab* in the meridian. And since the angle *abe* is a right angle, the ratio of the chord of double *ae* to the chord of double *ab* is equal to the ratio of the diameter of the sphere to the chord of the double arc which measures the angle *aeb*; thus, the angle *aeb* itself is found. 

However, if it were not the degree of the rising point that was given, but rather the point passing through the meridian (which may be *a*), the angle in the east would nonetheless be measured. For if we take *e* as the pole, describe the quadrant *fgh* of a great circle, and complete the quadrants *eag* and *ebh*: then—because the altitude *ab* in the meridian is given, *af* is the complement of the quadrant, the angle *fag* follows from earlier proofs, and angle *fga* is a right angle—the arc *fg* is found, as is its complement *gh*, the latter of which measures the sought-after angle in the east. From this it also becomes clear how, simultaneously with the degree passing the meridian, the rising degree is also found; for the ratio of the chord of double *gh* to the chord of double *ab* is as the diameter to the chord of double *ae*, as has been proven regarding spherical triangles.

We have prepared three tables regarding these relationships. The first contains the ascensions in the right sphere <note>the celestial sphere as seen from the equator</note> starting from Aries and proceeding by 6 to 6 degrees of the ecliptic. The second contains the ascensions for the oblique sphere, likewise from 6

# Chapter 11.
# On the Use of These Tables.

The use of these tables is already evident from their development. Namely, if one takes the **right ascension** <note>The distance of a celestial point measured eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox.</note> for a known degree of the sun, adds 15 degrees to it for every equal hour, and subtracts 360 degrees of a full circle—should the sum become larger—then the remainder of the right ascension yields the degree of the **ecliptic** <note>The apparent path of the sun across the sky.</note> which **culminates** <note>Reaches its highest point on the meridian.</note> at the given time, calculated from noon. Likewise, if one does the same for the **oblique ascension** <note>The arc of the celestial equator that rises with a star or point in a specific latitude.</note> of one's own region, one obtains the point of the ecliptic rising at the time calculated back from sunrise. 

Also for any stars located outside the ecliptic whose right ascensions are known, there results—as shown above—from the list that point of the ecliptic which, with the same right ascension calculated from the beginning of **Aries**, passes the **meridian** <note>The great circle passing through the celestial poles and the zenith of a specific location.</note> simultaneously with them. And from their oblique ascension, it is revealed which point of the ecliptic rises at the same time as them, depending on how the ascensions and degrees of the ecliptic are found in the relevant places in the tables. In the same way, but always at opposite positions, one proceeds for the setting. Furthermore, if a **quadrant** <note>A quarter-circle, or 90 degrees.</note> is added to the right ascension that culminates, one obtains the oblique ascension of the rising star. Thus, from the culminating degree, the rising degree is also found, and vice versa. 

There follows the table of the angles which the ecliptic forms with the **horizon**, and which are read according to the rising degree of the ecliptic. From this, it is also seen how much the 90th degree of the ecliptic rises above the horizon, which is very necessary to know in the case of **solar eclipses**.

# Chapter 12.
# On the Angles and Arcs of Those Circles Which Are Drawn Through the Poles of the Horizon to the Ecliptic.

We proceed to explain the relationship of the angles and arcs that arise at the intersection points of the ecliptic and the circles which pass through the pole of the horizon <note>The zenith and nadir.</note> and on which the altitude above the horizon is also measured. Now, however, the altitude of the sun in the meridian, or of any arbitrary culminating degree of the ecliptic, and the angle at which the latter intersects the meridian, have already been dealt with above; since the meridian itself is one of those circles drawn through the **zenith** <note>original: "Scheitel des Horizonts" (Vertex of the horizon).</note> of the horizon. The angle at the starting point has also been mentioned previously, in that its **complement** <note>The amount needed to complete a 90-degree angle.</note> is the angle which the quadrant of the quarter-circle encloses with the rising ecliptic. It remains, therefore, with the help...

Retaining the previous figure, we shall conduct the investigation using the intermediate points of intersection between the meridian and the semicircles of the ecliptic <note>The path of the Sun across the sky</note> and the horizon. Let us take any arbitrary sign of the ecliptic between the meridian line and the rising or setting points; let this be *g*. Through this point, we draw the quadrant of a circle *fgh* from the pole of the horizon *f*. Since the entire arc *age* lying between the meridian and the horizon is given by the time, and *ag* is given according to our premise—likewise *af* because of the given meridian altitude *ab*—it follows that along with the meridian angle *fag*, *fg* is also determined according to the theorems of spherical triangles <term>spherical triangles: trigonometry applied to the surface of a sphere, essential for mapping the heavens</term>. Consequently, the remainder *gh* is also found, representing the altitude of point *g*, as well as the angle *fga*, which is what we sought. We have borrowed this derivation of the angles and arcs of the ecliptic in brief from Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose "Almagest" was the standard text for over a millennium</note>, referring back to the general treatise on spherical triangles. If anyone wishes to practice this further, they may devise more applications for themselves than those we have just treated as examples.

# Chapter 13.

# On the Rising and Setting of the Heavenly Bodies.

The risings and settings of the stars also appear to belong to the daily rotation; not only those simple ones of which we have just spoken, but also that kind through which the stars become morning and evening stars. Although this latter type is connected with the annual revolution <note>The Earth's orbit around the Sun</note>, it seems most appropriate to discuss it here. The ancient mathematicians distinguish true from apparent morning and evening stars. In the case of the **true** ones, the morning rising of a star occurs when it rises simultaneously with the Sun; the morning setting occurs when the star sets as the Sun rises; and during this entire interval, it is called a **morning star**. An evening rising occurs when the star rises as the Sun sets; an evening setting, on the other hand, occurs when the star sets as the Sun also sets; and during this entire interval, it is called an **evening star**, being invisible by day and appearing by night. In the case of the **apparent** morning and evening stars, however, the morning rising of the star occurs when it prepares to rise and begins to appear during the morning twilight and before sunrise; the morning setting occurs when the star appears to be just setting as the Sun is about to rise; the evening rising occurs when the star is just rising at evening twilight; and the evening setting occurs when the star first ceases to be visible after sunset, and is otherwise hidden by the Sun as it rises.

is covered, until it appears earlier in the sequence during the **morning rising**. This occurs in the same way for the **fixed stars**, and also for the planets **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars**. However, **Venus** and **Mercury** form their rising and setting differently: for they are not, like the former, covered by the arrival of the sun, nor uncovered by its departure, but by moving forward, they immerse themselves into the brilliance of the sun and withdraw from the same. The former do not become invisible at all during the **evening rising** and the **morning setting**, so that they shine with their light almost throughout the entire night. These latter, however, disappear without distinction from setting to rising, and cannot be seen. There is also another difference, namely that for the former, the true morning risings and settings occur earlier than the apparent ones, but the evening risings and settings occur later, in that they precede the rising of the sun there, and follow its setting here. For the lower planets <note>The "lower" or inferior planets are Mercury and Venus, whose orbits are closer to the sun than Earth's.</note>, however, the apparent morning and evening risings are later than the true ones, while the settings are earlier. The method, however, by which they are to be determined, can be understood from what was said above, where we explained the **oblique ascension** <term>oblique ascension: the arc of the celestial equator that rises together with a star in a non-vertical orientation</term> of each star which occupies a known location, and with which degree of the **ecliptic** <term>ecliptic: the apparent path of the sun across the sky over the course of a year</term> it rises and sets. Now, when the sun appears in this point or in the one opposite to it: then the celestial body has a true rising or setting, in the morning or evening. From these, the apparent ones differ according to the brightness and size of the celestial body. Those which are distinguished by stronger light are hidden in the **sun's rays** for a shorter time than those which shine more weakly. And the limits of **invisibility** and **appearance** are determined by the arcs of the circles lying below the **horizon**, which are drawn through the poles of the horizon, between the horizon itself and the sun. They amount to almost 12° for the fixed stars of the first magnitude, 11° for Saturn, 10° for Jupiter, 11½° for Mars, 5° for Venus, and 10° for Mercury. In general, however, the remainder of the daylight, which constitutes the evening or **morning twilight**, gives way to the night at 18 degrees of the already designated arc; when the sun is that many degrees below the horizon: then the smaller stars also begin to become visible. Some assume the **parallel circle** lying below the horizon, and say, when the sun touches this, it is daybreak or the night is ended. If we therefore know with which point of the ecliptic a celestial body rises or sets, and know the angle of this arc of the ecliptic with the horizon at that same point, and if we then find between the rising point and the sun as many degrees of the ecliptic as are sufficient to make the depth of the sun below the horizon equal to the limit determined for the given celestial body: then we say its first appearance or disappearance takes place. But what we [said] about the height of the sun above the horizon in the preceding...

### Chapter 14.

### On Determining the Positions of the Stars and the Catalog of the Fixed Stars.

Now that the daily rotation of the terrestrial globe, along with its consequences, has been explained by us: the proof of the annual revolution should now follow. However, as some of the ancient mathematicians were of the opinion that the phenomena of the fixed stars <note>The "fixed stars" refer to the stars that appear to maintain their positions relative to one another, unlike the "wandering stars" or planets.</note>, being the foundation of the science, must come first; so we also deem it good to follow this opinion. Since we intend to assume, in the conflict of principles against hypotheses, that the sphere of the fixed stars is altogether immovable, so that the deviations of all planets may rightly be referred to them. 

But let no one take offense at our having made this arrangement because Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model dominated for over a millennium.</note> in his "Great Construction" <note>original: "grosse Construction," referring to the *Almagest*.</note> was of the opinion that the development of the fixed stars could only be undertaken if knowledge of the solar and lunar positions had preceded it, and therefore believed that the investigation of the fixed stars had to be postponed until then. If one understands this in relation to the numbers by which the apparent movement of the sun and the moon is expressed, then that may perhaps be correct; for the geometer Menelaus <note>Menelaus of Alexandria (c. 70–140 AD), known for his work in spherical trigonometry.</note> also derived the positions of most stars and their locations in numbers by means of lunar conjunctions <note><term>Conjunction</term>: When two celestial bodies appear close together in the sky.</note>. 

We shall, however, achieve this much better if we determine any star from the positions of the sun and the moon, carefully tested with the help of instruments, as we shall soon show. We are also warned by the futile attempts of those who believed that the length of the solar year could be derived simply from the equinoxes or solstices, and not also from the fixed stars; regarding this, agreement could never be reached up to our times, so that in no chapter has a greater dispute existed. Ptolemy had this in mind when he calculated the solar year in his time, not without the suspicion of an error that might emerge over time, and urged posterity to strive for the utmost certainty in this matter in the future. It has therefore seemed worth our effort to show how, with the help of instruments, the positions of the sun and the moon are found—namely, by how much they [differ] from the vernal equinox or from...

*...we have assumed as principles and hypotheses that the sphere of the fixed stars is entirely immobile...* <note>original Latin: "intu principia et hypotheses assumpserimus von erantium stellarum sphaeram omnino immobilem esse"</note>

distance from other main points of the world: which is then useful to us in the investigation of the other celestial bodies, so that we may thereby present to the eye the sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: "Fixsternsphäre"</note>, interwoven with brilliance, and its image. However, the instruments with which the distance of the tropics <note>original: "Wendekreise"</note>, the obliquity of the ecliptic <note>the 23.5-degree tilt of Earth's axis relative to its orbit</note>, and the inclination of the sphere or the height of the poles of the equator are measured, have been explained above. In the same way, we can obtain any desired noon altitude of the sun. This altitude, depending on its difference from the inclination of the sphere, will show us how much the sun deviates from the equator; and from this deviation, its position—calculated from the equinox <note>original: "Aequinoctium"</note> or solstice <note>original: "Solstitium"</note>—is recognized for noon itself. Since the sun appears to traverse almost one degree in a period of 24 hours, the hourly portion amounts to 2½ minutes, from which its position for any other hour can easily be calculated.

In order to observe the positions of the moon and the stars, another instrument is constructed, which Ptolemy <margin>Ptolemy 59)</margin> calls an **astrolabe** <note>a sophisticated historical astronomical "computer" used for solving problems relating to time and the position of the sun and stars</note>. Specifically, two circles or square-edged rings are produced so that their flat sides or "cheeks" intersect the concave or convex surface at right angles: entirely congruent and of a suitable size, so that they are not too cumbersome to handle due to excessive expansion, while on the other hand, the size is favorable for a more precise division of the degrees. Their width and thickness should amount to at least the thirtieth part of the diameter. They are then joined and connected at right angles to one another, so that their convex and concave sides fit together as if they belonged to the rounding of a sphere. Of these, let one take the place of the **ecliptic** <note>the sun's apparent path</note>, and the other the place of that circle which passes through the poles of the equator and the ecliptic. The circle representing the ecliptic is to be divided on its sides into equal parts, usually 360, which again receive subdivisions as far as the instrument allows. On the other circle, quadrants are measured out from the ecliptic. And there the poles of the ecliptic are marked; from these, one takes distances according to the measure of the obliquity of the ecliptic, and marks here the poles of the equator. After this is so arranged, two other circles are placed through the poles of the constructed ecliptic, around which poles one shall move on the outside and the other on the inside. Their thicknesses between the two flat surfaces are equal, but the widths of the cheeks are similar to those of the first circles; and they are so fitted that the concave surface of the larger touches the convex, and the convex surface of the smaller touches the concave surface of the ecliptic everywhere; in such a way, however, that their movement is not hindered, but that the ecliptic with its meridian, and those others, can pass by one another. These circles are carefully pierced diametrically, as are those poles of the ecliptic, and axes <note>original: "Axen"</note> are inserted into them, through which they are connected and guided.

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the construction and calibration of the armillary sphere (referred to here as an astrolabe) for determining stellar positions. It follows the discussion of the outer rings and moves into the practical application of the instrument using the moon as a bridge between the sun and the stars.</meta>

<page-num>92</page-num>

The inner circle is likewise divided into 360 equal parts, so that 90 stands at the poles in the individual quadrants. Within its curvature, moreover, another circle—a fifth one—is to be fitted, which is rotatable in the same plane; on its sides, a pair of plates are attached in a diametrical direction with openings or pins <note>original: "Stiften"</note>, through which the light of the star can enter and pass, as with <term>diopters</term> <note>A diopter is a sighting tube or vane used for aligning an instrument with a celestial body.</note>. On the diameter of the circle, markers are added on both sides as indexes for the numbers of the surrounding circle, in order to read the latitudes upon it. Finally, a sixth circle is required, which encompasses the entire <term>astrolabe</term> <note>Here referring to the armillary sphere, a model of objects in the sky consisting of a spherical framework of rings.</note>, holding it by pins at the points of the poles of the equator; it rests upon a column and is adjusted and fixed by this perpendicularly to the plane of the horizon. After the poles have also been adjusted according to the inclination of the sphere, let the meridian circle stand in the natural position of the meridian, and let it not waver from it at all.

When we wish to record the position of any star according to this arrangement of the instrument: we set the outer circle toward evening—or when the sun is just about to set, and at a time when we also have the moon in sight—to the degree of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the sun across the celestial sphere.</note> in which we know the sun to be from previous calculations. We then turn the parts of the circle toward the sun itself until both of them—namely the ecliptic and the outer circle passing through its poles—shadow each other uniformly. Then we turn the inner circle toward the moon, and after we have brought the eye into its plane, where we see the moon as if cut through by the plane: we note the position in the ecliptic of the instrument; this will be the longitude of the moon's position. Without this, there would be no way to determine the positions of the stars, since the moon alone among all celestial bodies belongs to both the day and the night. 

Thereupon, when night falls and the star whose position we seek can already be seen, we direct the outer circle toward the moon, whereby we adjust the setting of the astrolabe to the moon just as we had done to the sun. Then we likewise turn the inner circle toward the star until it appears to hang on the plane of the circle and is seen through the diopters located on the enclosed circle. In this way, we obtain the longitude and latitude of the star. While this is being done, one looks to see which degree of the ecliptic is culminating <note>Reaching its highest point in the sky.</note>, and from this, the time at which the observation is made is determined with certainty. 

Thus, for example, **Ptolemy**⁶⁰)—who, in the second year of the Emperor **Antoninus Pius**, on the ninth day of **Pharmuthi** (the eighth month of the Egyptians), in **Alexandria**, at the setting of the sun, wished to observe the position of that star at the breast of the Lion called **Basiliskus** or **Regulus**—found by the astrolabe adjusted to the just-setting sun (after five equinoctial hours had elapsed since noon, and while the sun stood in 3¹/₂₄ degrees of **Pisces**) through the adjusted inner circle, that the moon...

It cites Ptolemy's 2nd-century observation of the star Regulus as a practical example of this technique.</summary>
