--- Page 121 ---
<page-num>93</page-num>

the Sun by a distance of 92⅛ degrees; according to which the position of the Moon then appeared at 5⅙ degrees of Gemini. After half an hour, by which the sixth hour after noon was completed, and when the star had already begun to become visible, and when the 4th degree of Gemini was culminating <note>reaching its highest point in the sky</note>: he aligned the outer circle of the instrument with the position of the Moon just obtained, and, by shifting the inner circle, obtained the distance of the star from the Moon, in the order of the zodiac signs, as 57¹⁄₁₀ degrees. 

Since the Moon was distant from the setting Sun, as noted, by 92⅛ degrees—which angle determined the Moon to be at 5⅙ degrees of Gemini—and during half an hour the Moon moved by ¼ degree (since the hourly rate of the Moon's motion is approximately ½ degree), but because of the Moon's waning at that time, its half-hourly progress had to be slightly less than ¼, about ¹⁄₁₂ less, for which reason the Moon stood at 5⅓ degrees of Gemini—(once we have dealt with the lunar variations, it will be shown that the difference was not so great, so that it will become clear the observed position of the Moon exceeded 5 degrees of Gemini by more than ⅓, and hardly less than ²⁄₅)—and if 57¹⁄₁₀ degrees are added to this: the position of the star results in 2½ degrees of Leo, thus distant from the solstice by almost 32½ degrees, with a northern latitude of ⅙ degree. 

This was the location of <term>Basiliskus</term> <note>The star Regulus, the "Little King" in the constellation Leo</note>, from which the positions of the other fixed stars were also derived. This observation by Ptolemy was made, according to the Romans, in the year of Christ 139 on the 24th of February, in the first year of the 229th Olympiad. Thus that most eminent mathematician determined what position every star occupied at that time in relation to the <term>vernal equinox</term> <note>The point where the sun crosses the celestial equator in spring</note> and indicated the brightness of the heavenly bodies, by which he rendered significant service to our study. He supported us in this difficult labor so that we—who are of the opinion that the stellar positions should not be referred to the equinoxes, which change over time, but rather the equinoxes to the sphere of the fixed stars—can easily relate the determination of the stars to some other unchangeable starting point, namely to Aries as the first sign, and specifically to its first star, which stands in its head. 

In this, it was assumed that those stars which are, as it were, fixed and connected among themselves, shining in their forever-occupied places, always maintain one and the same unchangeable appearance. They have been divided, through the admirable effort and care of the ancients, into 48 constellations, with the exception of those stars separated by a circle that keeps them always invisible for the fourth <term>clima</term> <note>A geographical zone or latitude</note> passing approximately through Rhodes. These stars remained as formless as they were unknown. According to the opinion of the younger Theon, in the <term>Aratean description</term> <note>Referring to Aratus, a Greek poet who wrote about the constellations</note>, the stars were organized into constellations for no other reason than to categorize such a great multitude of them and to name them individually according to ancient custom.

to designate them; just as it is established that some were already named in the time of Job⁶¹) <note>original: "Hiob"; referring to the biblical Book of Job, which mentions specific constellations</note>, and we also read the names of the Pleiades, Hyades, Arcturus, and Orion in the works of Hesiod and Homer.⁶²) In designating their position by longitude, we therefore do not make use of the division into twelve parts <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac</note> which begin from the equinoxes and the solstices, but rather use the simple and customary numbers of degrees; for the rest, we follow Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose star catalog remained the standard for over a millennium</note>, with the exception of a few cases where we have recognized that the data are either corrupted or otherwise behave differently. <meta>This page marks the beginning of Book Three of Copernicus's seminal work, transitioning from the study of the fixed stars to the motions of the Earth and the phenomenon of precession.</meta>

# Nicolaus Copernicus's On the Circular Motions.

## Book Three.

### Chapter 1.

### On the Precession of the Equinoxes and Solstices.

Having set forth the appearance of the fixed stars <note>The stars that appear to remain in fixed positions relative to one another, as opposed to the "wandering stars" or planets.</note>, we must now pass on to those things which are subject to an annual revolution; and to that end, we wish first to treat of the change of the equinoxes <note>The two times each year when day and night are of equal length.</note>, because of which it has been believed that even the fixed stars move. Now, we find that the ancient mathematicians did not distinguish the change of the year—namely the natural one, which depends on the equinox and the summer solstice <note>The longest day of the year.</note>—from that which is calculated from any one of the fixed stars. Hence it happened that they considered the Olympic years, which began from the heliacal rising of Sirius <note>The first day the star Sirius becomes visible in the dawn sky after a period of invisibility.</note>, to be the same as those which begin from the solstice, as the difference between the one and the other had not yet been recognized.

However, Hipparchus of Rhodes, a man of admirable intellectual sharpness, first noticed that these differed from one another; and by observing the length of the year more attentively, he found that the year related to the fixed stars <note>The sidereal year.</note> was greater than the one depending on the equinoxes or solstices <note>The tropical year.</note>. From this, he concluded that the fixed stars also possessed a certain motion, but one so slow that it would not be immediately noticed. At present, however, through the passage of time, this motion has become very striking, so that we now observe a far different rising and setting of the constellations and stars than the ancients recorded; and the twelve parts of the signs of the Zodiac have receded by a rather large distance from those constellations which originally corresponded with their designation and position. This motion is, moreover, found to be non-uniform, and those who wished to provide the reason for this irregularity have put forward various views. Some believed...

<summary>Copernicus introduces the phenomenon of the precession of the equinoxes, crediting Hipparchus with the discovery that the solar year and the sidereal year are not identical in length.</summary>
<keywords>precession, equinoxes, solstices, Hipparchus, Sirius, Zodiac, sidereal year, tropical year, astronomy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial mechanics, specifically addressing the phenomenon of the precession of the equinoxes and the movement of the Earth relative to the fixed stars.</meta>

<page-num>132</page-num>

...that it consists of a certain oscillation of the floating world, just as one perceives such an oscillation in the latitudes of the planets; it would therefore one day recede by as much as it had advanced from certain limits, and its deviation on both sides, calculated from its center, would amount to no more than 8 degrees. But this now obsolete view <note>This refers to the theory of "trepidation," an ancient belief that the stars moved back and forth like a pendulum rather than in a continuous circle.</note> could primarily not be sustained because it is already sufficiently established that the head of the constellation Aries deviates from the vernal equinox point by more than three times 8 degrees, and this is the same for the other stars, while meanwhile, through so many centuries, no trace of a recession has been noticed. Others have been of the opinion that the sphere of the fixed stars <term>Fixed stars: stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to each other, unlike planets.</term> advances with an uneven movement, but they have given no definite measure. To this was added yet another riddle of nature: namely, as we have already said, the obliquity of the ecliptic <note>The angle between the Earth's equator and its path around the sun.</note> no longer appears as great to us as it did to Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer of antiquity.</note>, which is why some devised a ninth, others a tenth sphere in the hope of finding the cause thereby; nevertheless, they could not fulfill what was promised, and an eleventh sphere was already about to be added. 

However, we shall easily eliminate this number of spheres as superfluous by assuming a movement of the Earth. As we have already partially explained in the first book <insert>Chapter 4</insert>, the two movements—the annual declination and that of the center of the Earth—are not completely equal; indeed, the retrograde movement of the declination exceeds the revolution of the center by a small amount. From this, it must necessarily follow that the equinoxes and solstices seem to recede; not because the sphere of the fixed stars moves forward, but rather because the equator—which is itself inclined due to the inclination of the Earth's axis against the plane of the ecliptic—moves backward. 

Indeed, in consideration of the greater and the smaller, it appears more appropriate to say that the equator is inclined against the ecliptic than that the ecliptic is inclined against the equator. The ecliptic, which is described by the distance of the sun from the earth in its annual revolution, is namely much larger than the equator, which, as said, is determined by the daily movement of the earth around its axis. In this way, one sees those intersection points of the equinoxes, along with the entire inclination of the ecliptic, advance over the course of time, while the stars appear to recede. The measure of this movement, however, and the ratio of its irregularity, was so hidden from the ancients that they did not know how much the movement had amounted to until then, specifically because of its unobservable slowness; since for so many centuries, during which it initially remained unknown to mortals, it has scarcely covered the fifteenth part of the circle. Nevertheless, according to what the history of observations has handed down to us, we shall determine the same as far as we are able.

<summary>The author argues that the apparent movement of the stars and the changing equinoxes are caused by the Earth's own axial motion rather than the complex "spheres" of ancient astronomy. He rejects the old theory of trepidation, noting that observations over centuries prove the movement is more significant than previously thought.</summary>

<keywords>precession of the equinoxes, ecliptic, Ptolemy, Earth's axis, celestial spheres, fixed stars, astronomy, heliocentrism</keywords>

<header>History of the observations which prove that the precession of the equinoxes and solstices is non-uniform.</header>

In the first 76-year period of <term>Callippus</term><note>A Greek astronomer who refined the Metonic cycle to better align the solar year and lunar months.</note>, in the 36th year of that same period—which was the 30th year since the death of **Alexander**¹⁵)—the Alexandrian **Timochares**¹⁶), who was the first to concern himself with the positions of the fixed stars, recorded that **Spica**, which the **Virgo** holds, stood at 82 1/3° from the summer solstice point and had a southern latitude of 2°. He also recorded that the star which is the northernmost of the three in the forehead of **Scorpio**, and the first in the order of formation of this constellation, had a latitude of 1 1/3° and a longitude of 32° from the autumnal equinox point. And in the 48th year¹⁷) of the same period, he found the longitude of **Spica** in **Virgo** to be 82 1/2° from the summer solstice, while the latitude remained the same.

**Hipparchus**, however, in the 50th year of the third Callippic period—that is, in the year 196 after **Alexander**¹⁸)—found the star in the breast of the **Lion** called **Regulus** to be 29 1/2° and 1/3° <note>original: "29 1/2° und 1/3°", meaning 29 5/6°</note> distant from the summer solstice point. Following this, the Roman geometer **Menelaus** in the first year of the Emperor **Trajan**, which was the 99th year after **Christ** and the 422nd after **Alexander’s** death, gave the distance of **Spica** in **Virgo** as 86 1/4° longitude; and the star in the forehead of **Scorpio** as 36° minus 1/12° from the autumnal equinox point.

He was followed by **Ptolemy**, in the second year of **Antoninus Pius**, which was the 462nd year after **Alexander’s** death¹⁹); he claims to have obtained the longitude of **Regulus** in **Leo** at 32 1/2° from the solstice point, that of **Spica** at 86 2/3°, and that of the star in the forehead of **Scorpio** at 36 1/3° from the autumnal equinox, while the latitude had not changed in the slightest, as given above in the catalog.

And these data, as they have been handed down by those men, we have examined anew. For after a considerable time, namely in the year 1202 after **Alexander’s** death²⁰), follows the observation of **Mahometus Aracensis**²¹)<note>Also known as Al-Battani, a major astronomer of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>, who is most to be trusted; and in this year it was shown that **Regulus** or **Basiliscus** of **Leo** had reached 44° 5′ from the solstice point, and that star in the forehead of **Scorpio** had reached 47° 50′ from the autumnal equinox point. In all these cases, the latitude of each star remained the same, so that no further doubt is held regarding this.

We also, in the year of **Christ** 1525, the first after a leap year in the Roman reckoning, which is 1849 Egyptian years²²) distant from the death of **Alexander**, observed the oft-mentioned **Spica** in **Frauenburg** in **Prussia**, and its greatest height in the meridian circle appeared to be nearly 27°. We have found the latitude of **Frauenburg** to be 54° 19 1/2′ ²³). From this, the declination of the star is found to be 8° 40′ ²⁴) from the equator. Hereafter, its position is established as follows. We describe the meridian circle through both poles of the ecliptic and the...

This longitude is found in the following way: The angles <term>okp</term> and <term>acb</term> are equal to each other as corresponding angles, and <term>opk</term> is a right angle. Therefore, <term>op</term> relates to <term>ok</term> as the halves of the chords of double <term>ab</term> to <term>be</term> and as the halves of the chords of double <term>ah</term> to <term>hik</term>, because they form a triangle similar to <term>opk</term>. In our times, it is found to be no greater than 23° 28¹/₂'.⁹⁰) Thus, it results from this that the movement from Aristarchus to Ptolemy was the smallest, but from Ptolemy to Albategnius it was the greatest.⁹¹)

# Chapter 3.

# Hypotheses from which the change of the equinoxes, the obliquity of the ecliptic, and the equator is derived.

That the equinoxes and solstices change with non-uniform speed seems clear from the preceding. Perhaps no one could provide a better reason for this than a certain movement of the Earth's axis and the poles of the equator; and that seems to follow truly from the conception of the movement of the Earth; since it is certain that the circle which is placed through the middle of the signs <note>The Ecliptic</note> remains eternally unchangeable, as proven by the constant latitudes of the fixed stars, while the equator changes; for if the movement of the Earth's axis corresponded simply and exactly with the movement of the center, as has been said, no advancement of the equinoxes and solstices would appear at all. However, if these are different from one another, and indeed by a non-constant difference: then it is also necessary that the solstices and equinoxes advance with non-uniform speed relative to the positions of the stars. In the same way, the movement of the declination <note>The angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator</note> occurs, which changes the obliquity of the ecliptic, which however more correctly [belongs] to the equator...

<summary>The author compares historical astronomical data to demonstrate that the precession of the equinoxes and the tilt of the Earth's axis (obliquity) are not constant but vary over time. He proposes that these variations are best explained by the physical movement of the Earth's axis within his heliocentric model.</summary>

Therefore, two alternating movements, similar to the swinging of a pendulum <note>original: "Pendelschwingungen"</note>, must be assumed: since the poles and circles on a sphere are interconnected and correspond with one another. Namely, there will be one movement that changes the inclination of those circles, as the poles move up and down around central angles; and another which increases and decreases the progression of the solstices and equinoxes, as a lateral movement is performed by both poles. We call these movements, however, **librations** <term>libration: a slow oscillation, real or apparent, of a satellite or planet</term>, because, like pendulums, they are faster in the middle between their two limits and slowest at the limits themselves; such movements frequently occur in the elongations of the planets, which we shall consider in its proper place. They also differ in their revolutions, because the non-uniformity of the equinoxes recurs twice during one return of the obliquity. But just as in every appearing non-uniform movement a mean must be found by which the ratio of the non-uniformity can be measured: so one naturally had to seek mean poles, a mean equator, and mean equinox and solstice points, around which the poles and the Earth's equator—deviating to both sides—make those various movements appear uniform within fixed limits. Those two coinciding librations thus cause the Earth's poles to describe certain lines over time, similar to a twisted ring. Since, however, this cannot easily be expressed sufficiently with words, especially when it is only perceived by hearing and not simultaneously viewed with the eyes: we describe the **ecliptic** <note>the apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere</note> *abcd* on a sphere; let its northern pole be *e*, the beginning of **Capricorn** *a*, that of **Cancer** *c*, that of **Aries** *b*, and that of **Libra** *d*; and through the points *a* and *c* and the pole *e*, let the circle *aec* be placed. Let the greatest distance between the north poles of the ecliptic and the equator be *ef*, the smallest *eg*; and likewise let the pole *i* be in the mean position, around which the so-called mean—

Let the empty equator *bhd* be described, and let *b* and *d* be the mean equinoxes <note>The points where the celestial equator and ecliptic intersect</note>, both of which always move backward around point *e* in a uniform motion—that is, against the order of the signs in the sphere of the fixed stars—and, as stated, advance in a slow motion. Now, one will understand both connected pendulum-like movements of the Earth's poles: the one between the limits *f* and *g*, which may be called the movement of the anomaly <note>In astronomy, "anomaly" refers to an irregularity or a specific angular distance in an orbit</note>, i.e., the inequality of the declination; the other, moving sideways back and forth twice as fast as the former, which we shall call the anomaly of the equinoxes. These two movements occurring simultaneously in the poles deflect them in a remarkable way. For if we first place the North Pole of the Earth at *f*, the equator described around it will pass through the same points *b* and *d*, namely through the poles of the circle *afec*; but it will increase the angle of the obliquity <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis</note> in proportion to the arc *fi*. If the pole of the Earth is to pass from this starting point to the mean obliquity, namely to *i*: the other movement added to it does not allow it to proceed straight along *fi*, but leads it in a direct motion <note>original: "rechtläufig" - moving in the direction of the zodiac</note> on a detour through the greatest deviation, which may lie at *k*. In this position, the intersection of the true equator *oqp* will not be at *b*, but will lie behind it at *o*, and the precession of the equinoxes will be reduced by the segment *bo*. From here the pole turns around, and by proceeding in a retrograde motion <note>original: "rückläufig" - moving backward against the zodiac</note>, it reaches the center *i* through the two cooperating movements, and the true equator coincides with the mean in all points. Proceeding from here, the Earth's pole moves backward, separates the true equator from the mean, and increases the precession of the equinoxes to the other limit *l*. Turning back from here, it takes away from the equinoxes what it had just added to them, until, having arrived at point *g*, it produces the smallest obliquity at the same point *b*, at which point again the movement of the equinoxes and solstices appears slowest, in much the same way as at *f*. At this time, the inequality of the latter has evidently completed its revolution, since it has reached both extremes from the center; but the movement of the obliquity has only covered half the revolution from the greatest declination to the smallest. Continuing from here, the pole comes again in a direct motion to the outermost limit at *m*, and again in a retrograde motion, it meets with the mean, and after having again turned backward and passed through the limit *n*, it finally completes, as said, the twisted line *fkilgminf*. In this way, it is clear that during one return of the obliquity, the Earth's pole twice reaches the forward and backward limits.

# Chapter 4.
## How the reciprocal motion of libration consists of circular motions.

We shall immediately explain how this motion agrees with the observed phenomena. In the meantime, however, one might raise the question of how the uniformity of that <term>libration</term><note>Libration refers to a slow oscillation, real or apparent, of a celestial body. Copernicus is explaining how a back-and-forth straight-line motion can be created by two uniform circular motions.</note> can be understood. For it was asserted at the beginning that celestial motion is uniform, or at least composed of uniform circular motions; yet here, two motions, each between two limits, appear united into one, which must necessarily result in an irregularity. We admit that these are composite, but we derive them from uniform motions in the following manner.

Let *ab* be a straight line divided into four equal parts by the points *c, d,* and *e*. Around *d*, let concentric circles lying in the same plane be described with the diameters *adb* and *cde*. Somewhere on the periphery of the inner circle, a point *f* is taken; around this point *f*, with the radius *fd*, the circle *ghd* is described, which intersects the straight line *ab* at point *h*, and the diameter *dfg* is drawn. It must be shown that when the combined motions of the circles *ghd* and *cfe* take place simultaneously, the movable point *h* moves back and forth on the straight line *ab*. This will be proven once it is understood that *h* moves in opposite directions and twice as fast as *f*.

The <term>central angle</term><note>The angle subtended at the center of a circle.</note> *cdf* in circle *cfe*, which is simultaneously an <term>inscribed angle</term><note>original: "Peripheriewinkel". An angle formed by two chords in a circle that have a common endpoint on the circle.</note> in circle *ghd*, encloses arcs in both circles, of which *gh* is twice as large as *fc*. Now, let us assume the case that at some time, when the straight lines *acd* and *dfg* coincide, the movable point *h* falls on *g* (and thus also on *a*), and *f* falls on *c*. Thus, the center *f* has moved to the right through *fc*, and *h* has moved to the left through the arc *gh*, which is twice as large as *cf*. Consequently, *h* will move back into the line *ab* from the opposite side; otherwise, the part would be larger than its whole, which I believe is easy to see. However, the point *h* moves away from its former position *a* by the distance *ah*, being pulled back by the broken line *dfh* (which is equal to *ad*) by that amount which the diameter *dfg* is larger than the <term>chord</term><note>A straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc.</note> *dh*. And in this manner, *h* is carried forward to the center *d*.

<summary>Copernicus demonstrates a geometric proof showing how linear oscillation (libration) is actually produced by the combination of two uniform circular motions, maintaining the principle of celestial regularity.</summary>
<keywords>libration, circular motion, geometry, uniformity, Copernicus, astronomy, oscillation</keywords>

which lies at the point of contact of the circle *dhg* with the straight line *ab*, because then *gd* will stand at a right angle to *ab*. And after that, the point *h* reaches the other limit *b*, from which it is led back again in a similar manner <note>original: "zurückgeführt wird"</note>. It is therefore evident that from two circular motions, which are opposed to each other in this way, a rectilinear motion is composed; and from two simultaneous uniform motions, a non-uniform motion results. From this it also follows that the straight line *gh* is always at a right angle to *ab*, because these two lines enclose a right angle within the semicircle *dhg*. And therefore *gh* is half of the chord of the double arc *ag*, and the other line *dh* is half of the chord of that double arc which remains from the quadrant after subtracting *ag*, whereby the circle *agb* is twice as large as *hyd*, according to the diameters.

# Chapter 5.

# Proof of the non-uniformity of the precession of the equinoxes and the obliquity.

Some call this motion, for this very reason, the motion in the latitude of the circle, that is, in its diameter; however, they measure its period and its uniformity in the arc, but its magnitude in the chords. It can therefore easily be proven that this motion appears as non-uniform, namely as accelerated at the center and slower at the periphery. Let *abc* be a semicircle, *d* its center, *adc* the diameter, and let the semicircle be bisected at point *b*. Let the arcs *ae* and *bf* be made equal, and from the points *f* and *e* let the perpendiculars <term>Lothe: perpendicular lines dropped from a point to a line</term> *eg* and *fk* be dropped onto *adc*. Since double *dk* is the chord of double *bf*, and double *eg* is the chord of double *ae*: then *dk* and *eg* are equal to each other. But *ag* is, according to the seventh proposition of the third book of Euclid's *Elements*, smaller than *ge*, and thus also smaller than *dk*. Because of the equal arcs *ae* and *bf*, however, *ga* and *kd* are traversed in equal times; consequently, the motion in the vicinity of point *a* of the periphery is slower than in the vicinity of the center *d*. Having proven this, let the center of the Earth be assumed at *l*: so that the straight line *dl* stands at a right angle to the plane of the semicircle *abc*; through the points *a* and *c*, let the arc of a circle *amc* be described from the center *l*—

### Chapter 6.

### On the uniform movements of the precession of the equinoxes and the obliquity of the ecliptic.

Every circular motion that appears non-uniform proceeds in four stages: namely, at the extreme points where it appears slowest and where it appears fastest, and at the intermediate points where it is a mean <note>average</note> speed. From the cessation of deceleration and the beginning of acceleration, it passes into the mean; from the mean, it increases to the greatest speed; from this, it passes again into the mean, and from there it returns to the initial greatest slowness. By this, it can be recognized in which part of the cycle the position of the inequality or the anomaly <note>The angular distance from a planet's or point's slowest position</note> was for any given time, and from these data, the period of the anomaly is also obtained. In a circle divided into four parts, let *a* be the place of greatest slowness, *b* the place for the increasing mean speed, *c* the place where the growth ends and the decrease begins, and *d* the place for the decreasing mean speed. Since now, as was said above, the appearing movement of the precession of the equinoxes was found to be slower from the time of Timochares to Ptolemy <note>Timochares (c. 320–260 BCE) and Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE) were foundational Greek astronomers</note> compared to other times, and because it seemed to be uniform for a while, as shown by the observations of Aristyllus, Hipparchus, Agrippa, and Menelaus in the intervening time: this proves that the appearing movement of the equinoxes

By virtue of this abbreviation, one can find and read the uniform motions through these <term>compendious tables</term> <note>Abridged or concise reference tables used for rapid calculation.</note> at least within 3600 years by means of double entry for the intended years. The same applies to the number of days. In the calculation of celestial motions, we shall everywhere use <term>Egyptian years</term> <note>A calendar of exactly 365 days (12 months of 30 days plus 5 extra days), favored by astronomers for its mathematical regularity compared to leap-year systems.</note> as a basis, because these alone among civil years are uniform; and it is necessary that the measure corresponds with the measured, which is not the case with the Roman, Greek, and Persian years, in which intercalations are made not in one and the same way, but according to the pleasure of each nation. The Egyptian year, however, introduces no ambiguity because of the fixed number of 365 days, which are divided into twelve equal months.

# Chapter 7.
## What the greatest difference is between the uniform and the apparent precession of the equinoxes.

Now that the mean <note>average or uniform</note> motions have been explained, we must investigate how large the greatest difference is between the uniform and the apparent motion of the equinoxes—or, in other words, the diameter of the small circle in which the motion of the anomaly <note>the irregularity or deviation from uniform motion</note> proceeds. For once this is determined, it will be easy to define any other differences in these motions. 

As previously stated, 432 years passed between the first observation by Timocharis <note>an Alexandrian astronomer, c. 320–260 BCE</note> and that of Ptolemy in the second year of Antoninus; in this time, the mean motion amounted to 6° 10', while the apparent motion was 4° 20'. The difference between the two was 1° 40', while the motion of the double anomaly <note>the cycle of the irregularity</note> amounted to 90° 35'. It is therefore clear that in the middle of this period, or very nearly so, the apparent motion had reached the limit of its greatest slowness. At this point, the apparent and mean motions must coincide, and the true and mean equinoxes must lie at the same intersection of the circles. 

Therefore, on both sides lie the differences between the non-uniform and uniform motion which, if one halves the motion and the time, amount to 5/6°. These correspond to the arcs of the circle of anomaly on either side, encompassing 45° 17½'. However, since we are dealing here with very small arcs—as those of the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path</note> do not reach one and a half degrees—the chords are nearly equal to the arcs, and a difference is hardly found even in the "thirds" <note>sixtieths of a second</note>. Thus, we who are satisfied with minutes commit no error if we use straight lines instead of arcs. 

->![Diagram of a semicircle intersecting a line at points a, b, and c, with a perpendicular line db and a radius line ef]<-

Now, let *abc* be that part of the ecliptic in which the mean equinox lies at *b*. Around this, taken as a pole, let the semicircle *adc* be described, intersecting the ecliptic at points *a* and *c*. From the pole of the ecliptic, let *db* be drawn, which line also bisects the described semicircle at *d*, where the extreme limit of slowness and the beginning of acceleration may lie. In the quadrant *ad*, let *de* be taken as 45° 17½', and through point *e* let *ef* be drawn from the pole of the ecliptic, and let *fb* = 50'. It is required to find from this the entire difference *ab*. Now it is clear that double *bf* is the chord of the double arc of *de*. Since *bf* = 7107 relates to *ab* = 10000 as *bf* = 50' relates to *ab* = 70', it follows that *ab* = 1° 10'. This is the greatest difference between the

<summary>Copernicus calculates the maximum variation between uniform and apparent precession by comparing historical observations from Timocharis and Ptolemy. He uses geometric modeling of a small circle of anomaly to determine that the maximum difference is 1° 10'.</summary>
<keywords>precession of the equinoxes, anomaly, ecliptic, Timocharis, Ptolemy, geometric modeling, astronomy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical demonstration of the Earth's axial wobble (precession and nutation), specifically calculating the divergence between the mean and apparent equinoxes.</meta>

<page-num>150</page-num>
between the mean and the apparent movement of the equinoxes, which we were seeking; and from this it follows that the greatest deflection of the poles is 28 minutes. <note>Copernicus is calculating the "nutation" or the small nodding motion of the Earth's axis.</note>

Having determined this, let *abc* be an arc of the ecliptic <note>The sun's apparent path</note>, *dbe* the mean equator, and *b* the mean intersection of the apparent equinoxes, whether of Aries or Libra; and let *bf* lie through the poles of the arc *dbe*. On *abc*, however, equal arcs *bi* and *bk* of 70 minutes <note>original: 70'</note> are taken on both sides, so that the entire arc *ibk* amounts to 2 degrees and 20 minutes. Furthermore, let two arcs of the apparent equators *ig* and *hk* be described at right angles to *fb* and its extension. I say "at right angles," even though the poles of the arcs *ig* and *hk* often lie outside the circle *bf* because the lateral movement of the declination is added to it, as shown in the hypothesis; but because of the very moderate distance—which, at its greatest, does not exceed the 350th part of a right angle—we take those to be right angles for the sake of visualization, for no visible error will arise from it. Since, therefore, in the triangle *ibg*, the angle *ibg* is given as 66 degrees 20 minutes—because the complement to the right angle, *dba*, is 23 degrees 40 minutes (the angle of the mean obliquity of the ecliptic)—and angle *bgi* is a right angle; angle *big* is almost equal to *ibd* and side *ib* is 70 minutes: thus the arc *bg*, by which the poles of the mean and the apparent equator stand apart from each other, is given as 28 minutes. Likewise, in the triangle *bhk*, the two angles *bhk* and *hbk* are equal to the two *igb* and *ibg*, and side *bk* is equal to side *bi*; consequently, *bh* will also be equal to *bg*, which is 28 minutes. For *gb* will relate to *bh* as *ib* to *bk*, and the movements of both the poles and the intersection points will be similar.

# Chapter 8.
# Concerning the individual differences of these movements together with an explanation
# of their table.

If, therefore, *ab* = 70 minutes (in the first figure of the preceding chapter) is given—which arc does not seem to differ in its length from its chord—it is not difficult to determine any other individual differences for the mean and apparent movements. These the Greeks call <term>Prosthaphaireses</term> <note>From the Greek for "addition and subtraction"; corrections used to find the true position from the mean position.</note> and the moderns call <term>Equations</term>, by whose removal or addition the...

We shall make use of the Greek word <term>Prostaphärese</term> <note>From the Greek *prosthaphaeresis*, meaning the correction or difference added to or subtracted from a mean motion to obtain the true motion.</note> as the more suitable term. Now, if the arc <italic>ed</italic> were 3°: we would obtain from the ratio of <italic>ab</italic> to the chord <italic>bf</italic>, the prosthaphaeresis <italic>bf</italic> = 4' 11''. If the arc <italic>ed</italic> is 6°, it is 7' 11''; if 9°, 11' 11'' and so forth. Regarding the change in the obliquity <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit.</note>, we believe we must proceed in a similar manner, where the difference between the greatest and smallest obliquity, as previously stated, is found to be 24', which is traversed during the semicircle of the simple <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet or point from its last perihelion or apogee.</note> in 1717 years. The mean value at the quadrant of the circle amounts to 12', and the pole of the small circle of this anomaly belongs to the mean obliquity of 23° 40'. And in this way, as said, we will derive the remaining parts of the difference, approximately proportional to those previously given, as is contained in the following list.

Although the appearing motions can be composed in various ways according to these derivations: yet that method pleased us most by which each individual prosthaphaeresis is obtained for itself, whereby the calculation of these motions becomes easier for the understanding and agrees more with the developments set forth. We have therefore prepared a table of 60 lines, which advances by every 3 degrees of the circle. In this way, it will seem to have neither an extended prolixity nor a too-crowded brevity; just as we intend to proceed in later similar tables. The present one has only four columns, of which the first two contain the degrees of each of the two semicircles, which we call the common numbers, because the obliquity of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere.</note> is obtained through the simple number, and the doubled number serves for the prosthaphaeresis of the <term>equinoxes</term> <note>The two points in the year when day and night are of equal length.</note>, the beginning of which is taken from the start of the increase. 

In the third column, the prosthaphaereses of the equinoxes are set down, which correspond to the individual three-degree intervals, and are either to be added to or subtracted from the mean motion, which we begin from the first star of the Head of Aries toward the vernal equinox point. The prosthaphaereses to be subtracted correspond to the small semicircle of the anomaly, or the first column; those to be added correspond to the second column and the following semicircle. Finally, in the last column stand the minutes, which are called the proportional minutes of the obliquity, and rise at most to 60; for instead of the greatest and smallest deviation of the obliquity of 24', we set 60', from which we calculate the parts of the similar ratio according to the proportion of the remaining deviations, and therefore set 60 at the beginning and at the end of the anomaly. But where the deviation rises to 22', as with the anomaly of 33°, we set 55 in its place, likewise for 20', 50 as with the anomaly of 48°, and further in this manner, as is evident in the following diagram.

# Chapter 9.
## On the Examination and Correction of the Theory Developed Concerning the Precession of the Equinoxes.

Since we have assumed, based on mere conjecture, that the beginning of the increase of the non-uniform movement lies at the midpoint of the time between the 36th year of the first <term>Callippic Period</term><note>A 76-year cycle used by ancient Greek astronomers to synchronize solar and lunar years.</note> and the second year of <term>Antoninus</term><note>The Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius; his reign is a standard chronological marker for Ptolemy's observations.</note>; and we begin the movement of the <term>anomaly</term><note>The irregularity or deviation from uniform circular motion.</note> from this midpoint: we must still investigate whether we have acted correctly in this, and whether it agrees with the observations. Returning to those three observed stars of <term>Timochares</term>, <term>Ptolemy</term>, and <term>Albategnius</term><note>Al-Battani, a 9th-century Arab astronomer who refined the measurements of the solar year and precession.</note>: it is certain that the first period comprises 432, and the second 742 Egyptian years. The uniform movement in the first period was 6° 12′, the actual movement 4° 20′ 10″, and that of the double anomaly 90° 35′ 12″; the amount to be subtracted from the uniform movement was 1° 40′ 10″. In the second period, the uniform movement was 10° 21′ 12″, the actual 11° 30′ 12″, the double anomaly 155° 34′, and the amount to be added to the uniform movement was 1° 9′ 12″.

Now let *abc* be, as before, an arc of the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere.</note>, and from *b*, which is intended to be the mean <term>vernal equinox point</term><note>The point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator in spring.</note>, let the small circle *adce* be described with the radius *ab* = 1° 10′. Let the uniform movement of point *b* be taken toward side *a*, that is, backward, and let *a* be the western limit, at which the variable equinox has advanced the furthest, and *c* the eastern limit, at which the variable equinox has remained furthest behind. From the pole of the ecliptic, let the great circle *dbe* be drawn through point *b*, which, together with the ecliptic, divides the small circle *adce* into four equal parts, because they intersect each other at right angles due to the poles. Now, if the movement lags in the semicircle *adc* and advances in the other *cea*, then, because of the opposition to the precession of *b*, the center of the greatest slowness of the apparent equinox will be at *d*, while at *e* there will be the greatest velocity, because the movements mutually accelerate toward the same side. Before and after *d*, let the arcs *fd* and *dg* each be taken at 45° 17½′. Let *f* be the first point of the anomaly at the time of Timochares, *g* the second at the time of Ptolemy, and *p* the third at the time of Albategnius; and through these points, as well as through the poles of the ecliptic, *fn*, *gm*, and *op* are drawn, which are all very similar to straight lines within the small circle. The arc *fdg* will therefore amount to 90° 35′, if 360° are assigned to the circle *adce*, and this arc will decrease the mean movement by *mn* = 1° 40′.

## Chapter 11.
## On the determination of the positions for the uniform movements of the equinoxes and the anomaly.

After all this has been settled, it remains for us to establish the positions of the movements of the vernal equinox <note>The spring equinox</note> itself, which are called "roots" <term>roots: the starting values or 'radices' used for astronomical calculations at a specific epoch</term> by some, from which the calculations for any given time are derived. However, in following better-known times, we have found it sufficient to begin from the first Olympiad, which it appears preceded Nabonassar by 28 years, with the summer solstice forming the beginning, at which time Sirius rose for the Greeks (heliacally) <note>heliacal rising: when a star first becomes visible in the dawn sky after a period of invisibility</note> and the Olympic games were celebrated, as Censorinus and other recognized authors have stated. According to more precise chronology, which is necessary for calculations of celestial movements, it is 27 years and 247 days <note>original note 138</note> from the first Olympiad, or from the noon of the first day of the Greek month Hekatombaion, until Nabonassar, or until the noon of the first day of the Egyptian month Thoth. If one subtracts those 95° 45' from 21° 15' of the simple anomaly in the same way, 285° 30' remains as the position of the simple anomaly for that same beginning of the Olympiads. And if one again adds the motions according to the time periods, always subtracting 360° whenever they are exceeded, one obtains the positions or "roots" for Alexander: 1° 2' for the uniform motion and 332° 52' for the simple anomaly. For Caesar, the mean motion is 4° 55' and the simple anomaly is 2° 2'. For Christ, the mean position is 5° 32' and the anomaly is 6° 45'. And thus we obtain for the others the roots of the motions for the beginning of any desired time. <margin>144)</margin>

# Chapter 12.
## On the Calculation of the Precession of the Vernal Equinox and
## the Obliquity.

Whenever one wishes to obtain the position of the vernal equinox <note>The point where the sun crosses the celestial equator in spring</note>, one must first convert the years—if they are unequal like the Roman years commonly used—into equal or Egyptian years. For in the calculation of uniform motions, for the reasons previously stated <insert>145</insert>, we use no years other than Egyptian ones <note>Egyptian years consist of exactly 365 days, making them easier for astronomical math than leap-year systems</note>. If the number of years is greater than sixty, one divides them into groups of sixty and enters the Table of Motions with these groups. One skips the first column of motion as if it were superfluous and begins with the second column, which contains the degrees; if a number is found there, it is multiplied by sixty and combined with the other degrees, minutes, and so on. Then, one enters the table a second time with the remaining years and takes the degrees, minutes, etc., exactly as they appear starting from the first column. In this process, fractions of days or even whole days may be conveniently neglected due to the slowness of these movements, as the daily motion involves only seconds and thirds <note>sixtieths and thirty-six-hundredths of a degree</note>. After adding all this to the "root" <note>The starting value or epoch</note>, placing the respective signs in their positions, and removing multiples of sixty degrees whenever they arise, one obtains the mean position of the vernal equinox for the given time. This tells us how far it precedes the first star of Aries, or how far that same star follows the equinox.

In the same manner, one also seeks the anomaly <note>The angular distance used to find a planet's or point's irregular motion</note>. With this simple anomaly, one finds the recorded proportional minutes in the last column of the Table of Prosthaphaereses <insert>146</insert> <term>Prosthaphaereses: from Greek, meaning "addition and subtraction"; these are corrections used to convert "mean" or average motion into "true" observed motion</term>, which should be noted down separately. Then, using the doubled anomaly, one looks in the third column of the same table for the prosthaphaerese in degrees and minutes, which represents the difference between the true motion and the mean motion. This prosthaphaerese is subtracted if the doubled anomaly is less than a semicircle <note>180 degrees</note>; but if the latter is greater than a semicircle—containing more than 180 degrees—one adds this prosthaphaerese to the mean motion. The resulting sum or difference gives the true apparent motion of the precession of the vernal equinox. In other words: it shows how far the first star of Aries has moved from the vernal equinox. This distance is added to the longitude of any other star found in the star catalog to determine its current position.

### Chapter 13.

### On the Magnitude and Variation of the Solar Year.

That the precession of the equinoxes and solstices—which we have stated arises from the inclination of the Earth's axis—proceeds in such a manner, will also be confirmed by the annual motion of the center of the Earth as it moves around the Sun, which we must now discuss. For it must undoubtedly follow from this that the length of the year, when calculated from one equinox or solstice to the next, turns out to be unequal due to the unequal change of these points, since both are dependent on one another. One must therefore separate and distinguish the civil <note>original: "temporalis"</note> year from the sidereal <note>original: "sidereus"; measured by the stars</note> year. We call the year "natural" or "civil" when it defines the four seasons for us; but the sidereal year is that which returns to any fixed star. That the natural year, which is also called the tropical <note>original: "vertens"</note> year, is unequal, is proven by many observations of the ancients. For Callippus, Aristarchus of Samos, and Archimedes of Syracuse determined that it contains a quarter of a day in addition to 365 whole days; following the custom of the Athenians, they calculated the beginning of the year from the solstice. But Claudius Ptolemy, noticing that the determination of the solstices was difficult and uncertain, did not entirely trust their observations and relied instead on Hipparchus, who had recorded not so much the solstices as the equinoxes in Rhodes, and had noted that something was missing from the fourth part of a day. Ptolemy later determined this missing amount to be 1/300th of a day by the following method. He took as a basis the autumnal equinox observed very precisely by Hipparchus at Alexandria in the year 177 <insert>157</insert> <note>A correction or reference to the era of Alexander's death</note> after the death of Alexander the Great, according to the Egyptian calendar, at midnight on the third intercalary day, which was followed by the fourth intercalary day. With this, Ptolemy combined an observation of the same equinox made by himself at Alexandria in the 3rd year of Antoninus—which was the 463rd year after Alexander's death—on the 9th day of the 3rd Egyptian month, Athyr, about one hour after sunrise. Between this observation and that of Hipparchus, there were 285 Egyptian years, 70 days, and 7 1/3 hours, whereas it should have been 71 days and 6 hours if the tropical year contained 1/4 day in addition to the whole days. Thus, in 285 years, one day minus 1/20th of a day had been lost. <insert>158</insert>

From this it follows that in 300 years an entire day is lost. Likewise, he also carried out the derivation from the vernal equinox <note>The point in spring when day and night are of equal length</note>. Specifically, he mentions a note by Hipparchus <note>Greek astronomer, c. 190–120 BCE</note> from the year 178 after Alexander [the Great] on the 27th of Mechir, the sixth Egyptian month, at sunrise. He himself finds the same in the year 463 on the 7th of Pachon, the ninth Egyptian month, at 1 o'clock in the afternoon and slightly over; so that in 285 years there is likewise 1 day less ¹/₂₀ of a day missing. ¹⁵⁹) On the basis of these facts, Ptolemy determined the tropical year to be 365 days, 14 sixtieths, and 48 three-thousand-six-hundredths ¹⁶⁰). Following this, Albategnius ¹⁶¹) <note>Latinized name of Al-Battani, a famous Arab astronomer</note> in Raqqa ¹⁶²) in Syria observed the autumnal equinox with no less care in the year 1206 after the death of Alexander and found that it occurred in the night following the 7th of Pachon at 7²/₅ o'clock, that is, 4³/₅ hours before the dawn of the 8th day. In order to compare this observation of his with that of Ptolemy in the 3rd year of Antoninus, one hour after sunrise at Alexandria—which city lies 10° west of Raqqa ¹⁶³)—he reduced the latter to his meridian of Raqqa, for which it must have occurred 1²/₃ hours after sunrise. Consequently, in a period of 743 Egyptian years, there were 178 days and 17³/₅ hours in excess ¹⁶⁴); while the quarter-days accumulate to 185³/₄ days. Since, therefore, 7 days and ²/₅ hours are missing, it appears that ¹/₁₀₆ is still missing from the ¹/₄ [day] ¹⁶⁵). He therefore divided the 7 days and ²/₅ hours by the number of years, 743, obtained 13 minutes and 36 seconds, and subtracted these from ¹/₄ day. According to this, he stated that the natural year contains 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes, and 24 seconds ¹⁶⁶). We also have observed the autumnal equinox in Frauenburg <note>Modern Frombork, Poland, where Copernicus lived</note>, specifically in the year 1515 after the birth of Christ on September 14th; that was, after Alexander's death, in the 1840th Egyptian year on the 6th of Phaophi, half an hour after sunrise ¹⁶⁶). But because Raqqa lies approximately 25° ¹⁶⁷) east of our region, which makes a difference of 2 hours less ¹/₃ hour, there were 633 Egyptian years and 153 days 6³/₄ hours between our equinox and that of Albategnius, instead of 158 days 6 hours ¹⁶⁸). From that Alexandrian observation of Ptolemy, however, up to the place and time of our observation, it is 1376 Egyptian years, 332 days, and ¹/₂ hour, for we are situated approximately one hour ¹⁶⁹) away from Alexandria. Thus, from Albategnius until our time, in 633 years, 5 days less 1¹/₄ hours fell away, which is one day in 128 years; but from Ptolemy, in 1376 years, approximately 12 days, which is one day in 115 years; the year has therefore resulted unequally in both periods. We also observed the vernal equinox, which occurred in the following year 1516 after the birth of Christ at 4¹/₃ hours after midnight on March 11th, and the time difference from that vernal equinox of Ptolemy—if one reduces the same from the meridian of Alexandria to ours—amounts to 1376 Egyptian years, 332 days, 16¹/₃ hours, whereby it simultaneously results that the intervals between the vernal and autumnal equinoxes are also unequal. However, much depends on the fact that the solar [year] obtained in this manner—

year remains constant. The fact that during the autumnal equinoxes <note>The point in September when day and night are of equal length.</note> between Ptolemy and our own time, as has been demonstrated, a uniform division into years shows a deficiency of 1/115 of a 1/4 day, does not agree with the equinox observed by Albategnius <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD), a significant Arab astronomer.</note> in Raqqa by half a day. Furthermore, the difference between Albategnius and us—according to which 1/128 of a 1/4 day must be missing—does not agree with Ptolemy; rather, the calculation yields more than a whole day too much compared to his observation of the equinox, and even more than two days too much compared to that of Hipparchus. If one likewise takes the interval from Ptolemy to Albategnius as a basis, the calculated equinox exceeds the one observed by Hipparchus by two days.

Therefore, it is more correct to derive the uniformity of the solar year from the fixed stars. This was first discovered by Thabit ibn Qurra <note>original: "Thebites, der Sohn Chora's"</note>, who determined its length to be 365 days + 15/60 + 23/3600 <note>equivalent to 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 12 seconds</note>; he likely started from the assumption that the year appears longer when the equinoxes and solstices retreat more slowly, and shorter when they move faster, and this in a specific proportion. This could only occur if the uniformity existed in relation to the sphere of the fixed stars. In this regard, one should therefore disregard Ptolemy, who absurdly and inappropriately believed that the annual uniformity of the Sun was measured by its return to any of the fixed stars, and that this was no better than if one related it to Jupiter or Saturn.

From this, the reason also emerges why the civil year was longer before Ptolemy, because after him it became shorter due to the increased precession <note>The slow "wobble" of the Earth's axis that changes the position of the stars over centuries.</note>. It is true that an error can also occur in the sidereal year <term>asteroterida</term> <note>The time it takes the Earth to orbit the Sun once relative to the fixed stars.</note>, yet it is only a slight one and much smaller than the one we have already demonstrated. This is because the apparent motion of the center of the Earth around the Sun is unequal due to another double variation. Of these variations, the first and simple one has an annual period; the other, which consists of the changing of the first, is not perceived immediately, but only after a great span of time.

Therefore, the calculation of the annual uniformity is neither simple nor easy to perceive. For if one wished to derive it simply from the known specific distance from any fixed star—which can be done with the help of the astrolabe and the Moon, as we explained regarding Regulus <note>original: "Basiliskus des Löwen"</note> in the Heart of the Lion (Book II, Chapter 14)—one would not entirely avoid an error, unless at that precise moment the Sun, due to the motion of the Earth, had either no prosthaphaeresis <term>prosthaphärese</term> <note>A technical term for the correction added or subtracted to account for the difference between mean and true planetary positions.</note>, or by chance an identical and equal one for both points in time. If this is not the case, and a difference in their inequality occurs, then no equal revolution will result in equal times. But if for both points in time the entire derived inequality is included in the calculation...

...is taken into account, the result will be accurate. The determination of the inequality itself requires a preliminary knowledge of the mean motion, which we therefore wish to seek out. But to finally arrive at the solution of this knot <note>The "knot" refers to the complex mathematical problem of planetary motion.</note>, we have found four causes for the appearing inequality. The first is the inequality of the precession of the equinoxes <note>original: "Vorrückens der Nachtgleichen"</note>, which we have already developed. The second is that by which the sun appears to traverse unequal arcs of the ecliptic in equal times, and this has almost an annual period. The third, which also changes this one, and which we shall call the second inequality. The fourth, finally, which changes the perihelion and aphelion <note>original: "Sonnennähe und Sonnenferne"; literally the sun-nearness and sun-distance</note> of the center of the earth, as will become clear further below. Of all these, only the second was known to Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer.</note>, which alone could not produce the annual inequality, but rather causes it in connection with the others. However, to show the difference between the uniform and the appearing solar year, no completely exact calculation of the year is necessary; rather, it suffices if we take 365¼ days as the magnitude of the year in our calculation, in which time the motion of the first inequality is completed, since that which amounts to so little in a whole circle completely disappears when related to a smaller magnitude. But for the sake of a better and easier arrangement of the presentation, we wish to place first the uniform motions of the annual revolution of the center of the earth, to which we then add the differences between the uniform and appearing motion in their required explanation.

# Chapter 14.
# On the uniform, mean motions in the revolution
# of the center of the earth.

If we therefore multiply 360° of a circle by 365 days, and divide the product by 365 days, 15 minutes, 24 seconds, 10 thirds: we obtain the motion in one Egyptian year as 5 times 60° + 59° 44' 49'' 7''' 4'''' <insert>172)</insert>. And the motion of 60 such years, omitting the whole circles, as 5 times 60° + 44° 49' 7'' 4'''' <insert>173)</insert>. If we again divide the annual motion by 365 days: we obtain the daily motion as 59' 8'' 11''' 22''''. # Chapter 15.
# Preliminary investigations into the development of the inequality in the apparent motion of the Sun.

In order to penetrate more deeply into the apparent inequality of the Sun, we wish to demonstrate even more clearly that—while the Earth orbits the Sun (which stands in the center of the universe) as if around a midpoint, and the distance between the Sun and the Earth is, as stated, vanishingly small compared to the immensity of the sphere of fixed stars—the Sun appears to move in the same way in relation to any point or star of that same sphere in the ecliptic <note>The ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere as seen from Earth.</note>. Let `ab` be a great circle in the plane of the ecliptic, its center being `c`, and let the Sun stand in this center. With the distance of the Sun from the Earth being `cd`, in comparison to which the extent of the universe is immeasurable, let the circle `de` be described in the same plane of the ecliptic, in which the annual motion of the center of the Earth is said to take place. I assert that in relation to any point assumed in the circle `ab` or to a star of the ecliptic, the Sun appears to move in the same way. Suppose the Sun is seen from the Earth, located at `d`, in the direction `acd` at point `a`. Let the Earth move in any way through the arc `de`, and from point `e` let `ae` and `be` be drawn. The Sun now appears, seen from `e`, at point `b`. But because `ac` is infinitely large compared to `cd`: then, since `ce` is equal to `cd`, `ac` is also infinitely large compared to `ce`. We assume any point `f` on `ac` and draw `ef`. Since the two straight lines drawn from the endpoints of the base `ce` to the point `a` fall outside the triangle `efc`: then, according to the converse of the 21st proposition of the first book of Euclid's Elements <note>Euclid's Elements was the standard textbook for geometry for centuries; Proposition 1.21 concerns the properties of lines drawn within a triangle to its base.</note>, the angle `fae` is smaller than the angle `efc`. Therefore, the lines extended to infinity finally enclose such an acute angle `cae` that it can no longer be perceived: and by this angle, the angle `bca` is larger than the angle `aec` <note>The original text reads "acc", likely a transcription error for "aec".</note>. Because of this so insignificant difference, these angles appear equal, and the lines `ac` and `ae` appear parallel; consequently, the Sun appears to move in relation to any arbitrary point of the sphere of fixed stars just as if it circled around the center `c`, which was to be proven. Its inequality, however, is demonstrated by the fact that the motion of the center of the Earth and its annual orbit are not exactly around the center—

point of the Sun occurs. This can very well be imagined in two ways: either by an **eccentric circle**, that is, one whose center is not that of the Sun, or by an **epicycle** <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one.</note>, in which the Sun itself stands at the center of the main circle. This is explained from the eccentric circle as follows. 

Let **abcd** be an eccentric circle in the plane of the **ecliptic** <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note>; let its center **e** lie at a not very small distance outside the center of the Sun and the world, which shall be **f**; let the diameter through both centers be **aefd**. Let the **apogee** <note>The point in orbit farthest from the center.</note>, which is called *summa absis* <note>original: "summa absis" (Latin); the highest arch or turning point.</note> by the Latins, lie at **a**, as the place most distant from the center of the world; **d**, on the other hand, shall be the **perigee** <note>The point in orbit closest to the center.</note>, which is called *infima absis* <note>original: "infima absis" (Latin); the lowest arch or turning point.</note> and is the place nearest to the center of the world. 

Now, if the Earth moves uniformly in its orbit **abcd** around the center **e**, then, as stated, the movement around **f** appears non-uniform. If one makes the arcs **ab** and **cd** equal and draws the straight lines **be**, **ce**, **bf**, **cf**; then the angles **aeb** and **ced**, to which equal arcs around the center **e** belong, are equal. However, the exterior angle **cfd** is larger than the interior angle **ced**, and thus also larger than the angle **aeb**, which is equal to **ced**. But the exterior angle **aeb** is also larger than the interior angle **afb**; all the more so is the angle **cfd** larger than **afb**. Yet each of the two is traversed in equal times, because the arcs **ab** and **cd** are equal to one another. The uniform movement around **e** thus appears non-uniform around **f**. 

The same can be seen even more simply from the fact that the arc **ab** lies further from **f** than **cd**. For, according to the 7th proposition of the 3rd book of **Euclid's Elements**, the lines **af** and **bf** are larger than **cf** and **df**, and as is proven in **optics**, equal magnitudes appear larger when near than when at a distance. Therefore, what was asserted about the eccentric circle is now clear. <insert>The proof would be exactly the same if the Earth stood still at **f** and the Sun moved in the circle **abc**, as with **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Roman astronomer who championed the geocentric model.</note> and others.</insert> 

The same can also be explained by the **epicycle**, in which the Sun stands in the center of its **deferent** <note>original: "Hauptkreis" (main circle); the large circle upon which the center of an epicycle moves.</note>. Namely, let **bcd** be the main circle, **e** the center of the world in which the Sun also stands, **a** the center of the epicycle **fg** in the same plane, and through both centers the line **ceaf** is drawn. Let the apogee of the epicycle be **f**, the perigee **i**. Thus it is evident that a uniformity in **a**, a...

produces the irregularity of the appearance in the epicycle <term>fg</term> <note>An epicycle is a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in pre-modern astronomy to explain planetary paths.</note>. For, if **a** moves toward the side of **b**, that is, in a direct motion <note>original: "rechtläufig" — moving in the standard direction of the zodiac.</note>, but the center of the Earth moves retrograde from the apogee <term>f</term> <note>Apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note>, then **e** appears to move more in the perigee <term>i</term> <note>Perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the center of motion.</note>, because both movements, from **a** as well as from **i**, lie toward the same side. In the apogee **f**, however, the point **e** appears to be slower, because it moves only with the difference of the two opposing movements; and, if the Earth is assumed to be at **g**, it precedes the uniform motion, but at **k** it lags behind it, and indeed in each of the two cases by the arcs **ag** and **ak**, whereby the Sun also appears to move irregularly. Everything that occurs through the epicycle can be conditioned in the same way by the eccentric circle, which the movement of the celestial body in the epicycle describes uniformly in relation to the actual center and in the same plane, and whose eccentric center stands apart from the actual center by the magnitude of the radius of the epicycle; and this can happen in three ways. Namely, if the epicycle on the main circle and the celestial body in the epicycle complete equal revolutions, but the movements are opposite to one another: then a fixed eccentric circle, whose apogee and perigee occupy unchanging places, represents the movements of the celestial body. Let **abc** be the main circle, the center of the world **d**, the diameter **adc**; we assume that, while the epicycle were at **a**, the celestial body would stand in the apogee of the epicycle, thus at **g**, and its radius would fall in the straight line **dag**; we take from the center **b** the arc **ab** of the main circle, and let the arc **ef** be described in the epicycle with an equal rotation of **ag**, place **de** and **eb** in a straight line, and take the arc **ef** toward the opposite side and similar to the arc **ab**. The celestial body

or the Earth stands at **f**. We connect **b** with **f**, and take on the line **ad** the segment **dk** equal to **bf**. Now because the angles **ebf** and **bda** are equal: **bf** and **dk** are parallel and equal. But if straight lines are connected by equal and parallel straight lines: they are themselves parallel and equal, according to the 33rd proposition of the first book of Euclid's Elements <note>A reference to the foundational Greek mathematical work by Euclid of Alexandria.</note>. And because **d** and **ag** are made equal, one obtains, if one adds **ak** to both, **gak** equal to **akd**, and thus also equal to **kf**. The circle described around the center **k** with the radius **kag** thus passes through **f**, and the point **f** describes this circle through the movement composed of **ab** and **ef**, as an eccentric circle, equal to the main circle, which therefore also remains fixed. For if the epicycle makes equal revolutions with the main circle: it is necessary that the apsides <note>original: "Absiden" — the points of greatest or least distance in an orbit.</note> of the eccentric circle so described lie at the same place.

remain. But if the center of the epicycle and its periphery make unequal revolutions, then the movement of the celestial body will no longer describe a fixed eccentric circle, but rather one whose center and <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit where the celestial body is either closest to (perigee) or farthest from (apogee) the center of its system.</note> move in a <term>retrograde</term> <note>Appearing to move backward or opposite to the standard direction of the zodiac.</note> or <term>direct</term> <note>Moving in the standard direction of the zodiac; also called prograde.</note> fashion, depending on whether the movement of the celestial body is faster or slower than the center of its epicycle. Let *ebf* be greater than the angle *bda*, but equal to *bdm*: so it is likewise proven that if on the line *dm*, *dl* is taken equal to *bf*, the circle described around the center *l* with the radius *lmn* equal to *ad* passes through the celestial body *f*, whereby it becomes evident that through the composite movement of the celestial body, the arc *nf* of an eccentric circle is described, whose apogee has meanwhile traversed the arc *gn* in a retrograde direction from point *g*. Conversely, if the movement of the celestial body on the epicycle had been slower, the center of the eccentric circle would have moved in a direct fashion, and indeed by as much as the center of the epicycle had moved faster—as would obviously occur, for example, if the angle *ebf* were smaller than *bda* but equal to *bdm*, as I have asserted.

From all of this, it follows that the same inequality of appearance is always produced, whether by the epicycle on the main circle, or by an eccentric circle equal to the main circle, and that both do not differ from one another if only the distance of the centers is equal to the radius of the epicycle. Which of the two actually occurs in the heavens is therefore not easy to determine. Ptolemy <note>original: "Ptolemäus" — the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model dominated for over a millennium.</note> was of the opinion that where a single inequality and fixed, unchangeable locations of the apsides (as he suspected in the case of the Sun) are perceived, the justification through eccentricity is sufficient; however, for the Moon and the other five planets, which move with double or multiple inequalities, he assigned eccentric epicycles. 

Furthermore, using the method of the eccentric circle, it can easily be shown that the greatest difference between the uniform movement and the appearing movement occurs when the celestial body appears in the middle location between the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center.</note> and the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the center.</note>; according to the method of the epicycle, this is the case when the celestial body intersects the main circle, as has been proven in Ptolemy's work. This is proven through the eccentric circle as follows: Let *abcd* be a circle around the center *e*, its diameter *aec* passes through the Sun at *f* outside of the center. Let the line *bfd* be drawn perpendicularly through *f*, and let *be* and *ed* also be drawn.

<meta>This page concludes the geometric demonstration regarding the maximum difference between uniform and apparent motion and begins Chapter 16, applying these principles to the Sun's orbit as observed by Ptolemy and later astronomers.</meta>

Let the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit where a celestial body is at its greatest distance from the center of motion.</note> be $a$, the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit where a celestial body is at its closest distance to the center of motion.</note> $c$ — let $b$ and $d$ be the middle apparent positions. It is evident that the exterior angle $aeb$ represents the uniform motion, the interior angle $efb$ represents the apparent motion, and the difference between the two is the angle $ebf$. I assert that no greater peripheral angle than those at $b$ and $d$ can be constructed over the line $ef$. Let us take points $g$ and $h$ before and after $b$, and draw $gd, ge, gf$ and $hc, hf, hd$. Now, since $fg$ is closer to the center and therefore larger than $df$, the angle $gdf$ is greater than $dgf$. However, the angles $edg$ and $egd$ are equal, because $eg$ and $ed$ are equal sides <note>radii of the same circle</note>. Therefore, the angle $edb$, which is equal to $ebf$, is also greater than the angle $egf$. Likewise, $df$ is also greater than $fh$. The angle $fhd$ is greater than $fdh$, but the whole angle $ehd$ is equal to the whole angle $edh$, because $eh$ and $ed$ are equal; therefore, the remainder $edf$, which is equal to $ebf$, must also be greater than $ehf$. Therefore, a larger angle can nowhere be constructed over the line $ef$ than at points $b$ and $d$. Consequently, the greatest difference between uniform and apparent motion occurs at the middle position between the apogee and perigee.

### Chapter 16.

#### On the Apparent Inequality of the Sun.

This has been proven generally, and it can be adapted not only to the appearances of the Sun but also to the <term>inequalities</term> <note>In astronomy, "inequality" refers to the variations or irregularities in the speed or position of a celestial body compared to a perfectly uniform circular motion.</note> of other stars. Now we wish to treat that which is peculiar to the Sun and the Earth; and indeed, first that which we have received as handed down from Ptolemy and other predecessors, and then what more recent times and experience have taught us. Ptolemy $^{177)}$ found that between the <term>vernal equinox</term> <note>The moment in spring when day and night are of equal length.</note> and the solstice there were $94\frac{1}{2}$ days, and between the solstice and the <term>autumnal equinox</term> <note>The moment in autumn when day and night are of equal length.</note> there were $92\frac{1}{2}$ days. Thus, in proportion to the time, the mean uniform motion in the first period was $93^\circ$ $9'$, and in the second $91^\circ$ $10'^{178)}$. Let the circle of the year,

divided in this way, be $abcd$, with its center at $e$. For the first period, let $ab$ be taken equal to $93^\circ$ $9'$, and for the second, $bc$ equal to $91^\circ$ $10'$. From $a$, the Sun appears at the point of the vernal equinox; from $b$, at the summer solstice; from $c$, at the autumnal equinox; and finally from $d$, at the winter solstice. Let $ac$ and $bd$ be drawn; let these intersect each other at right angles at $f$, where we shall place the Sun. Now, because the arc $abc$ is greater
