Now, through the center *e*, draw the straight line *ieg* parallel to *afc*, which intersects *bfd* at *l*; and draw the straight line *hek* parallel to *bfd*, which intersects *af* at *m*. In this way, the right-angled parallelogram *lemf* is formed, whose diagonal *fe*, in its extension *fen*, indicates the greatest distance of the Earth from the Sun, and designates point *n* as the location of the apogee. Since the arc *abc* measures 184° 19', *ah* contains 92° 9 1/2'; when this is subtracted from *agb*, the remainder *hb* is 59'. If one again subtracts the <term>quadrant</term> <note>A quarter of a circle, or 90 degrees.</note> *hg* from *ah*, the remainder *ag* equals 2° 10'. The half-chord of the double arc *ag* <note>In modern trigonometry, this is equivalent to the sine of the angle.</note> consists of 377 units, of which 10,000 make up the radius, and this is equal to *lf*. The half-chord of the double arc *bh*, namely *cl*, contains 172 such units. From the two given sides of the triangle *clf*, the <term>hypotenuse</term> *ef* is found to be 414, approximately the 24th part of the radius *ne*. However, as *ef* relates to *cl*, so the radius *ne* relates to the half-chord of the double arc *nh*. Consequently, the arc *hn* is found to be 24 1/2°, and the angle *neh* is the same amount, to which the appearing angle *lfe* is again equal. By this distance, therefore, the apogee preceded the summer solstice in Ptolemy's time.

But since *ik* is a quadrant of the circle, if one subtracts *ic* and *dk* (which are equal to *ag* and *hb*), there remains *cd* equal to 86° 51'; and the remainder of *cda*, namely *da*, equals 88° 49'. Now, 86° 51' corresponds to 88 1/8 days, and 88° 49' corresponds to 90 1/8 days, or 3 hours; these are the times in which the Sun, given the uniform motion of the Earth, appeared to pass from the autumnal equinox to the winter solstice, and from the winter solstice to the vernal equinox. Ptolemy testifies that he found this no differently than it had been handed down before him by Hipparchus. Therefore, he concluded that for all succeeding time, the apogee would eternally remain 24 1/2° ahead of the summer solstice, and the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> would amount to the 24th part of the radius, as stated.

Both of these values, however, are now found to have changed by a considerable difference. **Albategnius** <note>Also known as Al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD), a pioneering Arab astronomer.</note> records 93 days 35' from the vernal equinox to the summer solstice, and 186 days 37' to the autumnal equinox^179), from which, according to Ptolemy's rule, he determined the eccentricity to be no more than 347 units (where 10,000 make up the radius). The Spaniard **Arzachael** <note>Also known as Al-Zarqali (1028–1087 AD), an influential Arab mathematician and astronomer from Córdoba.</note> agrees with him regarding the eccentricity, yet the latter gives the apogee as 12° 10' before the solstice, while Albategnius found it to be 7° 43'^180) before the solstice. From this, it is to be inferred that there is yet another inequality in the movement of the center of the Earth, which is also confirmed by the observations of our own time. For in the more than 10 years during which we have applied ourselves to the investigation of these matters, and specifically in the year of Christ 1515, we have found that from

# Chapter 17.
## **Presentation of the first annual inequality of the Sun along with its specific variations.**

Since several different inequalities <note>In this context, "inequality" refers to the observed irregularity or variation in the speed of the Sun's movement across the sky.</note> of the Sun are found, we believe we must first derive that which has an annual course and is more well-known than the others. For this purpose, we again take the circle *abc* around the center *e*, with the diameter *aec*; let the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the center of motion.</note> be *a*, the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the orbit closest to the center of motion.</note> be *c*, and the Sun be at *d*. Now it is proven that the difference between the uniform and the apparent motion is greatest at the apparent middle location between the two <term>apsides</term> <note>The two extreme points—apogee and perigee—of an elliptical or eccentric orbit.</note>. Let us erect at *d* a perpendicular line *bd* against *aec*, which intersects the circumference at point *b*, and draw the line *be*. Since in the right-angled triangle *bde* two sides are given—namely *be* as the radius of the circle, and *de* as the distance of the Sun from the center—the angle *dbe* is also given. This is the amount by which the angle of uniform motion *bea* differs from the apparent right angle *edb*.

However, as the distance *de* becomes larger or smaller, the entire shape of the triangle changes accordingly. Thus, before Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model dominated for over a millennium.</note>, the angle *b* was 2° 23′; in the time of Albategnius <note>The Latinized name for Al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD), a private astronomer whose observations were highly accurate for the Middle Ages.</note> and Arzachel <note>The Latinized name for Al-Zarqali (1029–1087 AD), a leading Arab mathematician and astronomer from Al-Andalus.</note>, it was 1° 59′; now, however, it is 1° 51′. Ptolemy found the arc *ab*, which the angle *aeb* encloses, to be 92° 23′, and *bc* to be 87° 37′. Albategnius found *ab* to be 91° 59′ and *bc* to be 88° 1′. Now *ab* is equal to 91° 51′ and *bc* is 88° 9′. From this, the other variations also follow. These differences must change, as already noted, whenever the side *ed* changes.

# Chapter 20.

## On the Second and Double Inequality of the Sun, Which Occurs Due to the Change of the Apsides.

A greater difficulty lies in the instability of the <term>apsides</term> <note>The "apsides" (singular: apsis) are the two points in an orbit where the celestial body is either closest to (perigee) or farthest from (apogee) the center of its system.</note> of the Sun. Ptolemy considered them to be fixed; others believed that their change followed from the motion of the sphere of the fixed stars, which led them to assume that the fixed stars moved as well. <term>Arzachel</term> <note>An 11th-century Arab astronomer from Muslim Spain, also known as Al-Zarqali.</note> was of the opinion that this motion was also uneven, so that it could even become retrograde <note>Moving backward relative to the stars.</note>. He concluded this because <term>Albategnius</term> <note>A 9th-century Arab astronomer also known as Al-Battani, whose work was a cornerstone for European astronomy.</note>, as previously mentioned <note>Reference 205</note>, had found the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the center.</note> to be 7º 43' ahead of the solstice. This meant it had advanced approximately 17º <note>Reference 206</note> in about 740 years from the time of Ptolemy; however, in the course of 193 years <note>Original: "200 less 7 years."</note> after that, it seemed to have regressed about 4 1/2º. And therefore he thought there was another motion of the center of the annual orbit, moving in a small circle, by which the apogee moved forward and backward, and simultaneously the distances between the center of that orbit and the center of the world changed. This was indeed a beautiful invention, but nonetheless unacceptable because it cannot be reconciled with the rest of the system as a whole. 

For if the course of this motion is considered sequentially—that it stood still for a time before Ptolemy, then advanced about 17º in 740 years, and then regressed 4 or 5º in 200 years, while in the remaining time until our own it has advanced, all while no further regression or more standstills have been noted during the entire period (which must necessarily occur in opposing motions)—this can in no way be derived from a regular and circular motion. Therefore, many suspect that some error occurred in those observations of the apsides. Both mathematicians are equal in zeal and diligence, so that it is doubtful whom we should rather follow. I confess that nowhere is there a greater difficulty than in observing the Sun's apogee, in which large values must be calculated from the smallest and barely perceptible ones. Since in the region of the perigee and the apogee, a whole degree of <term>prosthaphairesis</term> <note>A technical term from Greek meaning "addition or subtraction." It is the correction value used to adjust the "mean" or average position of a planet to find its "true" observed position.</note> results in a change of only 2 minutes; whereas in the region of the middle distances, 5 to 6 degrees correspond to a single minute: thus a small error can increase to a monstrous degree. Therefore, when we set the apogee at 6 2/3º of the...

# Chapter 25.

## On the Calculation of the Apparent Motion of the Sun.

From this, I believe, it is now sufficiently clear in what manner the apparent position of the Sun is calculated for any given time. Specifically, for any chosen moment, one must find the true position of the vernal equinox <note>The point in the sky where the sun crosses the celestial equator in spring, marking the start of the astronomical year</note>, or its precession along with its first simple anomaly, as we have explained previously<gloss>232)</gloss>. Next, one must find the simple mean motion of the center of the Earth—which, if one prefers, can also be called the motion of the Sun—and the annual anomaly from the tables of uniform motions; these are then added to their established starting points. 

Using the first simple anomaly, after looking up its value (or the value closest to it) in the first or second column of the preceding table, one finds the corresponding <term>prosthaphaeresis</term> <note>from the Greek for "addition and subtraction"; a correction value used to convert "mean" or average motion into "true" observed motion</note> of the annual anomaly in the third column, and notes down the following proportional minutes. This prosthaphaeresis is added to the annual anomaly if the first anomaly is less than a semicircle (or if its value is found in the first column); otherwise, it is subtracted from it. 

This sum or difference results in the adjusted anomaly of the Sun. By using this value, one again finds the prosthaphaeresis of the annual orbit in the fifth column, along with the subsequent "excess" value. If this excess, when divided by the previously noted proportional minutes, yields a significant quotient, this quotient is added to the last prosthaphaeresis. This process corrects the prosthaphaeresis, which is then subtracted from the mean position of the Sun if the value of the annual anomaly is in the first column or is less than a semicircle; conversely, it is added to the mean position if the anomaly is larger or stands in the second column. 

The difference or sum obtained in this way determines the true position of the Sun, measured from the first star of Aries <note>The traditional fixed starting point for the zodiac in ancient and Renaissance astronomy</note>. Finally, if the true precession of the vernal equinox is added to this, one immediately obtains the position relative to the equinox point in one of the twelve signs and in degrees of the circle's signs. 

If one wishes to proceed differently, they may take the uniform composite motion instead of the simple motion and perform the rest as described, except that instead of the precession of the equinoxes, one only adds or subtracts their prosthaphaeresis as the circumstances require. Thus, the calculation of the Sun’s apparent position from the motion of the Earth is established, agreeing with both ancient and modern observations; it is all the more certain that one can use this method to predict positions for the future. 

However, we also do not wish to leave unmentioned that if someone should think that the center of the annual revolution stands fixed as the center of the world, while the Sun is movable and follows two motions similar and equal to those which...

## Chapter 26.
### On the <term>Nychthemeron</term> <note>from the Greek for "night-day"; a full 24-hour period</note>, that is, on the Inequality of the Natural Day.

Regarding the Sun, it still remains to say something about the inequality of the natural day. By this time, we mean the duration of 24 equal hours, which we have used until now as the common and reliable measure of heavenly motions. Some define such a day as the time lying between two sunrises, such as the Chaldeans <note>an ancient people of Mesopotamia famous for their early astronomical records</note> and the Jews of antiquity; others as the time between two sunsets, such as the Athenians; others as the time from midnight to midnight, such as the Romans; and others as the time from noon to noon, such as the Egyptians. 

It is clear, however, that during this time the actual rotation of the Earth's globe is completed, including that which is added in the meantime by the annual motion in relation to the apparent motion of the Sun. But that this increase is unequal is proven mainly by the unequal apparent course of the Sun, and furthermore by the fact that the natural day depends on the rotation around the poles of the <term>equator</term>, while the annual motion takes place in the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>the sun's apparent path across the sky throughout the year</note>. Therefore, this apparent time cannot be a common and reliable measure of motion, since neither the days nor their parts remain unchanged and equal; and for that reason, it was practical to derive a "mean" <note>average or standardized</note> uniform day from the natural one, through which the uniformity of motion can undoubtedly be measured. Since 365 rotations around the poles of the Earth take place in the course of a entire year, and nearly one whole extra rotation is added to these through the daily increase caused by the Sun's apparent advancement: it follows that the 365th part of this total is what constitutes the natural day. Therefore, they have...

...we must separate and distinguish the uniform day from the apparently unequal one. The difference between these days, although slight, is not immediately noticed, but through accumulation over several days, it grows until it becomes perceptible. 

There are two causes for this difference: partly the inequality of the Sun's apparent motion, and partly the unequal <term>ascension</term> <note>The way different parts of the Sun's path rise over the horizon</note> caused by the tilt of the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky over the course of a year</note>. However, in the second cause—which depends on rising and setting—the greatest difference occurs between the semicircles of the two <term>solstices</term>. This difference also prevails between the shortest and longest days; it is highly variable and unique to each individual region. But the difference that depends on noon or midnight is always determined by four limits. Thus, 5° of the Equator are missing in one instance, while in the other, there are just as many in excess. 

The days contained in the first section exceed those of the second section by 10° of the Equator, which equals ⅔ of an hour. This also applies in the other semicircle in the regions between the limits diametrically opposite to those. The difference relating to the meridian, however, is the same everywhere and is simpler. The method for deriving uniform (mean) time from the unequal appearing (solar) time, so that all inequalities are accounted for, is as follows: 
When a specific time is given, one must find two points: the "mean" position of the Sun (calculated from the spring equinox using its average uniform motion, which we call "composite" motion) and the true "appearing" position of the Sun (calculated from the actual equinox). This must be done for both the beginning and the end of the time period in question. Furthermore, one must observe how many time-degrees have passed past the <term>meridian</term> <note>The imaginary north-south line in the sky used to mark noon</note> at noon or midnight, and the distance between the first and second true positions. 

If the number of degrees between the two "mean" positions is the same as the "true" positions, the given apparent time is equal to the uniform time. If, however, the number of time-degrees is greater, one adds the excess to the given time; if it is smaller, one subtracts the difference from the apparent time. By doing this, we obtain the sum or difference in converted uniform time, where we count each time-degree as 1/60th of an hour (or 10/60ths of a sixtieth of a day). If, conversely, a mean time were given and one wished to know the corresponding apparent time, one would follow this procedure in reverse.

# Nicolaus Copernicus: On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres <note>original: "Nicolaus Copernicus' Kreisbewegungen"</note>

## Book Four

After we have explained, as far as our modest ability allowed, the phenomena that occur because of the Earth's movement around the Sun; and since it is now our task to derive the movements of all the <term>wandering stars</term> <note>In the 16th century, the term "wandering stars" or "planets" included the Sun and Moon, as they appeared to move against the backdrop of the fixed stars.</note> from that same cause: let the course of the Moon now be discussed. This is because it is through the Moon—which participates in both the day and the night—that the positions of the stars are chiefly measured and investigated. Furthermore, of all the heavenly bodies, it alone refers its movements (which are also irregular) entirely to the center of the Earth and is most closely related to the Earth. Consequently, one notices nothing of the Earth’s movement in the Moon’s behavior, except perhaps for the daily rotation. For this reason, people were all the more convinced that the Earth was the center of the universe and the common center of all celestial movements. In deriving the Moon’s path, insofar as it travels around the Earth, we shall not depart from the opinions of the Ancients; however, we must introduce several other points which we have not received from the Ancients, which are more consistent, and by which we may establish the lunar movement with as much certainty as possible.

### Chapter 1.

### The Hypotheses of the Lunar Circles according to the View of the Ancients.

The motion of the Moon has the peculiar characteristic that it does not describe the middle circle of the signs <note>The "middle circle of the signs" refers to the ecliptic, the apparent path of the Sun.</note>, but rather its own inclined circle, which divides the former into two equal halves and is itself intersected by it, whereby the Moon passes into both latitudes <note>The "latitudes" here refer to the Moon's north and south deviation from the ecliptic path.</note>. This behaves almost like the <term>solstices</term> <note>The points where the Sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky at noon, marking the longest and shortest days.</note> during the annual movement, so that what the year is for the Sun, the month is for the Moon. The intersection points with the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; the plane of Earth's orbit.</note> are called <term>nodes</term> by some, and the <term>conjunctions</term> <note>When the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun (New Moon).</note> and <term>oppositions</term> <note>When the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon (Full Moon).</note> of the Sun and Moon are called "ecliptic" when they coincide with these nodes; there are no other points for both circles—

<meta>This page continues Chapter 1 of Book Four, describing the traditional Ptolemaic model of the Moon's orbit. The previous page introduced the Moon as the celestial body closest to Earth and began discussing the geometry of its movement.</meta>

points in common, and it is at these points that solar and lunar eclipses can occur. At all other points, the <term>inclination</term> <note>The tilt of the Moon's orbit relative to the Earth's orbit around the Sun (the ecliptic).</note> of the Moon causes the bodies to pass one another without an eclipse or occultation. This oblique lunar orbit, along with its four principal points, moves uniformly around the center of the Earth at a rate of approximately 3' <note>three arc-minutes</note> per day, completing a full revolution in 19 years. Within this path and plane, the Moon is observed to move always in <term>direct motion</term> <note>meaning from west to east, the same direction as the other planets</note>, though its speed varies from very slow to very fast. Specifically, it moves slower the further it is from the Earth, and faster the closer it is; this variation was easier to detect in the Moon than in any other celestial body because of its proximity. Therefore, it was assumed that this was caused by an <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one.</note>: as the Moon traveled along this small circle, its uniform motion would appear slower in the upper arc and faster in the lower arc.

It has been demonstrated that what occurs via an epicycle can also be explained by an <term>eccentric circle</term> <note>original: "excentrischen Kreis". An eccentric circle is one where the Earth is not at the exact center.</note> <note>reference 238: This refers to Copernicus’s earlier mathematical proof in Book III, where he shows the geometric equivalence of epicyclic and eccentric models.</note>. The epicycle was preferred, however, because the Moon seemed to possess a double inequality. Specifically, when the Moon was at the highest or lowest <term>apsis</term> <note>The points of greatest or least distance from the Earth.</note> of the epicycle, no deviation from uniform motion appeared. Yet at the intersection points of the epicycle, the deviation did not always appear the same way; it was significantly greater during the <term>quadratures</term> <note>The first and last quarter moons.</note> of the waxing or waning Moon than when it was full or new, and this occurred in a fixed and regular sequence. For this reason, it was assumed that the circle upon which the epicycle moved did not share a center with the Earth. Instead, they posited that the Moon moved in an eccentric epicycle according to this law: at every <term>opposition</term> <note>Full Moon</note> and <term>conjunction</term> <note>New Moon</note> of the Sun and Moon, the epicycle stands at the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point furthest from Earth.</note> of the eccentric circle, while during the intervening quadratures, it stands at the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point closest to Earth.</note>.

They imagined, therefore, that two equal and opposite motions took place around the center of the Earth: the epicycle moved in direct motion while the center of the eccentric circle (or its apsides) moved in <term>retrograde</term> <note>backward or westward</note> motion, while the line of the mean position of the Sun always remained exactly between the two. In this way, the epicycle would traverse the eccentric circle twice every month.

Now, suppose the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Earth.</note> of the eccentric circle moves in <term>retrograde</term> <note>original: "rückläufig"; motion in the opposite direction of the zodiac, from east to west.</note>, while the epicycle moves in <term>direct motion</term> <note>original: "rechtläufig"; motion following the order of the zodiacal signs, from west to east.</note>. The epicycle then becomes <term>perigeal</term> <note>original: "perigeisch"; at its closest point to Earth.</note> in the eccentric circle, as at point *g*. Having come closer to the Earth, it produces greater variations in irregularity. Indeed, when equal magnitudes are at unequal distances, those closer to the eye appear larger. These variations were smallest when the epicycle stood at *a*, and largest at *g*, because the ratio of the diameter of the epicycle *mn* to the line *ae* is the smallest of all, and to *ge* is the largest of all. This is because *ge* is the shortest line, while *ae* (equal to *de*) is the longest of all lines that can be drawn from the center of the Earth to the eccentric circle.

## Chapter 2.
### Regarding the Weakness of these Assumptions.

The ancients <gloss>239)</gloss> <note>This likely refers to Ptolemy's Almagest.</note> truly accepted such a combination of circles as corresponding to the appearances of the Moon. But if we consider this subject more carefully, we will find the <term>hypothesis</term> to be neither appropriate nor sufficient, as we can prove through calculation and observation. For while it is acknowledged that the motion of the center of the epicycle around the center of the Earth is uniform, one must simultaneously admit that this same motion is non-uniform in the circle which it actually describes. If, for example, one assumes the angle *aeb* to be 45º (or half a right angle), and *aed* to be equal to it, so that the entire *bed* is a right angle; and if one places the center of the epicycle at *g* and draws line *gf*: it is clear that the exterior angle *gfd* is larger than the opposite interior angle *gef*. Consequently, the unequal arcs *dab* and *dg* are both described in the same amount of time. Since *dab* is a quadrant, *dg*—which the center of the epicycle has described in the meantime—would have to be larger than a quadrant. But it stood...

<meta>This page continues the technical critique of the lunar model (likely the Ptolemaic system) described on the previous page. ...established that at the <term>quadrature</term> <note>The points in the lunar cycle—the first and third quarters—where the Moon is 90 degrees from the Sun.</note> of the Moon, each of the two arcs, **dab** and **dg**, is a semicircle: consequently, the movement of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one.</note> on the eccentric circle which it describes is non-uniform. But if this were so, what should we say to the principle that the motion of the heavenly bodies is uniform, even when it appears non-uniform? If the movement of the epicycle were to appear uniform, it would in fact have to be non-uniform; thus, the exact opposite of the established and accepted principle would occur. If, however, one were to object that the center of the epicycle moves uniformly around the center of the Earth, and that this is sufficient to preserve uniformity, we would ask: how can that uniformity be transferred to another circle, since its motion does not take place in that circle, but in the eccentric one?

Likewise, it rightly causes us wonder that they wish to have the uniformity of the Moon itself in its epicycle recognized not in relation to the center of the Earth—that is, through the line **egm**, with which the uniformity should properly be associated since it aligns with the center of the epicycle—but rather in relation to some other arbitrary point. They claim that the Earth stands in the middle between this point and the center of the eccentric circle, and that the line **igh** serves as a sort of index of the Moon's uniformity within the epicycle. This, too, is in fact sufficient to prove this motion to be non-uniform. The phenomena which partly follow from this hypothesis force this admission. We might just as well investigate how the argument would turn out if, while the Moon traversed its epicycle non-uniformly, we wished to explain the non-uniform appearance through the non-uniform motion. What else would we be doing but providing a handle to those who disparage our science? 

Furthermore, experience and even observation teach us that the <term>parallaxes</term> of the Moon, which the calculation of those circles yields, do not harmonize with the facts. For the parallaxes, which are called <term>commutations</term> <note>original: "Commutationen"; an old astronomical term for parallax, the apparent shift in a body's position when viewed from different locations.</note>, arise from the very noticeable size of the Earth compared to the distance of the Moon. Specifically, if one draws straight lines from the surface and from the center of the Earth to the Moon, they will not appear parallel, but will intersect at a noticeable angle within the body of the Moon. This must necessarily cause a difference in the appearance of the Moon, so that it appears in a different place to those who observe it from the Earth's surface at an oblique angle than to those who see it from the center—that is, at their <term>zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly overhead.</note>. These commutations vary according to the distance of the Moon from the Earth. According to the consensus of all mathematicians, the greatest distance is 64 1/6 Earth radii; however, according to the measurement of those men [the ancients], the smallest distance would have to be 33 11/20, so that the Moon [would be] at nearly half the distance...

...approached us more closely, and by logical conclusion, the <term>parallax</term> <note>The displacement in the apparent position of the Moon when viewed from different points on Earth; it is used to calculate distance.</note> at the smallest and greatest distances would have to differ from one another by approximately double. We see, however, that the parallaxes corresponding to the <term>quadratures</term> <note>The points when the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun (the quarter moons).</note> of the waxing and waning Moon—even at the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the Moon's orbit where it is closest to the Earth.</note> of the <term>epicycle</term>—differ very little or not at all from those that occur during solar and lunar eclipses, as we shall sufficiently prove in the proper place. The error is most clearly proven by the body of the Moon itself, which, for the same reason, would have to be seen as twice as large or twice as small in its diameter. But since circles relate to one another as the squares of their diameters, the Moon would have to appear four times as large when it stands closest to the Earth in its quadratures than when it is full in its opposition with the Sun; and when it shone with only its half-light, it would nonetheless have to shine twice as brightly as when it was full. If someone, even though the contrary is clear in itself, still wished not to be satisfied with the evidence of his own eyes, but to investigate this through the <term>Hipparchan Diopter</term> <note>An ancient observational instrument used to measure the angular diameter of the Sun and Moon, named after the astronomer Hipparchus.</note> or other instruments by which the diameter of the Moon is measured, he would find that the diameter only differs by as much as the epicycle requires, without that eccentric circle. For this reason, <note>Menelaus of Alexandria and Timochares of Alexandria were Greek astronomers whose observations of lunar occultations of stars provided long-term data for later scientists.</note> Menelaus and Timochares, in their investigations of the fixed stars using the position of the Moon, did not hesitate to always apply the same diameter for the Moon—namely, half of a degree—since the Moon usually appears to occupy that much space.

## Chapter 3.

### Another view of the movement of the Moon.

It seems, then, that the circle through which the epicycle appears larger or smaller is not an eccentric one, but belongs to another kind of circles. Let **ab** be an epicycle, which we shall call the first and larger one, and its center **c**; from the center of the Earth, which lies at **d**, let the straight line **dc** be extended to the highest <term>apside</term> <note>Also called an apogee; the point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion.</note> **a** of the epicycle. Around this point **a**, let another smaller epicycle **ef** be described; and let all of this lie in the same plane as the slanted lunar orbit. Let **c** move in a <term>prograde</term> <note>Moving in the "forward" direction of the zodiac (west to east).</note> direction, while **a** moves <term>retrograde</term> <note>Moving in the "backward" direction (east to west).</note>, and the Moon moves from **f** in the upper part of **ef** in a prograde direction again; and this is according to the rule that, while the line **dc** coincides with the mean position of the Sun, the Moon is always closest to the center **c** (that is, it is at **e**), whereas in the quadratures it is furthest away, at **f**. If one takes this as a basis, I maintain that the lunar phenomena stand in harmony with it. For it follows that the Moon traverses the small epicycle **ef** twice in one month, in which time **c** returns once to the Sun; and the New...

<meta>This page continues the author’s explanation of his revised lunar model. Having previously critiqued the Ptolemaic model for making the Moon appear too large at certain points in its orbit, the author now demonstrates how his system of epicycles accounts for the Moon's observed diameter and movement more accurately.</meta>

...and full moon appear to describe the smallest circle, the <term>radius</term> <note>The distance from the center of a circle to its edge.</note> of which is **ce**, while the first and last quarters describe the largest circle, with the radius **cf**. Thus, through these similar but unequal arcs around the center **c**, the Moon produces the smallest differences between its uniform movement and its observed appearance in the former case, and the greatest differences in the latter. 

Since the center **c** of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in pre-modern astronomy to explain complex planetary paths.</note> always remains on the circle <term>homocentric</term> <note>Sharing the same center; here, a circle centered exactly on the Earth.</note> with the Earth, it does not cause wildly varying <term>parallaxes</term> <note>The apparent shift in an object's position when viewed from different locations; used here to measure distance from the Earth.</note>, but only those that correspond to the epicycle itself. This immediately provides the reason why the body of the Moon appears to remain roughly the same size, along with all the other phenomena observed in the Moon's course. We intend to demonstrate these points one by one from our assumption; nevertheless, the same results can also be achieved using <term>eccentric circles</term> <note>Circles whose center is offset from the Earth, rather than centered directly upon it.</note>, provided the necessary proportions are observed, just as we did with the Sun. 

However, we wish to begin with the uniform motions, as we have done before; for without these, the non-uniform motions cannot be understood. Here, a great difficulty arises because of the previously mentioned parallax; for because of it, the position of the Moon cannot be accurately observed using <term>astrolabes</term> <note>An ancient instrument used to measure the altitudes of celestial bodies and solve problems in astronomy and navigation.</note> or other instruments. 

But the kindness of Nature has also anticipated human desires in this regard, so that the position of the Moon can be found more reliably than through the use of instruments, and free from the suspicion of error, through its <term>eclipses</term>. For while the entire rest of the world is bright and filled with daylight, night consists of nothing other than the shadow of the Earth, which rises in a conical shape and ends in a point; so that the Moon, when it enters this shadow, is darkened. When it has arrived in the middle of the shadow, it is clear that it stands in the position exactly opposite the Sun. 

The <term>solar eclipses</term>, however, which are caused by the intervention of the Moon, provide no reliable proof of the Moon's position. For in those cases, it happens that we see a <term>conjunction</term> <note>An alignment where two celestial bodies appear in the same place in the sky.</note> of the Sun and the Moon which, in relation to the center of the Earth, has either already passed or has not yet occurred, precisely because of the discussed parallax. This is why we do not see the same solar eclipse as being equal in size and duration in all countries, nor similar in its phases. In <term>lunar eclipses</term>, however, no such obstacle occurs; they are the same everywhere, because the axis of the Earth’s darkening shadow is in the direction...

## Chapter 4.

**On the Lunar Cycles and Their Particular Movements.**

Among the ancients who were concerned with passing down numerical data on this subject to posterity, we find Meton the Athenian, who flourished around the thirty-seventh <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used by the Ancient Greeks as a calendar system; the 37th Olympiad would be around 630 BCE, though Meton actually lived later, around 432 BCE.</note>. He stated that in 19 solar years, 235 months pass; for this reason, this great year is called the Metonic <term>Enneadekateris</term> <note>From the Greek "enneakaideka," meaning nineteen.</note>, that is, the nineteen-year period. This number found such great favor that it was posted in the marketplaces of Athens and other distinguished cities, and it is still accepted in common life to the present day, because it is believed that through it, the beginning and the end of the months are established according to a certain rule. The solar year of 365 1/4 days is also <term>commensurable</term> <note>Two quantities are commensurable if they have a common measure; here, it means the solar years and lunar months align perfectly within this cycle.</note> with this number of months. From this comes that Callippic period of 76 years, in which a day is intercalated nineteen times, and which has been called the Callippic year. 

But the genius of Hipparchus found that in 304 years, an entire extra day would be produced, and that this could only be corrected by reducing the solar year by the 300th part of a day. Therefore, this period of time has been called by some<note>240) original: "Einigen" refers to other contemporary astronomers or commentators on Hipparchus.</note> the Great Year of Hipparchus, in which 3760 months pass. However, this is stated superficially and without precision; therefore, Hipparchus himself undertook a closer investigation into the time in which the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The irregularity in a planet's or the Moon's speed as it moves through its orbit.</note> returns simultaneously with the <term>latitude</term> <note>The Moon's distance north or south of the ecliptic (the Sun's apparent path).</note>. After comparing his own records of very carefully conducted observations of lunar eclipses with those of the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>Astronomers and mathematicians from ancient Babylonia known for their precise celestial records.</note>, he determined the time in which the monthly movements return simultaneously with those of the anomaly to be 345 Egyptian years, 82 days, and 1 hour. In this time, 4267 months and 4573 cycles of the anomaly should be completed. 

Therefore, if the number of days—which amounts to 126,007 days and 1 hour—is divided by the number of months, one obtains a month equal to 29 days 31<sup>I</sup> 50<sup>II</sup> 8<sup>III</sup> 9<sup>IV</sup> 20<sup>V</sup><note>241) These Roman numerals represent "sexagesimal" fractions: minutes, seconds, thirds, fourths, and fifths (divisions of 60).</note>. From this, the movement for any given time was found. For if one divides the 360° of a monthly revolution by the duration of a month, the daily course of the Moon relative to the Sun results in 12° 11' 26'' 41''' 20<sup>IV</sup> 18<sup>V</sup><note>242) This represents the "elongation," or the daily increase in the angle between the Sun and the Moon.</note>. Taking this 365 times gives the annual movement of 12 full revolutions plus 129° 37' 21'' 28''' 29''''<note>243) This reflects how much further the Moon has traveled beyond its starting point after one solar year.</note>. Furthermore, since 4267 months and 4573 cycles of the anomaly contain the common factor 17, their ratio expressed in the smallest numbers is 251 to 269, in which ratio we...

<meta>This page continues the technical derivation of lunar cycles, building on the work of Hipparchus and Ptolemy. It transitions from general cycles to specific calculations of the Moon's anomaly and latitude movements using ratios from Euclid.</meta>

<margin>Egyptian</margin> <note>In this context, "Egyptian" refers to the Egyptian calendar year of exactly 365 days, which astronomers like Copernicus and Ptolemy used as a standard for calculation because it lacks leap years.</note>

...therefore, according to the 15th proposition of the 5th book of **Euclid**, have that [ratio] of the lunar course to the movement of the **anomaly**. So that, if we multiply the movement of the Moon by 269 and divide the product by 251, the annual movement of the anomaly results in: 13 full revolutions, 88° 43' 8'' 40''' 20''''<sup>244)</sup> and from this, the daily movement is 13° 3' 53'' 56''' 29''''<sup>244)</sup>. 

The <term>cycle of latitude</term> <note>Also known as the Draconic month, this is the time it takes the Moon to return to the same point (node) where its orbit crosses the ecliptic; this determines the timing of eclipses.</note>, however, has a different ratio and does not coincide with the time in which the anomaly returns; rather, one only sees the latitude of the Moon return when a later lunar eclipse is in every way similar and equal to an earlier one—that is, if in both cases equal eclipses occur from the same side, both in terms of magnitude and duration. This is the case when the Moon has equal distances from the greatest or the smallest **apsis** <note>The points in an orbit where the celestial body is closest to (perigee) or farthest from (apogee) the center of its motion.</note>. For then it is clear that the Moon passes through equal shadows in equal time. 

According to **Hipparchus**, such a recurrence occurs in 5,458 months, which correspond to 5,923 cycles of latitude. According to this ratio, the specific movements for years and days are calculated as before. Namely, if we multiply the movement of the Moon from the Sun by 5,923 and divide the product by 5,458, we obtain the movement of the Moon's latitude for one year as: 13 revolutions 148° 42' 46'' 49''' 3''''<sup>245)</sup> and for one day: 13° 13' 45'' 39''' 40''''<sup>245)</sup>. 

In this way, **Hipparchus** determined the uniform movements of the Moon, and no one came closer to them than he did. However, later centuries have proven that something had still been overlooked in all these numbers. **Ptolemy**, for instance, found the same mean movement of the Moon from the Sun as Hipparchus, but he found the annual movement of the anomaly to be smaller by 1'' 11''' 39''''<sup>246)</sup>, and the annual movement of latitude to be larger by 53''' 41''''. 

However, we, after the passage of a very long period of time, have found Hipparchus's mean annual movement to be too small by 1'' 2''' 49'''', while Hipparchus's movement of anomaly is short by only 24''' 49''''. The movement of Hipparchus's latitude, however, is too large by 1'' 1''' 44''''. Through this, the amount by which the annual uniform movement of the Moon differs from the annual movement of the Earth is 129° 37' 22'' 32''' 40''''; the movement of the anomaly is 88° 43' 9'' 5''' 9''''; and the movement of latitude is 148° 42' 45'' 17''' 21''''<sup>247)</sup>.

# Chapter 5.

## **Development of the first inequality of the moon, which occurs at the new and full moon.**

We have presented the uniform motions of the moon as far as they could be identified up to this point. Now we must develop the <term>inequality</term> <note>original: "Ungleichmässigkeit"; in historical astronomy, this refers to an "anomaly," or the way the moon's actual position deviates from its predicted "mean" or average position</note>. We intend to do this through the method of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>a small geometric circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle; this was the primary tool used by ancient astronomers to explain why planets sometimes appear to speed up or slow down</note>. We will begin with the inequality that occurs during the new and full moon, a phenomenon which the ancient mathematicians analyzed with admirable ingenuity by discussing three lunar eclipses. We wish to follow the path they cleared for us and compare three other carefully recorded eclipses with those observed by <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the most influential astronomer of antiquity, who lived in the 2nd century AD</note>, in order to test whether the uniform motions we have already described are accurate.

In presenting these, we follow the example of the ancients by using the mean motions of the sun and the moon from the point of the <term>vernal equinox</term> <note>the point where the sun crosses the celestial equator in spring</note> as uniform values. This is because the inequality that arises due to the uneven <term>precession of the equinoxes</term> <note>the slow, wobbling shift of Earth’s axis over thousands of years</note> is not noticeable over such a short span of time—even if it were a period of ten years. 

Ptolemy<sup>248</sup>) states that the first eclipse, according to the Egyptian calendar, occurred in the 17th year of the Emperor <term>Hadrian</term>, after the twentieth day of the month of <term>Payni</term> had passed; that was the year 133 of Christ, on the 6th of May<sup>249</sup>). The eclipse was total, and the time of its midpoint was three-quarters of a "mean hour" before midnight in Alexandrian time. According to the time in <term>Frauenburg</term> or <term>Krakow</term> <note>the locations where the author, presumably Nicolaus Copernicus, conducted his work</note>, this was 1 3/4 hours before the midnight that was followed by May 7th<sup>250</sup>). The sun was at 12º 15' of <term>Taurus</term><sup>251</sup>), but according to its mean motion, it was at 12º 21' of Taurus<sup>252</sup>).

The second eclipse is said to have taken place in the 19th year of Hadrian, after the passing of two days of the month of <term>Choiak</term> (the fourth Egyptian month); that was in the year of Christ 134, on October 20th<sup>253</sup>). The eclipse covered five-sixths of the moon's diameter from the north, and the time of its midpoint was one mean hour before midnight in Alexandrian time. Therefore, according to the time in Krakow, it was two hours before midnight<sup>254</sup>). The sun stood at 25º 10' of <term>Libra</term>, but according to its mean motion, it was at 26º 43' of Libra<sup>255</sup>).

The third eclipse took place in the 20th year of Hadrian, after the passing of 19 days of the month of <term>Pharmuthi</term> (the eighth Egyptian month), or after the passing of 135 years of Christ and 6 days of March<sup>256</sup>). The eclipse covered half of the diameter, again from the north, and the time of its midpoint was four mean hours after midnight in Alexandrian time. Therefore, according to the time in Krakow, it was 3 hours after midnight<sup>257</sup>), on the morning of March 7th. The sun stood at 14º 5' of <term>Pisces</term>, but according to its mean motion, it was at 11º 44' of Pisces<sup>258</sup>). It thus follows that in the period between the first and second eclipse, the moon had traveled as much as the sun...

in their apparent motion—that is, if we set aside full rotations—was 161° 55' <note>original footnote: 259</note>, and from the second to the third, it was 138° 55' <note>original footnote: 260</note>. In the first period, there were 1 year, 166 days, and 23¾ hours of apparent solar time <note>original footnote: 261</note>, which equals 23⅝ hours of mean solar time <note>original footnote: 262</note>; in the second period, there were 1 year, 137 days, and 5 hours <note>original footnote: 263</note>, which equals 5½ hours of mean solar time <note>original footnote: 264</note>. The combined uniform motion of the sun and moon in the first period, excluding full rotations, was 169° 37' <note>original footnote: 265</note> and the <term>anomaly</term> <note>the moon's position or "irregularity" along its small orbital circle</note> was 110° 21' <note>original footnote: 266</note>; in the second period, the uniform motion of the sun and moon was 137° 33' <note>original footnote: 267</note> and the anomaly was 81° 36' <note>original footnote: 268</note>. It follows, therefore, that in the first period, 110° 21' of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>a small circle whose center moves along a larger one</note> subtracts 7° 42' <note>original footnote: 269</note> from the moon’s mean motion, and in the second period, 81° 36' of the epicycle adds 1° 21' <note>original footnote: 270</note> to the moon’s mean motion. With these values established, let the lunar epicycle *abc* be constructed, in which the first eclipse occurred at *a*, the second at *b*, and the third at *c*, following the order of the moon's retrograde motion described above.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram of a circle representing a lunar epicycle. Points a, b, c, and e are marked on the circumference. The arc *ab* of 110° 21' causes a <term>retardation</term> <note>a slowing down of the observed position relative to the average speed</note>, as stated, of 7° 42'; the arc *bc* of 81° 36' causes an <term>acceleration</term> <note>a speeding up of the observed position</note> of 1° 21'. Therefore, the remaining arc *ac* of 168° 3' will cause an acceleration of 6° 21'. Since the <term>highest absis</term> <note>the apogee, or the point on the epicycle furthest from the Earth</note> of the epicycle does not lie within the arcs *bc* and *ca*—because both cause acceleration and are smaller than a semicircle—it must necessarily be located within arc *ab*. Let *d* be the center of the Earth, around which the epicycle moves uniformly; draw lines to the points of the eclipses *da*, *db*, *dc*, and connect *bc*, *be*, and *ce*. Since arc *ab* in the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>the sun's apparent path across the sky</note> measures 7° 42', the angle *adb* is 7° 42' where 180° equals two right angles; however, it is 15° 24' if 360° is taken as two right angles. The angle *aeb* is the <term>inscribed angle</term> <note>an angle formed by two chords meeting on the circumference of a circle</note> of 110° 21' and the <term>exterior angle</term> of the triangle *bde*. Thus, angle *ebd* is found to be 94° 57'. The sides of a triangle with given angles are also given; therefore, *de* is 147,396 and *be* is 26,798, assuming the diameter of the circle circumscribed around the triangle is 200,000. Furthermore, since arc *aec* in the ecliptic covers 6° 21', the angle *edc* is 6° 21' where 180° equals two right angles, or 12° 42' if 360° represents two right angles; under this latter condition, angle *aec* is 191° 57'.

Since the two sides **be** and **ec** are again given in triangle **bec**, and the inscribed angle **e** corresponds to the arc **bc** of 81° 36': we also obtain the third side **bc** according to the theorems of plane triangles as 17,960 of those same parts. 

If, however, the diameter of the <term>epicycle</term> <note>a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle</note> were 200,000 parts: then **bc**, as the <term>chord</term> <note>a straight line segment connecting two points on a circle's edge</note> of 81° 36', would be 130,684, and the others according to the given ratio: **ed** = 1,072,684 and **ce** = 118,637, and the arc **ce** itself = 72° 46' 10''. But since the segment **ae** is smaller than a semicircle, the center of the epicycle does not lie within it, but in the remainder **abce**. Let this center be **k**, and let the line **dmkl** be drawn through both <term>apsides</term> <note>the points in an orbit farthest from (apogee) or closest to (perigee) the center</note>, where **l** is the highest and **m** the lowest apsis. According to the 35th proposition <note>original footnote: 271. This refers to the 'Power of a Point' theorem: the product of the segments of any chord through a point is constant.</note> of the 3rd book of Euclid, the rectangle formed by **ad** · **de** = **ld** · **dm**. Since the diameter **lm** of the circle is bisected at **k**, and **dm** lies in its straight-line extension: the square of **dk** is greater than the rectangle **ld** · **dm** by the square of **km** <note>original footnote: 272</note>. 

From this, **dk** is found to be 1,148,556, if **kl** is 100,000, and it follows that the radius of the epicycle **lk** is 8,706, if **dkl** <note>the distance from the observer to the center of the epicycle</note> is 100,000. Following these determinations, let **kno** be drawn perpendicular to **ad**. # Chapter 6.

## **Confirmation of what has been said about the uniform motions of the longitude and anomaly of the moon.**

From what has been developed regarding <term>lunar eclipses</term> <note>events where the Earth's shadow falls on the moon</note>, it can also be judged whether the uniform motions of the moon, which we developed earlier, are correct. It has been shown that at the second of the first eclipses, the distance of the moon from the sun was 182º 47'<sup>279)</sup>, and the <term>anomaly</term> <note>the moon's angular distance from its furthest point from Earth</note> was 64º 38'. At the second of the later eclipses from our own time, the distance of the moon from the sun was 182º 51', and the anomaly was 74º 27'. In the intervening time, however, there are 17,166 full months and an additional 4 minutes, and the movement of the anomaly, omitting full circles, amounts to 9º 49'. The time that elapsed from the 19th year of <term>Hadrian</term> <note>Roman Emperor, r. 117–138 AD</note>, the second of <term>Choak</term> <note>the fourth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</note> 2 hours before midnight—which was followed by the 3rd day of the same month—until the year of Christ 1522 on the 5th of September at 1 1/3 hours true time, amounts to 1,388 Egyptian years, 302 days, and 3 1/3 hours, when everything is reduced to <term>mean time</term> <note>time measured by a clock running at a perfectly uniform rate, rather than by the slightly varying motion of the sun</note>, which gives 3<sup>h</sup> 34<sup>m</sup> after midnight.<sup>280)</sup> And in this time, the motion of the moon—besides 17,165 full revolutions or equal months—would have been 359º 38' according to <term>Hipparchus</term> <note>Greek astronomer of the 2nd century BC</note> and <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Roman-Egyptian astronomer of the 2nd century AD</note><sup>281)</sup>. However, regarding the anomaly, according to Hipparchus it was 9º 37', while according to Ptolemy it was 9º 11'<sup>282)</sup>. Thus, for the motion of the moon since those two, 26' are missing<sup>283)</sup>, and for the anomaly 38' are missing<sup>284)</sup>, which are added in our calculations; and this agrees with the numbers we have developed.

# Chapter 7.

## **Concerning the positions of the longitude and anomaly of the moon.**

Now, as before, the positions or the specific starting points for the years of the Olympiads, Alexander, Caesar, Christ, and any others that might be desired, must be established here. In this time, the motion of the moon according to our calculation is 332º 49'<sup>285)</sup>, and that of the anomaly is 217º 30'<sup>286)</sup>. If one subtracts these values respectively from those found at the eclipse: there remains as the mean position of the moon from the sun 209º 58'<sup>287)</sup> and for the anomaly 207º 7'<sup>288)</sup> for the beginning of the years of Christ at midnight on January 1st. Now, there are again 193 years until the beginning of the years of Christ...

### Concerning the second inequality of the Moon, and the ratio that the first epicycle has to the second.

Thus, the uniform motion of the Moon, together with its first <term>inequality</term> <note>a term for the Moon's deviation from perfectly circular motion</note>, has been developed. For then the <term>vertical circle</term> <note>the circle passing through the zenith and the object</note> intersects the ecliptic at a right angle and allows no change in longitude; rather, the entire change falls upon the latitude. ## Chapter 10.

->**How the apparent motion of the Moon is derived from the given uniform motions.**<-

Having established these foundations, we now wish to show how the apparent and uniform motion of the Moon is derived through geometric construction from those given uniform motions. We shall take an example from the observations of <term>Hipparchus</term> <note>a famous Greek astronomer of the 2nd century BCE whose work laid the foundation for mathematical astronomy</note>, through which the derivation may simultaneously be proven by experiment. In the year 197 after Alexander’s death, on the 17th of <term>Pauni</term> <note>the tenth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</note>, after the passing of 9 1/3 daylight hours, Hipparchus <note>Note 300: This observation is recorded in Ptolemy's Almagest</note> found at Rhodes, while observing the Sun and Moon with an <term>astrolabe</term> <note>an ancient instrument used to measure the altitudes and positions of celestial bodies</note>, that they were 48 1/10° apart, with the Moon following the Sun by that amount. Since he determined the position of the Sun to be at 10 9/10° of <term>Cancer</term> <note>Note 301: Original reads "11° less 1/10°"</note>, it followed that the Moon was at 29° of <term>Leo</term> <note>Note 302</note>. At that same time, the 29th degree of <term>Scorpio</term> was rising, while the 10th degree of <term>Virgo</term> was passing through the <term>meridian</term> <note>the imaginary north-south line passing through the zenith</note> of Rhodes, and the North Pole was at an altitude of 36° <note>Note 303: This refers to the geographical latitude of Rhodes</note>. From this, it appears that the Moon—which was then 90° away from the horizon on the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>the sun's apparent path across the sky</note>—suffered no <term>parallax</term> <note>the displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight</note> in longitude, or at least an unnoticeable amount. But since this observation was made on that seventeenth day at 3 1/3 hours past noon—which for Rhodes corresponds to 4 <term>equinoctial hours</term> <note>Note 304: Standardized hours of 60 minutes, unlike seasonal "temporary hours" which varied in length</note> <note>Note 305</note>—these were 3 1/6 equinoctial hours for Kraków, because Rhodes is closer to us than Alexandria by 1/6 of an hour. Therefore, according to the simple calculation, 196 years, 286 days, 3 hours and 10 minutes had elapsed since Alexander’s death; precisely, however, 3 hours and 20 minutes. During this time, the Sun reached its mean...

Thus, that lunar distance, which Hipparchus determined with his instrument to be 48° 6', agrees in a wonderful way, as if by prior agreement, with our calculation.

## Chapter 11.

### Derivation of the Table of Prosthaphaereses or Lunar Equations.

By this example, I believe, the method for calculating the lunar motions can be understood in general. The two sides **ge** and **ce** of the triangle **ceg** always remain the same; according to the angle **ceg**, which changes continuously but is always given, we calculate the third side **gc** together with the angle **ecg**, which provides the <term>prosthaphaerese</term> <note>original: "Prosthaphärese"; a correction or "equation" added to or subtracted from the mean motion to find the true position</note> for the adjustment of the anomaly. Furthermore, if in the triangle **cdg** the two sides **dc** and **cg** are given in numbers along with the angle **dce**: then the angle **d** between the uniform and the true motion at the center of the Earth is found in the same way. To make this even easier, we wish to establish a table of these prosthaphaereses containing six columns. Following the two common numerical entries for the circle, the third row contains the prosthaphaereses which, originating from the small epicycle in a two-month motion, change the uniformity of the first anomaly. The following column remains empty for now and is reserved for future figures. The fifth column we take for the prosthaphaereses of the first and larger epicycle, which occur in the

# Chapter 12.

## On the Calculation of the Moon’s Course.

The method by which the apparent motion of the Moon is calculated is derived from what we have already explained, and is as follows. We first convert the given time for which we are seeking the Moon’s position into <term>uniform time</term> <note>Also known as "mean time," this is time measured at a constant rate, ignoring the slight seasonal variations in the length of a day.</note>. Using this time, we derive the mean motions of the longitude, anomaly, and latitude in the same manner as we did for the Sun, calculating from the birth of Christ or another established epoch. We then establish the positions for each of these values for the given time. 

Next, we look up the <term>uniform longitude</term> of the Moon—or its double distance from the Sun—in the table, and note the <term>prosthaphaeresis</term> <note>original: "Prosthaphärese"; a correction added or subtracted to account for the difference between a planet's average "mean" position and its actual "true" position due to its elliptical or complex orbit.</note> listed in the third column, along with the subsequent proportional parts. If the number we used to enter the table is in the first column, or is less than 180°, we add the prosthaphaeresis to the Moon's anomaly. However, if it is greater than 180° and stands in the second column, we subtract it. The result is the <term>adjusted anomaly</term> of the Moon—its true distance from the highest <term>apsis</term> <note>The highest point (apogee) in the Moon's orbit where it is furthest from Earth.</note>. 

With this adjusted anomaly, we return to the table to find the corresponding prosthaphaeresis in the fifth column, as well as the "variation" in the sixth column. This variation represents the effect of the second <term>epicycle</term> <note>A smaller orbital circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle; used by early astronomers to explain the complex "wobbles" in planetary paths.</note> upon the first. The proportional part for this is calculated based on a ratio of 60 and is always added to this prosthaphaeresis. We subtract this total sum from the mean motion of longitude and latitude as long as the adjusted anomaly is less than 180°; we add it if the anomaly is greater.

In this way, we obtain the Moon's true distance from the Sun's mean position, as well as the adjusted motion of latitude. From this, we can determine the true position of the Moon, both relative to the first star of Aries (using the Sun's simple motion) and relative to the <term>vernal equinox</term> (using the composite motion corrected for <term>precession</term>). 

Finally, using the adjusted motion of latitude, we find the degrees of latitude—the Moon's distance from the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; the Moon's orbit is tilted slightly relative to this path.</note>—in the seventh and final column. This latitude will be northern if the motion of longitude <note>313) This likely refers to the argument of latitude rather than simple longitude.</note> is on the first side of the table (less than 90° or greater than 270°); otherwise, it is southern. Consequently, the Moon descends from the north until it reaches 180°, and then rises from that southern limit until it has completed the other half of its circle. In this manner, the apparent course of the Moon performs roughly as many movements around the center of the Earth as the center of the Earth performs around the Sun.

### Chapter 13.
### How the motion of the Moon’s latitude is investigated and derived.

Now we must also develop the calculation of the movement of the <term>Moon’s latitude</term> <note>The Moon's angular distance north or south of the ecliptic—the Sun's apparent path.</note>, which seems more difficult to determine because it depends on several factors. For, as we have stated above, if two lunar eclipses are entirely similar and equal—that is, if the eclipsed portions have the same northern or southern positions, occur at the same <term>ascending or descending node</term> <note>The two points where the Moon's orbit crosses the Sun's path. The "ascending" node is where it moves north; the "descending" node is where it moves south.</note>, and the distance of the Moon from the Earth and from the highest <term>apsis</term> <note>The apogee, the point where the Moon is furthest from Earth.</note> is the same—it can then be recognized that the Moon, upon reaching that same alignment, has completed full revolutions of its latitude. 

Because the Earth’s shadow is a cone—and when a straight cone is cut by a plane parallel to its base, the resulting circle is smaller at a greater distance from the base, larger at a smaller distance, and equal at an equal distance—the Moon will pass through equal circles of shadow at equal distances from the Earth, presenting us with equal portions of its disk during observations. From this it follows that if the Moon, being at the same location and at an equal distance from the center of the shadow, is obscured by the same amount, it confirms its identical latitude to us. From this, we must conclude that having returned to its previous position of latitude, it stands at the same distance in arc from the same point on the <term>ekliptik</term> <note>The Sun's annual path as seen from Earth.</note>—especially if the position for both celestial bodies matches. This is because both the Moon's own approaching and receding, as well as that of the Earth, changes the total size of the shadow, to a degree that can hardly be measured. 

Therefore, the more the timing for both matches, the more accurately we can obtain the movement of the Moon’s latitude, as has already been mentioned regarding the Sun. But since it rarely happens that one finds two eclipses that match in all these respects—at least, we have encountered none such until today—we wish to show that there is another way to achieve the same goal. If the Moon, while the other conditions remain the same, is eclipsed on opposite sides and at opposite nodes, this proves that at the second eclipse the Moon has reached a point diametrically opposite the former and, besides whole revolutions, has described a semicircle. 

This seems sufficient for the investigation of this matter. We have found two eclipses that come close to these conditions: the first in the 7th year of Ptolemy Philometor, which was the 150th year of Alexander, after—as Claudius ³¹⁴) <note>original: "Claudius"; referring to the Greco-Egyptian astronomer Claudius Ptolemy.</note> says—27 days of the seventh Egyptian month Phamenoth had passed, in the night followed by the 28th. The Moon was eclipsed from the beginning of the 8th hour to the end of the 10th hour in the nocturnal seasonal hours of Alexandria, at its maximum by 7 <term>digits</term> <note>original: "Zoll" (inches); in historical astronomy, a "digit" is 1/12th of the diameter of the celestial body.</note> of the lunar diameter from the North...

For the second eclipse, however, from the same beginning of the Era of Alexander, it was 1832 Egyptian years, 295 days, 11 hours, and 45 minutes in apparent time, but 11 hours and 55 minutes in uniform time. Therefore, the uniform movement of the Moon was 182° 18', the position of the anomaly was 159° 55', and the adjusted position was 159° 13'. The <term>prosthaphaeresis</term>, by which the uniform motion was smaller than the apparent motion, was 1° 44'.

It follows, therefore, that in both eclipses the distance of the Moon from the Earth was the same, and the Sun in both cases was at <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the center of attraction.</note>; however, in the amount of obscuration, there was a difference of one inch. But since the diameter of the Moon usually occupies about half a degree, as we shall prove later, its twelfth part (for one inch) amounts to 2 1/2 minutes. In the slanted circle of the Moon near the node, this corresponds to nearly half a degree, by which the Moon was further from the ascending node in the second eclipse than it was from the descending node in the first. From this, it is clear that the true motion of the Moon’s latitude, besides the full revolutions, was 179 1/2°. However, when we account for the 21 minutes by which the prosthaphaereses differ between the first and second eclipses, we find the uniform motion of the Moon’s latitude, besides the full revolutions, to be 179° 51'. The time between both eclipses was 1683 Egyptian years, 88 days, 22 hours, and 35 minutes of apparent time, which matches the uniform time. In this period, 22,577 revolutions and 179° 51' were completed, which agrees with what we have already developed.

## Chapter 15.

### Construction of the parallactic instrument. <note>original: <sup>320</sup>. This instrument is also known as the Triquetrum, used for measuring the zenith distance of stars and planets.</note>

Fate has not offered us the same opportunity to observe that the greatest latitude of the Moon—corresponding to the angle of inclination of its orbit against the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The sun's apparent path across the sky; the "highway" of the planets.</note>—amounts to five degrees (of which 360 make a circle), as it did for Claudius Ptolemy, because the <term>parallaxes</term> <note>The displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</note> of the Moon were a hindrance to us. If one subtracts 2 1/8° from 30° 58', there remain 28° 51 1/2', which exceeds the <term>greatest obliquity of the ecliptic</term> <note>The angle between the Earth's equator and its orbital plane, which determines the limit of the sun's north-south movement.</note>, which at that time amounted to 23° 51' 20'' ^321) <note>This likely refers to a specific reference number in the original manuscript or a scholarly edition.</note>, by approximately 5 full degrees; and this latitude of the Moon is found to be consistent with the other details up to the present day. 

The <term>parallactic instrument</term> <note>Also called a triquetrum, this was a pre-telescopic tool used to measure the zenith distance of celestial bodies.</note> consists of three rulers, two of which are equal and at least four cubits long, while the third is longer. This one and one of the other two are connected to the two ends of the third by skillfully crafted drillings and matching axes or pins, so that they rotate in one and the same plane, but cannot wobble at those joints in any way. 

On the longer ruler, starting from the center of its joint, a straight line is carved along its entire length, upon which a segment is marked off that is equal to the most accurately measured distance between the joints. This segment is divided into a thousand parts, or if possible into even more equal parts, and this division is continued in the same manner along the extension until the whole contains 1414 parts. This is the length of the side of a square that can be inscribed in a circle whose radius contains 1000 parts. The remaining portion, by which this ruler is longer, can be cut off as superfluous. 

Also on the other ruler, starting from the center of the joint, a line is drawn which contains one thousand of those parts, thus being equal to the section between the centers of the joints on the first ruler. This same ruler carries openings on the side, as is customary with a <term>diopter</term> <note>A sighting device or "aimer" used to align the instrument with a star.</note>, through which one looks, and which are so adjusted that the line of sight does not incline at all toward the line drawn along the length of the ruler, but remains everywhere equally distant from it. Care is also taken that this line, which reaches with its end to the longer ruler, can meet the divided line; so that in this way an isosceles triangle is formed from the rulers, the base of which consists of parts of the graduated line. 

Thereupon, a very well-squared and polished post is erected and fixed, to which the instrument is attached—using the ruler that carries the two joints—by means of some hinges, in which it can turn like a door. This is done so that the straight line passing through the centers of the ruler's joints is always vertical and directed toward the <term>zenith</term> <note>The imaginary point in the sky directly "straight up" from the observer.</note>, acting as the axis of the horizon. 

If one now wishes to find the <term>zenith distance</term> <note>The angular distance of a star from the point directly overhead.</note> of any star, one looks through the diopter of the ruler once the star is correctly sighted, and having observed the ruler with the divided line below, one sees how many parts span the angle lying between the line of sight and the axis of the horizon. Of these parts, the diameter of the circle contains 2000°, and one obtains from the table the required arc of the <term>great circle</term> <note>A circle on the surface of a sphere, like the equator, whose center is the center of the sphere.</note> between the star and the zenith.

Through this instrument, as stated, Ptolemy obtained the greatest latitude of the Moon at 5º. Thereupon he turned to the determination of its <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent change in position of an object when viewed from different points; in astronomy, it helps determine the distance to celestial bodies.</note>, and says that he found it in Alexandria to be 1º 7', while the sun stood at 5º 28' of Libra, the mean distance of the Moon and the Sun was 78º 13', the uniform anomaly 262º 20', the motion in latitude 354º 40', the <term>prosthaphärese</term> <note>original: "Prosthaphärese" — a correction factor used to find the true position of a celestial body from its mean position.</note> to be added was 7º 26', and consequently the position of the Moon was at 3º 9' of Capricorn. He further concludes from the movement of these same circles that the greatest distance of the Moon from the Earth, which is claimed to occur at the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> of the epicycle during the new and full moon, is 64 1/6 of these parts—while the smallest distance, which occurs at the <term>quadratures</term> <note>The points where the Moon is 90 degrees away from the Sun, such as the first and last quarter phases.</note> of the lunar quarters and at the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note> of the epicycle, amounts to 33 33/60 such parts. From this he also determined the parallaxes that occur at 90º from the zenith, specifically the smallest at 53' 34'' and the greatest at 1º 43', as can be seen further from what he developed on this subject. 

However, it is already clear from the outset to anyone who wishes to see that this matter behaves quite differently, as we have convinced ourselves through manifold experiences. ### Chapter 17.

## **The distance of the Moon from the Earth, and proof of the ratio it holds to the radius of the Earth.**

From this it now becomes clear how great the distance of the Moon from the Earth is; without this, no definite ratio of the parallax can be stated, for both exist in a reciprocal relationship. This is explained as follows: 

Let *ab* be a great circle of the Earth, and *c* its center, around which another circle is described, in relation to which the Earth has a noticeable size; let this circle be *de*, and let *d* be the pole of the horizon. Let the center of the Moon be at *e*, with its known zenith distance being *de*. Now, in the first observation, the angle *dae* was 82º 50' and angle *ace*, according to the calculation, was only 82º; thus their difference, *aec*, was 50', which was attributed to the parallax. 

In the triangle *ace*, the angles are given, and therefore also the sides. Because the angle *cae* is given, the side *ce* contains 99,219 of those parts of which the diameter of the circle circumscribed around the triangle *aec* contains 100,000, and *ac* contains 1,454. This results in nearly 68 such parts <note>Specifically, 68 Earth radii.</note> for *ce*.

Lines connect 'c' to 'e', 'a' to 'e', and 'a' to 'c', forming a triangle 'ace'. The line 'cd' serves as the vertical axis of the horizon.</image-desc>
