# Chapter 18.
## On the Diameter of the Moon and of the Earth's Shadow at the Point of the Moon's Passage.³²³) <note>This refers to the diameter of the shadow cast by the Earth at the specific distance where the Moon's orbit crosses it.</note>

Alongside the distance of the Moon from the Earth, the apparent diameters of the Moon and the shadow are also variable, which is why we must also discuss these. Although the diameters of the Sun and the Moon are measured correctly using the <term>diopter</term> <note>An early astronomical sighting instrument used for measuring the angular diameters of celestial bodies.</note> of Hipparchus, it is believed that this can be achieved much more accurately for the Moon with the help of certain selected lunar eclipses. These are eclipses in which the Moon is at an equal distance from its greatest and smallest <term>apsis</term> <note>The points in an orbit where the celestial body is farthest (apogee) or closest (perigee) to the Earth.</note>; especially if the Sun then aligns in such a way that the shadow circle, which the Moon must pass through in each case, is found to be the same—except that the eclipses extend over unequal parts. For it is evident that the difference between the eclipsed portions and the corresponding <term>latitudes</term> <note>In historical astronomy, celestial latitude refers to the angular distance of the Moon north or south of the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path.</note> of the Moon allows one to infer the size of the arc of a circle described around the center of the Earth which the Moon's diameter occupies. Once this is known, the radius of the shadow is also soon found.

This may be made clearer with an example. If, then, at the time of the middle of an earlier eclipse, three "inches" <note>The original German uses *Zoll* (inches), representing the astronomical "digit" (*digitus*), a unit equal to one-twelfth of the diameter of a celestial body's disk.</note> of the Moon's radius are eclipsed while its latitude is 47′ 54″, and in a later eclipse, where the latitude was 29′ 37″, ten "inches" were eclipsed, then the difference between the magnitudes of the eclipses is seven "inches," and the difference between the latitudes is 18′ 17″. Meanwhile, 31′ 20″—representing the apparent diameter of the Moon—corresponds to twelve "inches." It follows, therefore, that at the time of the middle of the first eclipse, the center of the Moon protruded from the shadow by a fourth part of its diameter; this corresponds to 7′ 50″ of latitude. Subtracting this from the 47′ 54″ of the total latitude, 40′ 4″ remains for the radius of the shadow. Likewise, in the second eclipse, the shadow extended beyond the center of the Moon by a third part of the Moon’s diameter, or a latitude of 10′ 27″; adding this to the 29′ 37″, one also obtains 40′ 4″ for the radius of the shadow.³²⁴) To be sure, it is Ptolemy's opinion that while the Sun and Moon are at their greatest distances from the Earth during their <term>conjunction</term> <note>The alignment of the Sun and Moon on the same side of the Earth (New Moon).</note> and <term>opposition</term> <note>The alignment of the Sun and Moon on opposite sides of the Earth (Full Moon).</note>, the Moon's diameter is 31′ 20″. He claims to have found the Sun's diameter to be just as large using Hipparchus's diopter, but the diameter of the shadow is said to be 1º 21′ 20″.

# Chapter 19.

## How the distances of the Sun and Moon from the Earth, their diameters, the diameter of the shadow at the point of the Moon’s passage, and the axis of the shadow are derived simultaneously.

Now, the Sun also has a <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points; in astronomy, this helps determine distance.</note>, which, because of its extreme smallness, is not easily recognized. It can only be discerned because the distance of the Sun and Moon from the Earth, their diameters, the diameter of the shadow at the point where the Moon passes through it, and the axis of the shadow are all mutually dependent; therefore, they reveal one another through a natural mathematical development.

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram illustrating the celestial alignment of the Sun and Earth to determine shadow dimensions. At the top, a large circle represents the Sun with center d and circumference points a, b, and c. Below it, a smaller circle represents the Earth with center k and circumference points g, f, and e. A vertical central axis line dks passes through the centers d and k, ending at the shadow apex s. Converging common tangent lines ag and ce meet at point s. Two horizontal lines are drawn between the Earth and the apex, representing the Moon's path at different distances: the first line nlp passes through point l on the axis (with point o also marked), and the second line qmr passes through point m on the axis. Diagonal lines connect the edges of the Sun (a, c) to the center of the Earth (k).</image-desc>

<column-break/>

First, let us examine the views held by Ptolemy regarding this <gloss>325)</gloss> <note>This refers to the 19th-century editor's note in the German edition, likely referencing Ptolemy’s *Almagest*, Book V.</note>, and how he proved them, so that we may draw from them that which appears to be truly certain. He assumes the apparent diameter of the Sun to be 31' 20'' <note>31 minutes and 20 seconds of arc.</note>, and employs this value as a constant; he sets the diameter of the full and new Moon, which are supposed to occur at <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note>, as equal to that of the Sun. He further asserts that the Moon is then 64⅙ Earth-radii distant from the Earth. From this, he derives the remaining values as follows:

Let the circumference of the Sun be *abc*, and its center *d*; let *efg* be the circumference of the Earth at its greatest distance from the Sun, with its center *k*; let the straight lines *ag* and *ce* be the shared tangents, which, when extended, meet at the apex of the shadow *s*. Through the centers of the Sun and the Earth, let the line *dks* be drawn, and in addition, let the lines *ak*, *kc*, *ac*, and *ge* be drawn—the latter two of which, due to the immense distance, are not distinguished from the actual diameters. On the axis line *dks*, the equal segments *lk* and *km* are marked off, corresponding to the distances which, in his opinion, the full and new Moon have at apogee, and which consist of 64⅙ such parts...

amount to, where *ek* is the unit of measure; let *qmr* be the diameter of the shadow at the point of the Moon's passage, and *nlo* be the diameter of the Moon, perpendicular to *dk* and extended to *p*. First, the ratio of *dk* to *ke* must now be found. Since the angle *nko* <note>The angular diameter of the Moon as seen from Earth.</note> is 31' 20'', its half, angle *lko*, is equal to 15' 40'', and the angle at *l* is a right angle. In the triangle *lko*, the angles are therefore given, and consequently also the ratio of the sides *kl* to *lo*. Thus, *lo* in its length is 17³³/₆₀ <term>sixtieths</term> <note>The author uses a sexagesimal system (base 60) for fractional parts, common in ancient and Renaissance astronomy.</note> of such parts of which *lk* contains 64⅙, or *ke* contains one part. And because *lo* is to *mr* in a ratio of 5 to 13, *mr* contains 45³⁸/₆₀ sixtieths of the same parts. But since *lop* and *mr* are parallel to *ke* at equal distances, the sum of *lop* and *mr* is twice as large as *ke*; if one subtracts *mr* and *lo* from this, the remainder *op* is equal to 56⁴⁹/₆₀ sixtieths.

According to the second proposition of the sixth book of Euclid’s <note>original: "Euklid's"</note> *Elements*, the ratios of *ec* to *pc*, *ke* to *oc*, and *kd* to *ld* are as *ke* to *op*, that is, as 60 to 56⁴⁹/₆₀. <note>326) These calculations follow the Euclidean principles of similar triangles to determine the height of the shadow cone.</note> Likewise, *ld* results in 56⁴⁹/₆₀ if *dk* is 60, and the remainder *kl* is 3¹¹/₆₀. Insofar as *kl* contains 64⅙ of such parts of which *fk* is one, then *kd* <note>The distance from the Earth to the Sun.</note> amounts to 1210. Now it has already been shown that *mr* contains 45³⁸/₆₀ sixtieths of such parts, and the ratio of *ke* to *mr* is as *kms* to *ms*; consequently, *km* also contains 14²²/₆₀ sixtieths of *kms*. Conversely, if *km* contains 64⅙, then 268 parts are assigned to *kms* as the axis of the shadow. <note>327) This calculates the length of the Earth's conical shadow to be 268 Earth radii.</note> Thus says Ptolemy.

Others after Ptolemy, however, when they found that this did not sufficiently correspond to the observed phenomena, established certain other assumptions. Nonetheless, they maintain that the greatest distance of the full and new Moon from the Earth is 64⅙ Earth radii, that the apparent diameter of the Sun at its <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> is 31' 20'', and that it relates to the diameter of the shadow at the point of the Moon's passage as 13 to 5, exactly as Ptolemy himself held. They say, however, that the apparent diameter of the Moon at that time is no greater than 29½', and therefore set the diameter of the shadow equal to 1° 16' 45''. They believe that from this, the distance of the Sun from the Earth follows as 1146 and the axis of the shadow as 254 Earth radii, and they attribute this discovery—which however cannot be proven—to that "Aratean philosopher." <note>328) Likely a reference to the medieval astronomer Al-Battani (Albategnius), whom Copernicus and others sometimes associated with the tradition of Aratus or earlier Greek observers.</note>

We, however, have had to arrange and improve this by setting the apparent diameter of the Sun at its apogee to 31' 40'' (for it must currently be somewhat larger than it was before Ptolemy); we set that of the full and new Moon, specifically at its greatest <term>apse</term> <note>The highest point in an elliptical orbit.</note>, to 30' and that of the shadow at the point of the Moon's passage to 80' 36''. For it is more fitting that this ratio be as 150 to 403, which is slightly larger than 5 to 13. The entire solar disk can only be covered by the Moon when the latter is at a distance of 62 Earth radii from the Earth. If one accepts this, it seems to hold together reliably both within itself and with the rest of the system, agreeing with the appearances of solar and lunar eclipses.

Therefore, if we maintain the greatest parallax of $3'$ throughout, we shall not appear to commit any error. We obtain the mean apparent diameters of the Sun from the mean distances, or, as some do, from the apparent hourly motion of the Sun, the ratio of which to its diameter they estimate at $5 : 66$ or $1$ to $14 \frac{1}{5}$. The hourly motion of the Sun is, however, nearly proportional to its distance.

### Chapter 24.

->**Derivation of the table of the individual parallaxes of the Sun and the Moon in the vertical circle.**<-

It will now no longer be difficult to obtain any individual <term>parallax</term><note>Parallax is the apparent shift in the position of a celestial body when viewed from different locations—in this case, the difference between a view from the Earth's surface and its center.</note> of the Sun and the Moon. Let *ab* again be taken as an arc of the Earth's circumference, passing through the center *c* and through the <term>zenith</term><note>The point in the sky directly above the observer.</note>. In the same plane, let *de* be the orbital path of the Moon, and *fg* that of the Sun.

Furthermore, let the straight line *cdf* be drawn through the zenith, and line *ceg* be drawn where the true positions of the Sun and Moon are imagined to be. The straight lines *ag* and *ae* connect these positions to the eye of the observer <note>The observer is located at point 'a' on the Earth's surface, while 'c' is the Earth's center.</note>. Thus, the parallax of the Sun is indicated by the angle *agc*, and that of the Moon by the angle *aec*. The difference between the parallaxes of the Sun and the Moon is represented by the angle *gae*, which is obtained by subtracting *agc* from *aec*. Now, we take the angle *acg* as our basis and wish to compare that difference with it. For example, if *acg* is 30°, it is known from the doctrine of plane triangles that if we set the line *cg* equal to 1142 Earth radii, the angle *agc*—by which the true altitude of the Sun differs from the apparent altitude—becomes 1' 30''. The same applies to the Moon for its four limits. ## Chapter 25.

### On the Calculation of Solar and Lunar Parallaxes.

We wish to briefly set forth the procedure for calculating the solar and lunar <term>parallaxes</term> <note>Parallax is the shift in the apparent position of a celestial body when viewed from different locations—here, the difference between a view from the Earth's surface versus its center.</note> from the table. Using the double <term>zenith distance</term> <note>The angular distance of a body from the point directly overhead.</note> of the Sun and the Moon, we find the corresponding <term>parallaxes</term> alongside them. This is done simply for the Sun, but for the Moon, it is found for its four boundaries. Using the double motion of the Moon, or its double distance from the Sun, we find the first <term>proportional parts</term> <note>Interpolation values used to find a precise number between two entries in a table.</note>. These latter values relate to 60 as the <term>correction</term> <note>The adjustment needed to make the data accurate for a specific moment.</note> to be found relates to the difference between the first and second, or the third and fourth boundaries. This yields the <term>corrections</term>, the first of which we always subtract from the next following <term>parallax</term> of the second boundary; the second of which we always add to the immediately preceding <term>parallax</term> of the third boundary. In this way, we obtain the two rectified lunar parallaxes for the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point where the Moon is farthest from the Earth.</note> and the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point where the Moon is closest to the Earth.</note>, which the small <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small mathematical circle used in ancient astronomy to account for variations in speed and distance in a planetary orbit.</note> increases or diminishes. 

Following this, we take the last <term>proportional parts</term> using the adjusted simple <term>anomaly</term> <note>An angle used to describe the Moon's position relative to its closest or furthest point from Earth.</note> of the Moon. These relate to 60 as the <term>correction</term> to be found relates to the difference of the two rectified lunar parallaxes just found. This yields the <term>correction</term> which we always add to the first rectified <term>parallax</term> (which occurs at the <term>apogee</term>) and always subtract from the second rectified <term>parallax</term> (which occurs at the <term>perigee</term>). Thus, one obtains the required <term>parallax</term> for the specific place and time, as shown in the following example. 

Let the <term>zenith distance</term> of the Moon be 54°, the mean motion of the Moon 15°, and its adjusted <term>anomaly</term> 100°. From this, I wish to find the lunar parallax through the table. The double <term>zenith distance</term> is 108°. To this corresponds a difference between the <term>parallaxes</term> of the first and second boundaries of 1' 48"; the <term>parallax</term> of the second boundary is 42' 50"; the <term>parallax</term> of the third boundary is 50' 59"; and the difference between the <term>parallaxes</term> of the third and fourth boundaries is 2' 46"—all of which I note down separately. The double motion of the Moon yields 30°, by which I find the first <term>proportional parts</term> to be 5. Now, 5 relates to 60 as the <term>correction</term> to be found relates to the difference of the <term>parallaxes</term> of the first and second boundaries (that is, to 108"). This yields a <term>correction</term> of 9", which I subtract from the 42' 50" of the second-boundary <term>parallax</term>; there remains, as the rectified <term>parallax</term>, 42' 41". Likewise, 5 relates to 60 as the <term>correction</term> to be found relates to the difference of the <term>parallaxes</term> of the third and fourth boundaries (that is, to 166"). This yields a <term>correction</term> of 14", which I add to the 50' 59" of the third-boundary <term>parallax</term>; this results in a rectified <term>parallax</term> of 51' 13". The difference between these two rectified <term>parallaxes</term> amounts to 8' 32". Next, with the simple adjusted <term>anomaly</term>, I find the last <term>proportional parts</term> to be 34. Now, 34 relates to 60 as the <term>correction</term> to be found relates to the difference

I add this to the first adjusted parallax and obtain 47' 31'', and this is the required <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent shift in the Moon's position against the background stars when viewed from the Earth's surface instead of its center.</note> of the Moon in the <term>vertical circle</term> <note>The imaginary circle passing through the point directly overhead (zenith) and the object in the sky.</note>.<sup>334)</sup> However, since the other lunar parallaxes differ so little from those occurring at the full and new moon, it seems sufficient to always remain within the mean limits which we most commonly use for the prediction of eclipses. For the rest, such a high degree of precision is not required, as it might perhaps serve curiosity more than practical application.

## Chapter 26.

### How the Parallaxes of Longitude and Latitude are Distinguished.

Parallax is simply distinguished by longitude and latitude; that is, the distance between the Sun and Moon <note>Meaning the displacement of the observed position from the true position.</note> is broken down into arcs or angles of the intersecting circles: the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The path the Sun appears to take across the sky over a year.</note> and the vertical circle. If the vertical circle stands perpendicular to the ecliptic, there is no <term>longitude parallax</term> <note>Displacement along the path of the ecliptic.</note>; rather, the entire parallax is transferred to <term>latitude</term> <note>Displacement perpendicular to the ecliptic.</note>, since the vertical circle and the circle of latitude coincide. However, if it happens that the ecliptic intersects the horizon perpendicularly and thus coincides with the vertical circle, and the Moon is located on the ecliptic, there is exclusively a longitude parallax. If the Moon deviates from the ecliptic, it does not entirely lose its longitude parallax.

For example, if **abc** is the ecliptic, which stands perpendicular to the horizon (whose pole let be **a**), then **abc**

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a spherical triangle and arcs. A vertical line labeled with points 'a', 'b', and 'c' (from top to bottom) is intersected at point 'b' by an arc labeled 'dbe' (left to right). Lines connect apex 'a' to points 'd' and 'e', forming an outer triangle 'ade'. Point 'b' lies on the central vertical axis.</image-desc>

is also the vertical circle of the Moon, to which no latitude is attributed. Let its position be **b**, and its entire parallax **bc** falls into longitude. But if the Moon also has a latitude, we place the circle **dbe** through the poles of the ecliptic, and then **db** or **be** may be the latitude of the Moon. Now it is obvious: that neither **ad** nor **ae** is equal to **ab**, nor are the angles at **d** and **e** right angles, for **da** and **ae** do not pass through the poles of **dbe**; and the parallax will participate more in latitude the closer the Moon stands to the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly above the observer.</note>. For if the base **de** of the triangle **ade** remains the same, the sides **ad** and **ae** will form more acute angles with the base the shorter they are; and the further the Moon stands from the zenith, the more these same angles will resemble right angles.

Now, let the vertical circle **dbe** of the Moon stand obliquely to the ecliptic **abc**, and let the Moon have no latitude, but stand at point **b** of the ecliptic; let the parallax in the vertical circle be **be**. We construct the arc **ef** of a circle that passes through the poles of **abc**: thus, in the triangle **bef**, the angle **ebf**...

We also obtain the **apparent latitude** from the parallax of latitude by adding the latter if they are on the same side; if they are on different sides, the smaller is subtracted from the larger, and the remainder is the apparent latitude toward the side on which the larger of the two lies.

## Chapter 27.

### **Confirmation of what has been developed regarding the parallax of the Moon.**

That the parallaxes of the Moon developed in this way agree with observations can be confirmed through several other sightings. We performed one such observation at Bologna on the 9th of March after sunset in the year of Christ 1497. We observed the Moon during its impending <term>occultation</term> <note>An event where the Moon passes in front of a star or planet, hiding it from view.</note> of the bright star of the Hyades, which the Romans call **Palilicium** <note>The star known today as Aldebaran, the "Eye of the Bull" in the constellation Taurus.</note>, and while waiting at the end of the 5th hour of the night, we saw the star just disappearing against the dark part of the lunar body between the Moon's horns, closer to the southern horn by about one-third of the Moon's diameter. Since the star was calculated to be at 2° 52' of Gemini with a southern latitude of 5 1/6°, it was clear that the center of the Moon was apparently ahead of the star by half its diameter, and therefore its apparent position in longitude was 2° 36' and in latitude nearly 5° 6'. From the beginning of the years of Christ, there were now 1497 Egyptian...

## Chapter 28.

### On the Mean Conjunction and Opposition of the Sun and the Moon.

From what has been said so far regarding the motion of the Moon and the Sun, the method for investigating their <term>conjunctions</term> <note>When the Sun and Moon align at the same longitude; a New Moon.</note> and <term>oppositions</term> <note>When the Sun and Moon are on opposite sides of the Earth; a Full Moon.</note> also becomes clear. Specifically, for a time that is close to the estimated moment of a conjunction or opposition, we look for the mean motion of the Moon. If this motion results in a value equal to a full circle, we recognize it as a conjunction; a half-circle indicates a Full Moon. However, since this will only rarely happen exactly: the distance between the two must be observed and then divided by the daily motion of the Moon. This allows us to learn how much time has passed since the event or how much time remains until it occurs, depending on whether the motion is calculated as greater or smaller. For this specific time, we then seek the movements and the positions, calculating the true New and Full Moons through them, and we distinguish the <term>eclipses</term> from the other occurrences, as we intend to describe further below. Once we have established this: the same can be applied to any other point in time and thus even to a span of many years. This is done with the help of the table containing the times of the twelve months and the mean motions of the anomaly of the Sun and Moon, as well as the latitude of the Moon; each of these is to be combined with the individual mean motions found previously. We also add the adjusted anomaly of the Sun so that we have it immediately at hand; for its change is not noticed in one or even several years due to the slowness of its beginning—that is, the <term>apogee</term> <note>original: "Abside"; the point in an orbit farthest from the center of attraction.</note>.

# Chapter 29.

## Investigation into the True Conjunctions and Oppositions of the Sun and the Moon.

When we have obtained the time of the mean <term>conjunction</term> <note>The alignment of two celestial bodies, specifically the "New Moon" when the Sun and Moon are at the same longitude.</note> or <term>opposition</term> <note>The position of two celestial bodies when they are on opposite sides of the sky, specifically the "Full Moon."</note> of these two celestial bodies in the manner described, along with their movement, their true distance—by which they precede or follow one another—is necessary to find the true conjunction or opposition. For if the Moon precedes the Sun in the conjunction or opposition, it is clear that the true event will only occur once the Sun has already passed the sought-after true position. This is determined, however, from the respective <term>prosthaphaereses</term> <note>original: "Prosthaphaeresen"; from Greek meaning "addition and subtraction." These are the mathematical corrections used to account for the difference between a body's mean (average) position and its true (observed) position.</note> of both.

If both corrections are zero or equal and have the same signs—that is, if both must be added or both must be subtracted—then the true conjunctions or oppositions clearly coincide with the mean ones at the same moment in time. However, if they are unequal, their difference itself reveals the distance between the two bodies; it indicates which body precedes or follows based on whether the correction is to be added or subtracted. But if both have different signs, then the body whose correction must be subtracted precedes by an even greater margin, while their sum provides the total distance between the bodies.

We can estimate this distance based on how much the Moon can travel in whole hours, by calculating two hours for every degree of distance. For example, if the distance is approximately 6°, we take 12 hours. For this determined time interval, we seek the true movement of the Moon relative to the Sun. This is easily carried out, as we know that the mean motion of the Moon covers 1° 1′ in two hours, but that the hourly and true motion of the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The irregular movement of a celestial body in its orbit, specifically the angle measuring its position relative to its closest or furthest point from Earth.</note> near the full and new moon is nearly 50′. This results in a uniform motion of 3° over six hours, and as many minutes as the true motion of the anomaly contains five degrees.

With this, we search the table of lunar corrections for the difference between the corrections and add it to the mean motion if the anomaly is in the lower part of the circle, but subtract it if it lies in the upper part. This sum or difference is then the true motion of the Moon during the hours in question. This movement is sufficient if it equals the previously existing distance; otherwise, we divide the distance (multiplied by the number of estimated hours) by this motion, or divide the simple distance by the obtained true hourly motion. We then obtain the true difference in time between the mean and true conjunction or opposition in hours and minutes. We add these to the mean time of the conjunction or opposition if the Moon is ahead of the Sun, or if it stands diametrically opposite the location of the Sun.

...but subtract them if the Moon follows the Sun: and in this way, we obtain the time of the true <term>conjunction</term> <note>The moment of the "New Moon" when the Sun and Moon share the same celestial longitude.</note> or <term>opposition</term> <note>The moment of the "Full Moon" when the Sun and Moon are directly opposite each other in the sky.</note>. Although we must admit that the irregularity of the Sun still changes this somewhat, it is rightly neglected here, as in the entire course of the calculation—even at the greatest distance, which extends over seven degrees—it cannot amount to even one minute. Therefore, this method of determining the <term>lunations</term> <note>The period of time between two successive identical phases of the moon, such as from new moon to new moon.</note> is more reliable than any other. For if one bases it only on the <term>hourly movement</term> of the Moon, which is called the <term>hourly excess</term> <note>The difference between the Moon's faster hourly speed and the Sun's slower hourly speed.</note>, one is sometimes deceived and is more often required to repeat the calculation; for the <term>hourly movement</term> of the Moon is variable and does not remain the same. For the time of the true <term>conjunction</term> or <term>opposition</term>, we also calculate the true movement of the <term>latitude</term> <note>The Moon's distance north or south of the ecliptic, which determines if its shadow will hit the Earth or if the Earth's shadow will hit it.</note> in order to learn the <term>latitude</term> of the Moon; and also the true location of the Sun from the <term>vernal equinox</term> <note>original: "Frühlingsnachtgleichenpunkte"; the point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator, marking the start of spring.</note> in the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note>, to recognize from this whether the Moon stands in <term>conjunction</term> or <term>opposition</term>; and since the time found in this way is mean and uniform <term>Krakow time</term> <note>Krakow was used as the reference meridian for many Central European astronomical tables in the 15th and 16th centuries, including those used by Copernicus.</note>, we <term>reduce</term> <note>Convert or adjust the mathematical value.</note> it to true time in the manner previously specified. If we then wish to transfer this to places other than Krakow, we take their longitude into account, allowing 4 minutes of time for every degree of this longitude, and 4 seconds of time for every minute of longitude, and add this to the <term>Krakow time</term> if the place lies to the east, but subtract it if the place lies to the west; and this sum or difference is then the time of the <term>conjunction</term> or <term>opposition</term> of the Sun and the Moon.

# Chapter 30.

## How one distinguishes the conjunctions or oppositions of the Sun and the Moon which are accompanied by eclipses from the others.

Whether <term>conjunctions</term> or <term>oppositions</term> are linked with eclipses or not is easily recognized in the case of the Moon. Specifically, if its <term>latitude</term> is smaller than the sum of the radii of the Moon and the shadow, a <term>lunar eclipse</term> occurs; if it is larger, such an eclipse does not occur. But with the Sun, this presents more difficulty, because the <term>parallaxes</term> <note>The difference in the apparent position of a celestial body as viewed from different points on Earth; this is why a solar eclipse might be visible in one city but not in another.</note> of both bodies have an influence, whereby a visible <term>conjunction</term> mostly differs from a true one. If, therefore, for the time of the true <term>conjunction</term> itself, and for the period of one hour before the true <term>conjunction</term> in the eastern, and after it in the western <term>quadrants</term> <note>A 90-degree section of the sky.</note> of the <term>ecliptic</term>, we have calculated the <term>longitude parallax</term> <note>The shift in the Moon's apparent position along its orbital path due to the observer's location.</note> between the Sun and Moon, we then seek the apparent longitude of the Moon from the Sun, in order to learn by how much the Moon's appearance moves away from the Sun in one hour. If we <term>divide</term> <note>original: "dividiren"</note> that <term>longitude parallax</term> by this hourly movement, we obtain the time—

difference between the true and apparent <term>conjunction</term> <note>The moment when the Sun and Moon align in the same celestial longitude.</note>. If this is subtracted from the true time of the conjunction in the eastern quadrant of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note>, and added to it in the western quadrant (for here the apparent conjunction precedes the true, whereas there it follows it), one obtains the required time of the appearing conjunction. For this time, we now calculate—through the explained <term>parallax</term> <note>The difference in the apparent position of a celestial body when viewed from the Earth's surface versus its center.</note> of the Sun—the apparent latitude of the Moon from the Sun, or the distance between the centers of the Sun and the Moon at the apparent conjunction. If this latitude is greater than half the sum of the diameters of the Sun and Moon, no solar eclipse occurs; but if it is smaller, such an event takes place. And from this it follows that, if the Moon has no <term>longitude parallax</term> <note>An apparent shift in the Moon's position along the path of the ecliptic due to the observer's location on Earth.</note> at the time of the true conjunction, the apparent conjunction coincides with the true. This occurs at the 90th degree of the ecliptic, taken from the East or West.

## Chapter 31.

### **How great a solar or lunar eclipse will be.**

Once we have recognized a solar or lunar eclipse, we easily find how great it will be; for the Sun, namely, from the apparent <term>latitude difference</term> <note>The vertical distance between the centers of the two celestial bodies in the sky.</note> which exists between the Sun and Moon at the time of the apparent conjunction. For if we subtract this from half the sum of the solar and lunar diameters, we obtain as a remainder that which is eclipsed of the Sun, calculated in diameter. If we multiply this by 12, and divide the product by the Sun's diameter, we obtain the number of eclipsed <term>inches</term> <note>original: "Zolle"; in historical astronomy, these are "digits" (lat. digiti), where the diameter of the celestial body is divided into 12 equal parts to measure the magnitude of the eclipse.</note>. If no latitude difference exists between the Sun and Moon, the Sun is totally eclipsed, or as much as the Moon can cover. We proceed in roughly the same way for a <term>lunar eclipse</term>, except that instead of the apparent latitude difference, we apply the simple latitude. After this has been subtracted from half the sum of the shadow and Moon diameters, the remainder is the eclipsed part of the Moon; provided, that is, the latitude of the Moon is not smaller than the quotient of the Moon's diameter by half the sum of the diameters; for then the Moon is totally eclipsed; and an even smaller latitude results, moreover, in some duration of the eclipse, which will be greatest when the latitude is zero—which, I believe, will be perfectly clear with some reflection. If, however, in a partial lunar eclipse, we multiply the eclipsed part by 12, and divide the product by the diameter of the Moon, we obtain the number of eclipsed inches, exactly as was said for the solar eclipse.

<summary>This page provides the mathematical procedures for determining whether an eclipse will occur based on the Moon's parallax and latitude, and explains how to calculate the magnitude of the eclipse in "inches" (digits).</summary>

## Chapter 32.

### **On Predetermining the Duration of an Eclipse.**

It remains for us to investigate how long an eclipse lasts. In this regard, it should be noted that we treat the arcs that occur between the Sun, Moon, and shadow as straight lines, because their extreme smallness makes no discernible difference compared to straight lines. Let point **a** be the center of the Sun and of the shadow; let the straight line **bc** be the <term>orbit</term> <note>The path the Moon follows through the sky.</note> of the Moon. Let **b** be the center of the Moon at the moment when it touches the edge of the Sun or the shadow at the start of the phenomenon, and **c** the same at the end of the eclipse. Draw lines **ab** and **ac**, and drop a <term>perpendicular</term> <note>original: "Loth"; a line meeting another at a right angle.</note> **ad** onto **bc**:

<image-desc>A geometric line diagram showing a triangle with its apex at point 'a'. The base is a horizontal line segment 'bc'. From apex 'a', lines are drawn to points 'b', 'e', 'd', 'f', and 'c' on the base line. Line 'ad' is the vertical altitude, perpendicular to 'bc'. The points are arranged from left to right as b, e, d, f, c.</image-desc>

Thus it is clear that when the center of the Moon is at **d**, the middle of the eclipse occurs; for **ad** is the shortest of all the lines that can be drawn from **a** to **bc**. **bd** is equal to **dc**, because **ab** and **ac** are the halves of the sum—in a solar eclipse—of the solar and lunar diameters, or—in a lunar eclipse—of the shadow and lunar diameters. Furthermore, **ad** is the true or apparent latitude of the Moon for the middle of the eclipse. If one now subtracts the square of line **ad** from the square of line **ab**, the square of line **bd** remains; consequently, **bd** is also given according to its length. If we divide this by the true <term>hourly motion</term> <note>The distance the Moon travels across the sky in one hour.</note> of the Moon (in a lunar eclipse), or by the apparent motion (in a solar eclipse), we obtain the time of the half-duration. 

Often the Moon remains in the middle of the eclipse for some time, which occurs when the half-sum of the diameters of the Moon and shadow exceeds the latitude of the Moon by more than its diameter, as we have already stated. We take **e** as the center of the Moon at the beginning of the <term>total eclipse</term> <note>The phase where the Moon is completely covered by Earth's shadow.</note>, where the Moon touches the periphery of the shadow from the inside, and **f** as the center at the second contact, at which it begins to emerge. By drawing **ae** and **af**, it is shown in the same manner as before that **ed** and **df** represent the halves of the <term>duration</term> <note>original: "Verweilen"; the time spent entirely within the shadow.</note> in the darkness. Since **ad** is known as the latitude of the Moon, and **ae** or **af** is known as the excess of the shadow's radius over the Moon's radius, **de** or **df** is revealed. Dividing these again by the true hourly motion of the Moon gives the sought-after half-time of the duration of totality. 

However, it must be taken into account that the Moon moves in its own orbit and cuts lengths on the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The Sun's apparent path across the celestial sphere.</note> that are not entirely equal to those it covers in its own orbit, and which intersect those circles drawn through the poles of the ecliptic. But the difference is very small, as in the entire 12-degree distance—which approximately constitutes the outermost limits of solar—

# Nicolaus Copernicus’ On the Revolutions.

## Book Five.

So far, we have dealt to the best of our ability with the circular motions of the Earth around the Sun and of the Moon around the Earth. We now move on to the motions of the five planets. The sequence and the sizes of their orbits are in wonderful harmony and reliable proportion with that very motion of the Earth, as we discussed generally in the first book when we showed that those orbits have their centers not so much in the Earth, but rather in the Sun. It remains for us, therefore, to prove all this in more detail and more clearly, and thus fulfill our promise as far as we are able, by utilizing especially the observations of phenomena that we have taken from both ancient and our own times, establishing through them the relationship of those motions more securely.<note>This is note 338 from the German source text, likely referencing specific astronomical tables or earlier commentators.</note> These five heavenly bodies <note>original: Gestirne</note> are named in Plato’s *Timaeus*, each according to its particular nature: Saturn, the Shining <note>original: φαίνων (phainon)</note>, as if the bright or visible one, for it is hidden for the shortest amount of time and reappears faster than the others after it has been obscured by the Sun; Jupiter, the Radiant <note>original: φαέθων (phaethon)</note>, from its brilliance; Mars, the Fiery <note>original: πυρόεις (pyroeis)</note>, from its fiery glow; Venus, sometimes the Light-Bringer <note>original: φωσφόρος (phosphoros)</note>, sometimes the Evening Star <note>original: ἔσπερος (hesperos)</note>, insofar as it shines either in the morning or the evening; finally, Mercury, the Sparkling <note>original: στίλβων (stilbon)</note>, from its sparkling and flickering light. — All of these move with greater deviations in longitude and latitude than the Moon.

---

### Chapter 1.

### On the Circular Motions of the Planets and Their Mean Motions.

---

Two very different motions in longitude appear in the planets: one arises from the aforementioned motion of the Earth, while the other is peculiar to each of them. The first has

--- Page 283 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to Book Five. Following the description of the individual planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury), Copernicus begins to explain how the Earth's own motion creates the illusion of irregular planetary paths, a concept he calls the "motion of parallax."</meta>

...is not without reason called the **motion of parallax**, because it is this which produces the appearances of **stations** <note>points in an orbit where a planet appears to stop moving before changing direction</note> and the **prograde** <note>moving forward</note> and **retrograde** <note>moving backward</note> movements in the appearance of all planets. This occurs not because the planet itself possesses these irregularities in its own motion—for the planet is always prograde in its own movement—but because this appears so according to the measure of the parallax, as conditioned by the motion of the Earth depending on the difference and the size of those orbits.

It follows, therefore, that the true positions of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are only perceptible to us when they rise in the evening <note>this refers to "opposition," when the Earth is directly between the planet and the Sun</note>, which occurs approximately in the middle of their retrograde movements; for then they stand in a straight line with the mean position of the Sun and are free from that parallax. With Venus and Mercury, the relationship is different. These are, when they stand in full light, invisible, and show themselves only in their deviations, which they make from the Sun to one side or the other, so that they are never found free of that parallax.

Thus, a specific parallactic revolution belongs to each planet—I call this the motion of the Earth in relation to the planet <gloss>339)</gloss>—and the planets exhibit the same toward one another. We claim, namely, that the parallactic motion is nothing other than that difference by which the mean movement of the Earth exceeds the movement of the planets (as with Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars) or is exceeded by the latter (as with Venus and Mercury). 

But since these periods of parallax are found to be unequal by a noticeable difference, the ancients believed that the movements of the planets were also non-uniform, and that their orbits possessed **apsides** <term>apsides: the points in an orbit where a planet is at its maximum or minimum distance from the center of its motion</term> at which their non-uniformities recurred, and that these had their unchangeable places in the sphere of the fixed stars. Through this, the way was opened to investigate the mean movements of the planets and their uniform periods. For, if one had received the transmitted position of any one of them according to its determined distance from the Sun and a fixed star, and recognized that the planet had returned to the same place after a certain period of time at the same distance from the Sun: then the planet seemed to have traversed all its non-uniformities and, through all these, returned to its previous position relative to the Earth. 

And so, from the time that had elapsed, one calculated the number of complete, uniform revolutions, and from these, the specific movements of the heavenly body. Ptolemy reworked these revolutions—as far as he indicates having received them from Hipparchus—anew according to **solar years** <gloss>340)</gloss>. By solar years, he wants to be understood those which are calculated from the **equinox** <note>original: Nachtgleichenpunkt</note> or from the **solstice** <note>original: Solstitium</note>. It has already been shown, however, that such years are not entirely equal; therefore, we make use of those calculated according to the fixed stars, and accordingly, the movements of those five stars have been corrected and established by us, insofar as we have found that they...

<summary>Copernicus explains that the apparent retrograde motion of planets is an illusion caused by the Earth's own movement (parallax) and argues for using sidereal years (fixed stars) rather than solar years (equinoxes) for more accurate astronomical calculations.</summary>

# PARALLACTIC MOVEMENT OF JUPITER FROM YEAR TO YEAR AND FROM SIXTY TO SIXTY YEARS.

<note>In the context of early modern astronomy, "parallactic movement" refers to the change in a planet's apparent position caused by the Earth's own motion around the Sun. For Jupiter, this table helps calculate the "anomaly"—the difference between its average orbital position and where it actually appears in the sky due to our changing vantage point.</note>

## Chapter 2.

### Presentation of the Uniform and Apparent Movement of the Planets According to the View of the Ancients.

This, then, is the nature of the mean <note>The "mean" movement refers to the idealized, average speed of a planet if its orbit were a perfect circle.</note> movements of the planets; we now turn to those that are apparent and non-uniform. The ancient mathematicians, who held the Earth to be immovable, imagined for Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus <term>eccentric epicycles</term> <note>A system where a planet moves on a small circle (epicycle), which itself moves along a larger circle (deferent) whose center is offset from the Earth.</note> and, in addition, another eccentric circle, in relation to which the epicycle moved uniformly, just as the planet moved within the epicycle. Let, for ex-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of planetary motion according to the Ptolemaic system. It depicts a large outer circle (the eccentric) and inner circles. A vertical diameter is labeled with points a (top), f, c (center of the eccentric), e, d (center of the Earth), b, and g. A smaller circle, the epicycle, is centered on point h, which lies on the periphery of an inner circle fg. Lines ihc and lme are drawn from points c and e through the center of the epicycle h, intersecting the epicycle at points i, k, l, and m.</image-desc>

ample, *ab* be the eccentric circle, *c* its center, and *acb* its diameter; let the center of the Earth lie at *d*, so that *a* is the <term>apogee</term> <note>original: "Apogeum"; the point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion.</note> and *b* is the <term>perigee</term> <note>original: "Perigeum"; the point in an orbit closest to the center of motion.</note>; let *dc* be bisected at point *e*, and around *e* a second circle *fg*, equal to the first but eccentric, be described; in its periphery, take any point *h* to be a center, and describe around it the epicycle *ik*; through its center, draw the straight lines *ihc* and *lhme*. One should imagine, however, the plane of the eccentric circle to be inclined against that of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The sun's apparent path across the sky; the plane of the Earth's orbit.</note> and also the plane of the epicycle against the plane of the eccentric circle, according to the latitude <note>The vertical distance a planet appears above or below the ecliptic.</note> which the planet displays. For the sake of presentation, let both circles initially lie in one and the same plane. Now, it is claimed that this entire plane, with points *e* and *c*, rotates around the center *d* of the ecliptic, following the movement of the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>Stars that do not seem to move relative to one another, unlike the "wandering" planets.</note>. This is intended to be understood such that those points *e* and *c* have their imagined locations within the sphere of the fixed stars. The epicycle is said to move along the periphery of the circle *fhg*, likewise following the movement of the fixed stars, but according to the line *ihc*, in relation to which the planet revolves uniformly within the epicycle *ik*. However, it is certain that the uniform motion of the epicycle must occur in relation to the center *e* of its carrying circle, and the revolution of the planet in relation to the line *lme*. Thus, one allows that a uniform circular motion can exist here around a foreign center, rather than its own <note>This refers to the "equant" problem, where Ptolemy assumed a planet's speed was uniform relative to a point other than the center of its orbit, which many later astronomers found physically impossible.</note>. Similarly, this is said to apply even more to Mercury; however, this has already been sufficiently refuted in the case of the Moon ³¹²) <note>original: "Mond". Note 312 likely refers to a previous proof in the manuscript showing that the Moon's observed size didn't match the predictions of the eccentric/epicycle model.</note>. This and similar points have led us to assume a movement of the Earth and another method of derivation, through which uniformity and the foundation of science are preserved, and the cause of the non-uniformity in the appearance is rendered more reliable.

<summary>This page explains the complex Ptolemaic system of eccentrics and epicycles used by "the ancients" to explain planetary motion. The author critiques these models for requiring uniform motion around a center that is not the orbit's own center, using this as justification for proposing a heliocentric (Earth-moving) system.</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemaic system, eccentrics, epicycles, apogee, perigee, ecliptic, uniform motion, equant, Mercury, Moon, planetary theory</keywords>

# Chapter 3.

## General Presentation of the Non-uniformity Appearing Due to the Earth’s Motion.

Since there are two causes by which the uniform motion of a planet appears non-uniform—namely, the motion of the Earth and the planet's own motion—we wish to explain each of these in general and separately through a visual representation, so that they may be better distinguished from one another. We shall begin with that <term>non-uniformity</term> <note>original: "Ungleichmässigkeit"; in astronomy, this refers to "inequality," or the observed variation in a planet's speed and direction compared to a perfectly circular path.</note> which occurs for everyone because of the motion of the Earth, and specifically first in relation to Venus and Mercury, which are enclosed by the Earth’s circular orbit.

Let the circle **ab** be <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circle whose center does not coincide with the center of another circle—in this case, the Sun.</note> to the Sun, and let the center of the Earth describe this circle in its annual revolution in the manner previously described; let **c** be its center. For now, we assume that the planet has no other non-uniformity than that which will occur if the circular orbit **de** of Venus or Mercury is concentric with **ab**. Although this orbit must be inclined toward **ab** because of its latitude <note>The vertical distance of a planet above or below the ecliptic plane.</note>, for the sake of a clearer presentation, let us imagine it as lying in the same plane as **ab**.

Assume the Earth is at point **a**. From this point, draw the <term>lines of sight</term> <note>original: "Absehenslinien"; the lines representing the observer's view from Earth to the planet.</note> **afl** and **agm**, which touch the planet's orbit at points **f** and **g**, and furthermore, draw the diameter **acb** common to both. Let the motion of both—the Earth and the planet—take place in the same direction, that is, <term>prograde</term> <note>original: "rechtläufig"; moving forward in the order of the zodiac signs (west to east).</note>, and let the planet’s motion be faster than the Earth's. To an eye located at **a**, the point **c** (and thus also the line **acb**) will seem to move in accordance with the <term>mean motion</term> <note>The idealized, average speed of the Sun.</note> of the Sun. The planet, however, in the circle **dfg**—as if in an <term>epicycle</term>—will travel through the arc **fdg** in a prograde direction over a longer period, and the arc **gcf** in a <term>retrograde</term> <note>original: "rückläufig"; appearing to move backward (east to west) against the stars.</note> direction in a shorter period. In the former case, the entire angle **fag** must be added to the mean motion of the Sun; in the latter, it must be subtracted from it.

Now, when the subtractive motion of the planet becomes greater than the additive motion of point **c**—especially in the region of the <term>perigee</term> <note>original: "Perigeum"; the point in the orbit closest to the Earth.</note> **e**—the planet appears to the observer at point **a** to move backward due to its faster speed. This occurs with the planets considered here because the ratio of the line **ce** to **ae** is greater than the ratio of the motion at **a** to the motion of the planet, according to the theorems of <note>Apollonius of Perga was a 3rd-century BCE Greek geometer whose work on "stations" defined the exact points where a planet appears to stop and change direction.</note> Apollonius of Perga, as shall be shown further below. But if the subtractive motion is equal to the additive motion, they cancel each other out, and the planet appears to stand still—all of which occurs in the observed phenomena. If, therefore, no other in-

<image-desc>
A geometric diagram illustrating planetary motion from a heliocentric perspective. A large outer circle (the Earth's orbit) contains a smaller inner circle (the orbit of Venus or Mercury). A vertical diameter line is labeled with "b" at the top, "c" at the center, and "a" at the bottom (representing the Earth's position). Two tangent lines, "agm" on the left and "afl" on the right, extend from the Earth at "a" and touch the sides of the inner orbit at "g" and "f". The inner circle's highest point is "d" (apogee) and its lowest is "e" (perigee).
</image-desc>

<summary>This page explains how the Earth's orbital motion creates the visual illusion of planets (specifically Venus and Mercury) slowing down, stopping, or moving backward. It introduces a geometric model where the planet's path acts like an epicycle relative to the moving Earth.</summary>

<keywords>planetary motion, non-uniformity, Venus, Mercury, prograde, retrograde, perigee, Apollonius of Perga, heliocentrism, lines of sight</keywords>

--- Page 298 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of planetary motion from a Copernican perspective. While the previous page focused on the interior planets (Venus and Mercury), this page transitions into explaining how the Earth's motion affects our observation of the "superior" planets (Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars) and why simple concentric circles do not fully explain the data.</meta>

If a certain <term>uniformity</term> <note>original: "Gleichmässigkeit"; in astronomy, this refers to a planet moving at a constant speed along its path.</note> in the movement of the planet existed, as Apollonius thought, this might be sufficient. However, the greatest <term>elongations</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from the Sun as seen from Earth.</note> of these planets from the Sun—measured by the angles **fae** and **gae** in the morning or evening—do not always appear equal. They are not equal on either side, nor in their sums, nor among themselves on one side; from this, it is clearly suspected that their revolutions do not occur in circles concentric with the Earth’s orbit, but rather in certain other paths through which they produce a second non-uniformity. The same can also be proven for the <term>superior planets</term>—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—which move in all directions around the Earth. To explain the 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two concentric circles representing planetary orbits. A central vertical axis passes through points d (at the top, outside the circles), a (top of inner circle), c (center), b (bottom of inner circle), and e (bottom of outer circle). Two lines originate from point d and are tangent to the inner circle at points f and g. The diagram illustrates the angular relationship between a planet and the Earth's orbit.</image-desc>

again-constructed circle of the Earth, let the outer concentric circle **de** be described, initially in the same plane, and let the position of the planet be assumed at any point **d**. From this point, straight lines **df** and **dg** are drawn, which touch the path of the Earth at points **f** and **g**; let **dacbe** be the common diameter. It is clear that, seen from point **a**, the true position of the planet only appears in the line **de** when it rises in the evening and stands closest to the Earth; for seen from the opposite point **b**, although it stands in the same line and in full light, it does not appear at all because of the intervention of the Sun at point **c**. Because the speed of the Earth is greater than that of the planet, the Earth seems to accelerate the motion of the planet by the entire angle **gdf** in the <term>apogeal</term> <note>original: "apogeisch"; referring here to the arc of the orbit furthest from the planet's perspective.</note> arc **fgb**, and to slow it down in the other arc **gaf**—and indeed for a shorter time in the smaller arc **gaf**. And when the motion of the Earth to be subtracted is greater than the corresponding motion of the planet, particularly in the region of point **a**, the planet appears to be displaced by the Earth, to move <term>retrograde</term> <note>original: "rückläufig"; the illusion of a planet moving backward in the sky.</note>, and to stand still where the difference between these two opposite movements appears smallest to the eye. Thus, it is again clear that through the single motion of the Earth, everything occurs that the ancients sought to derive through <term>epicycles</term> <note>A mathematical tool used by ancient astronomers like Ptolemy to explain why planets seem to change speed and direction.</note> for each individual planet. However, since—contrary to the opinion of Apollonius and the ancients—the motion of a planet is found not to be uniform, as the non-uniform orbital motion of the Earth is transferred to the planet, the planets do not move in concentric circles, but in another way, which we shall describe immediately.

## Chapter 4.

### **In what manner the proper motions of the planets appear non-uniform.**

Since the proper motions of the planets in terms of longitude follow almost the same law—with the exception of Mercury, which differs from the others—those four <note>Referring to Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus, which were known to the ancients alongside Mercury.</note> shall be treated together; however, a different place is assigned to Mercury. What the ancients <note>Referring to earlier astronomers like Ptolemy.</note> considered a single movement in two eccentric circles—as we have illustrated—we regard as two uniform movements from which the apparent <term>non-uniformity</term> <note>original: "Ungleichmässigkeit"; when a planet's speed or path appears to change to an observer even if its actual motion is steady.</note> is composed. This occurs either in an eccentric circle of an eccentric circle, or in an <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle.</note> of an epicycle, or even in an eccentric epicycle, all of which can produce the same non-uniformity, as we have previously demonstrated with the Sun and the Moon. 

Let **ab** be an <term>eccentric circle</term> <note>A circle whose center is shifted away from the center of the observer's position.</note> around the center **c**. Let its diameter **acb** be the line of the mean position of the Sun passing through the highest and lowest <term>apsides</term> <note>original: "Abside"; the points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the center of motion (apogee and perigee).</note> of the planet, and on this line let **d** be the center of the Earth’s orbit, such that **a** is the highest apsis. With one third of the distance **cd**, let the epicycle **ef** be constructed, in whose <term>perigee</term> <note>original: "Perigeum"; the point in the orbit of the planet where it is nearest to the center of its motion.</note> **f** the planet may stand.

and indeed both—namely the motion of the **epicycle** and that of the planet—move in matching cycles. Thus it will happen that, while the epicycle is at the highest **apsis** <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion.</note> of the **eccentric circle** and the planet is at the **perigee** <note>The point in the planet's small circular path (epicycle) that is closest to its own center.</note> of the epicycle, on the other side they will find themselves in opposite positions once each has completed its half-circle. In the **quadrants** <note>The four 90-degree quarters of a circle.</note> lying between these two, each will be at its middle apsis. Only in the first two positions do the diameters of the epicycle lie on the line *ab*; in the latter two, however, they stand perpendicular to *ab*. At all other points, they will lean toward *ab* at an acute or obtuse angle, all of which can be easily deduced from their movements.

From this, it also follows that the planet, in this combined motion, does not describe a perfect circle as the ancient mathematicians believed, though the deviation is nearly imperceptible. To demonstrate this, let the same epicycle be constructed around center *b*, called *kl*; likewise around point *g*, which is one quadrant away from *a*, let there be the epicycle *hi*. Finally, let *cm* be one third of *cd* and equal to *gi*. Let lines *gc* and *im* be drawn, intersecting at *q*. Now, since by our assumption the arc *ag* is similar to the arc *hi*, and the angle *acg* is a right angle, then the angle *hgi* is also a right angle. The vertical angles at *q* are also equal; therefore, the triangles *giq* and *qcm* have equal angles and matching sides, because *gi* was made equal to *cm*. Consequently, *qi* and *gq* are respectively equal to *qm* and *qc*. Since *qi* and *qm* face the larger angle, the entire line *iqm* is larger than the entire line *gqc*. However, *fm*, *ml*, *ac*, and *cg* are all equal to one another. If one now describes a circle around the center *m* through points *f* and *l*, which is thus equal to circle *ab*, it will intersect the line *im*. The same result occurs on the other side in the other quadrant. Therefore, by virtue of the uniform motion of the epicycle on the eccentric circle and the planet's own motion on the epicycle, the planet does not describe a perfect circle, but only something approximating it, which was to be proven <gloss>343)</gloss>. <note>Note 343 likely refers to a scholarly commentary on the geometric proof that planetary paths are slightly "oval" rather than perfectly circular in this specific model.</note>

At *r* is the **true apogee** <note>The point where the Earth appears furthest from the planet.</note> of the Earth in relation to the planet, and at *s* is the **mean apogee**. The angle *rds* (or *idp*) is therefore the difference between the mean and the apparent motion—namely, the difference between angles *acg* and *cdi*.

We begin, therefore, with Saturn, and take three of the opposition positions of the same once observed by Ptolemy. ## Chapter 6.

### Concerning Three Other Recently Observed Oppositions of Saturn.

However, since the calculation of Saturn's motion provided by <term>Ptolemy</term><note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the influential Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose planetary models the author is here refining.</note> differs significantly from our own time, and because it might not be immediately obvious where the error lies, we were compelled to make new observations. From these, we have once again obtained three midnight <term>culminations</term><note>The moment when a celestial body crosses the observer's meridian and reaches its highest point in the sky.</note>. The first took place in the year of Christ 1514 on May 5th, 1 1/5 hours before midnight, and Saturn was at 205° 24'. The second was in the year of Christ 1520 on July 13th <note>359) Copernicus originally wrote July 13, though some tables suggest minor variations.</note> at noon; Saturn was at 273° 25' <note>360) In the zodiac, this corresponds to 3° 25' of Capricorn.</note>. The third was in the year of Christ 1527 on October 10th, 6 2/3 hours after midnight; Saturn was at 0° 7' from the <term>Horn of the Ram</term><note>original: "Horn des Widders"; a reference to the First Point of Aries, the zero-point of the zodiac used to measure celestial longitude.</note>.

During this time, the appearing motion of Saturn is 68° 1'. From the second to the third opposition, there are 7 Egyptian years, 89 days, and 46 minutes, and the appearing motion of the star was 86° 42'. The mean motion of Saturn amounted to 75° 39' <note>361)</note> in the first period, and 88° 29' <note>362)</note> in the second. Now, according to the rule of Ptolemy, in seeking the highest apsis and the <term>eccentricity</term><note>A measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>, one must proceed as if the planet moved in a simple eccentric circle. Although this will not be sufficient, we shall nonetheless approach the truth and finally reach it. Let *abc* be the circle in which the planet moves uniformly; let the first opposition be at point *a*, the second at *b*, and the third at *c*. Let point *d* be assumed as the center of the Earth.

# Chapter 8.

## On the Determination of the Positions of Saturn.

From the beginning of the Christian era until the twentieth year of Hadrian <note>Publius Aelius Hadrianus, Roman Emperor from 117 to 138 AD. Ptolemy’s astronomical work relied heavily on observations from this period.</note> on the 24th of Mesori <note>The twelfth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note>, one hour before noon, when Ptolemy's observation took place, 135 Egyptian years, 222 days, and 27 minutes <gloss><sup>375)</sup></gloss> <note>Original: "27<sup>I</sup>". In early astronomy, these Roman numerals often refer to sexagesimal fractions of a day (1/60th).</note> have elapsed. During this time, the <term>parallactic motion</term> <note>In the Copernican system, this refers to the apparent motion of the planet caused by the Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note> of Saturn amounts to 328° 55' <gloss><sup>376)</sup></gloss>. Subtracting this from 174° 44' leaves a remainder of 205° 49' as the position of the distance of the mean position of the Sun from the mean position of Saturn. This is the parallactic motion of the latter at midnight, when the first of January begins. From the first <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used by the ancient Greeks for timekeeping; the first began in 776 BC.</note> until this point in time, for 745 Egyptian years and 12 1/2 days, the motion (excluding full revolutions) amounts to 70° 55'. Subtracting this from those 205° 49' leaves a remainder of 134° 54' for the beginning of the Olympiads at noon on the 1st of Hekatombäon <note>The first month of the Attic (Greek) calendar.</note>. From that point, in 351 Egyptian years and 247 days, the same motion (excluding full revolutions) amounts to 13° 7'. Adding this to the previous figure gives 148° 1' as the position for the beginning of the years of Alexander the Great at noon on the 1st of <term>Thoth</term> <note>The first month of the Egyptian calendar.</note> of the Egyptians. And up to the time of Caesar, in 278 Egyptian years and 118 1/2 days, the motion is 247° 20', and thus the position is 35° 21' at midnight, when the first of January begins.

# Chapter 9.

## On the Parallaxes of Saturn Resulting from the Earth's Annual Orbit, and How Great Its Distance Is.

The uniform and apparent motions of Saturn's longitude are set forth in this manner. The remaining phenomena that occur with it are, as stated, <term>parallaxes</term> <note>The displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</note> which result from the annual orbit of the Earth. For just as the circumference of the Earth acts parallactically in relation to the distance of the Moon, so too must its orbit, in which it revolves annually, act upon the five planets; however, these latter parallaxes are far more noticeable because of the great size of the orbit. Such parallaxes, however, cannot be determined unless the distance of the planet has been established beforehand. Yet, this distance can already be obtained through any single observation of the parallax. We conducted such an observation of Saturn in the year of Christ 1514 on the 25th of February, 5 <term>equinoctial hours</term> <note>Hours of equal length (60 minutes), as opposed to seasonal hours which varied with the length of the day.</note> after midnight. The position of Saturn was thus given by these stars. From the beginning of the Christian era until the hour of the observation, 1514 Egyptian years, 67 days, and 13 minutes <gloss><sup>378)</sup></gloss> have passed, and therefore the calculated mean position of the Sun is 315° 41' <gloss><sup>379)</sup></gloss>, the paral-

## Chapter 10.
### Presentations of the Motion of Jupiter.

Having dealt with Saturn, we wish to employ the same method and arrangement of derivation for the motion of Jupiter. We will first take up three positions handed down and calculated by Ptolemy, and restore them through the transformation of the circles shown above, making them either consistent or not deviating much from one another. The first **opposition** <note>The configuration where a planet is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun.</note> took place in the 17th year of Hadrian, on the first day of the Egyptian month Epiphi, one hour before midnight of the following day, and, as he says, at 23º 11' <gloss>386)</gloss> of Scorpio. ## Chapter 12.

### Confirmation of the uniform motion of Jupiter.

It has already been seen further above that at the last of the three oppositions observed by **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose work formed the basis for Western astronomy for over a millennium.</note>, the planet Jupiter stood at 4° 58' according to its mean motion, and at 182° 47' according to its parallactic anomaly. From this, it follows that in the time between the two observations, in addition to full revolutions, the parallactic motion of Jupiter increased by 1° 5', and its own motion increased by approximately 104° 54'. 

The time which elapsed from the first year of **Antoninus** <note>The Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius; his reign is a frequent chronological marker in ancient astronomical records.</note> on the 20th of the Egyptian month **Athyr**, 5 hours after midnight, until the year of Christ 1529 on the 1st of February, 19 hours after midnight, amounts to 1,392 <term>Egyptian years</term> <note>A year of exactly 365 days, without leap years, used by astronomers to make long-term calculations easier.</note>, 99 days, and 37 minutes <note>original: "37^I"; these are "first minutes" or sixtieths of a day.</note>. According to the calculation set forth above, this time corresponds to 1° 5' beyond the full revolutions, during which the Earth overtook Jupiter 1,276 times. In this, we have a reliable and tested figure that agrees with the observations. During this same period, however, both the highest and lowest **apsides** <note>The points in an orbit closest to (perigee) and farthest from (apogee) the center of motion.</note> of the eccentric circle advanced by 4° 30'. If this is distributed uniformly, it results in approximately 1° every 300 years.

## Chapter 14.

### On the determination of the parallaxes of Jupiter, and its distance in comparison to the radius of the Earth's orbit.

To determine the remaining phenomena regarding Jupiter which depend on **parallax** <note>The apparent change in the position of an object when viewed from different locations—in this case, caused by the Earth's movement around the Sun.</note>, we carefully observed its position on February 18, 1520, at 6 hours before noon. Through our instrument, we found that Jupiter was 4° 31' ahead of the brighter first star in the forehead of the **Scorpion** <note>This star is Beta Scorpii, historically used as a fixed reference point in the zodiac.</note>. Since the position of this fixed star is 209° 40', the position of Jupiter is determined to be 205° 9' in relation to the sphere of fixed stars. From the beginning of the Christian era, 1520 uniform years, 62 days, and 15 minutes <note>original: "15^I"</note> had elapsed up to the hour of this observation. From this, the mean motion of the Sun is calculated to be 309° 16', and the **parallactic anomaly** <note>The angle representing the Earth's position relative to the planet's mean position.</note> is 111° 15', whereby the mean position of the planet Jupiter is found at 198° 1'. Since the position of the highest **apsis** <note>The point in an orbit where the planet is farthest from the center of motion.</note> of the eccentric circle in our time has been found to be 159°, the anomaly of Jupiter's eccentric circle was 39° 1'.

From this it also follows that the greatest parallax of Jupiter at apogeum is equal to **10° 35'**, and at perigeum equal to **11° 35'**. Between the two there is a difference of **1°**. With this, both the uniform and the apparent motions of Jupiter are developed.

# Chapter 15.

## On the Planet Mars.

Now we must investigate the movements of **Mars**, by taking three ancient **oppositions** <note>An opposition occurs when a planet is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun; from our perspective, the planet and Sun are 180 degrees apart, making the planet appear brightest.</note>, and combining them with the movement of the Earth that was also taking place at that time. Of those which **Ptolemy** <sup>104)</sup> handed down, the first was in the 15th year of **Hadrian** on the 26th day of the 5th Egyptian month, **Tybi**, one **equinoctial hour** <note>original: "Aequinoctialstunde"; an hour of fixed length (60 minutes), unlike the "seasonal hours" common in antiquity which varied with the length of the day.</note> after the following midnight. He states that Mars stood at **21° of Gemini**, but in relation to the **sphere of the fixed stars**, it was at **74° 20'** <sup>105)</sup>. The second observation he recorded was in the 19th year of Hadrian on the 6th day of the 8th Egyptian month, **Pharmuthi**, 3 hours before the following midnight, at **28° 50' of Leo**, but in relation to the sphere of the fixed stars, it was at **142° 10'**. The third was in the 2nd year of **Antoninus** on the 12th day of the 11th Egyptian month, **Epiphi**, 2 equinoctial hours before the following midnight, at **2° 34' of Sagittarius**, but in relation to the sphere of the fixed stars, it was at **235° 54'**. 

There are, therefore, between the first and second observations, 4 Egyptian years, 69 days, and 20 hours (or 50 minutes of an hour), and the apparent motion of the planet during this time, excluding full rotations, amounted to **67° 50'**. Between the second and third oppositions, there are 4 years, 96 days, and 1 hour (or 2 minutes and 30 seconds of an hour), and the apparent motion of the planet is **93° 44'**. The **mean motion** <note>Mean motion is the theoretical uniform speed of a planet, assuming its orbit were a perfect circle.</note>, however, was **81° 44'** in the first period, excluding full rotations, and **95° 28'** in the second. He found the total distance between the centers to be 12 of such parts, of which the radius of the **eccentric circle** <note>A circle whose center is offset from the center of the universe, used to explain why planets seem to speed up and slow down.</note> contains 60; however, if the latter is assumed to be 10,000, the distance is **2000**. In mean motion, there were **41° 33'** between the first opposition and the **greatest apsis** <note>The "apsis" refers to the point in an orbit where a planet is at its maximum or minimum distance from its center of motion. The "greatest apsis" is the aphelion.</note>, **40° 11'** between the second and the greatest apsis, and **44° 21'** between the third and the **smallest apsis**. 

According to our assumption of uniform motions, however, there lie between the centers of the eccentric circle and the Earth's orbit three-quarters of those 2,000—that is, **1,500**—and the remaining quarter, equal to **500**, is the radius of the **epicycle** <note>A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one.</note>. Based on this, let the eccentric circle *abc* be constructed, let its center be *d*, and let the diameter through both apsides be *fdg*. Upon this line lies the center of the Earth's orbit, and let the points of the observed oppositions be, in order: *a*, *b*, and *c*. Let the arc *af* be equal to **41° 33'** <sup>106)</sup>, *fb* equal to **40° 11'**, and *cg* equal to **44° 21'**. Around the individual points *a*, *b*, and *c*, the epicycles are constructed, whose radii are one-third of the distance *de*, and the lines *ad*, *bd*, and *cd* are drawn. Within the epicycles, however, *al*, *bm*, and *cn* are drawn such that the angles *dal*, *dbm*, and *dcn* are equal to the angles *adf*, *bdf*, and *cdf*.

### Chapter 16.
