## Chapter 17.
## Confirmation of the Motion of Mars.

It was shown above that at the last of the three observations by Ptolemy, Mars was located at 244° 30' according to its mean motion, and at 171° 26' according to its parallactic anomaly. Therefore, in the intervening time, besides the full revolutions, an increase of 5° 38' has occurred. From the second year of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, the Roman Emperor during whose reign the astronomer Ptolemy worked in the 2nd century AD.</note>, the 12th day of the 11th Egyptian month Epiphi, 9 hours after noon—that is, 3 equinoctial hours before midnight of the following day, in relation to the meridian of Krakow—until the year of Christ 1523, the 22nd of February, 7 hours before noon, 1384 Egyptian years <note>Egyptian years: A calendar used by ancient astronomers consisting of exactly 365 days, making it easier to calculate long spans of time.</note>, 251 days, and 19/60ths of a day <note>original: "19<sup>I</sup>" (nineteen sixtieths, often used for minutes of a day).</note> have elapsed. In this time, according to the calculation given above, 5° 38' are added to the 648 full revolutions of the parallactic anomaly. The presumed uniform motion of the sun, however, amounts to 257° 30'; if one subtracts from this the 5° 38' of the parallactic motion, 251° 52' remain as the mean motion of Mars, all of which closely agrees with what was developed above.

## Chapter 18.
## Establishing the Positions of Mars.

One counts 138 Egyptian years, 180 days, and 52/60ths of a day from the beginning of the years of Christ until the 2nd year of Antoninus, the 12th day of the Egyptian month Epiphi, 3 hours before midnight. The parallactic motion during this time amounts to 293° 4'; if one subtracts this from the 171° 26' of the last Ptolemaic observation, there remains—while the number of full revolutions changes—238° 22' for the first year of Christ at midnight on the first of January. ## Chapter 19.

### Determining the Magnitude of the Orbit of Mars in Units of Which the Earth's Orbit is One.

To this end, we have observed a conjunction of Mars with the first bright star of Libra, which is called the Southern Scale <note>original: "südliche Schale"; this star is known today as Alpha Librae or Zubenelgenubi.</note>; this occurred in the year of Christ 1512 on the 1st of January. We found that at 6 equinoctial hours <note>Equinoctial hours are standard hours of equal length (1/24th of a day), regardless of the season.</note> before noon on that day, Mars was at a distance of a quarter of a degree from that fixed star toward the rising of the sun at the solstice <note>original: "Solstitium"; the summer solstice.</note>. This indicated that Mars was separated from the fixed star by 1/8º in longitudinal direction and by 1/5º in northern latitude. Now, the position of the fixed star is 191º 20' from the first star of Aries <note>Aries is the traditional starting point for astronomical measurements in the zodiac.</note>, with a northern latitude of 40'; thus, the position of Mars was at 191º 28' and its northern latitude was 51'. At this time, however, according to the calculation, the parallactic anomaly <term>Parallactic anomaly: The displacement in the apparent position of a planet caused by the Earth's movement in its own orbit.</term> was 98º 28'. The mean position of the sun was 262º, and the mean position of Mars was 163º 32'; its eccentric anomaly <term>Eccentric anomaly: An angular measurement used to describe the position of a body moving along an elliptical or eccentric path.</term> amounted to 43º 52'. Having established this, let the eccentric circle *abc* be described around the center *d*, and let the diameter *adc* be drawn so that *a* is the apogee <note>The point furthest from the sun.</note> and *c* is the perigee <note>The point closest to the sun.</note>. Let the eccentricity *de* be 1460 parts, of which *ad* contains 10,000. The arc *ab* is equal to 43º 52'. Around the center *b*, with a distance *bf* equal to 500 (where 10,000 are in *ad*), let the epicycle <term>Epicycle: A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent), used to explain complex planetary motions.</term> be described; let the angle *dbf* be made equal to angle *adb*, and let the lines *bd*, *be*, and *fe* be drawn. Around the center *e*, let the Earth's orbit *rst* be constructed, and let the diameter *ret* be drawn parallel to *bd*; in this lies the parallactic apogee of the planet at *r*, and its corresponding perigee at *t*. Let the Earth be at *s*, where the arc *rs*, according to the calculated uniform parallactic anomaly, is equal to 98º 28'. Let the straight line *fe* be extended beyond *e* to *v*; this line cuts...

...the line *bd* at point *x*, and the concave arc of the Earth's orbit at point *v*; here lies the true parallactic apogee <term>Parallactic apogee: The point in a planet's orbit where it appears furthest from the Earth's center due to the geometry of their combined motions.</term>. Now, in triangle *bde*, the two sides *de* (equal to 1460) and *bd* (equal to 10,000) <note>Early modern astronomers often used a standard radius of 10,000 for their trigonometric calculations to avoid working with small decimal fractions.</note> are given, along with the included angle *bde* of 136° 8'—this being the supplementary angle to angle *adb*, which is 43° 52'. From this, we find the third side *be* to be 11,097 of those same units, and the angle *dbe* to be 5° 13'.

Angle *dbf* is equal to angle *adb* by our initial premise; thus, the entire angle *ebf* is 49° 5'. This angle is enclosed by the known sides *eb* and *bf*. Consequently, angle *bef* is 2°, and side *fe* is 10,776, while *db* remains 10,000. Therefore, angle *dxe* is 7° 13', which is equal to the sum of the two interior opposite angles *xbe* and *xeb*. This is the prosthaphæresis <term>Prosthaphæresis: A Greek-derived term meaning 'addition or subtraction,' used for the correction angle applied to a planet's mean motion to find its true position.</term> to be subtracted, by which angle *adb* is greater than angle *xed*—or, in other words, the mean position of Mars is greater than its true position. The mean position was calculated at 163° 32', so the true position is 156° 19'. However, during the observation from point *s*, it was seen at 191° 28'; thus, its direct parallax <term>Parallax: The difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</term> amounts to 35° 9'.

It follows that angle *efs* is 35° 9'. Since *rt* is parallel to *bd*, angle *dxe* is equal to angle *rev*, and thus the arc *rv* is also 7° 13'. This makes the entire arc *vrs* 105° 41' as the corrected parallactic anomaly. From this, we find angle *ves* as the exterior angle of triangle *fes*. Consequently, the interior opposite angle *fse* is 70° 32' (with all angles stated such that 180° equals two right angles). In a triangle with given angles, the ratio of the sides is also given: *fe* is 9428 and *es* is 5757, when the radius of the circle circumscribed about the triangle is 10,000. But if *ef* is 10,776, then *es* becomes 6580, while *bd* is 10,000. This corresponds to what was found by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Alexandrian astronomer whose geocentric model this text seeks to refine.</note> and is nearly identical to it.

The entire line *ade* becomes 11,460, and the remainder *ec* is 8,540 units. If one subtracts the radius of the epicycle (500) from the former, the greatest apsis <note>original: "Abside"; the point of greatest distance in an orbit.</note> becomes 10,960. If one adds that same value to the latter, the smallest apsis becomes 9,040. Therefore, if we take the radius of the Earth's orbit as the unit of measure, we find that for the apogee (the greatest distance of Mars) we have 1. 39' 57'', for the perigee (the closest distance) 1. 22' 26'', and for the mean distance 1. 31' 11''. Thus, for Mars as well, the scale of its motion and distance has been developed through a certain logical conclusion derived from the motion of the Earth.

## Chapter 20.

### About the Planet Venus.

Now that the motions of the three higher planets that revolve outside the Earth's orbit—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—have been developed, we must speak of those which the Earth's orbit encloses. First, we discuss Venus, which allows for a simpler and clearer explanation of its motions.

...movement is more easily permitted than that of the others, provided that the necessary observations of certain positions are not lacking. Specifically, if the greatest distances of the planet <note>Referring to Venus, though not named until the next sentence.</note> from the mean position of the Sun are found to be equal on both sides—that is, in the morning and in the evening—we can conclude with certainty that halfway between those two solar positions lies either the highest or lowest **apside** <term>Apside: The two points in an elliptical orbit where a celestial body is either closest to (perigee) or farthest from (apogee) the center of its motion.</term> of the eccentric circle of Venus. These two points can then be distinguished from one another by the fact that equal movements appear smaller at the apogee and larger at the perigee. Finally, for the remaining positions, it is recognized without doubt from the differences by which they vary from one another how far they are removed from the highest or lowest apside of Venus's orbit, and how great its **eccentricity** is. Ptolemy has presented this most clearly, so that it would not have been necessary to repeat it in detail, except insofar as Ptolemy's own observations must be adapted to our assumption of the movement of the Earth.

As the first of these observations, he took, as he says ⁴¹⁵), the one that the Alexandrian mathematician **Theon** made in the 16th year of Hadrian, on the 21st of **Pharmuthi** <note>The eighth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note>, in the first hour of the following night; this was in the year of Christ 132, on the 8th of March, at twilight ⁴¹⁶).

**Venus** was seen at her greatest eastern distance, removed from the mean position of the Sun by 47º 15'; while this same mean position of the Sun was calculated to be at 337º 41' on the sphere of the fixed stars.

To this, he added another observation of his own, which he states he made in the 4th year of Antoninus on the 12th of **Thoth** <note>The first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note> at daybreak; thus in the year of Christ 140 ⁴¹⁷) at the dawn of July 30th. There, as he says, the outermost limit of the deviation of Venus, as the morning star, from the mean position of the Sun was again 47º 15', just as before. But the mean position of the Sun lay at 119º on the sphere of the fixed stars, whereas previously it had been at 337º 41'. Thus, the mean positions of the apsides lie in the middle between these, namely at 48º 20' and 228º 20' ⁴¹⁸) opposite each other. If one adds 6º 40' to both as the **precession of the equinoxes** <term>Precession of the equinoxes: The slow, continuous change in the orientation of Earth's rotational axis, which shifts the positions of the stars and zodiac signs over thousands of years.</term>, one obtains 25º of Taurus and of Scorpio, as Ptolemy states; and here the highest and lowest apsides of Venus must lie opposite one another.

For further confirmation of this fact, he took another observation of Theon from the 4th year of Hadrian at the dawn of the 20th of **Athyr** <note>The third month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note>; that was in the year 119 after the birth of Christ, on the morning of October 12th ⁴¹⁹), where Venus was again at her greatest distance of 47º 32' from the mean position of the Sun, which was at 191º 13'.

With this, he connected his own observation from the 21st year of Hadrian, or the year of Christ 136, on the 9th day of the Egyptian month **Mechir** <note>The sixth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note>, which according to the Roman calendar was December 25th, in the first hour of the following night, where the eastern distance was again found to be 47º 32' from the mean Sun at 265º.

In the preceding observation of Theon, the mean position of the Sun was however at

# Chapter 22.
## On the Dual Motion of Venus.

Around point $d$, however, the uniform motion of Venus is not simple, which is proven primarily by two observations made by Ptolemy ⁴²²). He conducted the first of these in the 18th year of Hadrian on the 2nd day of the Egyptian month of **Pharmuthi** <note>The eighth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar, roughly corresponding to late winter/early spring.</note>. According to the Roman calendar, this was the year 134 AD on the 18th of February at daybreak. At that time, the mean motion of the Sun was $318^\circ 50'$. Venus appeared as the morning star at $275^\circ 15'$ of the **ecliptic** <term>Ecliptic: The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere as seen from Earth.</term> and had reached the limit of its greatest **deviation** <note>In astronomy, this is often called "elongation"—the angular distance between the Sun and a planet as seen from Earth.</note> of $43^\circ 35'$. He made the second observation in the 3rd year of Antoninus on the fourth day of the same Egyptian month, Pharmuthi; according to the Roman calendar, this was the year 140 AD on the 18th of February at twilight. At that time, the mean position of the Sun was also $318^\circ 50'$, and Venus was at its greatest eastern distance from it by $48^\circ 20'$, and it was located at $7^\circ 50'$ of longitude. Following these determinations, let us assume that the Earth stands in its orbit at point $g$, so that $ag$ is a quadrant of a circle, and at the time of both observations, the Sun, according to its mean motion, was ahead of the **apogee** <note>original: "Apogeum"; the point in the orbit farthest from the center.</note> of the **eccentric circle** <term>Eccentric circle: An off-center circular path used in ancient astronomy to explain why planets seem to move at varying speeds.</term> of Venus. Now, draw $gc$ and parallel to it $dk$, furthermore the **tangents** <note>Lines that touch the circle at exactly one point, representing the maximum angular distance from the center.</note> $ge$ and $gf$ to the orbit of Venus, and finally $de$, $df$, and $dg$. Since the angle $egc$ as the western deviation in the first observation was $43^\circ 35'$ and $cgf$ as the eastern deviation in the second was $48^\circ 20'$, and both sum to the angle $egf$ of $91^\circ 55'$, then half of that, or the angle $dgf$, is equal to $45^\circ 57' 30''$ and $cgd$ equals $2^\circ 23'$. In triangles *cgd*, the angles are given, and thus also the ratio of the sides; *cd* is equal to 416 when *cg* is equal to 10,000. It was previously proven, however, that this distance between the centers was 208 of those same parts; thus, it is now twice as large. If one therefore bisects *cd* at point *m*, then *dm* equals 208, representing the entire difference of this oscillation <note>original: "Hin- und Herganges"; referring to the periodic variation in eccentricity.</note>; and if one bisects this difference again at point *n*, this point appears to be the mean position or the point of uniform motion. 

Thus, as with the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, a motion occurs in Venus that is composed of two uniform motions, whether this takes place in an eccentric epicycle, as it does for those planets, or in another of the ways previously described. However, this planet possesses something different from the others in the law and measure of these motions; this will, I think, be demonstrated more easily and conveniently by using an eccentric circle upon an eccentric circle. 

We therefore describe a small circle around the center *n* with the radius *dn* and assume that the orbital path of Venus is carried around and thereby altered on the periphery of this small circle, according to this law: as often as the Earth reaches the diameter *acb*—where the highest and lowest **apsides** <term>Apsides: The points in an orbit where a celestial body is at its maximum (apogee) or minimum (perigee) distance from the center of its system.</term> of the eccentric circle are located—the center of the planet’s orbit is always at the minimum distance, that is, at point *m*. At the middle apsides, however, such as at *g*, the center of the orbit reaches point *d*, and thus attains its greatest distance *cd*. 

From this, it can be understood that in the time it takes the Earth to complete one revolution of its orbit, the center of the planet's orbit completes two revolutions around the center *n*, and moves in the same direction as the Earth, which is **prograde** <term>Prograde (rechtläufig): Moving in the same direction as the Sun and most other planets through the zodiac, from west to east.</term>. By such an assumption regarding Venus, the uniform and the apparent motions are in harmony in every instance, as will soon be shown. All that has been developed so far concerning Venus is also shown to be in agreement with our own times, except that the total distance—which previously amounted to 416 parts—has decreased by nearly a sixth part and now contains 350 parts, as many observations teach us.⁴²³)

## Chapter 24.

### On the Positions of the Anomaly of Venus.

From the beginning of the <term>Olympiads</term> <note>A four-year period used in ancient Greek chronology, starting in 776 BCE.</note> until the 13th year of Ptolemy Philadelphus, at dawn on the 18th of Mesori, 503 Egyptian years, 228 days, and 40 minutes passed. # Chapter 25.

## Concerning Mercury.

We have shown in what way Venus is linked to the movement of the Earth, and where the uniformity of its circles is to be found. Mercury now remains; it will undoubtedly follow the same adopted principle, although it moves under even more veils <note>original: "Verhüllungen" — referring to the complexity or obscurity of its orbital paths compared to other planets.</note> than Venus, or indeed any of the others previously discussed. It is established through the experience of ancient observers that Mercury shows its smallest deviations from the Sun in the sign of Libra, and larger ones on the opposite side <note>In the sign of Aries.</note>, as is to be expected. However, it does not reach its greatest deviations at this latter location, but at certain others, on either side, such as in Gemini and Aquarius—especially during the time of Antoninus, according to Ptolemy's opinion <note>Note 434: Referring to Claudius Ptolemy's observations in the 2nd century AD recorded in the Almagest.</note>—which occurs with no other planet. 

Since the ancient mathematicians—who believed that the Earth was immobile and that Mercury moved in a large eccentric <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient astronomy to explain retrograde motion.</note>—realized that a single and simple eccentric circle could not satisfy these phenomena, even if it were assumed that this eccentric circle moved not around its own center, but around a foreign one: for that reason, they felt compelled to further assume that this same eccentric circle, while it guided the epicycle, moved upon another small circle, similar to what they had assumed for the eccentric circle of the Moon. 

Thus, there were three centers: first, the center of the eccentric circle guiding the epicycle; second, the center of the small circle; and third, the center of that circle which the moderns call the <term>equant</term> <note>original: "ausgleichenden" — a mathematical point used to explain the observed speed changes of planets while attempting to preserve the idea of uniform motion.</note>. Neglecting the first two, they assumed that the epicycle moved uniformly only around the center of the equant, which is quite foreign to the true center and its relationship, as well as to the other two centers. They also believed that the appearances of this planet could be preserved in no other way, as is explained at greater length in Ptolemy's *Almagest* <note>Note 435: The definitive astronomical manual of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, written by Ptolemy.</note>. 

However, to defend also this last planet against the injustice and reproach of such detractors, and to demonstrate its uniformity no less than with the others preceding it—under the assumption of the Earth’s motion—we assign to it, instead of what was regarded in antiquity as an epicycle, an eccentric circle of an eccentric circle. But this is done in a slightly different way than with Venus; nevertheless, an epicycle moves on that eccentric circle, in which the planet does not move along the periphery, but back and forth along its diameter, which can likewise result from uniform circular motions.

<summary>Copernicus introduces the unique complexities of Mercury's orbit and critiques the cumbersome Ptolemaic system of multiple centers and equants. He proposes a new model based on the Earth's motion that uses a combination of eccentric circles and linear movement along a diameter to maintain the principle of uniform motion.</summary>

In this manner, two twin motions occur: one for the center of the orbit on the periphery of the small circle ***ef***, and one for the planet along the diameter ***lk***. These motions correspond to one another and are **commensurable** <note>Meaning they share a common measure or timeframe.</note> with the period of one Earth year.

Furthermore, it follows that **Mercury**, in its own motion, does not always describe the same circular circumference. Instead, it describes very different ones depending on its distance from the center of its orbit: the smallest at point ***k***, the largest at ***l***, and the medium at ***i***. This is almost identical to the "epicycle of the epicycle" that one can observe in the **Moon's** orbit. However, what occurs on the periphery for the Moon happens along a diameter for Mercury, through a variable motion composed of uniform parts. We demonstrated how this works previously when discussing the **precession of the equinoxes** <note>The slow shift in the orientation of Earth’s axis, which Copernicus explains using similar geometric "librations" or oscillations.</note>. We shall provide further details on this later when discussing latitudes. This assumption accounts for all the phenomena seen in Mercury, as will become clear from the history of observations by **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Roman-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus was refining.</note> and others.

# Chapter 26.
### Concerning the position of the highest and lowest apsides of Mercury.

**Ptolemy** observed Mercury in the first year of the reign of **Antoninus** <note>Emperor Antoninus Pius; the year was 137 or 138 AD.</note> after sunset on the 20th day of the month of **Epiphi** <note>An Egyptian calendar month.</note>. At that time, the planet was an **evening star** and was at its greatest eastern distance from the mean position of the Sun. From the birth of Christ until this time, 137 Egyptian years, 188 days, 42 minutes, and 30 seconds had passed according to **Krakow time** <note>original: "Krakauer Zeit"; Copernicus calculated his tables based on the meridian of Krakow.</note>. Consequently, the mean position of the Sun, according to our calculation, was at 63° 50', and the planet was seen through the instrument, as Ptolemy says, at 7° of **Cancer**. 

If we subtract from this the **precession of the equinoxes**, which at that time amounted to 6° 40', the position of Mercury was 90° 20' from the first star of **Aries** in the sphere of fixed stars, and its greatest distance from the mean Sun was equal to 26° 30'. He made a second observation in the 4th year of Antoninus at the dawn of the 19th day of the month of **Phamenoth**, after the time since the birth of Christ...

## Chapter 27.

### **How great the eccentricity of Mercury is, and the ratio of its orbits.**

From this, the distance between the centers and the sizes of the orbits also emerge. <meta>This page continues the geometric and historical analysis of Mercury’s orbital eccentricity. Having established the base measurements for Mercury’s apsides (the points where it is closest to and farthest from the Sun), Copernicus now focuses on the "mean apsides"—the points where the planet is at its average distance. He uses specific historical observations from Theon and Ptolemy to refine the model of the "small circle" (epicycle) that explains the variations in Mercury's perceived distance.</meta>

Distance of the centers *cd* equals 8,658. If, however, *ac* were equal to 1, or 60' <note>60 minutes of arc, a standard unit in ancient and Renaissance astronomy.</note>, then the radius of Mercury's orbit would be 0° 21' 26'' and *cd* would be 0° 5' 41''. And if *ac* is 100,000, then *df* is 35,733 and *cd* is 9,479, which was to be demonstrated. 

However, even these values do not remain the same everywhere; indeed, they differ most at the points located in the region of the mean apsides <term>apsides</term> <note>The two points in an orbit where the planet is at its maximum and minimum distance from its center of motion.</note>, as we learn from the western and eastern elongations <term>elongations</term> <note>The angular distance between the Sun and a planet as viewed from Earth.</note> observed at these points, as reported by Theon and Ptolemy.

For Theon observed the greatest eastern elongation of Mercury in the 14th year of Hadrian, on the 18th day of the month of Mesori <note>The twelfth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note>, after sunset<sup>443</sup>), which is 129 Egyptian years, 216 days, and 45 minutes after the birth of Christ. At that time, the mean position of the Sun was at 93° 30'—that is, almost exactly at the mean apside of Mercury. Through the instrument, however, it was measured that the planet preceded the Basiliskus of Leo <note>The star known today as Regulus, the "Little King," the brightest star in the constellation Leo.</note> by 3° 50'; its position was therefore 119° 45', and its eastern elongation was 26° 15'. 

Ptolemy reports another "greatest elongation," observed by himself in the second year of Antoninus at the break of the 21st<sup>444</sup>) day of the month of Mesori; by this time, 138 Egyptian years, 219 days, and 12 minutes had passed since Christ. The mean position of the Sun was likewise 93° 39', and he found the greatest western elongation of Mercury to be 20° 15'. For Mercury was seen at 73° 24' on the sphere of the fixed stars.

Now, let *acdb* be, as before, the diameter of the Earth's orbit drawn through the apsides of Mercury, and at point *c*, let the line *ce* be erected at a right angle, representing the line of the mean motion of the Sun. Around point *f*, located between *c* and *d*, let the orbit of Mercury be described, to which the straight lines *eh* and *eg* are tangents <term>tangents</term> <note>Lines that touch the edge of a circle at exactly one point, used here to represent the maximum angle of visibility.</note>, and finally, let the straight lines *fg*, *fh*, and *ef* be drawn. 

The task once more is to find the location of point *f* and the ratio of the radius *fg* to the line *ac*. Since the angle *ceg* is given as 26° 15' and the angle *ceh* as 20° 15', the total angle *heg* measures 46° 30'. Its half, *hef*, is 23° 15', and thus the remaining angle *cef* is 3°. Consequently, in the right-angled triangle *cef*, the sides are: *cf* equals 524 and *fe* equals 10,014 of those parts where *ce* or *ac* contains 10,000. It was previously shown, however, that the entire line *cd* is equal to 948 of these same parts when the Earth is at the planet’s greatest or smallest apside. Therefore, the difference *df*—which is the diameter of the small circle described by the center of Mercury's orbit—is 424, and the radius *if* equals 212.

## Chapter 29.

### **Examination of the mean movement of Mercury.**

Among the ancient observations, it is found that in the 21st year of Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, ruler of Egypt; the 21st year of his reign corresponds to approximately 265 BCE.</note>, at the start of the 19th day of the Egyptian month Thoth $^{448)}$, Mercury was separated by two moon-diameters to the east from the straight line drawn through the first and second of those stars which stand in the forehead of the Scorpion <note>original: "Stirn des Skorpion"; these are the stars Beta and Delta Scorpii.</note>, and was one moon-diameter to the north of the first star. Now, it is known that the position of the first star is at 209º 40' longitude and 1º 20' northern latitude, and that of the second is at 209º longitude and 1º 40' southern latitude. From this, the position of Mercury was calculated to be 210º 40' longitude and 1º 50' northern latitude. Since the death of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great, whose death in 323 BCE served as a common chronological epoch for astronomers.</note>, however, 59 years, 17 days, and 45 minutes $^{448)}$ <note>The "minutes" here refers to 45/60ths of a day, or 18 hours.</note> had passed, and the mean position of the Sun was therefore, according to our calculation, 228º 8', while the western elongation <note>term: elongation (the angular distance between the Sun and a planet as seen from Earth)</note> of the planet was 17º 28'. This latter was still increasing, which was noted again 4 days later $^{450)}$, from which it emerged that the planet had not yet reached its greatest western elongation, or the tangent of its orbit, but was still moving in the lower arc, closer to the Earth. But since the highest apsis <note>The aphelion, the point furthest from the Sun.</note> lay at 183º 20', Mercury was 44º 48' distant from the mean position of the Sun. # Chapter 30.

## **On more recent observations of the movement of Mercury.**

The ancients previously mapped out this method for us to examine the course of our planet. They were favored by a clear sky, as the Nile, so they report, does not breathe out such vapors as the Vistula does in our region. But for us, who live in a harsher climate, nature has denied this convenience, as the air is less frequently calm. Furthermore, because of the great obliquity of the celestial sphere <note>Copernicus refers to the high northern latitude of Poland and Germany, where the angle of the horizon makes Mercury much harder to see near the sun</note>, there are fewer opportunities to see Mercury. Even when it is at its greatest distance from the sun, such as when the sun is in Aries or Pisces, it does not rise within our view; nor can its setting be seen when the sun is in Virgo or Libra. Moreover, in Cancer or Gemini, it does not appear at all, neither in the evening twilight nor the morning dawn—and never at night—unless the sun enters the most favorable part of Leo. For this reason, this planet has caused us much trouble and labor to calculate its irregularities.

To this end, we have borrowed three positions from those which were carefully observed in Nuremberg. The first was observed by Bernhard Walther$^{153)}$, a student of Regiomontanus, in the year of Christ 1491, on the 9th of September, 5 equal hours after midnight. By comparing it with the star Aldebaran <note>a bright orange giant star in the constellation Taurus, often used as a reference point</note> using an astrolabe, he found that Mercury was at 13° 30' of Virgo, with a northern latitude of 1° 50'. At that time, the planet was beginning to disappear as a morning star, as its western deviation had been continually decreasing over the previous days. From the beginning of the years of Christ, 1491 Egyptian years, 258 days, 12 hours, and 30 minutes had passed. The simple mean position of the sun was at 149° 48', but 26° 47' into Virgo from the vernal equinox point; therefore, the distance of Mercury was approximately 13° 15'.

The second observation was made by Johannes Schöner* in the year of Christ 1504, on the 9th of January, 6 1/2 hours after midnight, when the 10th degree of Scorpio was culminating <note>at its highest point in the sky</note> at Nuremberg. The planet stood at 3° 20' of Capricorn, with a northern latitude of 45'. According to calculations from the vernal equinox point, the mean position of the sun was at 27° 7' of Capricorn$^{154)}$, and Mercury preceded it to the west by 23° 42'.

The third observation is by the same Johannes, also in the same year 1504, on the 18th of March, in which he, by comparing the planet with the...

## Chapter 31.

### On the Determination of the Positions of Mercury.

Now, from the beginning of the Christian era until the last observation in 1504, 1504 <term>Egyptian years: years consisting of exactly 365 days, used by ancient and Renaissance astronomers for ease of calculation</term> 87 days and 48 minutes <note>These are sexagesimal minutes of a day, where 60 minutes equal one day.</note> have elapsed. During this time, the movement of Mercury’s <term>parallactic anomaly: the angular distance of the planet from the furthest point of its small orbital circle</term>, after removing the full revolutions, amounts to 63º 14'. If one subtracts this from 109º 38' <note>This was the value calculated for the observation in 1504.</note>, there remains 46º 24' as the position of Mercury's parallactic anomaly for the beginning of the Christian era. Counting backward from there to the beginning of the first <term>Olympiad: a four-year period used in ancient Greek dating, starting in 776 BCE</term>, there are 775 Egyptian years 12 days and 30 minutes <gloss>460</gloss>; for this period, the calculated movement is 95º 3', excluding full revolutions. Subtracting this from the position at the time of Christ—by "borrowing" a full 360-degree circle—leaves 311º 21' as the position for the first Olympiad. From this, using the same calculation for the 451 years and 247 days until the death of <note>Alexander the Great, whose death in 323 BCE served as a common reference point for astronomers.</note> Alexander, this position is found to be 213º 3'.

## Chapter 32.

### On Another Method of Deriving the Oscillation.

Before we leave Mercury, we wish to examine another perspective, which is no less acceptable than the one above, through which that <term>libration: a back-and-forth oscillation or "swinging" motion</term> could be thought to have arisen.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of concentric and eccentric circles used to model planetary motion. A large circle is labeled with points g (top), h (left), p (right), and k (bottom). A horizontal line connects h and p through the center f. A vertical line connects g and r (at the very bottom). A small central circle is labeled with m at the top and l at the bottom. Around point l, another circle is drawn, labeled with points o and r on the vertical axis.</image-desc>

Let there be a circle, *ghkp*, divided into four equal parts by its center *f*; with this, let the small circle *lm* be <term>concentric: having the same center</term>, and around the center *l*, with the radius *lfo*, equal to *fg* or *fh*, let a third circle *or* be described. Now let us assume that this entire arrangement of circles, with their intersecting lines *gfr* and *hfp*, moves <term>prograde: in the direction of the signs of the Zodiac, from west to east</term> around the center *f* daily by approximately 2º 7' from the apogee of the planet's eccentric circle; for the parallactic motion of the planet is greater than the motion of the Earth in the <term>ecliptic: the path the Sun appears to follow through the stars over a year</term> by that amount. Meanwhile, the planet, starting from point *g*, completes the remainder of its own parallactic motion in circle *or*, closely matching the motion of the Earth. Furthermore, imagine that during this same annual revolution, the...

...the center of the circle guiding the planet moves in a back-and-forth motion along the diameter *lfm* twice as fast as we previously assumed. If, according to these determinations, we place the Earth in its mean motion opposite the <term>apogee: the point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion</term> of the <term>eccentric circle: a circular path whose center is offset from the observer's position</term> of the planet, and at the same time the center of the circle guiding the planet is at *l*, while the planet itself is at point *o*: then the latter, at its smallest distance from *f*, describes the smallest circle of its motion, the radius of which is *fo*. 

From this it follows further that when the Earth is in the region of the <term>mean apsides: the middle points between the furthest and nearest distances in an orbit</term>, and the planet is at point *h*, the latter—because of its greatest distance from *f*—describes the largest arcs, specifically in a circle whose center is *f*; for then the guiding circle *or* coincides with the circle *gh*, because they share the common center *f*. 

Moving from here, if the Earth advances further into the region of the <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the center of motion</term>, and the center of the circle *or* moves to the other extreme point *m*, the circle *or* also extends beyond *gk*, and the planet at *r* returns to its smallest distance from *f*; and now the rest proceeds as from the beginning. For here the three equal revolutions coincide: namely, the motion of the Earth with that of the apogee of Mercury’s eccentric circle; the back-and-forth motion of the center along the diameter *lm* with the motion of the planet from the line *fg* back to the same; and from these, only the motion in the sections *gh* and *kp* deviates from the <term>apside: a point of extreme distance in an orbit</term> of the eccentric circle, as we have said. 

Thus, Nature plays with this planet in such a wondrous variation, even as she remains bound to an eternal, certain, and unchanging order. It must be noted here, however, that the planet does not pass through the middle regions of the quadrants *gh* and *kp* without an inequality in longitude; for as the change of the centers is added, the planet will necessarily produce a <term>prosthaphaeresis: the angle added to or subtracted from the mean motion to find the true position</term>; and such a variability of its center does exist. 

For if, for example, while the center remained at *l*, the planet moved forward from *o*, then a greatest difference would occur in the region of *h* according to the measure of the <term>eccentricity: the degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</term> *fl*. But it follows from the premises that although the planet begins to move away from *o* and promises to pass through the difference belonging to the distance *fl* of the centers, as the movable center approaches the mean *f*, it is more and more hindered from this sought-after variation. Its effort is so far thwarted that at the middle points *h* and *p*, where one would expect the greatest difference, it becomes zero. Yet even if a small difference were to occur, we must nonetheless admit that it would be hidden within the rays of the Sun; and that the planet, when it appears in the East or West as the <term>Morning Star: the planet Venus or Mercury seen before sunrise</term> or <term>Evening Star: the planet Venus or Mercury seen after sunset</term>, is not seen exactly at the edge of the circle. However, we have [developed] this no less rational view—

# Chapter 33.

## **On the Tables of the <term>Prosthaphaereses: mathematical corrections added or subtracted to account for the difference between a planet's average motion and its observed motion</term> of the Five Planets.**

We have developed these points regarding the uniform and apparent motion of Mercury and the other planets and explained them with numbers; through these examples, the path is now open to calculate any other positions and differences in motion. To make this goal easier to achieve, we have set up special tables for each planet with six columns and thirty rows, arranged in intervals of three degrees, as is our custom. 

The first and second columns contain the common numbers <note>These are the input values, or "arguments," used to look up values in the table, representing the degrees of a circle from 3 to 180 and 180 to 360.</note>, used for both the anomaly of the <term>eccentric circle: an orbital path where the center is not the Earth</term> and the parallactic anomaly. In the third column, one finds the total corrections of the eccentric circle; specifically, the complete differences that occur between the mean and the irregular motion of those orbits. 

The fourth column presents the proportional parts as sixtieths <note>original: "Sechzigstel" (scrupula). Just as an hour is divided into sixty minutes, a degree is divided into sixty parts for precision.</note>, by which the <term>parallaxes: the apparent change in a planet's position caused by the Earth’s own motion</term> must be increased or decreased due to the greater or lesser distance from the Earth. In the fifth column are those corrections arising from the Earth's orbit for the parallaxes at the <term>apogee: the point where the planet is furthest from the sun or center of motion</term> of the planet’s eccentric circle. Finally, the sixth column contains the differences by which the corrections occurring at the <term>perigee: the point where the planet is closest to the center of motion</term> are greater. The tables follow here.

## Chapter 34.

->How the Longitudes of the Positions of the Five Planets Are Calculated.<-

With the help of these tables we have established, we can calculate the longitudes of the positions of the five planets without difficulty. In all of these, the method of calculation is nearly the same, although the outer planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note> differ somewhat from Venus and Mercury. First, we wish to speak of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, where the calculation consists of finding—for any given time, in the manner indicated above—the mean motions: namely, the simple motion of the Sun and the <term>parallactic motion: the apparent shift in a planet's position caused by the Earth's own movement in its orbit</term> of the planet. Following this, the position of the greatest <term>apsis: the point in an orbit where a celestial body is farthest from the center of motion</term> of the planet’s <term>eccentric circle: an orbital path that is not centered on the Earth</term> is subtracted from the simple position of the Sun, and from the remainder, the parallactic motion is also subtracted. What then remains is the <term>anomaly: the angular distance of a planet from its apsis</term> of the planet’s eccentric circle. We look up this value among the common numbers in one of the first two columns of the table; next to it, in the third column, we find the <term>prosthaphaeresis: a mathematical correction used to account for the difference between a planet's mean and true position</term> of the eccentric circle, and further along, the proportional parts. We add this prosthaphaeresis to the parallactic motion and subtract it from the anomaly of the eccentric circle if the number we used to enter the table was found in the first column; conversely, we subtract it from the parallactic motion and add it to the anomaly of the eccentric circle if the number is in the second column. The resulting sums or differences represent the equated <note>or "adjusted"</note> anomaly of the parallax and the eccentric circle. We set aside the proportional parts for a use to be specified shortly. We likewise look up the parallactic anomaly, thus equated, among the first common numbers, and take from the fifth column the prosthaphaeresis of the parallax, along with its excess from the final column next to it. For this excess, we take the corresponding portion from the proportional parts and always add it to the prosthaphaeresis. This sum gives us the true parallax of the planet, which must be subtracted from the equated parallactic anomaly if the latter is smaller—and added if it is larger—than the semicircle <note>180 degrees</note>. In this way, we obtain the true and apparent distance of the planet from the mean position of the Sun in a <term>retrograde: directed or moving backward</term> sense. If we subtract this distance from the position of the mean Sun, the remainder is the sought-after position of the planet in relation to the <term>sphere of fixed stars: the background of stars that appear not to move relative to one another</term>. When, finally, the <term>precession: the slow, conical motion of Earth's axis that changes the arrival of the equinoxes</term> of the equinoxes has been added to this, we have the position of the planet from the <term>vernal equinox point: the position of the Sun at the start of spring, used as the zero point for celestial longitude</term>. For Venus and Mercury, instead of the anomaly of the eccentric circle, we take the distance of the greatest apsis from the mean position of the Sun, and by means of this anomaly, we equate the parallactic motion and the anomaly...

of the eccentric circle, in the manner just indicated. If, however, the <term>prosthaphaeresis: the mathematical correction used to find a planet's true position</term> of the eccentric circle has the same sign as the adjusted <term>parallax: the apparent displacement of a celestial object when viewed from different positions, here caused by Earth's orbit</term> or is of the same kind, their sum is added to or subtracted from the mean position of the Sun. But if they have different signs, one subtracts the smaller from the larger magnitude, and proceeds with the remainder in the specified manner, according to the positive or negative sign of the larger number; thus the sought-after apparent position is obtained <note>original: "erscheinende Ort"; reference 461 in original text</note>.

## Chapter 35.

### On the Stations and Retrograde Motions of the Five Planets. <note>reference 462 in original text</note>

In addition to the determinations of movement in relation to longitude, there is also the knowledge of the <term>stations: the points where a planet appears to stop in the sky before changing direction</term> and the <term>retrograde motions: the apparent backward movement of a planet</term>; namely where, when, and to what extent these occur. Mathematicians, and especially <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240 – 190 BC) was a Greek geometer known for his work on conic sections and planetary models.</note> Apollonius of Perga, have also dealt much with this; but they did so as if the planets moved with only a single inequality—specifically in relation to the Sun—which is the inequality we have called "parallax" due to the motion of the Earth in its orbit. 

For if the orbits of the planets were concentric with the Earth's orbit, and the planets moved in them with unequal speeds, all in the same direction—that is, in <term>direct motion: movement in the same direction as most other bodies in the solar system</term>; — and if a planet in its orbit within the Earth's orbit, like Venus and Mercury, is faster than the motion of the Earth; and a straight line drawn from the Earth intersects the orbit of the planet so that half of the segment within the orbit has the same ratio to the segment between our eye (the Earth) and the lower convex arc of the intersected orbit, as the movement of the Earth has to the speed of the planet: then the point determined by such a line separates the arc toward the <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the Earth</term> of the planetary orbit (representing the retrograde motion) from the arc of the direct motion. Thus, the planet appears to stand still when it is at this very point. 

Likewise, for the other three outer planets, whose motion is slower than the speed of the Earth, if a straight line drawn through our eye intersects the Earth's orbit so that half of the segment located within the Earth's orbit has the same ratio to the segment lying between the planet and our eye (located in the nearer and convex arc of the Earth's orbit) as the motion of the planet has to the speed of the Earth: then the planet at this location presents to our eye the appearance of a station. # Nicolaus Copernicus’ *On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres*.

## Sixth Book.

We have demonstrated, as far as we were able, the influence and effect that the assumed circular motion of the Earth has on the apparent motion of the planets in **longitude** <term>longitude: the position of a celestial body measured East-West along the ecliptic</term>, and the certain and necessary laws to which this motion constrains them all. It now remains for us to occupy ourselves with those movements of these stars by which they change their **latitude** <term>latitude: the distance of a planet North or South of the ecliptic (the Sun's apparent path)</term>; and to show how the same motion of the Earth also holds dominion here and prescribes laws to the planets in this regard as well. This part of the science is necessary because the latitudinal movement of the planets produces a significant variation in the phenomena of rising and setting, of appearing and disappearing, and other matters which have been generally established earlier. It is also necessary because one cannot say that the true places of the planets are known until their longitude is established simultaneously with their latitude in relation to the **ecliptic** <term>ecliptic: the apparent path of the Sun across the sky, which serves as the reference plane for the solar system</term>. What the ancient mathematicians attempted to prove here through the immobility of the Earth, we shall perhaps carry out more concisely and conveniently by means of its motion.

### Chapter 1.

#### General Explanation of the Motion of the Five Planets in Relation to Latitude.

The ancients found that two irregularities of latitude occur in all the planets, corresponding to the twofold irregularity of the longitude of each; they believed that one arose from the **eccentricity** <term>eccentricity: the amount by which a planet's orbit deviates from a perfect circle or is off-center</term> of the orbits, and the other from the **epicycles** <term>epicycles: small circular paths that planets were once thought to follow while simultaneously moving along a larger circular orbit</term>. In place of these epicycles, we employ the single orbit of the Earth, which we have already used so often. It is not as if this orbit itself deviates in any way from the plane of the **Zodiac** <note>original: "Thierkreis"</note>—which it occupies once and for all, since the two are the same—but rather that the orbits of the planets are inclined against this plane at a var—

<meta>The previous page introduced Book 6, shifting the focus from the East-West movement of planets (longitude) to their North-South deviations (latitude). It established that Earth’s own motion influences how we perceive these deviations.</meta>

...are inclined at varying angles. This change, however, depends on the positions and movements of the Earth in its orbit. Just as the three superior planets—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—move according to slightly different laws regarding **longitude** than the other two [Venus and Mercury], they also differ significantly in their movement in **latitude**. Therefore, we first investigated where their northernmost limits of latitude lie and how great the deviation is. Ptolemy found these <note>Note 468 in the source text</note> for Saturn and Jupiter at the beginning of **Libra**, but for Mars at the end of **Cancer**, nearly at the **apogee** <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion</term> of the eccentric circle. In our own times, we have found these northernmost limits for Saturn at 7° of **Scorpio**, for Jupiter at 27° of **Libra**, and for Mars at 27° of **Leo**. The apogees have shifted by this same amount up to our time, for the inclinations of the planetary orbits and their principal points of latitude follow the same motion. 

When these planets are at a distance of a **quadrant** <term>quadrant: 90 degrees, or one-quarter of a full circle</term> of their orbits from these limits—whether measured by their mean or apparent motion—they appear to make no deviation in latitude at all, regardless of where the Earth may be at that time. At these middle distances, one recognizes that the planets are at the shared intersection points of their orbits with the Earth's orbit, just as the Moon is at the intersection points of its orbit with the **ecliptic** <term>ecliptic: the Sun's apparent path, used as the reference "flat" plane of the solar system</term>. Ptolemy <note>Note 468</note> calls these intersection points **nodes** <term>nodes: the two points where a planet's tilted orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit</term>; specifically, the "ascending node" is where the planet passes into the northern half, and the "descending node" is where it passes into the southern half. 

It is not as if the Earth’s orbit—which always remains in the plane of the ecliptic—causes any latitude for those planets; rather, every latitudinal deviation stems from the planets themselves. This deviation changes most significantly at those points where the planets, during their **opposition** <term>opposition: when a planet is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, appearing brightest and largest</term> with the Sun or at their midnight **culmination** <term>culmination: reaching the highest point in the sky</term>, always show a greater deviation to the approaching Earth than at any other position of the Earth. In the northern semicircle, this deviation is toward the North, and in the southern semicircle, it is toward the South; and this difference is greater than what the mere narrowing or widening of the distance to the Earth would require. 

From this circumstance, one recognizes that the inclinations of those orbits are not fixed, but change through fluctuating movements that are **commensurable** <term>commensurable: having a common measure; here meaning the planet's wobble is synchronized with the Earth's orbital period</term> with the circular motions of the Earth's orbit, as shall be discussed further below. **Venus** and **Mercury**, however, appear to deviate in latitude in a somewhat different manner, yet in a specific dependency on the highest, the lowest, and the two middle **apsides** <term>apsides: the points in an orbit closest to or farthest from the center (apogee and perigee)</term>. For at the middle distances—namely, where the line of the mean motion of the Sun is a quadrant away from the highest and lowest apsides of the planets, and the planets themselves (as morning or evening stars) are a quadrant of their own orbits away from that same line of the Sun's mean motion—no deviation from the ecliptic was found in them. From this, it was recognized that the planets were then in the shared line of intersection between their orbits and the ecliptic. This line of intersection...

...moves through the **apogees** and **perigees** <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the center of motion</term>. Because of this, the planets show noticeable deviations as they move further from or closer to the Earth. The greatest deviation occurs at their maximum distance from the Earth—that is, when they first become visible in the evening or disappear in the morning. At these times, **Venus** appears at its furthest point north, while **Mercury** appears at its furthest south. Conversely, when they are closer to the Earth—as they cease to be evening stars and begin to appear in the morning—**Venus** is positioned to the south and **Mercury** to the north. 

When the Earth is at the opposite point in its orbit (at the other middle **apsis** <term>apsis: the highest or lowest point in an orbit</term>, where the **anomaly** <term>anomaly: the angular distance of a planet from its apogee</term> of the eccentric circle is 270°), the positions reverse: at its greatest distance from Earth, **Venus** appears to the south and **Mercury** to the north; when closer to Earth, **Venus** is to the north and **Mercury** to the south. 

However, as the Earth approaches the apogees of these planets, Ptolemy found that the latitude of **Venus** was northern when it was a morning star and southern when it was an evening star. For **Mercury**, the opposite was true: southern in the morning and northern in the evening. This pattern flips again in the opposite region (the perigee), where **Venus** as a morning star appears southern and as an evening star northern, while **Mercury** appears northern in the morning and southern in the evening. 

Furthermore, in both of these positions, **Venus** was found to have a greater northern latitude than southern, while **Mercury** had a greater southern latitude than northern. From these observations, astronomers concluded there were two types of latitude for this region—and three in total. They named the first (at middle distances) **inclination**; the second (at the greatest and smallest apsides) **obliquation**; and the third, which is linked to the second, **deviation**. This **deviation** is always northern for **Venus** and always southern for **Mercury**. Between these four boundary points, these movements blend together, alternately increasing, decreasing, and displacing one another. We shall explain the specific circumstances of how this occurs in more detail.

## Chapter 2.

### Hypotheses regarding the circles in which the planets move in latitude.

One must therefore imagine that the orbits of the five planets are tilted against the plane of the **ecliptic** at angles that change regularly, and that their shared lines of intersection form diameters of the ecliptic. For **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars**, the angle of inclination undergoes a certain oscillation <note>Latin: *libratio*</note> around that intersection line, much like an axis. We demonstrated a similar motion when discussing the **precession of the equinoxes** <term>precession: the slow "wobbling" of Earth's rotational axis</term>. However, this is a simple oscillation that is proportional to the **parallactic motion** <term>parallactic motion: the apparent shift of a planet caused by Earth's own movement</term>, which causes the angle of inclination to increase and decrease at specific intervals. Thus, whenever the Earth is closest to the planet...

Specifically, at the midnight culmination <term>culmination: the moment a celestial body reaches its highest point in the sky</term>, the greatest inclination <term>inclination: the tilt of a planet's orbit relative to the Earth's orbit</term> of the planetary orbit occurs; in the opposite position, the smallest; and in the middle position, the average. When the planet is at the point of its greatest northern or southern latitude, this latitude appears much larger when the planet is near the Earth than when it is at its greatest distance. While this difference in distance could alone explain the variation—since a closer object naturally appears larger than a distant one—the latitudes of the planets show an even greater variation in their increase and decrease. This can only be explained by the fact that the orbits themselves oscillate <note>original: "schwanken"</note> in their positions. However, as we have stated previously, in the case of such oscillations, a certain mean must be assumed between the extreme limits.

This is how the three superior planets <note>The "upper" or superior planets are those further from the Sun than Earth: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> behave. Venus and Mercury differ from these not a little, both in longitude and in latitude, because the common intersection lines of their orbits are situated through the apogees <term>apogee: the point in an orbit furthest from the Earth or center</term> and perigees <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the Earth or center</term>. Both oscillations are commensurable with the circular motion of the Earth, but not in one and the same way. 

The first oscillation is such that while the Earth returns once to the apsides of these planets, the motion of this oscillation itself completes two cycles. This occurs around a fixed axis which, as stated, represents the intersection line lying through the apogees and perigees; thus, as often as the line of the mean motion of the Sun passes through the perigee or apogee of these planets, the greatest angle of inclination occurs, whereas in the middle distances, the smallest angle always occurs. The second oscillation, which is added to this one, differs in that it takes place around a movable axis, so that when the Earth is at the middle distance, both Venus and Mercury always stand in the axis—that is, in the common intersection line—of this oscillation. In this case, when the apogee or perigee of the planet is turned toward the Earth, Venus is, as stated, always deflected furthest to the north, and Mercury to the south; yet, because of the earlier simple inclination, they ought to have no latitude at all at that time. Since the obliquation <term>obliquation: the slanting or tilting of the planet's orbital plane relative to the ecliptic</term> was found to be greater than the declination <term>declination: here referring to the angular distance of the planet north or south of the ecliptic</term>, it was recognized that this arises from a certain oscillation. This oscillation occurs around the intersection line *fg* as its axis, as was stated further above. Therefore, if these angles of inclination on both sides are known to us, we can easily find from their difference how much that oscillation amounts to, from its smallest to its largest value. 

Now, imagine another circle of deviation which is inclined against the circle *gkfl*. For Venus, this circle shares the same center; for Mercury, however, it is eccentric to its eccentric circle, as shall be shown hereafter. Let their common intersection line be *rs*, serving as an axis in rotation for this oscillation. Thus, when the Earth is at point *a* or *b*, the planet reaches the outermost limit of its deviation somewhere at point *t*. As the Earth advances from *a*, the planet moves just as far from *t*, during which time the inclination of the circle of deviation decreases. By the time the Earth has traversed the quadrant *ab*, the planet has reached the node *r* of its latitude. 

But since the planes then coincide in the mean oscillation and pass into the opposite positions, the other semicircle of deviation, which previously lay to the south, now moves to the north. As Venus moves along this semicircle, it becomes northern again, skipping the south entirely; through this oscillation, it is never deflected to the south. Likewise, Mercury maintains its southern deviation, which is further distinguished by the fact that it oscillates in a circle that is not homocentric <term>homocentric: sharing the same center</term> with the eccentric circle, but is itself eccentric. For this planet, we employed an epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to explain complexities in planetary motion</term> when deriving the inequality of its motion in longitude. However, since longitude is considered there without latitude, and here latitude is considered without longitude—yet both have the same revolution and repeat at the same time—it is sufficiently clear that it is a single motion and the same oscillation that can produce both changes, being simultaneously eccentric and oblique. There is no other assumption than the one we have just discussed, and which we shall discuss in more detail below.

### Chapter 5.

## **On the Latitudes of Venus and Mercury.**

There remain Venus and Mercury, whose movements in latitude, as mentioned, are derived from three interacting deflections. However, so that these may be distinguished from one another individually, we shall begin with that which is called the declination, as it can be treated most simply. With this one alone <note>original note 473</note> is it possible at times to separate it from the others—namely, in the region of the mean distances, or the nodes <term>nodes: the two points where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the ecliptic</term>—when the Earth, according to the mean movements in longitude, is 90º away from the planet's apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</term> and perigee <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the Earth</term>. In this position, the southern and northern latitude has been found to be 6º 22' for Venus and 4º 5' for Mercury when near the Earth, and 1º 2' for Venus and 1º 45' for Mercury <note>original note 474</note> when at the greatest distance from the Earth. From this, with the help of the established tables of adjustments <note>original note 475: likely referring to tables of prosthaphairesis, used to correct for orbital irregularities</note>, the angles of inclination for this position are calculated. To these, the locations of Venus correspond to 1º 2' <note>original note 476</note> at the greatest distance from Earth and 6º 22' at the nearest distance on both sides of the path, corresponding to an arc of nearly 2º 30'; for Mercury, however, the upper position is 1º 45' and the lower is 4º 5', which requires an arc of its orbit of 6º 15'.

## Chapter 6.

### Concerning the second latitudinal deviation of Venus and Mercury,
### according to the obliquity of their orbits at <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> and <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth</note>.

The preceding related to the latitudinal deviations of both planets which occur at the mean distances of their orbits, and which, as mentioned, are called <term>declinations</term>. Now we must deal with those that occur at the <term>perigee</term> and <term>apogee</term>, where—differing from the three upper planets—that third deviation, the <term>deviation</term> <note>Specifically referring to the 'reflexion' or 'deviation' in the Ptolemaic model</note>, is added, and indeed so that this may be more easily understood and distinguished, as follows. For Ptolemy observed that those latitudes appear greatest when the planets stand at the tangents drawn from the center of the Earth to their orbits, which, as said, occurs at their greatest western and eastern distances from the Sun; and he found the northern latitudes of Venus to be 20' greater than the southern, but for Mercury the southern were almost 1º 30' greater than the northern ⁴⁸⁷). However, wishing to avoid the difficulty and labor of the calculation—especially since he estimated the resulting error to be imperceptible, as we shall also soon show—he assumed, according to a certain mean ratio for the two sides of the latitude, 2º 30'. ## Chapter 7.

### How great the angles of the <term>obliquations</term> <note>The tilting or slanting of the planetary orbits relative to the ecliptic</note> of the two planets, Venus and Mercury, are.

<note>Image Description: A geometric diagram showing a circle with center b. A vertical axis runs through points c, b, f, e, and a. Point d lies on the circle's circumference. After these preliminary remarks, we now wish to see how large an angle is formed by the orbital planes of the two planets under the influence of the <term>inflexion</term> <note>A specific type of latitudinal oscillation in the Copernican model</note>. We recall what was said above<sup>488</sup>): namely, that for each of the two planets, the angle between the greatest and smallest distance on both sides of the Earth's orbit amounts to 5º, and of this, the majority usually falls on the northern or southern half. The passage of Venus through the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the center</note> and <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the orbit closest to the center</note> of its eccentric circle, or its apparent difference, yields a deviation slightly larger or smaller than 5º; however, the passage of Mercury yields one that is larger or smaller by half a degree. The angle dag is assumed to be half as large as the specified latitude difference of each of the two planets, thus equal to 2º 30', where 360º constitutes four right angles. Their lengths result as: *ag* at 6940 and *fg* at 4988. If *ag* is 10000, then *fg* is 7187 and the angle *fag* is 45° 57'; and if *ad* is 10000, then *df* is 7193, and the angle *daf* is 46°. At the greatest obliquation, the **prosthaphaeresis** <note>term: Prosthaphaeresis; a technical term in pre-Keplerian astronomy referring to the correction required to convert mean motion to true motion.</note> of the parallax becomes smaller by about 3'. We have already added the prosthaphaereses to the individual points of the orbits in the tables of irregular movements. For both planets, we will calculate the portion corresponding to how much each prosthaphaeresis is smaller than the greatest, based on those 2º 30', and place these portions in the table set out below next to their numbers; in this way, we obtain all the specific latitudes of the obliquations <note>the "slanting" or tilting of the orbital planes</note> which apply to the greatest and smallest distance from the Earth, just as we have entered the latitudes of the declinations for the middle quadrants and the mean distances. What lies between these four boundary points, however, can be developed with mathematical precision from the assumed theory of circles, though certainly not without effort. Ptolemy <sup>495)</sup> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose geocentric model this text engages with</note> however, who strives for simplicity everywhere as much as possible, noticed that both types of latitudes, both as a whole and in all their individual parts, increase and decrease proportionally to the lunar latitude; and by multiplying each of them by 12—because his greatest latitude amounts to 5º, which number is the twelfth part of 60—he produced from them the proportional parts, which he considered applicable not only for these two planets but also for the three upper ones <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, as will be seen further below.

### Chapter 8.

## **Regarding the third type of latitude in Venus and Mercury, which is called Deviation.**

After these developments, only a few things remain to be said about the third movement of latitude, the deviation. The ancients, who view the Earth as standing firm in the center of the world, believe that this arises through an inclination of the eccentric circle <note>a circular orbit whose center is not the Earth</note>, in connection with a similar inclination of the epicycle <note>a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one</note>, around the center of the Earth; specifically when the epicycle is located in the apogee or perigee, for Venus always one-sixth of a degree toward the North, for Mercury always three-quarters of a degree toward the South, as we have already stated previously. It is not sufficiently clear, however, whether they thought of this inclination as always equal and the same; their numerical determinations point to this, as they established that for the deviation of Venus 10' <note>minutes of arc</note> must always be taken, and for Mercury always 45', which would only be permitted if the angle of inclination always remained as many minutes large as they take as a basis. And yet it is not quite comprehensible how this latitude-movement of those planets, while the angle of inclination remained always the same, from the ge-

However, we are dealing here with a motion that is not jerky, but by its nature uniform. One must therefore admit that a certain oscillation <note>Latin: libratio; a swinging motion like a pendulum</note> occurs within it, which causes the parts of the circle to move toward opposite sides, as we have explained; from this, it must follow that the numerical values for Mercury differ by one-fifth of a degree. It should therefore be all the less surprising if this latitudinal motion, according to our assumption, is also variable and does not appear to be so simple, yet causes no noticeable error, so that it can be clearly recognized in all its differences.

In a base plane perpendicular to the ecliptic <note>The apparent path of the Sun; the reference plane for planetary orbits</note>, let there be a common line of intersection *cbea*. In this line, let *a* be the center of the Earth and *b* be the center of a circle *cdf* which passes through the poles of the inclined orbital circle itself, and through the points of the greatest and least distance from the Earth <note>Apogee and Perigee</note>. Now, while the center *b* of the circle is at the apogee or perigee in relation to *a*, the planet possesses its greatest deviation, regardless of which point on the circle parallel to the orbit it occupies.

Now let *df* be the diameter of this circle parallel to the diameter *cbe*, and these two straight lines are the common lines of intersection of these planes perpendicular to the plane *cdf*. Let *df* be bisected at *g*, so *g* itself is the center of the parallel circle; furthermore, the lines *bg*, *ag*, *ad*, and *af* are drawn, and the angle *bag* is assumed to be one-sixth of a degree, as in the case of the greatest deviation of Venus. In the triangle *abg*, which is right-angled at *b*, we have the ratio of the sides *ab* to *bg* as 10,000 to 29. The whole line *abc* <note>The distance to the furthest point of the orbit</note> is 17,193 in the same units, and the remainder *ae* <note>The distance to the nearest point</note> is equal to 2,807. 

The half-chord of the double arc *cd* and *ef* is equal to *bg*; thus, the angles *cad* are equal to 6' <note>minutes of arc</note> and *eaf* to 15'. The former differs by 4' and the latter by 5' from the angle *bag*. These differences are mostly neglected because of their smallness. Therefore, the apparent deviation of Venus, when the Earth is at its apogee or perigee, will be slightly greater or less than 10', regardless of which point of its orbit the planet is in. However, since for Mercury the angle *bag* amounts to three-quarters of a degree, the ratio of *ab* to *bg* is as 10,000...

Through the arc **fg**, the line **eg** (considered as a straight line not differing from the curved one) becomes known, as does **ef** and the remainder **be** in parts of **bf**. # Chapter 9.

## **On the Calculation of the Latitudes of the Five Planets.**

The procedure for calculating the latitudes of the five planets from these tables is as follows: first, for Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, we adjust the individual corrected anomaly <note>The "anomaly" refers to the angular distance of a planet from its furthest point from Earth (apogee).</note> of the eccentric circle to the common numbers. We leave this unchanged for Mars, decrease it by 20º for Jupiter, and increase it by 50º for Saturn. Now, we note the sixtieths, or the proportional minutes, which are found in the last column. Likewise, using the individual parallactic anomaly <note>The "parallactic anomaly" relates to the planet's position relative to the Sun as viewed from Earth.</note> for each planet specifically, we take the corresponding latitude—namely the first or northern latitude, if the proportional minutes are on the first page (which occurs when the anomaly of the eccentric circle is less than 90º and greater than 270º); or the southern or second latitude, if the proportional minutes are on the second page (which occurs when the anomaly of the eccentric circle is greater than 90º or less than 270º). If one then multiplies one or the other of these latitudes by their proportional minutes, the result is the northern or southern distance from the ecliptic <note>The ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere; latitude measures how far a planet sits above or below this path.</note>, depending on the designation of the arcs used.

In the case of Venus and Mercury, one must first take the three corresponding latitudes of declination, obliquation <note>term: obliquation (the slanting or inclination of the planet's orbit)</note>, and deviation through the individual parallactic anomaly and note them separately. However, for Mercury, one must decrease the obliquation by one-tenth if the number of the anomaly of the eccentric circle is on the first page of the table; conversely, increase it by the same amount if the number is found on the second page; and then apply that remainder or sum. Their designations, however—whether they are northern or southern—are decided as follows: if the individual parallactic anomaly lies in the apogean semicircle (i.e., it is less than 90º and greater than 270º) and at the same time the anomaly of the eccentric circle is less than the semicircle; or if the parallactic anomaly lies in the perigean semicircle (i.e., it is greater than 90º and less than 270º) and at the same time the anomaly of the eccentric circle is greater than the semicircle: then the declination of Venus is northern, and that of Mercury is southern. If, on the other hand, the parallactic anomaly lies in the perigean semicircle and the anomaly of the eccentric circle is less than the semicircle; or if the parallactic anomaly lies in the apogean semicircle and the anomaly of the eccentric circle is greater than the semicircle: then, conversely, the declination of Venus is southern and that of Mercury is northern. Regarding obliquation, it is as follows: if the parallactic anomaly is less than the semicircle and the anomaly of the eccentric circle is simultaneously apogean <note>apogean: relating to the point in the orbit furthest from the Earth.</note>; or if the parallactic anomaly is greater than the semicircle and the anomaly of the eccentric circle is simultaneously perigean <note>perigean: relating to the point in the orbit closest to the Earth.</note>; then the...
