<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of planetary latitudes, specifically focusing on the complex calculations for the inner planets, Venus and Mercury.</meta>

# 363

The obliquation <note>The "slanting" or tilting of the planet's orbit relative to the ecliptic</note> of Venus is northern, while that of Mercury is southern. The converse <note>The opposite case</note> of this also applies. The deviations, however, always remain northern for Venus and southern for Mercury. Furthermore, one takes the proportional minutes <note>Small adjustments used to scale the planetary latitude based on the planet's position</note>—which are common to all five planets, though only listed alongside the outer planets—using the specific anomaly <note>The angular distance of a planet from its furthest point (apogee) in its eccentric orbit</note> of the eccentric circle, and adds them to the obliquation and the deviation. 

Following this, one adds 90° to the eccentric anomaly and uses this sum to find the common proportional minutes again; these are then added to the latitude of the declination <note>The angular distance of the planet north or south of the celestial equator</note>. Once all of this has been set in order, the three individually calculated latitudes are each multiplied by their respective proportional minutes. These products then provide all three corrected latitudes for the specific place and time. Finally, if all three have the same name <note>Meaning they are all northern or all southern</note>, they are added together to obtain the final latitude of these two planets. If they do not have the same name, at least two will be the same; these are added together, and this sum may be smaller or larger than the third, differently-named latitude. One then calculates the difference between the two, and this result is the latitude being sought.

<meta>This page begins a historical and bibliographical analysis of the first edition of Nicolaus Copernicus's seminal work, focusing on the disputed title and the controversial anonymous preface.</meta>

1) The title of the first edition of the present work reads in translation: "Six Books on the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres by Nicolaus Copernicus of Thorn. You receive, diligent reader, in this newly created and completed work, the movements of both the fixed stars and the wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" refers to the planets.</note>, established from ancient and modern observations, and equipped with new and wonderful theories. At the same time, you receive the most useful tables, from which you can calculate these movements for any given time as conveniently as possible. Therefore buy, read, and enjoy. **Let no one untrained in geometry enter** <note>original Greek: "Ἀγεωμέτρητος οὐδεὶς εἰσίτω" — a famous motto famously inscribed over the entrance to Plato's Academy.</note>. Nuremberg, published by Joh. Petrejus in the year 1543."

On the title page of the copy in the Wolfenbüttel Library, there is a handwritten note in Latin, which reads in translation:
> "Copernicus took the title of his work from a passage in Proclus's astronomical hypotheses, where he says: Sosigenes the Peripatetic in his '**On the Revolving [Spheres]**' <note>original Greek: "περὶ τῶν ἀνελιττουσῶν"</note> i.e., on the circular motions; he himself did not add 'of the heavenly spheres' <note>original Latin: "orbium coelestium"</note>, but someone else did."

Abraham Gotthelf Kästner, in his "History of Mathematics. Göttingen 1797. Vol. II. page 367," identifies Andreas Osiander as the one who added the phrase "of the heavenly spheres." However, in Copernicus's preface to the Pope, the full expression "revolution of the heavenly spheres" <note>original Latin: "revolutio orbium coelestium"</note> appears, where it certainly originates from Copernicus himself. Likewise, the heading of the 10th chapter of the 1st book, "On the order of the heavenly spheres" <note>original Latin: "De ordine coelestium orbium"</note>, also contains the words in question.

From a copy of the first edition kept in the University Library at Uppsala, which Rheticus <note>Georg Joachim Rheticus, Copernicus's only pupil and the man responsible for bringing the work to publication.</note> presented to the Canon Georg Donner at Frauenburg, the correctness of Kästner's statement does indeed seem to emerge. On the title page of this copy, the words "of the heavenly spheres" are crossed out in red. Since Donner, who was a close friend of Copernicus and certainly knew the author's intentions, must have made this mark, it is to be assumed that Copernicus did not write them. This is also confirmed by the autograph manuscript of the work in Prague, where in one place—the only one where a kind of title appears—it is written in Copernicus's hand: "The fifth book of revolutions ends" <note>original Latin: "Quintus revolutionum liber finit"</note>, and thus nothing of "heavenly spheres" is to be found.

2) Regarding these introductory words, which are completely foreign to the idea of the entire work, Humboldt says (Cosmos II. p. 345—346): "It is an erroneous and, unfortunately, even in recent times (Delambre, History of Modern Astronomy Vol. I. p. 140) very widespread opinion that Copernicus, out of fear and in apprehension of priestly persecution, presented the planetary motion of the Earth and the position of the Sun in the center of the entire planetary system as a mere hypothesis, which fulfilled the astronomical purpose of conveniently subjecting the orbits of the celestial bodies to calculation, 'but need be neither true nor even probable.' To be sure, one reads these strange words in the anonymous preface with which Copernicus's work begins, titled 'On the Hypotheses of this Work' <note>original Latin: "de Hypothesibus hujus operis"</note>; but they contain expressions which, being entirely foreign to Copernicus, stand in direct contradiction to his dedication to Pope Paul III. The author of the preface is, as Gassendi (Life of Copernicus p. 319) states most definitely, a mathematician then living in Nuremberg, Andreas Osiander, who with Schoner [supervised] the printing of the—

### To Joachim Rheticus.

Having returned from the King's wedding celebration in Krakow, I find the two copies sent by you of the recently printed work of our Copernicus, whose passing I did not hear of until I had set foot on Prussian soil. I might have balanced the pain over the loss of the brother and great man by reading the book, which seemed to bring him back to me alive; but right at the beginning I noticed the faithlessness and—you use the right expression—the villainy of Petrejus <note>Johannes Petrejus, the printer of the first edition</note>, which aroused an indignation in me greater than the preceding sadness. For who would not be enraged at such a great crime committed under the protection of trust? Yet it is perhaps to be attributed not so much to this printer, who is dependent on others, as to the envy of a man who, perhaps out of pain at having to abandon the old confession should this book gain fame, has abused the simplicity of the printer to withdraw the trust in the work. But so that he who has allowed himself to be bribed by another's deceit does not go unpunished, I have written to the Senate in Nuremberg and indicated in the letter what is necessary, in my opinion, to restore trust in the author. I am sending the letter with a copy of the work to you, so that you may judge according to the circumstances how the matter is to be initiated. For in pursuing the same with the Senate, no one seems to me so suitable or so willing as you, who played the role of the chorus leader <note>term: "Chorfürhers" (coryphaeus) - the leader of the chorus in Greek drama, here meaning the primary promoter of the work</note> in the performance of the piece, so that you must be no less concerned than the author with the restoration of what has been distorted. If this is important to you, I urgently request you to carry out everything with the greatest care. When the first sheets to be reprinted arrive, you should, it seems to me, add a preface, so that even the copies already issued may be freed from the error of distortion. Indeed, I even wish that the biography of the author might be sent ahead, which I have read in the attractive composition by your hand; I believe nothing further is missing from it but the end of his life, which was brought about by a hemorrhage with added paralysis of the right side on May 24, after memory and mental vigor had already vanished many days before. He only saw the work in its completion at his last breath on the same day that he passed away. That it appeared in print before his death is of no consequence; for the year matches, and the printer did not add the day on which the printing was completed. I wish that the little treatise, through which you freed the movement of the earth from the reproach of a contradiction with the Holy Scripture, might also be added. Thus the work receives its proper scope, and you will at the same time make up for the grievance that the teacher did not mention you in the preface of the work, which in my opinion he omitted not out of indifference toward you, but as a result of his heaviness and carelessness, especially since he was already faint, as I well know how highly he was accustomed to value your assistance and your kindness. For the copies sent to me, I return great thanks to the giver; they will serve me as an everlasting monument to the memory not only of the author, whom I have always loved, but also of you, who stood powerfully by his side in his work as a Theseus <note>A mythological reference to a loyal companion or hero</note>, and have now contributed through your efforts and through your care to the fact that we do not lack the enjoyment of the completed work. How much we all have to thank you for these efforts of yours is not in...

The passage to which Copernicus refers here is found in Cicero, *Academic Questions* <note>original: "Academicae quaestiones"</note> Book IV, Chapter 29, and reads: "Nicetas of Syracuse, as Theophrastus says, believes that the heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars, and finally all things above, stand still; and that nothing in the world moves except the earth, which, while it turns and twists around its axis with the greatest speed, produces all the same effects as if the heavens moved while the earth stood still. While the latter rolls and turns around its axis with the greatest speed, everything is brought about just as if the heavens turned while the earth stood still. <image-desc>Two geometric diagrams labeled Fig. I and Fig. II. 
Fig. I: A larger circle on the left with center point W and a vertical radius labeled ρ (rho). To its right is a smaller circle with center point L and a horizontal diameter labeled δ (delta). 
Fig. II: A composite diagram where the smaller circle (diameter δ, center L) is placed inside the larger circle (center W). The smaller circle touches the top inner edge of the larger circle. The larger circle's vertical radius is labeled ρ' (rho prime). The center W is located directly below center L.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

If in Fig. I, W is the center of the water-sphere and ρ <note>the Greek letter rho</note> its radius; likewise L is the center of the land-sphere and δ <note>the Greek letter delta</note> its diameter: then let δ³ : (2 ρ)³ = 1:7, then δ = 1.0455161 · ρ ; it follows, therefore, that if the water-sphere were 7 times as large as the land-sphere, and each of the two existed for itself, the diameter of the land-sphere would still be somewhat larger than the radius of the water-sphere.

Fig. II. If one were to submerge this land-sphere into the water-sphere, and the water-sphere then restored its spherical shape: the whole body would now be eight times as large as the land-sphere alone. If we designate the radius of this new sphere in Fig. II as ρ' : then we have δ³ : (2 ρ')³ = 1:8, therefore δ = ρ' ;

and the land-sphere consequently would only touch the water-sphere from the inside, while the center of the whole body would lie only on the surface of the land-sphere. The land-sphere could therefore no longer protrude from the water's surface without leaving the center of the whole body to the water alone. Regarding the origin and history of the doctrine of the [earth] submerged in a water-sphere—

⁹) That Copernicus understands nothing else by the expression "middle circle" <note>original: "circulus medius"</note> than the 180th degree of longitude from Ferro (or from the Fortunate Islands), is evident from the fact that Ptolemy—whom Copernicus cites in the text—says in his *Geography*, Book VI, at the beginning of Chapter 16 (which deals with the location of Serica <note>An ancient name for Northern China</note>): this Serica borders on the east with unknown land, specifically between 35 and 63 degrees of latitude at the meridian which has a geographical longitude of 180º. However, as is well known, Ptolemy calculates his geographical longitudes from the Fortunate (Canary) Islands, thus approximately from Ferro. With this determination of the eastern border of Serica, the remark of Ptolemy in *Geography*, Book I, Chapter 12—"The known length of the whole [earth] from the meridian through the Fortunate Islands to the Seres is 177 and one-fourth parts"—stands in no contradiction; for this determination of longitude refers to the capital city Sera (Sera Metropolis), whose geographical longitude is determined in the aforementioned Book VI, Chapter 16, as 177º 15' at a northern latitude of 38º 36'. The mathematician Giovanni Antonio Magini (born in Padua 1551, died in Bologna 1617), who produced a Latin edition of Ptolemy's *Geography* with commentaries, designates the location of Sera in the latter on page 24 as 7 hours and 55 minutes—that is, 118º 45' east of Alexandria. Since, according to Ptolemy in the aforementioned Book IV, Chapter 5, the longitude of Alexandria is given as 60º 30', the longitude of Sera would accordingly be 179º 15'. Currently, the longitude of Alexandria is known to be 47º 30' east of Ferro, and the view is held that modern-day Xi'an <note>original: "Singanfu"</note> on the Wei River, which lies 126º 20' east of Ferro and 34º 6' northern latitude, is that ancient Sera which, until Ptolemy's time, formed the easternmost point that merchants still reached.

¹⁰) Cathagya is the same land which is otherwise also called Cataya or Catayo <note>Cathay</note>. Compare *The Geography of Claudius Ptolemy* by author J. A. Pliny, and after him even more so Ptolemy (Pliny, *Natural History* VI, c. 24 and Ptolemy VII, c. 3), first learned there of the nomadic Scythians and the trading Serer people as far as the land of the distant Sinae; only since then has the great name of this region, corresponding to the culture of the land, come into use with Ptolemy VI, c. 15—namely, as the land of the nomads outside, i.e., to the east of the Imaus (*Scythia beyond the Imaus*). The same stretch of land has been very frequently referred to by Muhammadan-Asian and Christian-European authors since the Middle Ages—though always only in its further explored eastward extent—by the very indefinite name Cathay, Kathai. The similarity of the name with Cathea Sophitis (in Strabo XV, f. 699 and Quintus Curtius IX, 1) in India, from the time of Alexander the Great, is analogous only in sound but not in content (Andr. Müller, *Geographical and Historical Disquisition on Cathay*, Berlin 1671, p. 79). This name is rather to be derived from the Mongol-Tungusic people of the Khitan (plural *Kithat* according to A. Rémusat, compare Klaproth on the different names of China in *Memoirs relating to Asia*, Paris 1828, III, p. 259), who rose to a widespread power in high Inner Asia even before the Mongol period, since the 10th century, on the throne of Northern China and westward in Tangut."

...daily change both their positions and their circles. For none of these stars rises in the same place where it rose the day before. If this is the case, there is no doubt that the sun has 183 circles, through which it either descends from the summer solstice to the winter solstice, or ascends from the latter to the summer solstice. But while the sun possesses the specified number (of circles), Mars describes twice as many, Jupiter twelve times, and Saturn twenty-eight times as many circles, which are also called parallel circles. All these movements advance with the (fixed-star) world and encircle the earth with rising and setting. On the other hand, although Venus and Mercury show daily rising and setting, their paths do not go around the earth at all, but rather group themselves around the sun, which is larger in circumference; in short, they place the center of their paths in the sun, so that they move sometimes above it, mostly below it, closer to the earth; and indeed Venus deviates from the sun by one sign and a half degree. <summary>This page discusses the planetary orbits of Mercury and Venus around the Sun and provides scholarly annotations regarding Hermes Trismegistus and classical literary references used by Copernicus. --- Page 402 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of planetary motion, specifically addressing the transition from Copernican natural motion to the mechanical "attraction theory" (Newtonian physics) and the debate over the "motion of declination."</meta>

the Earth its natural foundation, and it becomes something non-essential to the Earth, brought about by external causes—that is, by mechanical forces—and therefore accidental. This has now occurred through the <term>theory of attraction</term><note>Newtonian gravity</note>, in which one has felt compelled to assume that every planet originally received an "impulse" <note>a tangential force or "shove"</note> which ensures that it cannot fall into the sun, but must instead orbit the sun in a path. From this mechanical view arose the objections against the <term>motion of declination</term><note>Copernicus's "third motion," which he proposed to explain why the Earth's axis remains parallel to itself as it orbits the sun</note> and, finally, its theoretical rejection. Lalande says of this (*Astronomy 1792. I No. 1100*):

> “At the time when all parts of the Earth were hurled forward by a lateral impulse, they all received parallel and equal velocities and directions; this, therefore, changes nothing in the position which they have relative to one another, and which they must continue to have. One can thus assume that the Earth, which originally rotated around a fixed axis, was hurled forward in any given direction. Since all parts received the same impulse, there is a complete equalization of the upper parts with the lower, and they all retain the rotational motion which they had before; that is, every particle moves in a direction parallel to that which it initially had when the Earth stood still. When a body has begun to move around its axis, its two poles—or the points which do not rotate around the axis—have received the same motion through the impulse applied to the center, which produced the progressive motion; but if they have received the same motion, there is no reason for one of these points to travel a greater distance than the other; and if they both travel the same distance, they will necessarily always remain on a line parallel to that on which they were at the beginning of the motion.”

— And referring to this, the same author (*III. No. 3220*) adds:

> “We have proven that the axis of rotation must always remain parallel to itself, whatever the motion of revolution may be.”

— And Gassendi, who can probably be regarded as the first to have come out against the “motion of declination,” expresses himself (*Astronomical Institution, London, 1653, Book III. 3.*) as follows:

> “The motion of declination is that turning away of the Earth's axis from its position parallel to the axis of the ecliptic, and the maintenance of a direction parallel with itself occurring in all positions, whereby it always remains parallel with the axis of the world; thus, this motion could be called not so much a truly new motion, but rather a law of the other two motions. It can, in fact, be understood in the same way in which the axis of a child’s spinning top remains parallel to itself or persists in a vertical position while it turns on a plane and describes various circles with its tip.”

Nonetheless, it might appear questionable to compare the movements of celestial bodies—or even to identify them—with those movements which we can bring about in earthly objects through external, mechanical forces or impulses. The dubiousness of assuming such impulses for celestial bodies has not escaped prudent experts, as can be felt from their occasional remarks; thus Mädler says (*Popular Astronomy. Berlin, 1846, p. 86*):

> “It is by no means asserted here that an actual, material impulse took place in the very beginning, but only the nature of the effect is designated by this comparison.”

One has also sought to find reassurance by imagining that rectilinear, uniform velocity—which would be the nature of the effect of an impulse—was originally inherent to all planets. This explanation, however, is only an apparent one, in that it merely shifts the assumption of that unnatural impulse into an immemorial past. Copernicus was far from thinking of such a force, or such an impulse, as the cause of planetary motion; he says instead:

> “Rectilinear motion <note>motion in a straight line</note> seizes only those bodies which have gone away or been pushed from their natural place, or are in some way outside of it. Nothing opposes the order and form of the whole world so much as being-outside-of-one's-place. Rectilinear motion, therefore, only occurs when things do not behave correctly and are not perfectly in accordance with nature, by separating themselves from their whole and leaving its unity.”

From these words, it is evident that Copernicus imagined the movements of the planets as essentially natural to them and therefore not produced by external causes or forces. And for this very reason, it could not occur to him to suspect that the Earth's axis of rotation should remain parallel to itself because its progressive motion was produced by a cause external to it. — But since he sought the cause of this phenomenon in the essence, in the natural determination of the Earth itself, he could only find it in a motion necessarily belonging to the Earth, a motion <term>immanent</term><note>inherent or internal</note> to it; and from this conviction, he drew the concept of the “motion of declination.”

<summary>This page contrasts the mechanical Newtonian view of planetary motion (caused by an external "impulse") with the Copernican view that motion is an inherent, natural property of celestial bodies. It specifically examines why Copernicus proposed a "third motion" (declination) to explain the stability of the Earth's axis, a concept later dismissed by astronomers like Lalande and Gassendi as a simple consequence of inertia.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the critical commentary on Nicolaus Copernicus's seminal work, specifically addressing his editorial changes and the inclusion of Pythagorean traditions.</meta>

37) Deviating from the Latin text: <note>original: "Quoniam declivitas aequinoctialis ad a e lineam per revolutionem diurnam detornat sibi tropicum hiemalem parallelum, secundum distantiam, quam sub e a h angulus inclinationis comprehendit"</note> "Since the equinoctial decline toward the **a e** line, through the daily revolution, carves out for itself the parallel winter tropic according to the distance contained within the angle of inclination **e a h**," I have taken the liberty of reading it here as: "Since through the equinoctial decline toward the **a e** line, the daily revolution carves out the parallel winter tropic etc." In the verb *detornare* <note>to turn on a lathe or carve out</note>, the "equinoctial decline" does not seem well-suited to be the subject; rather, the "daily revolution" is the subject, and it is not clear what relationship the "for itself" <note>Latin: sibi</note> would then have.

38) In the original manuscript, these closing words are followed by two and a half pages which are crossed out with very black ink, and with which Copernicus intended to close the first book. Chapters 12, 13, and 14 originally constituted the second book along with the table of chords, which Copernicus combined with the first book partly by striking text and partly by shortening it. The editors of the Jubilee Edition have added the material crossed out by Copernicus in the remarks, and these words read in English translation as follows:

Even if we were to admit that the course of the sun and the moon could be derived even with the immobility of the Earth, this is nonetheless less permissible for the remaining planets, and it is to be assumed that from these and similar causes Philolaus <note>A Greek Pythagorean philosopher who was among the first to suggest the Earth moves</note> recognized the mobility of the Earth; just as some say that Aristarchus of Samos <note>An ancient Greek astronomer who proposed a heliocentric model</note> was of the same opinion, even if not moved by that conclusion which Aristotle cites and rejects (On the Heavens II. 14). But since this is of such a nature that it cannot be grasped without a sharp mind and without long-sustained diligence, it remained, as Plato relates, mostly hidden from the philosophers at that time, and there were only a few who knew the cause of the movement of the stars at that time. But even if it was known to Philolaus or any Pythagorean, it is nonetheless probable that they did not surrender it to posterity. For it was the custom of the Pythagoreans not to hand down the secrets of philosophy in books, nor to open them to everyone, but solely to entrust them to the loyalty of friends and relatives, and to pass them from hand to hand. As a document for this fact, there is a letter from Lysis to Hipparchus, which I wish to include here because of its thoughts worth taking to heart, and so that it may be clear how highly they esteemed philosophy among themselves, and with the same I wish to close this first book. I have translated the content of the letter from the Greek as follows (namely into Latin):

->Lysis greets Hipparchus.<-

> After the death of Pythagoras, I would never have believed that the connection of his students would be dissolved. Although we are, contrary to expectation, scattered and dispersed like those who have suffered a shipwreck, one here, another there, it is nonetheless a holy duty to remain mindful of his divine teachings and not to communicate the treasures of philosophy to those who have not even dreamed of the purification of the spirit. For it is not fitting to surrender to everyone that which we have acquired with such great effort. Just as it is not permitted to open the secrets of the Eleusinian goddesses <note>Demeter and Persephone; their "mysteries" were sacred rites of ancient Greece</note> to ordinary people, and with completely equal right would the one or the other be considered ill-intentioned and forgetful of duty. It is worth the effort to consider how much time we needed to erase the stains that clung to our minds, until after the passage of five years we became receptive to his teachings. As painters, after cleaning, fix the color of garments with a certain mordant <note>A substance used to set dyes</note> so that they soak up the indelible coloring which cannot easily fade afterward: so did that divine man prepare the friends of philosophy, so that he would not be deceived in the trust which he had placed in the capability of anyone. For he did not sell science as a commodity, nor did he connect the use of truth with snares in which many Sophists <note>Teachers in ancient Greece often criticized for using clever but fallacious arguments for money</note> catch the minds of youths, but he was a teacher in divine and human things. Many imitators of his teaching do much and great things, but in an unseemly manner and not as it is fitting to instruct a youth, whereby they make their listeners reckless and impudent. For they stain the pure principles of philosophy with impetuous and impure customs. It is as if someone pours pure, clear water into a deep well filled with filth; the filth is set in motion and lets the water through <note>meaning the water becomes contaminated by the mud</note>. So it goes for those who teach and are taught in such a manner. Dense and dark forests cover the understanding and the heart of those who are not initiated in the proper way, and disturb the entire gentleness and discretion of the spirit. All kinds of vices penetrate into this forest, which consume and prevent anything rational from emerging from it. As mothers of those intruders, we wish to name mainly self-interest and greed. Both are very fertile. For self-interest gives birth to unchastity, gluttony, desecration, unnatural lusts, and many violent impulses that lead to death and destruction. For some have already been so carried away by desire that they...

neither the mother nor the children were spared; she led them astray against the laws, against the fatherland, against the state, and against the rulers, laying snares for them and bringing those she captured to the severest punishments. From greed, however, are born robberies, murders, sacrilege, the mixing of poisons, and other sisters of the same kind. Although she could have sold them for much money, she did not wish to do so, but valued poverty and the commands of her father higher than gold. It is also said that the dying Dama left the same to her daughter, Vitalia, as a trusted possession. We, however, of the male sex, are forgetful of our duty toward our teacher and are transgressors of our confession. If you therefore improve yourself, I shall love you; if not, you are dead to me.”

The heading of Chapter 12, “On the Magnitude of Straight Lines in a Circle,” which follows here in the printed editions, is missing in the original manuscript; instead, one finds the heading “On the Straight Lines which are Chords in a Circle.” The beginning of the chapter as it appears in the editions, as well as some preceding sentences, are crossed out in the manuscript. These crossed-out words read in translation as follows:
> “What appeared necessary from natural philosophy as principles and assumptions for our development—namely, that the world is spherical, immense, and similar to the infinite; further, that the sphere of fixed stars encompasses everything and is immobile, but that the motion of the other celestial bodies is circular—we have treated in general terms. We have also added that the Earth is involved in several circular motions, upon which we lean as a foundation for the development of our entire theory of the stars. But because the developments which we employ in almost the entire work deal with straight lines and arcs, and with plane and spherical triangles, and although much regarding this is already available in the Elements of Euclid, one still does not possess what is chiefly required here—namely, how one can find the sides from the angles and the angles from the sides—so etc.” Compare Chapter 12.

60) This observation is found in: *Almagest* VII. 2. The reduction of its Egyptian date can easily be carried out as follows. The first Egyptian regnal year of Augustus begins on August 31st, or on the 1st of Thoth, thus on the 243rd day of the 4684th year of the Julian Period, at 12 o'clock noon Alexandria time; cf. Ideler, *Handbook*, I. 157. — From the beginning of the Julian Period until Augustus, there had therefore elapsed: 4683 years 242 days 12 hours Julian. The interval between Augustus and Aelius Antoninus, the latter being identical with the Antoninus Pius of the text, amounts to 166 Egyptian years. The observation in question took place on the 9th of Pharmuthi, thus on the 219th day of the second year of Antoninus Pius, which is 167 years 218 days Egyptian, or 167 years 176 days 6 hours Julian after Augustus. If one adds to this those 4683 years 242 days 12 hours, one obtains 4851 years 53 days 18 hours after the beginning of the Julian Period.

Copernicus was not acquainted with the Julian Period <note>A chronological system used by astronomers to provide a single count of days starting from 4713 BCE.</note> used here, because it was first formed forty years after his death by Joseph Scaliger in his work "On the Improvement of Time, Paris 1583," through the multiplication of the three cyclic numbers 28, 19, and 15. According to this, with the beginning of this period, the Solar, Lunar, and Indiction cycles begin simultaneously, and this period begins anew every 7980 Julian years. Within such a period, every year is characterized by its own unique cyclic numbers. Now, for the first year of the Christian era, the Solar cycle was 10, the Golden Number <note>The year's position in the 19-year lunar cycle.</note> was 2, and the Indiction <note>A 15-year tax cycle used in the Roman Empire.</note> was 4, from which it follows that the 4714th year of the Julian Period is the first year after Christ. Compare Ideler, *Handbook*, II. 587. —

63) The conclusion of this chapter is rendered according to the wording of the Nuremberg edition, although it appears from the Thorn Secular Edition that the same deviates somewhat in the original manuscript. Might Copernicus have felt prompted to make this change because it already appeared doubtful to him whether Job was a historical person, and whether the Book of Job therefore possessed such a high antiquity that it could be cited as proof of the "ancient custom" of certain star names?

$^{67}$) This star, in the time of Ptolemy, had a polar distance of 8° 52'; it was therefore the bright star closest to the pole and would have deserved the name "Pole Star" at that time.

$^{68}$) The name *Helice* means "winding" or "spiral," from the Greek *helix* <note>original: ἑλίξ</note>, and is attributed to the Great Bear because its seven main stars form a serpentine line if one imagines the quadrilateral as a semicircle open to the north. Compare Ideler, *Star Names*, page 8.

$^{69}$) *Arctophylax* <note>original: Ἀρκτοφύλαξ</note> = Guardian of the Bear (Ovid, *Tristia* I. 10, 15.) = Bear-keeper, since *Arctos* is the mythological name for the Great Bear. Originally the name was *Arcturus*, which likewise means Bear-keeper, since *ouros* <note>original: οὖρος</note> = *phylax* <note>original: φύλαξ</note> = Watchman. This name, Arcturus, later became the name of the brightest star in this constellation.
->*Bootes* <note>original: Βοώτης</note> = Ox-driver; this is connected to the idea that Bootes was meant to drive the wagon, *amaxa* <note>original: ἅμαξα</note>, i.e., the Great Bear. Compare Ideler, *Star Names*, page 47.<-

$^{70}$) The star $\mu$ in the Shepherd’s Staff is called *Incalurus* in the Arabic-Latin *Almagest* and in the Alfonsine Tables, but more correctly *Alkalurops* in newer star charts. It is actually the Greek *kalaurops* <note>original: καλαῦροψ</note>, "shepherd’s staff," with the Arabic article prefixed. Ptolemy used the more unusual *kollarobon* <note>original: κολλάροβον</note> in his catalog, which is still missing from dictionaries and likely derived from *kalauropon* (this form is found in Hesychius). Later it was also written as *kalabrops*. Compare Ideler, *Star Names*, pages 49 and 50.

$^{71}$) According to the testimony of Avienus, the epic poet Panyasis (468 BC) was the first to give the name *Hercules* to this constellation, and Eratosthenes (272 BC) consequently placed a club in his hand, designated by the star $\omega$. Previously, the Greeks called the constellation *En gonasin* <note>original: ‘Ἐν γόνασιν‘</note> = "the one on his knees," and the Romans likewise called it *Engonasin*, or in translation *Nixus in genibus* (kneeling), *Geniculatus* (bent-kneed), etc.

$^{72}$) Regarding this star, Bode remarks in *Claudius Ptolemy's Observations and Descriptions of the Stars*, p. 117: "the new star of 1604." Kepler, in the star catalog compared with Tycho's and his own observations (*Rudolphine Tables* 1627, p. 108), lists this same star, "the one in the right shin," exactly as it is designated in the star catalogs of Ptolemy and Copernicus, and notes: "mine is lacking," meaning his catalog does not contain it.

$^{73}$) *Fl.* stands for Flamsteed, who included Ptolemy's star catalog in his *Historia Coelestis*, Volume III, and brought many stars that did not align into agreement through the correction of errors and reduction.

The month of Elaphebolion <note>A month in the Attic calendar, typically falling in early spring</note> is the ninth month of the Greek year, so 8 months and 15 days have elapsed from the beginning of the 36th Callippic year <term>Callippic year: A 76-year cycle used by Greek astronomers to improve the accuracy of the 19-year Metonic cycle</term>. Now, the duration of a Callippic month is 29 days, 12 hours, 44 minutes, 2.5 seconds; according to this, 8 months amount to: 236 days, 5 hours, 52 minutes, 20 seconds. If one adds the 15 days of the 9th month, one obtains 251 days. The 5th of Tybi is the 125th day of the Egyptian year, and November 5th is the 309th day of the Julian year. 308 + 125 — 365 = 68. The year 294 BC is a common year <note>a non-leap year</note> and the 68th day of a common year is March 9. The observation was therefore made on March 9, 294 before our era."

⁷⁶) The observations listed here are found in the *Almagest* <note>Ptolemy's 2nd-century mathematical and astronomical treatise</note> VII. 3.

⁷⁷) This would be the year 282 BC according to the superficial calculation 330 — 48 = 282. However, Ptolemy gives the date of this observation as follows: <note>original Latin: "Asserit etiam, quod in 48 ejusdem periodi anno..."</note> "He also asserts that in the 48th year of the same period, on the sixth day of the ending of Pyanepsion, but on the seventh of Thoth (the tenth hour having passed by half of one hour), Spica <note>The brightest star in the constellation Virgo</note> was seen to exactly touch the northern part of the Moon above the eastern horizon; and it is the year 466 from Nabonassar <term>Era of Nabonassar: A chronological era starting in 747 BC, used by ancient astronomers to record celestial events</term>, on the seventh of Thoth according to the Egyptians, the eighth following, as he himself writes, at 3:30 temporal hours after midnight, which are approximately 4:7:30 equinoctial hours." Thus, 465 Egyptian years or 169,725 days and 7 days of the first month, Thoth, have passed; therefore 169,732 days since the epoch of the Era of Nabonassar. According to Julian calculation, these are 464 Julian years and 256 days. Since the epoch of the Era of Nabonassar is February 26, 3967 <note>Julian Period year</note>, one obtains the Julian year of the observation by adding 3967 + 464 = 4431; this year is not a leap year, so the 256th day after February 26 is November 9. To determine the Christian Julian year more precisely than at the beginning of this note, we have to subtract 4431 from 4714, and thus obtain November 9, 283 BC as the date of the observation.
The month of Pyanepsion is the 5th of the year; 4 Callippic months are 118 days, 2 hours, 54 minutes, 10 seconds; if one adds 6 more days, then 124 days, 2 hours, 54 minutes, 10 seconds have elapsed since the beginning of the 48th Callippic year. If one now counts back these 124 days from November 9 according to Julian calendar days: the beginning of the 48th Callippic year results as July 8.

⁸¹) The passage in which Albategnius <note>Latinized name of Al-Battani, a famous 9th-century Arab astronomer</note> conducts the same investigation, based in part on the same older observations as Copernicus does here, is found in his already mentioned work "On the Motion of the Stars" (*de motu stellarum*) in the Nuremberg edition of 1537, Chapter 51, folio 79, and reads as follows: <note>original Latin: "Stellarum fixarum qualitates..."</note> "We have foretold in this book the qualities of the fixed stars in their rising and setting, and in their culmination, as well as in their stay above the earth and below the earth, and also in their distances and proximities in individual regions. Indeed, the pole of the motion of the fixed stars was found to be upon the two circles of the signs <note>the ecliptic</note>. And since their motion was detected to depart from it in no way, and their latitudes likewise were not altered. And likewise the longitudes between them are held invariably from the time they were observed, and therefore the fixed stars are called 'fixed' in longitude. For the motion of all of them is one and the same, as if they were moved in the same circle, whether they are moved naturally by themselves, or the circle revolves them by its own motion from west to east... We found their locations according to longitude and latitude in Ptolemy's book in the first year of King Antoninus, which is the year 886 from King Nebuchadnezzar <note>Nabonassar</note>; in one of those observations through which Ptolemy worked was the observation of Menelaus, which he used in the year 842 from King Nabonassar, and he said that the northern star, which is placed between the two eyes of the Scorpion, just as he tested by the Moon with the sphere of circles, existed in that year at 2 degrees and 22 minutes of Scorpio, and according to what he himself had written in his book, the Heart of the Lion <note>Regulus</note> in that same year was at 2 degrees and a sixth of Leo, but Leumia <note>likely a corruption of a star name, possibly in Gemini</note> ought to have been at the 17th degree of Gemini.
We also observed these and other stars very often in continuous years, and one of our observations in which we have the most confidence was made in the year 1191 of Alexander <note>the Seleucid era</note>, also observing the Moon and the transits of stars through the middle of heaven, their distance from the equinoctial circle..."

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of historical astronomical observations, specifically focusing on the calculations of Al-Battani (Albategnius) and his reconciliation of various ancient eras (Nabonassar, Alexander, and the Seleucid era) to determine the motion of fixed stars.</meta>

...and the parts of the signs with which the heavens are mediated to them, we have discovered their transitions through these; through these we have apprehended to which parts of the circle of signs in longitude and latitude their locations have reached. And we found the northern star, which revolves between the two eyes of the Scorpion <note>The star Beta Scorpii (Acrab)</note>, at 17 degrees and 20 minutes of Scorpio, while we found the Heart of the Lion <note>Regulus</note> at 14 degrees of Leo; the year of this observation was 1627 of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosor"</note>. And when these 11 degrees and 50 minutes, which are held between the first location and that location in which we ourselves found them, are divided by the 783 years which are between the two observations, we find their motion in every 66 solar years to be one degree; and thus we have described them in the tables of the motions of the fixed stars, which are extracted through collected and expanded years and months. Similarly, we also added 11 degrees and a half and a third <note>11 degrees and 50 minutes</note> to the locations in which we found them written in Ptolemy's book, and we recorded their locations in the year 1191 of the Era of the Two-Horned One <note>original: "ad Hilcarnain," referring to the Seleucid Era; "Dhul-Qarnayn" is an epithet for Alexander the Great</note>. In most of the stars which we observed more closely, we found no notable difference in latitude. Therefore, we established tables in which we placed their locations in longitude and latitude, as well as in part and quantity, so that the locations they reach after this year may be truly apprehended through their motions, which are extracted from the tables when they have been added to their locations in the year 1191.

In the canon of Assyrian and Median rulers, as given by Ideler in the *Handbook of Chronology* Vol. I, p. 111 after Halma, the ruler named Nebuchadnezzar in the above words of Albategnius is written as Nabocolassar, and it is noted therein that this is the Babylonian king who is called Nebuchadnezzar in the Hebrew historical books, and Nabuchodonosor by the Septuagint <note>LXX</note> and Josephus.

A confirmation of this identity is also provided by the date of Ptolemy's observation, which falls in the 2nd year of Antoninus, and finds mention both in the above words of Albategnius and in the text of Copernicus's work. This year is the 462nd after Alexander's death, as Copernicus also correctly writes. Alexander's death, however, falls 424 years after Nabonassar—cf. Note 75—thus the 2nd year of Antoninus is the $462 + 424 = 886$th year after Nabonassar, and in agreement with this, Albategnius writes "year 886 from King Nebuchadnezzar." Albategnius gives his own observation as "made in the year 1191 of the Two-Horned One." By this "ad Hilcarnain" is understood the Philippic or Seleucid Era, which begins 12 years after Alexander's death. — Cf. Albategnius Ch. XXX. fol. 36. a, and Ideler, *Astronomical Observations of the Ancients* p. 258. — Therefore, Albategnius also says, e.g., Ch. XXVII. fol. 27. a., that in the year 1206 after Alexander's death, or 1194 of the years of the Two-Horned One, on the 19th of Elul or the 3rd of Pachon, he observed the autumnal equinox. Elul = Eilul is the twelfth Syrian month, while the Syrian year began with Tishri I falling on October 1st, so the 19th of Elul = September 19th. In the year 1206 after Alexander's death, i.e., 1627 after Nabonassar, the 1st of Thoth fell on January 17th, according to which the 3rd of Pachon was likewise = September 19th. The two date entries are thus indeed identical. The difference between the year numbers 1206 – 1194, however, correctly amounts to 12.

Regarding the two observations of $\alpha$ Virginis <note>Spica</note> and $\beta$ Scorpii by Menelaus, the year number "842 from Nebuchadnezzar" contained in the text of Albategnius's work has evidently become incorrect through a printing error. The first year of Trajan is the 845th of Nabonassar, as Ptolemy in *Almagest* VII. 3 and, in agreement with him, Ideler (loc. cit. p. 35) have correctly reduced it.

...and the declination of the zodiacal circle from the equatorial circle <note>The "obliquity of the ecliptic," or the tilt of the Earth's axis</note> occupies only half of these parts, which is 23 degrees and 35 minutes, and this is the space contained between the two poles of the two circles." In the text of the Nuremberg, Basel, and Thorn editions of Copernicus's work, the obliquity of the ecliptic is given here as 23° 26' and in the 6th Chapter of the III Book as 23° 25'. The Amsterdam edition posits at least 23° 35' as more correct. From the report of Rheticus <note>Georg Joachim Rheticus (1514–1574), Copernicus's sole pupil</note>, in which the correct figure of 23° 35' is found, it appears that all deviating figures are likely based only on printing or clerical errors.

88) **Arzachel**, **Archazel**, **Azrachel**, actually **Abraham Eizarakil** <note>Al-Zarqali (c. 1029–1087), a leading Arab mathematician and astronomer of Al-Andalus</note>, lived in Toledo in 1080 AD, according to the text 1069 AD. In a folio manuscript volume of the Wolfenbüttel Library, with the shelfmark 65 MS., a work begins on folio 171 with the words: <note>original Latin: "Incipiunt Canones Arzachelis..."</note> "Here begin the Canons of Arzachel, or the rules established upon the astronomical tables for the city of Toledo." In this work, on folio 173, there is a chapter with the heading: "On the ascensions of the signs in the direct circle." In this chapter are the following words: "You shall take the total declination, which according to what Ptolemy reported is 23 degrees and 51 minutes, and according to Jahiben, son of Albumasar <note>likely referring to Yahya ibn Abi Mansur</note>, an admirable observer, 23 degrees and 33 minutes and 30 seconds, which among us is said to be truer; the first of these we know by rumor, and this latter we have learned through observation." The work ends on folio 180 with the words: "Here end the canons of Arzachel established upon the astronomical tables for the meridian of the city of Toledo. In the year of the incarnation of Jesus Christ 1455 by Wilhelm Gezenstorffer." Here, therefore, the obliquity of the ecliptic is stated to be 30'' smaller than in the text. In other writings by the same author, however, the obliquity of the ecliptic also appears as 23° 30'; for example, in a quarto manuscript volume of the Wolfenbüttel Library, with the shelfmark 24 MS., there is a work which begins: "Here begin the Rules of the Universal Astrolabe, which Azarchel wrote in letters to King Maymon of Toledo." The second part of this work begins with: "The first part is finished with the praise of God and His help, and the second follows." In this second part, the second chapter begins: "In the knowledge of the degree of declination, which you wish from the equinox of the day; after this work, place a mark above that degree in the zodiac as it proceeded; after this, place some pointer of the 'rete' <note>the star-map part of an astrolabe</note> in the northeastern quadrant on the limb above the maximum declination, which is 23 and a half degrees; after this, see if the mark falls under the middle of the rete, then see the *mamar* <note>an Arabic astronomical term for a specific line or passage</note> which passes over that degree, and place a mark in it above the place where it fell." <margin>Behold the axial declination of Arzachel, 9 minutes more than that which is now posited.</margin>

King Maymon of Toledo, to whom this letter is addressed, was originally, under the name Adafer Ali Maymon, governor of Toledo during the reign of the Umayyad Caliphs, but made himself independent in the year 1024; from then on, Toledo existed under him and his descendants as its own kingdom until Alfonso VI, King of Castile, conquered the city and kingdom on May 25, 1085.

In the work printed at Nuremberg in 1534: "29 Problems of the Saphaea, a noble astronomical instrument, by Johannes de Monteregio" <note>Regiomontanus</note>, the second part of which is titled: "The more recent teachings on the Saphaea of the father Abrusahk Azarchel," one likewise finds in Doctrine IV: "nearly 23 and a half degrees," in Doctrine VI "23 and a half degrees," and in Doctrine VIII "23 and a half degrees."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Copernicus’s sources, specifically focusing on the Jewish astronomer Prophatius (Jacob ben Machir ibn Tibbon) and his calculations regarding the tilt of the Earth's axis.</meta>

“...located in Oxford (according to Coxe’s Catalog p. 57). Copernicus has Prophatius ‘writing’ 230 years later, thus around 1300. The work of which Copernicus speaks is the Tables (i.e., the so-called *Almanac*), in the preface of which Jacob b. Machir himself places Al-Zarqali <note>original: "Zarkali"; an 11th-century Andalusian astronomer</note> around 400 of the Hegira <note>The Islamic calendar; 400 AH corresponds to roughly 1010 AD</note>. It is probable, however, that only the century is indicated here, and the tens and ones are missing. This *Almanac* has the year 1300 as its root date <term>Radix: the base date used for astronomical calculations</term>. It is likely not necessary to go into the two works of Prophatius which deal with astronomical instruments—namely one translated from Arabic (probably by Ahmed Ibn al-Saffar) and the other his own invention of the quadrant—although both exist in Latin translation, as I believe Copernicus had the *Almanac*, or a note taken from it, before him. Further investigations must still be made into the manuscripts of the *Almanac*, as the information from bibliographers is of little value, and a translation of the Arabic work by Ibn al-Haytham <note>original: "Ibn el Heithem"</note> must also be considered. I know from personal inspection <note>original: "Autopsie"</note> the Bodleian manuscript of the Hebrew original of these tables. Furthermore, I have received a copy of the beginning of the Latin Codex Bodl. 464, compared with Codex Rawlinson C. 117 (*Canons of the Almanac of Prophatius the Jew*), and have therefore recognized the identity of the tables with the *Almanac*. Finally, regarding the figures for the obliquity of the ecliptic <term>Obliquity of the ecliptic: the angle between Earth's equator and its orbit around the sun</term>, I have already pointed out in general in the article ‘Jewish Literature’ in the *Encyclopedia of Ersch and Gruber* Vol. 27, p. 439, that these are difficult to trust, as copyists sometimes substituted other numbers. In the English translation of that article, which Mr. Spottiswoode arranged in London and which appeared in 1857, I wrote the following on p. 186: The obliquity of the ecliptic stated by Al-Battani <note>original: "Albatani"</note>, Ibn Ezra (middle of the 12th century) and Levi ben Gerson (who wrote an original astronomical work in 1330–1340, which is in Hebrew in Paris and is recommended to specialists by Munk) as 23° 33' is reduced by Prophatius to 23° 32'. My source for Al-Battani, Ibn Ezra, and Levi was the work printed in Paris in 1521: *On the Motion of the Eighth Sphere* <note>original: "De motu octavae sphaerae"</note> by Augustinus Ricius (a student of Abraham Zacuto <note>original: "Abraham Zakul"</note>) leaf 36. b.; whether this was also the source for Prophatius, I am not certain, but I suspect it, as I wrote the note at the same time, and it is Ricius’s tendency to point out such changes in astronomical determinations, although his own theme is the precession of the equinoxes.”

The above words, according to which Prophatius is said to have given the obliquity of the ecliptic as 23° 32', are in full harmony with the text, while the claim that Al-Battani set the same at 23° 33' contradicts the citation given in Note 87 from the work of Al-Battani <note>original: "Albategnius"</note> himself, according to which the obliquity of the ecliptic is determined there as 23° 35'.

According to a note by Mr. Curtze in the *Thorn Newspaper* No. 133, June 12, 1877, a large number of books are found in the library at Uppsala which once belonged to the Cathedral Library at Frombork <note>original: "Frauenburg"</note> or the Jesuit Library at Braniewo <note>original: "Braunsberg"</note>, and all bear the inscription *Book of the Warmian Library* <note>original: "Liber Bibliothecae Varmiensis"</note>. Among these, the aforementioned gentleman lists under No. 10: “A volume that belonged to the Jesuit Library in Braniewo, but in its older parts originates from the library of the Friars Minor in Braniewo; the newer components only entered it after Copernicus’s death. In it, however, is a parchment manuscript of the *Almanac of Prophatius the Jew* from 1302, which Copernicus may very well have used, as he mentions Prophatius several times in his work.” My efforts to obtain an authentic copy of Prophatius’s statement on the obliquity of the ecliptic, which is surely to be found in this manuscript, have unfortunately remained unsuccessful.

In *Zedler’s Universal-Lexicon* Part 29, p. 842, it is said of Prophatius that he was a rabbi in Montpellier, and according to Christmann’s *Astronomical Illustrations* and Ricius in the *Preface to Ptolemy’s Almagest*, as well as Lucas Gauricus in his speech *In Praise of Astronomy*, he flourished in the 13th century, and that King Alfonso X, the Wise, of Castile (1252–1284), made heavy use of him when he prepared his *Alfonsine Tables*. Of his writings, all of which still remain unprinted, the following are located:
1. Various works in the Vatican Library in Rome in the Latin language,
2. *Treatise on the Quadrant* <note>original: "Tract. de quadrante"</note>, in the Paduan Library,
3. *Tables*, in the Bodleian Library,
4. *Treatise on the Eclipse of the Sun and Moon* <note>original: "Tract. de eclipsi solis et lunae"</note> and
5. *Canons on the Almanac*, in the Bodleian Library.

According to the notes from Mr. Steinschneider shared above, numbers 3 and 5 would be identical and would be the writing from which Copernicus drew the information about the obliquity of the ecliptic. Regarding Prophatius, see the recently published treatise: *The Preface to the Almanac of Prophatius the Jew of Montpellier (1300), hitherto unpublished, from two ancient versions (one also interpolated) together with the Hebrew text edited for the first time from manuscripts, with a literal Latin translation added by Moritz Steinschneider* (Boncompagni Bulletin, Vol. IX, 1876, 595–614).

$^{91 a)}$ In the original manuscript, Copernicus had originally added several sentences here that were later crossed out, from which it appears that he sensed the elliptical shape of the planetary orbits! It says there:
> And it should be noted here in passing that if the circles **hg** and **cf** were unequal, while the other conditions remained the same, they would describe not a straight line, but a conic or cylindrical section, which mathematicians call an ellipse; but more on these matters elsewhere. <note>original Latin: "Estque hic obiter animadvertendum... sed de his alias." This is a significant passage because it suggests Copernicus glimpsed the possibility of elliptical orbits decades before Kepler proved them.</note>

(Centenary Edition of the *Revolutions* p. 166, Note to line 26).

$^{92)}$ Book III. Chapter 2.

$^{93)}$ Aristyllus was a contemporary of Timochares, thus living around 290 BC, and likely observed together with Timochares in Alexandria. Ptolemy uses the observations of both in *Almagest* VII. 3 as being simultaneous. Lalande, *Astronomy* I. p. 111. No. 315 remarks on both:
> "The first Greeks who cultivated astronomy in Alexandria were Timocharis and Aristyllus. Ptolemy, in his *Almagest*, ensures that Hipparchus had employed their observations, although imperfect, and had recognized by their means the movement of the stars in longitude (Ptol. VII. 1. 2. 3.). Ptolemy himself cites several of their observations: the oldest is from the year 294 before the common era. Timocharis saw the northern edge of the moon touch the northern star in the forehead of the Scorpion: this observation is one of the best we have for knowing the movement that the fixed stars have had. I used it to advantage in a memoir, where I established, both by theory and by observations, the change of the stars in latitude (*Memoirs of the Academy* 1758)." <note>Lalande was an influential 18th-century French astronomer.</note>

$^{94)}$ Hipparchus was born in Nicaea in Bithynia around 160 BC; his observations were made partly in Rhodes and partly in Alexandria. From him comes the first catalog of fixed stars. A detailed report on his significant works can be found in Lalande’s *Astronomy* I. p. 113—115. No. 321—327.

$^{95)}$ Agrippa observed, according to *Almagest* VII. 3, in Bithynia, likely in Nicaea, in the twelfth year of Domitian, or in the 840th year of Nabonassar <note>The Era of Nabonassar is a chronological scale starting in 747 BC, used by ancient astronomers</note>, thus in the year 93 AD, and was consequently a contemporary of Menelaus.

$^{96)}$ Menelaus observed in Rome, in the first year of Trajan, or in the 845th year of Nabonassar, thus in the year 98 AD; compare Ideler, *Historical Investigations* p. 35.

$^{97)}$ This period extends from 139 to 881 AD, and thus encompasses 742 years.

$^{98)}$ It is to be regretted that Copernicus did not share the method of his more detailed calculation; however, if one accepts the statement (not further proven) that the movement of the <term>anomaly of the precession of the equinoxes</term> <note>The variation or "wobble" in the rate at which the equinoxes shift over time</note> in 1819 years exceeded its full revolution by 21° 24', then the proportion
->381²/₅ : 360 = 1819 : **x**<-
yields for **x** indeed 1716.937 years, for which 1717 years are then set in the text.

$^{99)}$ If one compares, for example, the observations of Menelaus with those of Ptolemy, there is a period of about 40 years between them, and in this time the precession of the equinoxes amounted to 25'; thus in 96 years 1°; this yields for a time of 102 years 1° 3.75', for which 1° 4' is set in the text. Had the precession in the above period of 40 years amounted to 25.098', exactly 1° 4' would have resulted for 102 years. Since from Timochares' time to Copernicus, i.e., in 1819 years, the precession had amounted to 25° 1', it yields for 1717 years 25° 1' — 1° 4' = 23° 57'.

$^{100)}$ Since in 1717 years the precession is supposed to be 23° 57', a period of 25808.768 years would be required for one full revolution, and not 25816 years as in all old editions. The Warsaw edition has 25809 (cf. Centenary Edition p. 171, note to line 18). According to this, 15¹/₃₉ revolutions of the anomaly would occur for one cycle of precession. Compare Note $^{104)}$.

Copernicus, Book II, Chapter 14, assumes that Ptolemy determined the star positions he observed for noon on the 24th of February in the year 139 AD—which corresponds to the year 4852 of the Julian Period, or the year 886 of Nabonassar <note>The Era of Nabonassar is an astronomical epoch beginning in 747 BC, used extensively by Ptolemy</note>, or the 462nd year after Alexander’s death, or the 2nd year of Aelius Antoninus, on the 10th of Pharmuthi <note>An Egyptian month</note>.

which is 138 years and 88.5 days; in all editions, the half-day is missing.

Admittedly, this latter date contradicts Ptolemy's own statement in *Almagest* VII. 5, which specifies the beginning of the reign of Antoninus (the 20th of July) as the time for which his observations are valid.

which gives 914 years and 101 days (Egyptian). For this period, one obtains from the tables for the uniform movement of the equinoxes: 12º 44' 57'' 42'''
->the text instead gives: 12º 44'<-
as the simple anomaly: . . . . . 95º 51' 0'' 3'''
->the text instead gives: . . . . . 95º 44'<-

Both discrepancies are explained by the fact that Copernicus found the period between the start of the Olympiads and the Era of Nabonassar to be 1 year too small. — At the time of Ptolemy's observations, the observed position of the vernal equinox point was 6º 40', and the double anomaly was 42º 30'. The latter, according to the tables, yields a <term>prosthaphärese</term> <note>A correction or "equation" added or subtracted to convert mean motion to true motion</note> of 47' 40'', for which the text reads 48'. Adding this prosthaphärese to the observed position of the vernal equinox point (6º 40') gives the mean position of the vernal equinox point at the time of Ptolemy's observations as 7º 27' 40'', for which the text has 7º 28'. Adding 360º to this and subtracting the precession of 12º 44' 57'' 42''' mentioned above results in the mean position of the vernal equinox point at the start of the Olympiads as 354º 42' 18''', for which the text has 354º 44'. The vernal equinox point thus followed <term>γ Arietis</term> <note>Gamma Arietis, a star in the constellation Aries used as a reference point</note> by 5º 17' 17'' 42'''. If one adds 360º to the simple anomaly at the time of Ptolemy (namely 21º 15') and subtracts the simple anomaly of 95º 51' calculated above, one obtains the position of the simple anomaly at the start of the Olympiads: 285º 24', whereas the text finds 285º 30'. From that point on, the positions or "roots" for the dates named in the text can easily be calculated using the tables and the intervening times. In the small table below, the more precisely calculated positions are placed alongside those given in the text for comparison.

170) Thabit ibn Qurra <note>original: "Thebit Ibn Chora"</note>, also known as Thabit ben Korrah or Thabet Ebn Korra Ebn Merwan, the Sabian, lived at the time of al-Ma'mun, Caliph of Baghdad, in Harran and died in 901 AD. He was the first to accurately distinguish the sidereal year from the tropical year <term>tropical year: the time the sun takes to return to the same position in the cycle of seasons, as seen from Earth</term>, declared the former to be the true orbital period of the sun, and determined its duration to be 365.25639 days, almost entirely in agreement with the latest astronomical determinations. Compare Ritter's *Geography* <note>original: "Erdk." for Erdkunde</note> XI. 1844. pages 298 & 306, Abulfeda's *Mesopotamian Tables* edited by Reiske in Büsching IV. p. 240, Bar Hebraeus's <note>original: "Abul Pharag."</note> *History of the Dynasties* p. 184. La Lande, *Astronomy* I. No. 356. p. 123.

^205) Book III. Chapter 16.

^206) Before Ptolemy, the apogee <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> was ahead of the solstice <note>original: "Solstitium"</note> by 24º 30' Book III. Chapter 16.
At the time of Albategnius <note>The Latinized name of Al-Battani, a famous 9th-century Arab astronomer.</note> it was 7º 43' in the same place.
Thus the apogee had lagged behind by 16º 47, for which the text says "nearly 17º" <note>original: "prope 17º"</note>.

^207) The 1514 years are Roman years, so we must add $\frac{1514}{4}$ = 378 days; it is therefore 1515 years 13 days or 25 $\times$ 60 + 15 Egyptian years and 13 days. For this, one finds in the tables of Book III. Chapter 6 the simple anomaly <note>The angular distance of a planet from its perihelion or apogee.</note> for:
25 $\times$ 60 = 157º 15' 3''
15 = 1 34 21 2'''
13 = 0 0 13 26
Position of Christ from Book III. Chapter 11 = 6 45
Total = 165º 34' 37'' 28'''
For which the text says "nearly 165º 39'" <note>original: "165º 39' fere"</note>, a difference which would assume that Copernicus refers his determination to September 12th of the year 1515 AD, which corresponds very closely with his own statement of September 14th.

^208) The position of Christ for the anomaly is 6º 45'
Subtract from this the anomaly for 60 years: 6º 17' 24'' 9'''
Remaining: 0 27 35 51
Subtract from this the anomaly for 4 years: 0 25 9 36
Remaining: 0 2 26 15
Subtract from this the anomaly for 2 $\times$ 60 days: 0 2 4
Remaining: 0 0 22 15
Subtract from this the anomaly for 21 days: 0 0 21 42
Remaining: 0 0 0 33''', which are to be neglected; thus the time from the beginning of the anomaly is 64 years 141 days, for which the text has set "nearly 64 years" <note>original: "64 Jahre fere"</note>.

^210) The Secular Edition <note>The "Säcular-Ausgabe" refers to the 1873 commemorative edition of Copernicus's *De revolutionibus*.</note> has here, and repeatedly hereafter, 4º 23' instead of the 4º 13' of the old printings; however, it is easy to see that the old reading is the correct one; for, if we set 360º = 2 Right Angles <note>original: "2 R"</note>, then it was found: Angle **acb** = 341º 26'
**cab** = 14 21
Total: 355º 47'

^211) The Secular Edition reads 366, while the old printings have 369. This discrepancy is explained thus: the Secular Edition has **bd** = 318, the old edition **bd** = 321; to this is added $\frac{1}{2}$ **ad** = **df** = 48, **df** = 48
this gives **bf** = 366 **bf** = 369

^244) The annual motion of the Moon amounts, according to note ^243), to 13,456,411,200° / 3,024,169; if one multiplies this fraction by 269 / 251, one obtains 3,619,774,612,800° / 759,066,419 as the annual motion of the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The anomaly refers to the angular distance of a planet or the moon from its perigee or apogee; essentially its position in its elliptical or epicyclic orbit.</note>, and the execution of the division yields:
->13^c 88° 43' 9'' 9''' 1'''' 56^V.<- <note>The "c" stands for "circuli" or full circles/revolutions.</note>

To calculate the daily motion of the anomaly, the reasoning is as follows: in 345^a 82^d 1^h, i.e., in 3,024,169 / 24 days, the anomaly completes 4,573 x 360°, thus in one day (4,573 x 360 x 24) / 3,024,169 or 39,510,720° / 3,024,169 = 13° 3' 53'' 56''' 34'''' 21^V 4^VI.

^247) The numerical data of this chapter present, unfortunately, a great deal of confusion due to the different readings; in order to create some order in them, I have throughout the text initially retained the readings of the Secular Edition, but in the following I have tested them by recalculation and compared them with the readings of the old editions and the *Almagest*. It concerns three determinations in general, namely:
1. the annual mean motion,
2. the annual motion of the anomaly, and
3. the annual motion of the latitude of the Moon.
1. Hipparchus and Ptolemy (*Almagest* IV. 7.) found the annual mean motion of the Moon to be in agreement, namely = 12^c 129° 37' 21'' 28''' 29'''' I.

This figure, which is also found in all editions of Copernicus, is however not exact according to note ^243) following the method followed by Hipparchus and Ptolemy, and rather reads:
12^c 129° 37' 21'' 55''' 16'''' 5^V II.
Copernicus himself gives the same in the Secular Edition as 12^c 129° 37' 22'' 32''' 40'''' III.
and in the old editions 12^c 129° 37' 22'' 36''' 25'''' IV.

In the tables immediately following, the data III is used as the basis in the Secular Edition, and data IV in the old editions. According to a note by Mr. M. Curtze, the data IV is written by a foreign hand in the original manuscript <note>original: "Mnscpte."</note> under the last column of the tables.

$^{303)}$ The geographical latitude of the Mole of Rhodes is given in Rümker's *Navigation* as 36$^o$ 26' 53''.

$^{304}$ Equinoctial hours <term>equinoctial hours: hours of equal length (60 minutes), as opposed to seasonal hours</term> are synonymous with our uniform hours, i.e., they each amount to 1/24th of a civil day, and they take their name from the fact that at the time of the equinoxes they are equal to the civil day and night hours, *horae temporales* <note>seasonal hours</note>. The equinoctial hours, which among the ancients were called *equinoctial hours* <note>original Greek: ὥραι ἰσημεριναί</note> or *horae aequinoctiales*, are synonymous with today's astronomical hours; while the *seasonal hours* <note>original Greek: ὥραι καιρικαί</note> or *horae temporales* divided the respective length of the day or night into twelve parts. The latter therefore change with the geographical latitude of the place and with the seasons; the former remain the same for all observation sites and seasons. Compare Ideler, *Handbook* I. pages 86 and 87.

$^{305)}$ Ptolemy says in *Almagest* V. 5:
> "since the observation was made after noon on the 17th day of Pauni at 3:20 seasonal hours, which then in Rhodes made nearly four equal hours" <note>original Latin: "quoniam post meridiem diei 17 Pauni 3. 20 horis temporalibus facta observatio fuit, quae tunc in Rhodo quatuor proxime faciebant aequales"</note>

and later adds: "simply 4, but exactly 3:40." — This contrast between *simply* and *exactly* refers to the conversion of seasonal hours into equinoctial hours. To carry out this conversion, the date of the discussed observation must first be reduced to the Christian calendar. In Book III, Chapter 11 and the notes therein, we have seen that there have elapsed:

³³⁵) Copernicus evidently intends here to designate the star α Tauri, that is, Aldebaran. The name Palilicium—perhaps better Parilicium, also Parelicium—encompasses the entirety of the Hyades, as is evident from Pliny's *Natural History* <note>original: "Historia naturalis"</note> XVIII. 26, where it says: "On the 14th day before the Kalends of May in Egypt, the little pigs" <note>original: "suculae"</note>, the Hyades, "set in the evening, a violent constellation and turbulent on land and sea; on the 16th for Attica, the 15th for Caesar, they signify for four continuous days; however, for Assyria on the 12th day before the Kalends of May; this is commonly called the constellation Parilicium, since the 11th day before the Kalends of May is held as the birthday of the city of Rome, on which serenity is generally restored; it gave clarity to observation; the Greeks call these stars Hyades as evidence of rain-clouds <note>original: "nimborum"</note>, but our people, thinking from the similarity of the Greek name that it was imposed because of pigs <note>original: "propter sues"</note>, called them 'little pigs' <note>original: "suculas"</note> out of ignorance." Edition by Julius Sillig Vol. III. p. 200. — The Hyades were so named by the Romans because they disappeared in the evening twilight around the 21st of April—the 11th day before the Kalends of May—on which day the shepherd's festival, Parilia or Palilia, was celebrated, and according to an old tradition, Rome was founded. See Ideler's *Investigations into the Origin and Meaning of Star Names* <note>original: "Untersuchungen über den Ursprung und die Bedeutung der Sternnamen"</note> page 140.

³³⁶) This sentence is found in Archimedes' *Measurement of a Circle, Proposition 3* <note>original: "᾿Αρχιμήδους κύκλου μέτρησις • πρότασις γ´"</note> and reads there:
> "The circumference of every circle is three times the diameter, and further exceeds it by a part less than a seventh of the diameter, but greater than ten seventy-firsts." <note>original Greek: "Παντὸς κύκλου ἡ περίμετρος, τῆς διαμέτρου, τριπλασίων ἐστὶ, καὶ ἔτι ὑπερέχει, ἐλάσσονι μὲν ἢ ἑβδόμῳ μέρει τῆς διαμέτρου, μείζονι δὲ ἢ δέκα ἑβδομηκοστομόνοις."</note>

The Latin translation of the Oxford edition of 1792 by Torelli reads as follows:
> "The circuit of any circle is triple the diameter, and still exceeds it by a certain part, which is indeed less than a seventh part of the diameter, but greater than ten seventy-firsts," <note>original Latin: "Cujuslibet circuli ambitus diametri est triplus, et adhuc parte quadam excedit, quae quidem minor est septima diametri parte, major vero decem septuagesimis primis,"</note>

$^{356}$) For this number, the manuscript and the Nuremberg and Basel editions read 1016; however, the figure of 1139 included in the text of the translation from the Secular Edition <note>original: "Säc.-Ausg." referring to the 1873 anniversary edition of Copernicus's *De revolutionibus*</note> is the correct one. The proportion $60 : 6 \frac{5}{6} = 10000 : x$ yields $x = 1138.88...$ and not 1016. Furthermore, the numbers immediately following in the aforementioned editions refer to the correct value of $x = 1139$ and do not fit 1016; for $\frac{3}{4} \times 1138.888...$ is $= 854.166...$ and $\frac{1}{4} \times 1138.88...$ is $= 284.722...$, for which the latter number 285 is used in the text.

$^{357}$) In the old editions, $18^\circ 26'$ is written here; the errata list of the Nuremberg edition, the manuscript, and the Secular Edition read $18^\circ 36'$, while the Warsaw edition alone has $18^\circ 38'$. The remaining numerical data regarding the angles to be considered here can only be reconciled with the latter reading: for the supplementary angle $bdf$ of the angle $bde$, which is supposed to be $161^\circ 22'$, can only be $18^\circ 38'$. Likewise, the interior angles $ebd = 1^\circ 27'$ and $bed = 17^\circ 11'$ require the exterior angle $bdf = 18^\circ 38'$, and so on. Therefore, in the text of the translation, this angle is set at $= 18^\circ 38'$.

$^{358}$) In all editions without exception, "of the earth" <note>original: "terrae"</note> appears here instead of "of the sun" <note>original: "solis"</note>; nevertheless, the sense of the passage requires "of the sun," and the text of the translation has proceeded accordingly.

**399)** In Book I, Ch. 10, the orbital period of Jupiter is assumed to be 12 years; consequently, in the 1392 years calculated in the previous note, there are 116 revolutions of Jupiter
and 1392 revolutions of the Earth;
consequently, the Earth has overtaken Jupiter 1276 times in this period; instead, all editions say 1267, which is all the more striking as this number is written out in words. <note>This suggests a long-standing typographical or transcription error in the historical printed versions of Copernicus's work.</note>

**400)** Book V, Ch. 10, toward the end, gives 154° 22' for the Ptolemaic result.
Book V, Ch. 11, gives 159° for the Copernican result.
The difference is 4° 38',
for which 4° 30' is set in the text.

**401)** The third observation of Ptolemy took place, according to Book V, Ch. 10, in the year 136, 314 days, 5 hours Egyptian after Christ; for these 5 hours, 10 <term>sixtieths</term> are set in the text. The reason for this is that Copernicus takes the time in Krakow to be 1 hour less than in Alexandria; accordingly, it is 4 hours, and this correctly makes 0 days and 10 <term>sixtieths</term>, whereas 5 hours would be 0 days, 12 <term>sixtieths</term>, and 30 <term>sixtieth-sixtieths</term>.

3. $2^\circ \text{ } 34' \text{ } ♐$ (Sagittarius) $= 242^\circ \text{ } 34' - 6^\circ \text{ } 40' = 235^\circ \text{ } 54'$.
