The text from the deleted pages, according to the Secular Edition <note>original: "Säc. Ausgabe," referring to the 1873 Säcular-Ausgabe of Copernicus's works</note>, is now as follows: "He saw, namely, between the moon and the first shining star—the northernmost of those located in the brow of the Scorpion <note>The constellation Scorpius</note>—Venus situated on the same straight line, one and a half times as far from the moon as from the fixed star. Since the location of this fixed star is known, namely 109º 40' longitude and 1º 20' north latitude, it was worth the effort to determine the apparent position of the moon in order to find the position of Venus. From the birth of Christ until the hour of the observation, 138 Egyptian years, 18 days, 4 hours, and 45 minutes after midnight Alexandria time (or 3 hours 45 minutes Krakow time—adjusted to 3 hours 41 minutes or 18 days 9 hours 32 minutes) had elapsed. Since the sun, according to its simple mean motion, stood at 255º 30', and according to its apparent motion at 23º of Sagittarius, the uniform distance of the moon from the sun amounted to 319º 18', its mean anomaly <note>The angle used to calculate a body's position in a non-circular orbit</note> was 87º 37', and the mean anomaly of the northern latitude was 12º 19'. From this, the true position of the moon is calculated as 209º 4' longitude and 4º 58' north latitude. However, if one adds the precession of the equinoxes <note>The slow change in the orientation of Earth's rotational axis</note>, which at that time amounted to 6º 41', one obtains the moon at 5º 45' of the Scorpion. Since the culmination <note>The point at which a celestial body reaches its highest altitude</note> of the second degree of Virgo was observed through the instrument at Alexandria, 25º of the Scorpion was rising; therefore, according to our calculation, the parallax <note>The displacement in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight</note> of the moon amounted to 51' in longitude and 16' in latitude. In this way, the observed and verified position of the moon at Alexandria results in 209º 55' longitude and 4º 42' north latitude. Now, let **ab** be the orbit of the Earth, its center **c**, and its diameter through both apsides <note>The points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the center</note> **acb**; from **a**, let the orbit of Venus be..."

<meta>This page continues the mathematical demonstration of Venus's orbit, specifically calculating the planet's anomaly based on observations from the time of Ptolemy, likely referencing Copernicus's "De revolutionibus."</meta>

“seen in the apogee <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> at 48° 20', and from the opposite point *b* at 228° 20'. In the diameter, let *cd* = 312 of such parts, of which 10,000 go to *ac*, and around *d* with the distance *df* = 1/3 *cd* = 104, a small circle is described. Since the mean position of the sun was at 255° 30', the distance of the Earth from the lowest apsis <note>The point in an orbit closest to the center of motion.</note> was 27° 10'. Therefore, let *be* be an arc of 27° 10', and *ec*, *ed*, and *ef* be drawn so that the angle *cdf* is twice as large as *bde*. Then describe the orbit of Venus around *f*, whose periphery intersects the extended line *ef* at *l* and the diameter at *o*; finally, let *fk* be drawn parallel to *ce* as far as the periphery. Let the planet be at point *g*, and draw *ge* and *gf*. According to these constructions, the angle *ceg* and the arc *kg* are to be found; the latter arc is the distance of the planet from the mean apogee of its orbit, since *k* designates this apogee. Now, since in the triangle *cde* the angle *dce* is 27° 10' and the side *cd* is 312 of such parts of which 10,000 go to *ce*, the side *de* contains 9,724 of the same parts, and the angle *ced* is 50'. Because likewise in the triangle *def* the two sides *de* = 9,724 and *df* = 104 of such parts are given, of which *ce* contains 10,000—and because *cdf* = 54° 20', and *fdb* as the supplementary angle = 125° 40', the whole angle *fde*, which is enclosed by the given sides, is = 152° 50';—thus the third side *ef* = 9,817 of the same parts, the angle *def* = 16', and the whole angle *cef* = 1° 6', by which the mean motion of the center *f* differs from its apparent motion, i.e., the angle *boe* from the angle *eob*. Therefore, the angle *boe* = 28° 16' is given, and that was required first. Furthermore, since the angle *ceg* = 45° 44', namely equal to the distance of the planet from the mean position of the sun, the whole angle *feg* is also = 46° 50'; but *ef* is given as = 9,817 of such parts of which *ae* contains 10,000, and of these parts *fg* contains 7,193 according to the above. Consequently, in the triangle *efg*, the ratio of the sides *ef* and *fg* along with the angle *feg* is given. It follows then that the angle *efg* = 83° 19' and its exterior angle *lfg* = 131° 6'. This is also the size of the arc *lkg*, or the distance of the planet from the apparent apogee of its orbit. But since the angle *kfl* = *cef* = the distance between the mean and true apsis = 1° 6', as has been proven, there remains, if one subtracts this from 131° 6', 130° as the arc *kg* between the planet and its mean apsis, and the rest of the circle, namely 230°, is the uniform anomaly <term>anomaly: the angular distance of a planet from its perihelion or aphelion</term> taken from point *k*. By this we have obtained that in the second year of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, Roman Emperor.</note> or in the year of Christ 138, at Krakow, on the 15th of December at 3:45 AM, the uniform anomaly of Venus was 230°, which is what we sought.”

<sup>431)</sup> If one bases the calculation on the data in the text, one obtains 90º 31' — 252º 5' = 198º 26', as the Centennial Edition <note>original: "Säc. Ausg." referring to the 1873 Thorn edition</note> consistently reads; however, the Nuremberg and Basel editions have 188º 26'. If, on the other hand, one uses the number resulting from Note <sup>429)</sup>, one obtains 90º 31' — 250º 44' = 199º 47'.

<sup>432)</sup> Book V. Chapter 1.

<sup>433)</sup> Since, according to Note <sup>423)</sup>, a different observation originating from Ptolemy was used for comparison at the beginning of Chapter 23 in the original manuscript—instead of the observation by Timochares discussed in the old editions—the conclusion of that same chapter had to be phrased differently to correspond. Consequently, according to the remarks in the Centennial Edition page 375, the concluding words found in the printed text from "In the observation of Timochares" etc. until the end of the chapter are missing in the original manuscript. They are replaced by the following conclusion: "In the preceding observation by Ptolemy, however, it was 230º. In the intervening time, therefore, 220º 31' have accrued beyond the full revolutions. The time from the second year of Antoninus at 8:15 AM <note>8 hours 15 minutes before noon</note> before the <term>Cracow noon</term> <note>Copernicus often calculated time relative to the meridian of Cracow</note> on the 28th of Tybi," — here the original says *vigesimi* instead of *noni vigesimi* <note>20th instead of 29th</note>, see Note <sup>423)</sup> — "until the 1529th" — here the original says 1528th — "year of Christ on the 12th of March at 7:30 PM, amounts to 1391 Egyptian years 49 days 39 minutes 23 seconds. In this time, 220º 31' are calculated beyond the full revolutions, of which there were 808 according to the table of mean motions; thus, everything is correct. The positions of the <term>apsides</term> <note>the points in an orbit closest or furthest from the center</note> of the eccentric circle remained unchanged in the meantime at 48º 20' and 228º 20'." Following this in the original is:

->**"Chapter 23."**<-

->**"On the positions of the mean anomaly of Venus."**<-

"From this, the positions of the <term>parallactic anomaly</term> <note>the angular distance of a planet from its apogee as seen from the sun</note> are easily established. From the birth of Christ to the observation of Ptolemy, 138 Egyptian years 18 days 9 minutes 30 seconds have elapsed, and the motion corresponding to this time amounts to 105º 25'. When subtracted from the 230º of Ptolemy's observation, this yields the anomaly of Venus at midnight before the first of January as 123º 35'. Furthermore, according to the ratio of the often-repeated motion and time, one finds the position for the start of the Olympiads to be 318º 9', for Alexander 79º 14', and for Caesar 70º 49'." As can easily be seen, these numbers do not agree with those in the text of any of the editions, including the Centennial Edition.

453) Bernhard Walther was born in Nuremberg in 1430. After the death of Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a pivotal Renaissance mathematician and astronomer</note>, he purchased the books and manuscripts left behind and continued his observations. Although he had studied Latin and Greek, he felt he still lacked proficiency in the latter language to fully understand the many Greek manuscripts in Regiomontanus's estate. Therefore, he acquired a handwritten lexicon, which is still held in the Nuremberg City Library, under the title: <term>Greek Onomasticon</term> <note>original: "Onomasticum graecum"</note>, prepared at the care and expense of Bernhard Walther, 1496. — According to Doppelmayer's report, Walther's willingness to publish Regiomontanus's works was of little service to the public of that time, as he neither made them known nor shared them otherwise. Walther was involved in the improvement of the great Nuremberg clock in 1488. He also noticed that the refraction <note>The bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere</note> of stars near the horizon was considerable; however, Alhazen, Vitello, and Bacon had already known of astronomical refraction. Walther died in 1504. He recommended his and Regiomontanus's scholarly estate to his heirs and their guardians, who, being unlearned, paid little attention to it, sold off some items, and only through the Nuremberg Magistrate was some of it saved. Compare Ptolemy's *Geography* by Werner § 11. In the work: <term>The Astronomical Basis of the Nuremberg Urania</term> <note>original: "Uranies Noricae basis astronomica"</note>, or the accounts of the annual motion, from observations of the sun made in this our century and the third century prior at Nuremberg by Johann Philipp von Wurzelbau, Nuremberg 1709, Walther's and Wurzelbau's observations are contained. On the copperplate title page, there is an illustration of the Ptolemaic rules <note>likely referring to the triquetrum or "Ptolemy's Rules," an instrument for measuring zenith distances</note> as Walther used them for observations of the sun's zenith distances in 1475. Compare *History of Mathematics* by A. G. Kästner Vol. II. Göttingen 1797, pages 324 to 326.

<meta>This page serves as a chronological appendix to the preceding astronomical discussions, providing a consolidated list of the empirical data used by Copernicus to support his heliocentric theory.</meta>

In conclusion, let the list of observations made by Copernicus himself and used in this work—which was also included in the Secular Edition <note>The "Säcular-Ausgabe" refers to the 1873 commemorative edition of Copernicus's works marking the 400th anniversary of his birth.</note>—find its place here.
